# Cardiff Beekeeper Devastated After Hive Theft as Cases Rise Across Wales

A Cardiff beekeeper has spoken of her distress after discovering one of her hives had been stripped of its entire honey bee colony, in what appears to be part of a growing trend of hive thefts across Wales.

Elaine Spence found one of her hives without its roof in March, with the colony completely removed. She estimates that a colony of bees could sell for more than £200 on the black market and believes the thieves had expert knowledge of beekeeping.

"I looked at my hive and there was no roof on it. I was lost for words," Ms Spence told BBC Wales' Eye on Wales programme. "I lifted what remained of the hive to have a look and it was just empty inside."

The theft was particularly devastating as Ms Spence had already lost one of her three colonies to poor weather conditions over the winter months. She keeps her hives on industrial land at a secret location in Cardiff.

"All bee-keepers strive to ensure that their bees last through the winter: you care for them, they're a bit like part of your family, really," she said. "And to come and find that they have just been taken from you - it was really distressing."

Ms Spence said she knows of approximately 10 other hives being stolen in the past year alone, although no official figures are kept on such thefts. She believes the perpetrators were experienced beekeepers who came equipped with the necessary tools.

"To steal a colony of bees, you need to know what you're doing. A person walking the street would not know how to come in and effectively remove a colony of bees," she explained.

She suspects the thieves used small carrying boxes designed for transporting bees, which can hold about six frames. "They lifted the six frames out of the hive complete with the colony on it, put them in the box, shut the box up, Bob's your uncle, away they go," she said.

In a twist of irony, Ms Spence noted that the stolen bees were particularly aggressive, having sent her to accident and emergency the previous year after stinging her. "Maybe there might be some poetic justice," she suggested.

The programme also explored other challenges facing beekeepers, including the recent two-year ban on neonicotinoid pesticides imposed by the European Commission. James Byrne of the Wildlife Trust expressed concerns that these pesticides could be damaging bees' navigation systems.

However, Pembrokeshire arable farmer Perkin Evans, representing Wales' arable farmers for the National Farmers' Union, warned that the ban could reduce crop yields by up to 20%.

The programme also followed regional bee inspector Francis Gellatly during inspections for the invasive varroa mite and met Newport beekeeper Dave Crewe, who lost two of his finest colonies to poor weather conditions.

Eye on Wales was broadcast on BBC Radio Wales and is available on the BBC iPlayer.

# Michelle Dockery Pulls Out of Donmar's Les Liaisons Dangereuses Production

Michelle Dockery has unexpectedly withdrawn from the Donmar Warehouse production of Les Liaisons Dangereuses just six weeks before its scheduled opening night. The actress was set to portray the role of Madame de Tourvel in the classic tale of seduction and betrayal.

Producers have not provided any explanation for Dockery's departure from the production. She will be replaced by Elaine Cassidy, known for her role in The Paradise, who previously appeared at the Donmar in last year's production of Fathers And Sons.

Josie Rourke, the Donmar's artistic director, expressed her hopes "to work with Michelle in the future" while welcoming Cassidy to the production. "I can't wait to work with Elaine and our fantastic company when rehearsals start on Monday," Rourke stated.

The production features a stellar cast including Dominic West as Vicomte de Valmont, Janet McTeer as the Marquise de Merteuil, and Una Stubbs. Christopher Hampton's adaptation of Choderlos de Laclos' controversial 1782 novel explores the dangerous games of seduction between two former lovers in pre-revolutionary France.

Les Liaisons Dangereuses will run from 11 December to 13 February, with a live cinema broadcast in partnership with National Theatre Live on 28 January 2016.

# Chesterfield's O'Shea Double Sinks Struggling Millwall

Chesterfield secured a crucial 2-0 victory over Millwall at the Den, with Jay O'Shea scoring twice to condemn the Lions to their fourth consecutive League One match without a win.

The Spireites made an impressive start to the contest, taking the lead after just 17 minutes when O'Shea unleashed a volley from the edge of the penalty area that cannoned in off the post, giving Jordan Archer no chance.

Millwall pushed for an equaliser but were thwarted by outstanding goalkeeping from Tommy Lee, who produced a spectacular one-handed save to deny Jimmy Abdou's deflected effort and preserve Chesterfield's advantage.

O'Shea sealed the points deep into injury time when his shot took a deflection past the helpless Archer to make it 2-0.

The defeat leaves Millwall in a precarious position, sitting just two points above the League One relegation zone. Manager Neil Harris expressed his frustration, acknowledging his side's poor first-half performance but praising their second-half improvement, despite their inability to find the crucial goal.

Chesterfield's victory provides a welcome boost to their league campaign.

# England Drop to 10th in FIFA World Rankings - Lowest Position Since Keegan Era

England have slumped to their lowest position in the FIFA world rankings in over a decade, falling three places to 10th - a slot they have not occupied since the aftermath of Kevin Keegan's tenure as manager.

The drop represents a significant decline for Roy Hodgson's side, who reached an all-time high of third place just last August, despite their quarter-final exit at Euro 2012.

Spain continue their dominance at the top of the rankings with 1,514 points, maintaining the position they have held since September 2011. The reigning European and World champions are followed by Argentina, who climbed two places to second with 1,263 points, and Germany in third.

Elsewhere in the British Isles, the news is equally disappointing. Wales dropped to 52nd, the Republic of Ireland fell to 59th, and Scotland slipped to 63rd. However, Northern Ireland provided a bright spot, rising 23 places to 86th - though this improvement is somewhat ironic given their embarrassing 3-2 defeat to Luxembourg this week. The 127th-ranked team had not won a home World Cup qualifier since 1972.

Belgium continued their impressive rise, jumping four places to sixth, while the USA made the most significant leap inside the top 20, climbing from 19th to 13th. Uruguay also entered the top ten, rising five positions to seventh.

# Care Home Worker Who Poisoned Drinks with Bleach Faces Hospital Order

A care home worker who poisoned drinks with bleach, endangering dozens of residents and staff, has been detained under a hospital order.

Melissa Swift, 24, from West Bromwich, admitted three counts of attempted murder following an investigation into her conduct at the Goldfield Court care home in West Bromwich. The former special constable with West Midlands Police also pleaded guilty to two counts of making threats to kill in February.

Swift contaminated drinks at the facility with bleach, leaving them accessible to everyone at the home. As a result, 25 residents and seven staff members required hospital treatment.

In addition to poisoning drinks, Swift sent anonymous letters threatening to kill two members of staff, including her older sister.

At Birmingham Crown Court, Judge Philip Parker QC granted an interim hospital order lasting up to three months after hearing Swift may suffer from a mental disorder. She is expected to be transferred to Rampton Hospital, a high-security psychiatric facility near Retford, Nottinghamshire, within 28 days.

Swift is due to be formally sentenced later this year.

# Chris Ashton: England wing accepts international career is over after Toulon move

England wing Chris Ashton has accepted his international career is over following his decision to join French club Toulon next season.

"That was when I felt I needed to get out of England," Ashton told BBC Sport. The Toulon-bound Saracens wing said "obstacles on both sides" meant he accepted his Test career is over.

"I enjoy it here [Saracens] but I always want to play for England and by going to France it took that out of the picture," he told 5 live's Rugby Show.

His move to Toulon puts the former Northampton and Wigan rugby league winger out of the running for an England recall, with the Rugby Football Union not allowing players based outside the Premiership to be picked.

"It is hard to watch England, although now I have made my decision it is a lot easier," he added. "The burning desire is always there and always will be, it just changes its path slightly and going to France takes that away."

Ashton has scored 19 tries for England in his 39 caps, the last of which came in the summer of 2014.

## Disciplinary issues affected England chances

He was given a 13-week ban after being found guilty last year of biting Northampton prop Alex Waller, returning to action in December 2016.

It was Ashton's second lengthy suspension after he was banned for 10 weeks in 2015 for eye-gouging, which cost him his place in England head coach Eddie Jones' first Six Nations squad.

"I can't feel hard done by, well obviously I can, but I think that was the easy option," said the prolific try scorer.

"I have put myself in those situations. It can look the way it looks because I have put myself in that place so there is definitely a responsibility on my side.

"Whether I agree with someone telling me I have done something or not is completely different."

## Lions tour 'very nice' suggestion

Saracens director of rugby Mark McCall believes Ashton should be considered for this summer's British and Irish Lions tour of New Zealand.

Ashton said: "I think that is just Mark being very nice to me.

"He is always a good guy and always been very supportive of me but I think he was just being very nice."

# Spanish Man Jailed for Sexually Assaulting Children at Enniskillen Swimming Pool

A Spanish national has been sentenced to 14 months in prison for sexually assaulting three young girls at a swimming pool in Enniskillen, County Fermanagh.

Cristian Diaz, 35, who was living in the town at the time of the offences, pleaded guilty to carrying out the attacks at the Lakeland Forum leisure centre during February and March 2015. He approached the children - aged nine, 10 and 11 - on three separate occasions while they were swimming.

At Dungannon Crown Court, the judge described the offences as particularly serious because they had taken place in a "public arena" and had involved children of a "tender age". He emphasised that the swimming pool was a place "where the children should have been able to feel safe and where parents allow them to go in safety".

The court heard that the attacks had left the young victims "understandably confused, distressed and upset at what happened to them".

## Details of the Assaults

A prosecution lawyer told the court that following one of the assaults, Diaz told the child he was "sorry", but the victim was too shocked to reply and swam away from him. The incidents were subsequently reported to police, who identified Diaz from CCTV footage obtained from the leisure centre.

## Defence and Sentencing

A defence lawyer explained that Diaz was a graduate of Madrid University who had been working in Europe as an electrical engineer before moving to Enniskillen to improve his English. His address was given as East Bridge Street in the town.

"The accused accepts the three complainants were bound to be frightened, stressed and suffer as a result of his actions and for what it's worth he's asked me to apologise for his actions," the defence lawyer told the court. The lawyer added that Diaz had described what had happened "as the greatest mistake of his life".

Diaz has since returned to Spain to live with his father and was accompanied to court by two of his sisters.

Judge handed down a 14-month sentence, with half to be served in prison, and placed Diaz on the sex offenders' register for 10 years.

## Victims' Families Respond

The parents of the three children sat in the public gallery and watched as Diaz shrugged his shoulders before being led away in handcuffs.

The mother of one victim said afterwards: "He came in here as Cristian Diaz, but he's going out as a registered sex offender."

In a statement, the parents thanked the PSNI in Enniskillen for the "sensitive, professional and tenacious manner in which they dealt with this enquiry to ensure this predator was stopped from causing more or greater harm".

They added: "This case has spanned nearly two years with the offender only admitting his guilt the day before his trial was due to start. The children were very brave to come forward and should be very proud of themselves in helping to stop further harm to members of the public."

# Glasgow and South Lanarkshire Councils Reject Teacher Numbers Funding Deal

Glasgow and South Lanarkshire councils have made a controversial decision regarding their budgets for the coming year, standing firm against Scottish government pressure to accept funding tied to maintaining teacher numbers.

The Scottish government is offering councils across the country money specifically to maintain teacher numbers, but has warned that authorities will lose cash if teacher numbers drop. This condition has sparked a major dispute between many councils and the government, representing the most serious conflict between local and central government since devolution.

Local authorities face a Friday deadline to inform the government whether they intend to accept the cash. Despite significant opposition from some non-SNP councils, it is expected that most will ultimately agree to the terms.

## The Funding Dispute

The government is offering councils across Scotland almost £11 billion for the coming year. Typically, each council receives around 80 pence of every pound it spends from the government. However, the row centres on a relatively small portion of this total - £51 million to maintain teacher numbers, including £10 million councils may receive in January.

Teacher numbers in Scotland have declined in recent years to approximately 51,000, and the government is determined to halt this trend. Teachers are employed by councils, and if teacher numbers fall, councils will not receive their share of the £10 million and may even have cash clawed back.

## Council Concerns

While many councils have accepted the funding offer as expected, several non-SNP authorities remain deeply unhappy. Some object to the principle of central government dictating that they must maintain teacher numbers, even when they agree with the objective itself.

Others believe there may be better uses for their funding and argue the government should judge them on attainment in schools rather than a raw measure like teacher numbers. Some councils fear being penalised for small annual drops in teacher numbers due to circumstances such as sickness on the day numbers are counted, although government sources have attempted to address this concern.

## Wider Implications

The dispute reflects far broader issues than just teacher numbers. For some in local government, it raises fundamental questions about how councils are funded and whether they have become subservient to central government.

Cosla, the local government body which Glasgow and South Lanarkshire are officially leaving shortly, held "robust" discussions with the government earlier this week. It has suggested finding a way to maintain teacher numbers nationally while allowing numbers to fall locally.

If the vast bulk of councils accept the funding offer, it will be viewed as a significant victory for the government.

# Australia Sets 2030 Emissions Target Ahead of Paris Climate Talks

Australia has announced its target to cut greenhouse gas emissions by 26-28% by 2030, based on 2005 levels, Prime Minister Tony Abbott revealed on Tuesday. However, the target falls short of commitments made by comparable nations including Canada and the United States.

The announcement represents a significant increase from Australia's previous climate goal of reducing emissions by just 5% by 2020, calculated from 2000 baseline levels. The new target comes as nations prepare for crucial international climate negotiations scheduled for December in Paris, where world leaders will attempt to forge a new global climate strategy.

Australia faces unique challenges in reducing emissions, as the nation remains heavily reliant on coal power and ranks among the world's largest coal exporters. Prime Minister Abbott emphasized that economic considerations must balance environmental objectives.

"It is very much that everything we do has this in mind: how do we promote jobs and growth... and climate change policy is no different," Abbott said during a press conference in Canberra. "We have to reduce our emissions... but in ways that are consistent with continued strong growth."

The Prime Minister defended the target as being within the middle range of commitments from similarly sized economies, estimating the economic cost at approximately 0.2% to 0.3% of Australia's gross domestic product.

However, the target has drawn sharp criticism from climate scientists. Dr. Tim Flannery from the independent Climate Council said that even if Australia achieves the 26% reduction, Australians would still emit more per person than Americans and "significantly more" than British citizens on a per capita basis.

"These targets are vastly inadequate to protect Australians from the impacts of climate change and do not represent a fair contribution to the world effort to bring climate change under control," Professor Flannery stated.

The Climate Council maintains that limiting global temperature rise to 2°C would require Australia to cut emissions by 60% by 2030 from 2000 levels. Australia currently ranks as the world's 13th largest greenhouse gas emitter with one of the highest per capita emissions rates globally.

# Bangladesh Central Bank Governor Resigns After $81m Cyber Heist

Bangladesh's central bank governor, Atiur Rahman, has resigned following one of the largest cyber heists in banking history, in which hackers stole approximately $81 million from the country's foreign currency reserves.

Mr Rahman submitted his resignation to Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina after it emerged that unknown hackers had stolen the money from the bank's account with the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. The theft happened in February, but Mr Rahman did not tell the government. Finance Minister A M A Muhith said he had learnt of it from press reports.

According to media reports quoting banking officials, the gang behind the raid used stolen credentials to make requests to transfer cash look legitimate. If all the requests had gone unchallenged, the gang would have got away with about $1bn. However, the transfers were stopped when the volume of requests raised suspicions at other banks.

To commit the attack, the gang spent time studying the internal processes of Bangladesh's central bank, so they could convincingly pose as officials when requesting the transfers. However, the sheer number of transactions and a spelling mistake helped alert bank staff to the theft.

The spelling mistake in the name of one recipient of funds led Deutsche Bank, which was helping to route the cash, to ask for clarification from the central bank, which then stopped the transaction. At about the same time, the Federal Reserve Bank of New York had alerted the Bangladesh central bank to a series of suspicious requests to transfer money.

The requests are believed to have been flagged because they were to private accounts rather than other banks and because there were so many of them.

The money that the hackers did steal ended up in accounts in Sri Lanka and the Philippines. Part of the money was recovered from Sri Lanka, but the rest was laundered through casinos in the Philippines. The central bank said it was working with authorities there to recover the remaining amount.

Bangladesh's government has publicly blamed the New York Fed for not spotting the suspicious transactions earlier.

# Coroner: Bed Shortage May Have Cost Brain Bleed Patient Her Life

A coroner has concluded that a woman with a brain bleed might have survived if she had been transferred promptly to a specialist unit, highlighting critical shortages in neurosurgical beds across the NHS.

Mary Muldowney, 57, from Crawley, died last July after doctors at East Surrey Hospital struggled for hours to find her an available bed at a neurosurgical unit. A scan had revealed severe brain bleeds requiring immediate specialist intervention.

Despite requests for an urgent transfer, three nearby units - St George's Hospital, King's College Hospital in London, and the Royal Sussex County Hospital in Brighton - all refused due to lack of capacity. Several other hospitals also reported no available intensive care beds.

Coroner Mary Hassell described how an East Surrey doctor, in "desperation," contacted a former colleague at the Royal London Hospital (RLH), utilizing personal connections to secure a bed. Ms Muldowney was finally transferred and taken directly to surgery at 4:40pm.

Tragically, during the ambulance journey to the Royal London, Ms Muldowney's pupils became fixed and dilated - a grave neurological sign. Surgery could not save her.

In her letter to NHS England, Ms Hassell wrote: "If she had been transferred promptly, it probably would have." The coroner recorded a narrative verdict.

NHS England's medical director, Sir Bruce Keogh, acknowledged the case raised a "serious safety issue" and expressed sympathy for the circumstances. He confirmed the delay in securing a bed was just under two hours.

Sir Bruce noted a "clear difference in perspective" between doctors at East Surrey and St George's hospitals and said a meeting would be arranged between clinicians. The findings will inform broader reviews of inter-hospital referral processes.

The case underscores mounting pressure on specialist NHS services and the potentially fatal consequences of bed shortages.

# Ancient Temple Discovered at El Paraiso Archaeological Site in Peru

Archaeologists in Peru have uncovered a temple believed to be up to 5,000 years old at the El Paraiso archaeological complex, one of the most significant sites on the country's central coast.

The rectangular structure, measuring 6.82 metres by 8.04 metres (22 feet by 26 feet), was found in the right wing of the main pyramid during conservation work carried out by Peru's Ministry of Culture. Entry to the temple was through a narrow passageway, and at its centre, researchers discovered a hearth used for burning ceremonial offerings.

The temple walls were constructed from stone and covered with fine yellow clay, which also contained traces of red paint. The structure had been hidden beneath sand and rocks for millennia before its recent discovery.

**Religious Significance**

Archaeologist Marco Guillen, who led the excavation team, explained the religious importance of the hearth. "The main characteristic of their religion was the use of fire, which burnt in the centre," he told the BBC. "The smoke allowed the priests to connect with their gods."

**Interconnected Communities**

The discovery suggests that communities during the Late Pre-ceramic Age (3500 BC to 1800 BC) were more interconnected than previously believed. Peru's Deputy Minister for Culture, Rafael Varon, described the temple as the first structure of its kind found on Peru's central coast.

"It corroborates that the region around Lima was a focus for the civilisations of the Andean territory, further bolstering its religious, economic and political importance since times immemorial," Mr Varon stated.

The Paraiso settlement once supported a community of hundreds of people who relied on farming and fishing. With ten ruins spread across the site, El Paraiso remains one of the largest archaeological complexes in central Peru.

Thousands of ruins are thought to remain undiscovered throughout Peru, making it a prime destination for archaeologists, though also vulnerable to looting.

# Welsh Government Air Service Records Decline in Passengers Despite Public Funding

A Welsh Government-funded air service has seen passenger numbers drop to 9,862 in 2016-17, marking a decrease of 128 passengers despite small increases in previous years. The service continues to operate at only half capacity, filling just 50% of available seats.

Since its launch in 2007, the service has received approximately £1.2 million in public funding annually. However, a Welsh Government spokesman defended the latest figures, stating they aligned with the previous year's numbers and represented an improvement on the 2012-15 period.

The service's performance has been inconsistent since inception. Initial uptake was strong, with over 14,000 passengers in the first two years, but numbers have remained below 10,000 since then. Last year, the Welsh Government commissioned a viability review, following a 2014 report that highlighted underperformance.

Operational challenges have plagued the twice-daily weekday service. In March, Eastern Airways assumed operations after Citywing's liquidation, prompted by its Czech operator Van Air having flight permissions suspended by the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA). Previously, in 2015, Links Air ceased operations when the CAA revoked its licence due to safety concerns.

Opposition parties have called for the service to be scrapped, whilst others argue it requires improved transport links and marketing to succeed.

With a maximum capacity of 18,720 seats available annually, the service has never achieved more than 78% utilization, reached during its second year of operation. The Welsh Government maintains that the current passenger levels demonstrate stability following several years of fluctuation.

# Brazil Unveils Massive Infrastructure Investment Plan to Revive Slowing Economy

Brazil's government has announced an ambitious infrastructure investment program worth more than $60bn (£38bn) over the next 25 years, with over half of the funding allocated for the next five years, in a bid to revitalize the country's sluggish economy.

The comprehensive plan includes construction of 8,000 kilometres of new roads and 8,000 kilometres of railways. Additional announcements regarding investment in ports and airports are anticipated in the coming weeks.

The infrastructure push comes as Brazil faces its weakest economic performance since 2009, with growth predicted to reach less than 2% this year—a dramatic decline from the impressive 7.5% expansion recorded in 2010. Previous government stimulus measures, including currency devaluation and progressive interest rate reductions, have failed to jumpstart growth.

Neil Shearing of Capital Economics welcomed the initiative, noting it would address supply-side constraints hampering the economy. However, he cautioned that the full benefits would take several years to materialize.

Brazil's recent economic expansion has relied heavily on credit growth and consumer spending, a strategy that exposed significant infrastructure deficiencies. The government is now actively encouraging private sector participation to address these gaps.

The Brazilian business community has applauded the infrastructure commitment, though many argue the action comes too late. President Dilma Rousseff is simultaneously preparing to reduce industrial energy costs by approximately 10% through the elimination of certain federal taxes.

Brazil is also counting on an economic boost from hosting the 2016 Olympic Games, hoping the combination of infrastructure improvements, energy reforms, and the global sporting event will restore the country's economic momentum and return it to robust growth.

# Rafael Benitez Appointed Napoli Manager After Chelsea Exit

Rafael Benitez has been confirmed as the new manager of Napoli, bringing an end to his interim spell at Chelsea and embarking on a fresh challenge in Italian football.

The 53-year-old Spaniard will replace Walter Mazzarri, who has departed the club to join Serie A rivals Inter Milan. Benitez arrives at a club in good health, with Napoli having finished second in Serie A last season and secured qualification for next season's Champions League competition.

The appointment comes on the back of Benitez's Europa League triumph with Chelsea, a victory that brought his managerial trophy haul to an impressive 10 titles across his distinguished career.

"I am very happy and very satisfied for having committed to a great club with an illustrious heritage like Napoli," said Benitez upon his appointment. "I understand the history of the city and how the club forms a fundamental part of the culture and traditions of Naples."

The former Liverpool manager expressed particular enthusiasm about working with Napoli's famously passionate supporters. "I must confess that I am extremely excited because I can share my passion for football with the fans of Napoli; it is proven that they are very, very special," he added. "I look forward to experiencing each and every one of the fans of Napoli and their strong support for this project that we will begin."

Benitez will bring trusted members of his backroom staff with him from London, including first-team fitness coach Paco de Miguel and first-team opposition analyst Xavi Valero.

The appointment was first made public by Napoli club president Aurelio De Laurentiis, who posted a photograph on Twitter showing himself shaking hands with the new manager. "Rafa Benitez is the new coach of Napoli," he tweeted. "A man of great international experience. A leader."

The club later issued a formal statement confirming the appointment and describing Benitez as a "prestigious" coach.

Benitez brings an impressive curriculum vitae to Naples. He won La Liga twice with Valencia and also secured a Uefa Cup triumph with the Spanish club. His six-year tenure at Liverpool, beginning in 2004, yielded Champions League glory in 2005 and FA Cup success in 2006. A brief stint at Inter Milan brought Club World Cup success before he spent nearly two years out of club management.

His return to English football came in November 2012 when he accepted the interim manager's position at Chelsea following Roberto Di Matteo's departure. Despite delivering Europa League glory, a third-place Premier League finish ensuring Champions League qualification, and reaching multiple cup semi-finals and the Club World Cup final, Benitez remained unpopular with sections of the Chelsea support.

The Spaniard had made clear his intention to leave Stamford Bridge at the end of the season, with Chelsea expected to re-appoint Jose Mourinho following the Portuguese manager's departure from Real Madrid.

In a statement, Chelsea said: "Everybody at Chelsea Football Club would like to place on record our thanks to Rafa and his staff for their work at the club, and wish them success for the future."

Benitez now faces the challenge of building on Napoli's strong second-place finish and establishing the club as genuine title contenders in Serie A while competing in Europe's premier club competition.

# Indian Court Rules on Fate of "Man-Eating" Tiger Ustad

India's Supreme Court is set to hear an appeal concerning Ustad, a nine-year-old tiger relocated from Ranthambore National Park to a zoo following three fatal attacks on humans, including a forest guard.

The tiger was tranquilised and transported 400km (250 miles) to a zoological park in Udaipur district earlier this month, where he now resides in an enclosure smaller than a football field. The move followed the death of a 53-year-old forest guard on 8 May. Ustad had previously been linked to the deaths of a 23-year-old local man in 2010 and a 19-year-old boy in March 2012.

Chandramauleshwar Singh, a tiger enthusiast and regular Ranthambore visitor, challenged the relocation in Rajasthan's high court, arguing the decision violated India's wildlife laws. Singh claimed authorities acted "without any scientific probe or investigation into the circumstance of the attack" and suggested the move was driven by pressure from the local tourist industry, which feared visitors would avoid the park due to concerns about a man-eating tiger.

However, the Rajasthan high court dismissed the petition, ruling that the decision to relocate Ustad "can under no stretch of imagination be held to be hasty, arbitrary or unreasonable." The judges rejected claims of tourism industry influence, stating that "tourism thrives on the tigers of Ranthambore and it is not the other way round."

Singh has now escalated the matter to India's Supreme Court.

The case highlights broader challenges facing tiger conservation efforts in India, which has successfully increased its tiger population to 2,226 as of 2014. The country is home to 70% of the world's tigers, with the 400 sq km (99,000-acre) Ranthambore National Park being particularly popular for tiger safaris.

However, as tiger numbers have grown, their natural habitat has diminished, resulting in increased human-tiger encounters. More than 60 people are killed by tigers annually in India, raising difficult questions about balancing conservation success with human safety.

The Supreme Court's decision could set an important precedent for managing similar situations as India continues its tiger conservation efforts while protecting local communities.

# Government Awards £1.3bn Contract for HMS Anson Submarine Construction

The Ministry of Defence has announced a £1.3 billion contract to complete construction of HMS Anson, the fifth Astute Class submarine being built at BAE Systems' Barrow shipyard.

The substantial package will fund the vessel's design finalization, remaining construction work, and comprehensive testing over the next five years. This announcement continues a pattern of incremental contractual commitments that successive governments have made to the Astute programme since the 1990s.

HMS Anson is part of Britain's ambitious seven-submarine Astute Class fleet. Currently, two submarines are operational, whilst a third is conducting sea trials. A fourth vessel has reached advanced construction stages, and preliminary work has commenced on the sixth submarine.

The programme has never operated under a single overarching contract, with funding consistently released in segments throughout its lifespan.

Philip Dunne, Minister of State for Defence Procurement, explained the approach: "Building submarines is not a simple endeavour. Every element of it is quite complex, including securing the right contractual arrangements around it."

Tony Johns, Managing Director of BAE Systems Submarines, welcomed the agreement: "Signing this contract is an important milestone in the Astute programme. This is a hugely complex national endeavour and we are proud of the role we play in helping to protect our nation's interests."

# Eddie Redmayne to Star in New Harry Potter Film

Oscar-winning actor Eddie Redmayne will take on the leading role of Newt Scamander in the upcoming Harry Potter spin-off film. The character is described as a 'magizoologist' who embarks on adventures searching for magical creatures in New York, set 70 years before Harry Potter's story unfolds.

The film draws inspiration from J.K. Rowling's short book, marking her debut as a screenwriter for the franchise. The director expressed tremendous enthusiasm about the collaboration, praising Redmayne as "a fearless actor, brimming with invention, wit and humanity."

Fans will need to exercise patience, as the film's release is scheduled for 18th November 2016. This date holds special significance, arriving just two days before the 15th anniversary of the first Harry Potter book, "The Philosopher's Stone," creating a magical celebration for devoted followers worldwide.

# Northern Ireland Firms Report Strong Growth

Two major Craigavon-based manufacturing companies have reported strong financial performances, offering positive news for Northern Ireland's manufacturing sector.

Pharmaceutical company Almac more than doubled its pre-tax profits to £23m in the year ending September 2015, whilst Thompson Aero Seating recorded a 27% increase in pre-tax profits to nearly £14m for the year ending March 2016.

The positive results come at a time when parts of Northern Ireland's manufacturing sector have faced challenges, with several job losses reported over the past year.

Almac's turnover grew from £342m to £394m, with staff numbers exceeding 3,500. A key factor in the profit increase was $20m (£14m) received from licensing oncology and diagnostic test products. While the company primarily serves other pharmaceutical firms, it is increasingly developing its own products, particularly in cancer diagnostics.

Thompson Aero achieved its profit growth on a turnover of £65m, which the company described as "encouraging". The business class aircraft seat specialist has experienced rapid expansion over five years, supplying major airlines including Aer Lingus, Qantas and Air Canada.

# Liverpool Teenager Ben Woodburn Makes Senior Debut as Klopp Promises Academy Pathway

Liverpool manager Jürgen Klopp has praised young prospect Ben Woodburn following his senior debut, whilst emphasising the importance of patience in the teenager's development.

Seventeen-year-old Woodburn came off the bench late in Liverpool's victory over Sunderland, becoming the third youngest player ever to represent the Merseysiders in senior competition at just 17 years, one month and 11 days old.

Klopp described the moment as significant not just for Woodburn, but for the entire Academy system at Anfield. "I thought it was a good moment, not only for Ben, but to show it for all the other boys in the Academy," the German manager said. "There is a way [to the first-team], especially for you, whoever you are, as long as you are here and train hard and work hard, everything can be possible."

The Cheshire-born forward has committed his international future to Wales and recently impressed in the U19 Euro 2017 qualifiers, though he remains eligible for England. Woodburn has recently signed a new long-term professional contract with Liverpool, underlining the club's faith in his potential.

However, Klopp remained cautious about promising the teenager regular first-team football. "Ben is a wonderful boy, but I'm not sure," he admitted when asked about Woodburn's immediate prospects. "A lot of signs are very positive signs, not only with him. That's good to have."

The manager stressed that whilst Liverpool's first team is strong, opportunities would continue to arise for talented youngsters. "We can all speak a lot of times about opportunities for the young boys in our squad," Klopp added, "and sometimes we have to show it."

# Driver "Too Far Right" Before Fatal Crash, Court Hears

A driver was travelling too far to the right of the road before a collision that killed his passenger, a court has heard.

Joel Jones, now 24, is accused of causing the death of Jack McKenzie, 18, in a crash near Peterchurch, Herefordshire, on 3 September 2010.

Hereford Crown Court heard Mr Jones, of Skenfrith, Monmouthshire, struck a hay baler's wheel because he was driving too far to the right of the road. The prosecution said he was driving at "more speed" than was appropriate, though not exceeding the speed limit.

His speed was estimated at between 40mph and 50mph when the crash happened at 23:30 BST, the court was told.

The two students at Hereford Sixth Form College were in a Vauxhall Corsa when it collided with a seven-tonne hay baler being pulled by a tractor. A "competent driver" would have slowed down or pulled over while passing the tractor, prosecutors said.

Following the crash, a Fiat Punto was also involved in a collision with the Corsa, which had been on the opposite side of the road to the tractor.

Mr McKenzie, originally from Hereford, died in the collision. Mr Jones was also injured.

The trial continues.

# Catholic Church in Scotland Publishes Safeguarding Audit Revealing 15 Abuse Allegations

The Catholic Church in Scotland has published its Diocesan Safeguarding Audit for 2013, revealing details of 15 allegations of abuse made during that year, in what it describes as a commitment to transparency and openness.

According to the audit, six of the allegations were historical, dating from the 1980s or earlier. Ten allegations involved sexual abuse, with three of those cases also involving physical abuse. The remaining allegations comprised physical abuse alone, emotional abuse, and verbal abuse.

Of the 15 allegations, ten were reported to police authorities. A Church spokesman explained that the five unreported cases related to incidents such as shouting at groups of children, poor boundaries, and abuse of power – actions not considered illegal but requiring intervention from the Diocesan Safeguarding Advisor and Bishop.

As of November 2014, no prosecutions had resulted from the 2013 allegations. The outcomes varied significantly: two cases were reported to the procurator fiscal, two alleged perpetrators had died, three individuals were removed from ministry, one person was no longer serving as a volunteer, and two outcomes remained unknown to the Church.

A Catholic Church spokesman emphasized the organization's commitment to protecting people of all ages involved with the Church and its organizations. "The publication of this audit is an example of the commitment to transparency and openness made previously by Scotland's Catholic Bishops," he stated.

The spokesman also announced that an external review of safeguarding protocols conducted by Dr. Andrew McLellan would report in 2015, alongside a statistical review of all historic abuse cases from 1947 to 2005.

The Church confirmed its support for an evidence-based inquiry into abuse in care facilities across Scotland.

# AO World Reports Mixed Results After Profit Warning

Online electrical retailer AO World has released its annual results following a profit warning issued in February that sent shockwaves through the market.

The company had issued a profit warning in February, revising down expectations for its results. Revenues for the year to the end of March were 24% higher at £477m - in line with the revised expectations. The company said it was "on track" with its plans so far in the new financial year.

AO World floated on the stock exchange in February last year. Its valuation at the time - a market capitalisation of £1.2bn, despite profits of less than £8m - stunned the City.

"Despite missing our financial expectations for the year, we have continued to take market share in the UK," said AO World chief executive John Roberts. Mr Roberts said he was also "encouraged by progress" in its German business, which launched in October last year.

In February, the firm said sales had slowed in the final quarter of the year and that it had "become apparent" that it couldn't maintain the year-on-year growth boosted by the publicity surrounding its float.

Shares in the firm fell sharply after February's profit warning, and are now trading at about 176p - still well below their 285p flotation price.

# Bernhard Langer Wins Record Ninth Senior Major Championship

Bernhard Langer has made history by capturing his record ninth senior major championship, surpassing golfing legend Jack Nicklaus at the top of the all-time list.

The 59-year-old German overcame a one-shot deficit entering the final round, firing a four-under-par 68 to defeat Vijay Singh, who carded a 70, at Trump National Golf Club in Washington DC.

"It was a very tight race until we got to 16 and 17. Then I got in front by two and never looked back," Langer explained after his victory.

The seniors majors are contested by players aged 50 and over. Next on the calendar is the US Senior Open in late June, followed by the Senior Players Championship in July, where Langer seeks his fourth consecutive title. The British Seniors Open concludes the season at Royal Porthcawl from 27-30 July.

# Police Officer Disciplined After Year-Long Delay in Child Assault Investigation

A police officer has been disciplined following a Police Ombudsman investigation that revealed serious failings in handling a case involving a young boy who suffered serious injuries during a brutal 2014 assault.

The victim sustained a broken wrist, broken tooth, and extensive bruising after being punched and kicked during the attack. His mother filed a complaint after experiencing persistent difficulties in progressing the case through proper channels.

According to the ombudsman's findings, while the investigating officer made some preliminary enquiries, he subsequently failed to advance the investigation in any meaningful way. The boy's mother made numerous unsuccessful attempts to contact the officer throughout the investigation period. Her only successful contact occurred when she managed to reach him after discovering he had not submitted crucial paperwork related to the case.

During questioning by Police Ombudsman investigators, the officer could not provide adequate justification for the extensive delays. He cited workload pressures and being reassigned to other duties as contributing factors. Significantly, he admitted to forgetting his voicemail password and acknowledged failing to return at least one message.

Perhaps most concerning was the officer's admission that it took nearly a year to obtain consent for accessing the victim's medical and dental records—a delay he attributed simply to forgetting about the requirement.

Superintendent Jonathan Roberts addressed the case, stating: "We regret that on this occasion the conduct of this officer fell below that which the public, and we in the PSNI, expect. We accept and have implemented the ombudsman's recommendations."

The case has raised questions about police accountability and case management procedures within the service.

# FDA Panel Backs Controversial Female Sexual Desire Drug Despite Safety Concerns

A panel of medical experts has recommended approval of flibanserin, a controversial drug designed to treat low sexual desire in women, despite acknowledging modest results and significant safety risks.

The advisory committee backed the medication but emphasized it must carry strong warnings about potentially serious side effects, including fainting and tiredness. The final decision now rests with the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), which typically follows expert recommendations but has already rejected flibanserin twice since 2010.

Clinical trials showed women taking the drug experienced between 0.5 and one additional sexually satisfying event per month—results experts openly described as "modest." However, Dr. Julia Heiman of the Kinsey Institute at Indiana University argued that "even modest results can make a lot of difference when you're at a certain point in the clinical problem."

Patient testimonials highlighted the drug's emotional significance. "I want to want my husband, it is that simple," said Amanda Parrish, who called flibanserin "a relationship-saving and life-changing drug."

The approval push gained momentum from Sprout Pharmaceuticals, the drug's developer, and women's rights group Even the Score, which accused the FDA of gender bias for approving multiple male erectile dysfunction treatments without comparable options for women.

Critics, however, condemned the campaign. Dr. Adriane Fugh-Berman of Georgetown University warned that approval "will set the worst kind of precedent—that companies that spend enough money can force the FDA to approve useless or dangerous drugs."

If approved, flibanserin would target pre-menopausal women, with the panel recommending strict risk management measures, including requiring physicians to obtain certification before prescribing.

# Health Secretary Jeremy Hunt to Make £14m from Sale of Education Business

Health Secretary Jeremy Hunt is set to receive approximately £14 million from the sale of his stake in an education listings company he co-founded two decades ago.

The firm, which runs websites listing courses for students around the world, is being bought for £30 million by the Australian firm IDP Education. Mr Hunt owns a 48% stake in Hotcourses, which is therefore valued at just over £14 million.

The health secretary has pledged to use the proceeds to fund campaigns after he leaves politics. "I am incredibly proud to have set up a successful business, even prouder of the current Hotcourses team who have taken it from strength to strength, and intend to use a significant proportion of the proceeds to campaign for causes I believe in when I eventually leave frontline politics," Mr Hunt said.

He helped to set up the firm, which initially printed a directory of educational courses, in 1996. The MP for South West Surrey stepped down as a director in 2009 but retained his shareholding.

The company now runs several educational websites, such as Postgraduate Search and The Complete University Guide, as well as Hotcourses. Headquartered in London, it employs more than 300 staff in the UK, Australia, the US and Asia.

It has more than two million registered users for its websites, which list half a million courses offered by more than 5,000 educational institutions in 48 countries.

IDP Education, based in Melbourne, is half-owned by a consortium of 38 Australian universities and recruits and advises university students around the world who want to study abroad. It is also a co-owner of the English language testing business IELTS.

IDP Education said that it and the Hotcourses businesses would retain their identity and continue to operate separately, but would collaborate.

Chief executive of the Hotcourses group, Simon Emmett, said: "The Hotcourses Group and IDP Education are both longstanding members of the international education community, and this agreement brings together a world leader in education search technology and tools, with a world leader in student placement and preparation."

Hotcourses was previously up for sale in 2013 but no deal materialised.

# Syrian Forces Launch Major Ground Offensive North of Homs Following Russian Air Strikes

Syrian government forces, backed by intense Russian air bombardment, launched a major ground offensive on rebel-held territory north of Homs on Thursday, according to opposition activists and monitoring groups.

The assault on the rebel enclave began in the early hours of Thursday morning and was preceded by heavy aerial bombardment that reportedly shook the city of Homs several miles away. The offensive targeted several towns including Teir Maaleh, Talbiseh, and Ghantu, with significant civilian casualties reported.

Bebars al-Talawy, an activist based in Homs, described the intensity of the attack to the Associated Press: "Shells were raining on civilian homes. The air raids even shook the city of Homs" despite being several miles from the front lines.

According to Mr. Talawy, the strategic objective of the offensive appears to be reopening the motorway connecting Homs to the northern city of Hama, a vital supply route for government forces.

The Syrian state news agency Sana confirmed the operation, citing a military source who said troops were conducting a major assault against "terrorist organisations" in the Homs countryside. The source claimed government forces had seized control of the village of Khalidiya near Dar al-Kabireh and destroyed two "terrorist operations rooms" in Talbiseh and Teir Maaleh.

The Syrian Observatory for Human Rights, a UK-based monitoring organisation, reported that Russian warplanes conducted at least 15 air strikes on Talbiseh and surrounding areas, killing 10 people, including six rebels. Meanwhile, the Local Co-ordination Committees, an opposition activist network, reported 17 civilian deaths when Russian aircraft allegedly bombed a civilian shelter in Ghantu. Additional casualties were reported in Teir Maaleh and Dar al-Kabireh.

The ground offensive represents one of several launched by the Syrian military and its allies since Russia began its air campaign in Syria two weeks ago. While Russia maintains it is targeting "terrorists," primarily Islamic State militants, numerous reports indicate that many strikes have hit civilian areas and Western-backed rebel positions.

The assault coincided with significant statements from Iran, another key Assad ally. Alaeddin Boroujerdi, chairman of the Iranian parliament's national security and foreign policy committee, said during a visit to Damascus that Tehran would consider deploying ground forces to Syria if requested by the government.

"If Syria makes a request, we will study the request and make a decision," Mr. Boroujerdi stated, adding that Iran is "serious about the fight against terrorism" and has already supplied aid, weapons, and military advisers to Syria and Iraq.

Unconfirmed reports suggest that approximately 1,500 Iranian military personnel have arrived in Syria over the past two weeks, flown to Damascus airport and subsequently transported to a military base in Latakia province. Regional officials also indicate that Hezbollah, the Lebanese Shia Islamist movement, is sending reinforcements to support government assaults in northern and central Syria.

While Iran has long acknowledged sending military advisers to Syria, it has consistently denied having ground forces in the country.

# Tesco Settles US Class Action Lawsuit Over Accounting Scandal

Tesco has agreed to settle a US class action lawsuit stemming from an accounting scandal that rocked the supermarket giant in 2014, according to court documents filed in Manhattan.

The settlement, which requires court approval, was disclosed on Wednesday in the US District Court. While Tesco has not admitted any liability in the matter, the agreement resolves claims that the retailer violated US securities laws by overstating its profit guidance.

The controversy erupted in September 2014 when Tesco announced it had overstated its half-year profit guidance by £250 million due to incorrectly booking payments from suppliers. The figure was subsequently revised upward to £263 million. The revelation caused Tesco's New York-listed shares to plummet 15% the following day, affecting holders of American Depositary Receipts (ADRs), which represent approximately 2% of Tesco shares.

The incident triggered investigations by the Serious Fraud Office and other regulatory bodies, plunging the UK's largest supermarket group into crisis.

Kim Miller, a partner at Kahn Swick & Foti representing the claimants, described the settlement as an "outstanding recovery." Court documents indicate investors will receive an average of 37 cents per ADR before deducting fees and expenses of approximately 30%.

Following the settlement announcement, Tesco shares rose 1.5% to 171.1p in Thursday morning trading, though they remain down nearly 10% for the year.

Analysts at Shore Capital praised chief executive Dave Lewis and his management team for stabilising the organisation during this turbulent period, maintaining their "hold" recommendation on the stock.

Meanwhile, midfielder Aaron Wildig, 25, has signed a new two-year contract with the Shrimps, while forward Kevin Ellison, 38, midfielder Alex Kenyon, 24, and midfielder Andy Fleming, 29, have all agreed new one-year deals.

# New Plastic £5 Notes Enter Circulation in UK

The Bank of England has introduced new polymer £5 banknotes, marking a significant change in British currency. These innovative notes are slightly smaller than traditional paper versions and incorporate advanced security features designed to prevent counterfeiting.

According to the Bank of England, the plastic banknotes offer several advantages: they're cleaner, more secure, and significantly more durable than their paper predecessors. Existing paper £5 notes remain legal tender and can still be used for transactions, but they will gradually be phased out as they're deposited into banks.

The UK joins over 30 countries worldwide that have already adopted polymer currency technology, including Scotland, Australia, New Zealand, and Canada.

The transition to plastic currency will continue with new polymer £10 notes scheduled for summer 2017, followed by £20 notes in 2020.

# DUP-Tory Deal: £1bn Windfall Dominates Northern Ireland Headlines

Northern Ireland's newspapers have given extensive coverage to the controversial confidence-and-supply agreement between the Conservative Party and the Democratic Unionist Party, with front pages dominated by the £1bn financial package secured for the region.

The Irish News features a striking political cartoon depicting Prime Minister Theresa May up a ladder shaking a "money tree" while DUP leader Arlene Foster gleefully collects falling cash in her dress. The News Letter celebrates with the headline "One billion smiles," featuring a photograph of DUP MPs Nigel Dodds and Sir Jeffrey Donaldson alongside Mrs Foster and a more reserved-looking Mrs May. # Officers Face Misconduct Probe Over Man's Broken Neck During Arrest

Four police officers remain on active duty while facing potential gross misconduct charges following an investigation into an arrest that left a young man paralyzed with a broken neck.

Julian Cole, then a 23-year-old student, suffered catastrophic spinal injuries outside Elements nightclub in Bedford in May 2013. The incident has been the subject of a lengthy investigation by the Independent Police Complaints Commission (IPCC).

After examining the circumstances surrounding the arrest, the IPCC has concluded there may be a case to answer for gross misconduct and has referred the matter to prosecutors. Bedfordshire Police confirmed that four officers involved in the incident remain on active duty, while a fifth has since retired from the force.

The investigation findings indicate four officers could face charges relating to honesty and integrity, while one officer could face misconduct proceedings for use of force, though this is not believed to be directly linked to Julian's spinal injury.

The IPCC described the inquiry as "complex and lengthy," involving examination of over 900 documents, witness interviews, multiple medical expert opinions, CCTV analysis, and forensic examination. The Crown Prosecution Service will now determine whether criminal charges should be brought against any of the officers.

Julian's mother, Claudia Cole, told BBC News the announcement was "welcome" but noted the investigation had taken far too long. "It has been the hardest three years waiting for the IPCC investigation to conclude," she said. "Julian is still alive, but it cannot be said that he is really living."

The case has profoundly changed Julian's life. Once an energetic and athletic young man passionate about football and Arsenal FC, he now requires round-the-clock care and is completely dependent on nursing staff and his devoted parents for all his daily needs.

The exact circumstances of how Julian sustained his injuries remain unclear and may never be known with complete certainty. However, under new rules, any misconduct hearings will be open to the public, providing greater transparency in what has become a deeply serious case requiring public scrutiny.

The family continues to seek answers about what happened that night outside the Bedford nightclub, moving one step closer to understanding the truth behind the incident that changed their lives forever.

**Supreme Court Rejects News Group Appeal in Sheridan Defamation Case**

The Supreme Court has dismissed an attempt by News Group to overturn a defamation case won by former MSP Tommy Sheridan against the now defunct News of The World in 2006.

News Group, the paper's owner, sought to have the original ruling "struck down" following Mr Sheridan's 2010 conviction for perjury. However, the Supreme Court ruled they had failed to "raise an arguable point of law of general public importance".

The decision follows a hearing at the Court of Session in Edinburgh last year, where News Group attempted to obtain permission to have the original trial rerun. That application was rejected in November. The company subsequently appealed to the Supreme Court, which has now also declined to hear the case, upholding the Edinburgh judgement.

In a statement, the court explained: "The Court ordered that permission to appeal be refused because the application does not raise an arguable point of law of general public importance, which ought to be considered at this time, bearing in mind that the case has already been the subject of judicial decision and reviewed on appeal".

The judgement finally concludes an 11-year legal saga that began when the newspaper published articles about Mr Sheridan's private life. The former Scottish Socialist Party leader and Glasgow MSP was awarded compensation after winning the defamation trial in 2006, though it is understood he was not paid the money at that time.

In 2010, Mr Sheridan was found guilty of perjury for giving false evidence during the earlier case and was jailed for three years. He was released from prison after serving just over a year of his sentence.

# Wales Forwards: Lydiate Returns to Training as Williams Makes Comeback

Wales forwards coach Robin McBryde has delivered positive news regarding key players' fitness ahead of the Six Nations, confirming that Osprey Dan Lydiate has returned to training following a neck injury, while Liam Williams successfully completed 60 minutes for the Scarlets last weekend.

Lydiate, meanwhile, has been sidelined since being forced off during Ospreys' New Year's Day victory over Newport Gwent Dragons. His return to training represents a significant boost for Wales' back-row options.

# Lord Bilimoria Champions "Good Immigration" as Government Faces Criticism

As net migration figures are set to be released this week, the immigration debate in Britain has reached fever pitch, with critics lining up to attack current government policy. However, one prominent voice is bucking the trend – Lord Karan Bilimoria, the newly installed Chancellor of the University of Birmingham, who insists there is such a thing as "good immigration".

He criticised the government's approach as counterproductive, arguing that whilst they claim to have lost control of illegal immigration – challenging Home Secretary Theresa May to say how many illegal immigrants there actually are – they are instead targeting legitimate students who contribute significantly to Britain's economy and universities.

The financial stakes are considerable. The University of Birmingham's 4,500 international students bring in nearly £60 million in fees annually. Neighbouring Warwick University, the other Russell Group institution in the Midlands, reports that its 5,000-plus international students generate nearly £90 million – money that is reinvested to benefit British students.
