# Rome Metro Accident: Woman Dragged Along Platform After Bag Caught in Train Door

A woman was left in intensive care after being dragged along a Rome metro platform when her bag became trapped in closing train doors, according to CCTV footage that has emerged of the incident.

Natalya Garkovich, 43, was boarding a train at Rome's Termini station when she changed her mind at the last minute and attempted to exit the carriage. As she backed out, her bag became caught in the closing doors, trapping her as the train began to move.

The footage shows fellow passengers on the platform desperately trying to free Ms Garkovich, but they were unable to release her before the train started pulling away. Local media report that Ms Garkovich, believed to be a Belarusian national, suffered broken bones in the incident but has since been moved out of intensive care and her condition has improved.

The incident has raised serious questions about safety systems on Rome's metro network. Reports indicate that passengers aboard the train pulled multiple emergency levers in an attempt to halt the train's advance, but none of the emergency braking systems responded.

The CCTV footage also captured train driver Gianluca Tonelli eating while the train was at the platform. However, Mr Tonelli has defended his actions, insisting he followed proper protocol.

"I know that I was wrong and I am devastated by what happened to that woman," Mr Tonelli told Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera. "But in the video it can also be seen that I looked twice in the mirror, I was not reckless."

According to reports, Mr Tonelli was unaware of the accident until he pulled into the next station. It is believed Ms Garkovich was not dragged into the tunnel.

Carlo Rienzi, president of consumer rights group Codacons, argued that the failure of both the door sensors and emergency braking systems meant the driver could not be held fully responsible.

"The emergency systems on board must function properly," Mr Rienzi said in a statement. "Therefore we consider it outrageous and offensive to say the train driver is entirely responsible, when you should thoroughly investigate the Rome subway security systems and their proper operation."

Stefano Bottoni, national secretary of trade union Sul, called for additional safety measures, suggesting that cockpit cameras might prevent similar accidents in future.

The incident remains under investigation.

# Warburton Admits He May Not Be Ready for First Lions Test Despite Captaincy

British and Irish Lions tour captain Sam Warburton has admitted he may not be ready to feature in the first Test against New Zealand, despite recovering from injury to lead the side in their midweek fixture against the Highlanders on Tuesday.

The Wales open-side flanker has been sidelined with an ankle injury but has returned to captain the Lions in Dunedin. However, with intense competition for back-row positions, Warburton acknowledges his current form may not guarantee him a starting spot in the crucial opening Test.

"If I play Tuesday and I still feel I'm a bit undercut, then I might not be ready for that first Test," Warburton said candidly. "Maybe that would be the situation, or maybe I could have a blinder on Tuesday and feel absolutely fine so we'll see how it goes really."

The Lions face three matches before the first Test against the All Blacks on 24 June at Eden Park, where coach Warren Gatland will finalise his selection from the 41-strong squad. Gatland faces an embarrassment of riches in the back-row, with options including Warburton's Wales teammates Justin Tipuric, Taulupe Faletau and Ross Moriarty, Ireland's CJ Stander, Peter O'Mahony and Sean O'Brien, and England lock Maro Itoje, who has also played in the position.

The 28-year-old Cardiff Blues player missed the final six weeks of the domestic season with a knee injury and admits he needs more game time to reach his peak performance level.

"I definitely need more games. I definitely admit that and I knew that coming into the tour," Warburton explained. "I've learned from experience that it takes me at least two games and then the third game I'll probably be playing some good rugby but Gats knew that."

Despite holding the prestigious position of tour captain, Warburton maintains a realistic view of his Test prospects. "I've received this role as tour captain and I know there's every chance that I might not even get involved in that first Test because there's every other player," he said. "I see it as I'm tour captain, and if I've made the Test then that would be a bonus for me."

Warburton is renowned for his expertise at the breakdown, specialising in winning turnovers and protecting possession. He acknowledges that this will be crucial to his selection hopes.

"When I play well and I am match-fit, I am aggressive in the tackle; I'll contribute a handful of good carries, and you become a lineout option," said Warburton. "More importantly, which hasn't really been a factor in the last three games, is turnovers. My one specialist element is the contact area. I guess I have to deliver in that area on Tuesday. That's my role of expertise."

# Welsh Funding Deal Lacks Certainty, Says Finance Minister Jane Hutt

Welsh Finance Minister Jane Hutt has criticized the coalition government's funding offer, telling BBC Sunday Politics Wales that the deal fails to provide adequate certainty for public spending in Wales.

Mrs Hutt's comments echoed those of First Minister Carwyn Jones, who previously stated that promises of fair funding were lacking in crucial detail.

Prime Minister David Cameron recently pledged to protect the Welsh budget through a "funding floor" mechanism, a measure Welsh ministers have long sought. However, the specific amount will remain unknown until after the general election, when the next UK government spending review takes place.

The proposal would shift Wales away from complete reliance on annual Treasury grants, with the Welsh government instead raising some revenue through devolved taxes. Mr Cameron argues this funding floor—designed to prevent the Barnett formula from squeezing Wales's budget—removes any justification for delaying a referendum on income tax-varying powers.

However, Mrs Hutt expressed frustration that the coalition had not provided more comprehensive details about the funding floor's terms. "They took us for granted and they can't do that," she said.

"This is not about being told at the last minute 'We'll give you this, you do that'. That is not about an agreement. That is not about a respect agenda," the finance minister added.

Mrs Hutt indicated that the Welsh government could support tax devolution, but only with proper guarantees. "If we get that reassurance, that clarity we can sign up to it, then of course you could consider beginning to make a start in terms of considering tax devolution," she stated.

# Toy Dog Astronaut Reaches Edge of Space in School Science Project

A toy dog named Sam has completed a remarkable journey to the edge of space after being launched by helium balloon from a Morecambe hotel.

Attached to a special camera and sent skywards by a helium balloon, he reached an altitude of 15.5 miles (25km). Sam left mission control - the Midland Hotel - as part of a school science initiative on Tuesday.

It was the climax of a project by Morecambe Bay Primary School which joined forces with the hotel and SenditintoSpace.com.

Trudi Wilkinson, business manager of the school, said: "It was brilliant - we loved it."

Children tracked Sam using images and other data in a project that has helped them learn more about space exploration. The cuddly cosmonaut's ascent was charted using GPS tracking equipment and specialist cameras.

It is understood his flight was not too "ruff".

# Syrian Air Strikes Kill at Least 25 in Aleppo After Brief Lull

At least 25 people, including children, have been killed in renewed air strikes on rebel-held areas of eastern Aleppo, monitoring groups report.

The bombardment follows a temporary lull called by the Syrian government, partly to allow civilians to leave rebel areas in the east of the city. It has come under intense aerial attack since a ceasefire brokered by the US and Russia collapsed last month.

The air strikes came as Russian President Vladimir Putin cancelled a planned visit to France. He had been due to meet French President Francois Hollande later this month but pulled out after Paris said talks would be confined to Syria, French presidential sources said.

On Monday, Mr Hollande suggested Russian officials could face war crimes charges over the bombardment of Aleppo. On Tuesday UK Foreign Secretary Boris Johnson told the UK parliament Russia was in danger of becoming a pariah nation because of its involvement in Syria.

Moscow has repeatedly denied attacking civilians, and says it targets terrorist groups in Syria.

## Heavy Casualties Reported

The UK-based Syrian Observatory for Human Rights reported that at least 25 civilians were killed in Tuesday's air strikes and considerable damage was inflicted on several areas.

The observatory said Russian war planes had dropped so-called "bunker busters" and other bombs, with children thought to be among the dead. Footage shared by activists showed lifeless bodies of toddlers wrapped in sheets, with their parents distraught beside them.

Some of the most intense attacks have come in the Bustan al-Qasr and Fardos neighbourhoods near the citadel, which sits near the front line with the government-held west.

Aid organisation Medecins Sans Frontieres said on Tuesday there were now only 11 working ambulances left in the city because five had been hit by bombs and another eight were missing essential spare parts.

Meanwhile, Syrian state media reported rebel attacks on government-held western Aleppo, in which it said four people were killed and 14 injured.

## Diplomatic Efforts Stalled

Diplomatic efforts to revive the ceasefire have so far come to nothing. The UN has warned that eastern Aleppo, where an estimated 275,000 people still live, could face "total destruction" in the space of two months.

Last week, Russia vetoed a UN Security Council resolution drafted by France calling for an end to the bombing in Aleppo.

# Student Motorcyclist Dies in Collision Near Welshpool

A university student from Tamworth has died following a motorcycle collision in Powys while returning from a day trip with her boyfriend.

Melanie Lakin, from Glascote, was killed in the crash on the A458 between Llanfair Caereinion and Welshpool on Sunday afternoon. The 19-year-old had been enjoying a picnic at Bala lake with her boyfriend, with the couple travelling on separate motorbikes.

The incident occurred at approximately 4:30 PM and has been voluntarily referred to the Independent Police Complaints Commission (IPCC) by Dyfed-Powys Police due to a police vehicle being in the vicinity at the time.

According to police reports, a marked police motorcyclist was conducting routine vehicle checks in the area, resulting in several cars stopped in a line of traffic. Initial investigations indicate Ms Lakin's motorcycle collided with one of the stationary vehicles in the queue.

In a heartfelt tribute, Ms Lakin's family described her as "a keen motorcyclist who loved life, people, nature and animals especially her cats Hector and Cleo." She had just completed her first year studying diagnostic radiography at Birmingham City University and was enthusiastic about pursuing a career in the NHS.

Her family highlighted her creative passions, noting her "keen eye and appreciation for photography, music and art," which she often combined by photographing bands and musicians at music festivals.

Ms Lakin is survived by her mother Pam, father Nigel, brother Jody, his partner Elena, boyfriend Oliver, and numerous friends and colleagues who knew and loved her.

**Wales Updates Alcohol Guidelines After 20 Years**

Wales' chief medical officer Dr Ruth Hussey has joined her UK colleagues in updating 20-year-old alcohol consumption guidelines, warning against several common drinking habits.

One key recommendation advises people not to "save up" their 14 weekly units of alcohol to consume on just one or two days. The guidelines also challenge the popular belief that one or two glasses of red wine can protect against heart disease, stating this benefit is "less significant" than previously thought.

The proposed changes are currently subject to a UK-wide consultation running until April. The guidelines recommend several measures to reduce health risks associated with alcohol consumption.

The Change4Life Wales alcohol campaign is already encouraging people to have at least two alcohol-free days a week. Dr Hussey said the updated guidelines "draw on the latest evidence on how different levels of drinking affect health risks for individuals" and help people "make informed decisions about their drinking".

The announcement comes as the Welsh government launched a three-year strategy to tackle substance and alcohol abuse, particularly targeting "risky drinking behaviour" among those under 24 and older people. Hospital admissions in Wales for over-50s with alcohol issues have risen for three consecutive years.

The Department of Health is leading the consultation, with Mark Bellis, director of policy at Public Health Wales, involved in developing the guidelines.

# Sir Christopher Bland, Former BBC Chairman, Dies After Battle with Cancer

Sir Christopher Bland, the former chairman of the BBC board of governors and a distinguished figure in British broadcasting and business, has died peacefully at home after a three-year battle with cancer.

Sir Christopher was chairman of the BBC board of governors between 1996 and 2001. He also held a number of senior roles in business, including chairman of BT, and was head of the Royal Shakespeare Company (RSC). His son, Archie, said: "He was as sweet and gentle and wise as he was tough and bold and brave."

BBC director general Tony Hall said: "Sir Christopher Bland was an outstanding chairman of the BBC. He was a great communicator who both understood the creativity of broadcasting as well as the business of it. "He was hugely admired and will be greatly missed."

In a statement, Sir Christopher's family said he had died peacefully at home, having defied cancer for three years. The statement continued: "He relished every day of his life, and to those that loved him he is irreplaceable. We're enormously proud of everything he achieved, from steering the BBC through tough times to his late flowering as a novelist, and we'll miss him more than we can say."

Sir Christopher, who also spent time as head of London Weekend Television (LWT), spoke out in support of the BBC on a number of occasions after he left the corporation. Two years ago, he criticised the government for transferring the funding of free licence fees for the over-75s to the BBC, saying it was "the worst form of dodgy Whitehall accounting". In 2008, when Jonathan Ross and Russell Brand were suspended from the BBC for leaving lewd messages on actor Andrew Sachs's phone, Sir Christopher said "the meal that those who are not natural lovers of the BBC have made out of it all is excessive".

After leaving the BBC, he became chairman of BT, turning the company around at a time when its senior management had come under sustained criticism from investors. Between 2004 and 2011 he was chairman of the RSC, overseeing a £112m re-development of the company's home in Stratford-upon-Avon. On artistic director Michael Boyd's departure, he said: "If the RSC is in good shape now, it is in large part due to the expert, passionate and playful chairmanship of Sir Christopher Bland."

Archie Bland reported his father's death on Twitter, ending his message with the words, "God I'll miss him". BBC News presenter Huw Edwards offered his sympathy, writing that "at the BBC many of us remember him as an exemplary chairman". Master of Selwyn College, Cambridge, and former head of BBC News and BBC Sport Roger Mosey said: "[He] was the best BBC chairman in recent times. Tough, independent, wise and fair."

BBC media editor Amol Rajan wrote: "Christopher Bland is just about the most kind, impressive and inspirational man I ever met. "Goodbye hero. I commend his spirit to the living."

Sir Christopher is survived by his wife Lady Jennifer, his son and his four step-children.

# Teen Skipper Honored for Bravery After Abandoning Sinking Crabbing Boat

A teenage fisherman has been recognized for his courage and composure after his boat began sinking off the Welsh coast when he was just 16 years old.

Jake Bowman-Davies from Neyland, Pembrokeshire, faced every skipper's nightmare when his Milford Haven-based crabbing vessel started taking on water at night off the Llyn Peninsula in Gwynedd. After spending two hours desperately trying to pump out the water, he made the difficult decision to abandon ship.

The incident occurred at 22:30 GMT on 12 February, just weeks after Jake had assumed command of his father's 15-metre vessel, Cesca. Woken by his three crew members—aged 30, 23, and 20—the young skipper discovered the boat was rapidly flooding.

Despite the engines cutting out before coastguards arrived, Jake maintained his composure. "I just knew if I kept calm it would be better," he explained. "You realise what you're doing and what they've told you in training just kicks in."

As the vessel rolled and pitched heavily, Jake led his crew over the side into an inflatable life raft. Within 20 minutes, an RAF helicopter arrived and airlifted all four men to safety.

Now 17, Jake has received a commendation from the Shipwrecked Mariners' Society at London's Fishmongers' Hall. Olympic sailing legend Ben Ainslie called Jake's actions "impressive."

The Shipwrecked Mariners' Society has been recognizing skill and gallantry at sea since 1851.

# Passengers Stranded for Hours After Rail Chaos at York Station

Hundreds of passengers were left stranded at York station over the weekend after severe disruptions left them stuck on trains for hours with minimal information about their journeys.

Middlesbrough passenger Mike Oyston described the scene as "just chaos," adding: "There was no information at all." He was among approximately 1,000 people who found themselves waiting at York station, many having been brought there after lengthy delays on their original services.

A spokesman for train operator East Coast issued an apology for the disruption, stating: "We sincerely apologise for the queues and inconvenience." The company attempted to keep passengers informed by deploying staff to York station, though the spokesman acknowledged significant challenges.

"Part of the problem was that we didn't know the exact times when this situation would be resolved so the amount of information we had was limited," he explained. "Clearly we had a difficult weekend."

Mr Oyston expressed frustration at having to arrange for a friend to drive from Middlesbrough to collect him. "We were directed to the back car park and left to get on with it. We're not happy at all," he said.

Grandmother Pat Feetham from Hull spent almost five hours stuck on a train from Scotland. "They ran out of food, it was very cold and we didn't know what was happening until a police officer got on the train and said there were buses to take us to York," she said.

East Coast confirmed that passengers would be eligible for compensation under its "delay repay" scheme. Most services resumed normal operation on Sunday, though National Rail Enquiries warned that some disruption continued as train crews and rolling stock remained out of position. Passengers were advised to check before travelling.

# School Admissions Too Complex for Parents, Warns Watchdog

England's schools adjudicator has raised serious concerns about the complexity of school admission systems, warning that some are so complicated that parents may need to begin studying them "several years" before applying for a place for their child.

In her annual report, chief schools adjudicator Elizabeth Passmore highlighted that for the second consecutive year, too many schools were failing to comply with the admissions code – the rules designed to ensure school places are allocated fairly.

The report reveals particular problems with sixth-form admissions, suggesting that some state schools which select by ability at age 16 are setting tougher entry standards for external applicants than for pupils already attending the school. While only grammar schools can select by ability at age 11, this restriction does not apply to sixth-form entry at 16.

Ms Passmore called for all schools to fully comply with the admissions code, noting that some institutions were breaching the rules in various ways: through the criteria they set, by inadequately consulting parents about their plans, or by failing to publish admission arrangements on their websites in a timely manner.

The watchdog expressed particular concern about the labyrinthine nature of some schools' admissions processes. "Some secondary schools have arrangements that are complicated and require a parent to be well organised and study the arrangements carefully, sometimes several years before applying for a place, to ensure that their child will have a realistic chance of gaining a place at the school," the annual report states.

Parents face additional challenges when children must take entrance tests for multiple schools on different days. The situation becomes even more convoluted when schools use banding systems – taking proportions of children from different ability levels – alongside other criteria such as catchment areas, designated feeder schools, or religious faith requirements.

The report warns that "complex arrangements, especially some with points systems, risk falling far short of" the code's requirement that "parents should be able to look at a set of arrangements and understand easily how places for that school will be allocated."

Another issue identified involves new schools or academies taking over admissions responsibility from local authorities. Ms Passmore urged the Department for Education to "ensure that there is clear guidance, for new schools and those that change their status to become their own admission authority, about the requirements and timetable to be followed concerning admission matters."

Under the government's academy and free school programme, an increasing number of schools are assuming control of their own admissions processes. While they can establish their own rules, these must align with the admissions code.

The watchdog reported handling 212 new cases this year, down from 265 the previous year, with the majority involving admissions complaints. The adjudicator also deals with disputes over changes to school land use, including playing fields, examining 10 such cases this year – the same number as last year.

The report underscores growing concerns that the admissions system is becoming increasingly difficult for ordinary parents to navigate effectively.

# New RNLI Lifeboat Centre Planned for Burry Port Harbour

The Royal National Lifeboat Institution (RNLI) has unveiled plans to replace Burry Port's aging boathouse with a modern facility that will house both lifeboats under one roof.

The proposed centre will feature contemporary training and changing facilities designed to enable faster launch times for the volunteer crew. Additional amenities include a dedicated workshop and a public viewing area, allowing visitors to observe operations.

The new building will be located between the current lifeboat station and the western slipway, next to the cycle track.

Alun Wells, Burry Port RNLI Lifeboat press officer, described the development as a "major step forward in the regeneration of Burry Port Harbour." He emphasized that the project will guarantee "an RNLI presence and legacy for the local community for many years to come."

# Bestselling Author Identifies Lost 1069 Battlefield in Devon

Bestselling author Nick Arnold has claimed to have discovered the location of a forgotten Norman battlefield in Devon, describing the 1069 clash as the crucial "sequel" to the Battle of Hastings.

Mr Arnold, famous for writing the Horrible Science series of children's books, believes a field between Appledore and Northam in North Devon was the site of a bloody encounter that ultimately sealed Norman control of England. Academics have hailed the discovery as "significant" to British history.

The author began his research five years ago, inspired by a story passed down from his grandfather. His investigation revealed that Harold Godwinson's sons launched a revenge attack three years after their father's defeat at Hastings in 1066.

According to Mr Arnold's findings, more than 3,000 people perished when Godwine and Edmund, sons of the vanquished King Harold, arrived at Appledore on 26 June 1069 with 64 longships "crammed with armed men." The invasion force had sailed from Ireland, seeking to reclaim the English throne from Norman control.

The Anglo-Saxon army faced a defending force comprising Normans, Bretons, and English troops led by Brian of Brittany. The day-long battle ended in comprehensive defeat for Harold's sons. "The showdown settled once and for all who would rule England," Mr Arnold said.

The discovery adds a new chapter to the well-documented Norman Conquest timeline. Following Edward the Confessor's death in January 1066, Harold seized the crown with support from English magnates. His reign lasted just nine months before William defeated him at Hastings on 14 October 1066. William secured his position through negotiations with English nobles and was crowned on Christmas Day 1066.

Mr Arnold combined scientific analysis of the estuary with historical battle accounts to pinpoint the location. "By combining scientific data on the estuary with accounts of the battle it's possible to locate the fighting in a small area," he explained.

His research drew on original sources including the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, landscape histories, and calculations of historical tide times and sunset hours. "The amazing cast of supporting characters include a treacherous Abbot, a conscience-stricken Queen and a headless saint," he added.

The Devonshire Association has published Mr Arnold's research paper, which is being republished by the Battlefields Trust. Dr Benjamin Hudson from Pennsylvania State University called it "a significant contribution to the history of medieval Britain." Professor Elisabeth van Houts of Cambridge University praised the work as "an exemplary piece of lucid writing, research and detective work."

# Army Reservist Uses Morse Code SOS to Signal Wife After Breaking Leg on Dorset Beach

An army reservist who broke his leg after slipping on seaweed at a remote Dorset beach used his torch to signal for help in Morse code, leading to his dramatic rescue.

Sgt Tim Robinson, 54, was walking alone on the Jurassic Coast at Seatown, near Lyme Regis, when disaster struck on Tuesday afternoon. The experienced soldier, who has completed three tours in the Middle East, slipped on seaweed and fell, breaking his leg with an audible crack.

"I stepped on some seaweed and slipped, then my leg snapped," said Sgt Robinson, who was visiting from Derbyshire. "I fell backwards and I heard it go with a large crack, my foot was at a 45 degree angle."

Stranded two miles from the nearest town without a mobile phone as darkness fell, the reservist drew on his military training to mount a rescue operation. After crawling and staggering for approximately two hours, he took out a miniature torch and began signalling towards his hotel more than a mile away, where he hoped his wife would spot him.

Sgt Robinson systematically flashed the international distress signal - SOS in Morse code - then swung the torch overhead, a technique army officers use to signal helicopters. He crawled 50 yards before repeating the process.

After three attempts, his wife successfully located him by following the light signals and immediately called emergency services. The RNLI assisted in transporting Sgt Robinson to an ambulance at 19:10 GMT.

He is currently recovering at Dorset County Hospital, awaiting an operation on his leg and foot.

# Jason Gillespie Named Kent's Interim Assistant Coach Until Allan Donald Arrives

Former Australia fast bowler Jason Gillespie has been appointed as Kent's temporary assistant coach while the county waits for Allan Donald to obtain the necessary work visa.

The 41-year-old, who enjoyed remarkable success at Yorkshire, will support head coach Matt Walker until Donald can join on a full-time basis. During his tenure at Yorkshire, Gillespie guided the team to promotion from Division Two and secured back-to-back County Championship titles before departing at the end of last season.

"To get Jason on board is a brilliant coup," Walker said. "To have an experienced ex-head coach come into our ranks is great for me and the lads. His bowling expertise is like-for-like with Allan."

Gillespie, who has coached Adelaide Strikers in the Big Bash and Kings XI Punjab in the Indian Premier League, left Yorkshire in September to return to Australia for family reasons.

"The opportunity to assist Kent on a short-term basis was one that I couldn't resist and works well with my current situation," Gillespie explained. "I look forward to helping Matt Walker and Sam Northeast over the next couple of months until I hand over to Allan Donald."

Walker and Donald were announced as Kent's new coaching partnership in January, following Jimmy Adams' departure from Canterbury.

# Police Warn of Rising Cyber-Stalking Threat in Northern Ireland

Police in Northern Ireland have issued a warning about the growing prevalence of cyber-stalking, stating that victims span all age groups across the region.

Authorities are urging the public to take immediate action by reviewing their privacy and security settings on social media platforms and ensuring anti-spyware software on their devices remains up-to-date. Officials emphasized that education about cyber-stalking risks is essential to combat the problem.

The warning follows last year's investigations into multiple cases where Northern Ireland residents were targeted by international crime gangs. These cases mirror the tragic circumstances surrounding Ronan Hughes, a 17-year-old from Coalisland, County Tyrone.

In June 2015, Ronan took his own life after falling victim to webcam blackmail. He was deceived into sharing intimate images online, which were subsequently distributed to his friends when he refused to pay a ransom demanded by a Nigerian-based gang.

His family has since campaigned to raise awareness about such predatory online practices.

# Surf Industry Pioneer Jack O'Neill Dies at Seaside Home

**SANTA CRUZ, CALIFORNIA** - Jack O'Neill, the pioneering entrepreneur who revolutionized cold-water surfing and built a global surfwear empire, passed away peacefully at his seaside home in Santa Cruz, California, surrounded by family, friends confirmed to KSBW news.

O'Neill opened his first surf shop in San Francisco in 1952, launching what would become one of the world's largest surfwear brands. He is widely credited with popularizing the neoprene wetsuit, an innovation that transformed surfing from a warm-weather pursuit into a year-round sport accessible in colder climates.

"Surfing for me was a very important part of my life," O'Neill said in a 2011 interview. "I'd work downtown in San Francisco and I'd get all screwed up, and I'd go out and I'd jump in the ocean and everything would be all right again."

His business ambitions were initially modest. "All I wanted to do was surf, and when I opened that shop in my garage, I thought I would have a few guys there to sell suits and have guys to surf with," he recalled. A skeptic once told him he would "sell to the five guys on the beach" and go out of business. "Nobody is more surprised than I am about how this business has grown," O'Neill admitted.

After serving as a pilot in the Naval Air Corps during the 1940s, O'Neill moved to San Francisco and joined a dedicated group of cold-water surfers at Ocean Beach. There, he began experimenting with neoprene, a material already used by the U.S. Navy. He scoured surplus stores and started sewing pieces into vests, according to the San Francisco Chronicle, eventually developing the full-body wetsuit that made his name.

While not credited as the wetsuit's inventor, O'Neill was among the pioneers of the neoprene version. In the early 1970s, he lost sight in his left eye while testing an early surfboard leash prototype, thereafter wearing his characteristic eye patch.

His son assumed control of the business in 1985. Despite his commercial success, O'Neill remained intensely private, rarely speaking to the press. "O'Neill was one of the least-known, and least-talked-about titans of the surf world," Surfer magazine noted in his obituary.

O'Neill said his proudest achievement was the Sea Odyssey programme, which introduced schoolchildren to marine conservation.

# Liverpool New Year's Fireworks Display Criticized as "Disappointing" After Waterfront Move

Liverpool City Council is facing a barrage of criticism after relocating its New Year's Eve fireworks display to the waterfront for the first time, abandoning traditional celebrations in suburban parks across Liverpool and Wirral.

Hundreds of spectators took to social media following the event to express their disappointment, with many describing the display as "rubbish" and poorly executed. Council officer Claire McColgan confirmed the authority would "assess feedback" from the controversial event.

The revamped celebration was designed to allow crowds to gather on both sides of the River Mersey, watching fireworks launched from barges positioned on the water. However, the ambitious plan failed to meet expectations for many attendees.

Common complaints included fireworks being too distant to properly view and a notable absence of musical accompaniment. Twitter user Zoe Whittingham wrote: "Travel to Liverpool to see the firework display on the docks and what a load of rubbish! No music and the worst fireworks I've seen!"

Caitlin Austin questioned the council's planning, asking "what were you playing at?" while Alexandra Jones lamented the lack of atmosphere and poor organization.

Despite the criticism, some attendees defended the event. Nicola Bolton praised the "great view" and "great fireworks," noting that Liverpool was well-attended.

Ms McColgan, Liverpool City Council's head of culture, acknowledged that plans for a smartphone app enabling musical accompaniment were inadequately communicated. She defended the warm-up event featuring drumming and aircraft pyrotechnics as successful.

"We tried to do something new this year. Some people didn't like it, some did," Ms McColgan said, adding that the council would learn from the experience. She admitted the Mersey's size presented challenges for the display.

When asked about returning to local park displays, Ms McColgan responded: "Of course. We will consider everything."

A council spokesman noted that private sector funding supported the fireworks themselves.

# Luke Fitzgerald Retires from Rugby After Neck Injury Setback

Irish international Luke Fitzgerald has announced his retirement from professional rugby after a persistent neck injury forced him to end his distinguished career.

The Leinster wing, who earned 34 caps for Ireland, has battled with a serious neck problem for several years, with his final setback coming during Leinster's Pro12 final defeat to Connacht in May.

"I've had a wonderful rugby career which makes it easy for me to move on to the next stage of my life," Fitzgerald said in a statement.

The 29-year-old enjoyed considerable success during his career, winning a Grand Slam with Ireland in 2009 and a Six Nations Championship in 2015. He also claimed three Heineken Cups with Leinster, establishing himself as one of Irish rugby's most talented players.

Fitzgerald burst onto the international scene in 2006 but injury problems consistently interrupted his progress. He missed the 2007 and 2011 World Cups before finally making his tournament debut against Canada last September.

His standout season came in 2009 when he played in every match of Ireland's Grand Slam campaign, earning selection for that summer's British and Irish Lions tour to South Africa, where he won one cap.

The former Blackrock College student amassed 154 appearances for Leinster, winning three Pro12 titles alongside his European honours.

"It's been an honour and a privilege to represent my province, my country and the British & Irish Lions during my career and I'm glad to finish my career as a 'one club man'," Fitzgerald added.

His retirement represents the second significant loss for Leinster coach Leo Cullen this week, following scrum-half Eoin Reddan's decision to retire.

# Walmart Names Sean Clarke as New Asda Chief Executive

Walmart has appointed Sean Clarke as the new chief executive of struggling UK supermarket chain Asda, in a surprise move aimed at revitalizing the retailer's fortunes amid fierce competition.

The appointment comes after Asda has now reported seven straight quarters of declining sales, with the company facing intense pressure from discount competitors and rivals who have improved their operations. Sean Clarke's experience in managing structural change is expected to help "reposition the business" in an increasingly competitive market.

Sean Clarke started his retail career at Asda in 2001 and has since gained extensive international experience working for parent company Walmart in Japan and Canada. His broad background within the Walmart organization has earned him recognition as a rising star capable of handling major transformations.

The leadership change comes as a surprise after outgoing chief executive Andy Clarke indicated last week in an interview that he would be succeeded by Roger Burnley, who is joining Asda from Sainsbury's. Instead, Mr Burnley has been named as Asda's deputy chief executive and chief operating officer. David Cheesewright, president and chief executive of Walmart International, said Mr Burnley was "a top talent and a future CEO."

Andy Clarke has served as Asda's chief executive for six years in an increasingly tough market. It appears he is departing earlier than anticipated. Last month, the retailer said like-for-like sales in the first quarter of the year fell 5.7% in the face of "fierce competition."

Although Andy Clarke moved faster than his main rivals to try to counter the threat of the discounters, Asda has been haemorrhaging sales for the last seven quarters. Mr Clarke promised to narrow the price gap but the discounters are still the cheapest grocers on the high street meanwhile Tesco, Sainsbury's and Morrisons have all upped their game, leaving Asda trailing behind.

Mr Cheesewright said: "Sean is one of our most experienced global executives, and through his leadership we will build upon the momentum of Project Renewal to reposition Asda in a very competitive market place." Project Renewal is a programme designed to overhaul Asda's product range, modernise its 95 largest stores and reduce costs.

Asda is attempting to recoup sales by narrowing the price gap with the discounters and widen its price advantage over its three biggest rivals. All of the four major UK supermarket chains - Tesco, Sainsbury's, Asda and Morrisons - have been engaged in a long-running price war as part of an attempt to slow gains in market share by discounters such as Aldi and Lidl.

Last week, online retailer Amazon launched its fresh grocery service in the UK, adding to competition in the sector.

# Gucci Asks Hong Kong Shops to Stop Selling Knockoff Paper Products for the Dead

Luxury fashion house Gucci has requested several Hong Kong shops to stop selling paper replicas of its products intended to be burned as offerings for the dead, though the company emphasized it would not pursue legal action.

Paper replicas of items like mansions, cars, iPads and luxury bags are burnt in the belief that deceased relatives can use them in the afterlife. Demand for these products is highest during the Qingming "tomb-sweeping" festival, which happened last month.

The shops were sent letters but there was no suggestion of legal action. "We fully respect the funeral context and we trust that the store owners did not have the intention to infringe Gucci's trademark," Gucci Hong Kong said in a statement. "Thus a letter was sent on an informational basis to let these stores know about the products they were carrying, and by asking them to stop selling those items."

## An Ancient Tradition Meets Modern Luxury

The ancient tradition of venerating one's ancestors, even after death, is alive and well in the Chinese speaking world. It is based on the idea that these spirits continue to influence the lives of the living. If you want to avoid bad luck, the belief goes, then you'd better keep your ancestors happy.

How? Traditionally, it was by regularly tending their graves, bringing them fresh fruit and gourmet food and drink and burning joss paper. Also known as "hell money" or "ghost money", they are pieces of paper money in outrageous denominations, which are meant for use in the afterlife.

And these days, devotees can burnish their reputation with their deceased ancestors by offering items that many were never able to enjoy while still alive: luxury cars with European drivers, brand-name clothing. One of the best sellers at these shops are enormous villas complete with swimming pools, multiple car garages and Western domestic helpers.

Gucci has not said which shops or how many had received the letter. In Hong Kong, some of the shops that had reportedly received the letters had removed their Gucci wares. But other brands, including Louis Vuitton, Yves St Laurent, Burberry and New Balance were still on sale.

Hong Kong residents shared a mixture of comedy and scorn on social media. "Does Gucci want to open branches in the underworld?" Vincent Charles asked.

Sammi Ng said on Facebook: "Maybe Gucci should launch their own paper offering products."

Sai Ken made reference to Gucci pricing: "Living people cannot afford (Gucci products), and they still do not let you own Gucci products after death!"

# Bomb Disposal Experts Called to Suffolk Scrap Metal Site

Bomb disposal experts were summoned to a recycling facility in Great Blakenham, Suffolk, after staff discovered three suspicious devices around midday.

The incident occurred at Sackers scrap metal site when vigilant employees spotted the unusual items among materials. Suffolk Police confirmed the bombs, believed to be World War Two-era training devices, contained no explosives and posed no threat to the public.

David Dodds, Sackers' managing director, expressed his astonishment at the discovery. "I was gobsmacked as to why someone would take the bombs to a scrap metal site," he said, praising staff vigilance for the quick identification.

Following established safety protocols, operations were immediately quarantined and police notified. Additional devices were found later that afternoon around 3:00 PM.

Mr Dodds explained the bombs were likely tracer devices used during World War Two pilot training. "They held a very small explosive, so on impact the bomb would let off a puff of smoke so the pilot could see where it landed," he said.

The site has since resumed normal operations.

# Texas Pool Party: Protesters Demand Officer's Dismissal After Video Shows Teen Pinned to Ground

**McKinney, Texas** - Hundreds of protesters marched through a Texas suburb Monday night demanding the dismissal of a white police officer captured on video forcibly restraining a black teenage girl in a bikini during a pool party incident.

The controversial video, filmed Friday in McKinney, shows Corporal David Eric Casebolt pinning 15-year-old Dajerria Becton to the ground with his knees while she screams for her mother. The footage, which runs more than seven minutes, also shows the officer swearing at black youths, pointing his gun at others, and pulling the girl by her arm before restraining her.

Casebolt has been placed on administrative leave while the incident is investigated. He has not publicly commented and remains in hiding, according to US media reports.

The incident began when McKinney police were called to a community swimming pool after several uninvited guests refused to leave. According to a police statement posted on Facebook, a fight broke out, prompting additional emergency calls.

Nearly 800 demonstrators participated in Monday's march through the city of almost 150,000 residents, walking from a local school to the pool while carrying signs reading "My skin colour is not a crime" and "Don't tread on our kids."

Becton told local broadcaster KDFW that she believes more severe consequences are necessary. "Him getting fired isn't enough," she said.

Civil rights leaders in McKinney are calling for a US Justice Department investigation and Casebolt's termination. However, opinion remains divided. Radio host Benet Embry, who witnessed the incident, defended police actions, stating: "That's what they are supposed to do - protect us. I don't know any other way he could have taken her down or established order."

Numerous comments on the police department's Facebook page have also supported the officer's response.

The McKinney incident occurs amid heightened national scrutiny of police interactions with minorities, following deaths of several African Americans in police custody since July 2014, including Michael Brown in Ferguson, Missouri, Eric Garner in New York, Freddie Gray in Baltimore, and Tamir Rice in Cleveland, Ohio.

Police said the video "raised concerns that are being investigated."

# Chinese Billionaire Liang Wengen Set to Join Communist Party Leadership

Construction magnate Liang Wengen, 55, is poised to become the first entrepreneur to join China's Central Committee, marking a historic shift in the Communist Party's relationship with business leaders.

Mr Liang, who topped both Forbes and Hurun rich lists with wealth exceeding $9bn (£6bn), has reportedly completed the vetting process for the 300-strong body that effectively governs China. His approval is expected at the party's 2012 congress in October.

The BBC's Martin Patience in Beijing describes this as "a hugely symbolic shift in the party's view of business." China's Communist Party only began admitting businessmen a decade ago and is now actively courting the nation's wealthy elite.

Mr Liang's company Sany, a leading manufacturer of cranes and excavators, has prospered significantly from China's ongoing construction boom, cementing his position among the country's most influential business figures.

# Board Game Creator Faces FTC Action Over Misused Kickstarter Funds

A board game developer has become the subject of the first Federal Trade Commission enforcement action against crowdfunding misrepresentation after allegedly spending backer money on personal expenses rather than game development.

Erik Chevalier raised more than $122,000 (£79,000) in 2012 through Kickstarter to create a board game called The Doom That Came to Atlantic City. The project originally sought just $35,000 but exceeded expectations due to involvement from well-known game designers and artists.

According to the FTC, despite providing regular updates to backers, Mr Chevalier made little progress on developing the game. The project was abruptly cancelled in mid-2013, with Mr Chevalier citing his inexperience and unspecified "challenges" as reasons for the shutdown.

Investigators found that much of the raised capital was diverted to personal expenses, including rent, personal equipment, and moving costs. The funds reportedly supported Mr Chevalier's relocation to Oregon and helped finance a separate, unrelated project.

Although Mr Chevalier initially promised refunds to backers following the cancellation, the FTC states no money was returned to contributors.

Under the settlement terms, Mr Chevalier is permanently barred from misrepresenting any future crowdfunding campaigns and from withholding refunds. The agreement includes a repayment order of $111,793.71, though this has been suspended due to Mr Chevalier's claimed inability to pay. The full amount would become immediately due if the FTC discovers he possesses greater financial resources than disclosed.

Jessica Rich, director of the FTC's bureau of consumer protection, acknowledged the popularity of crowdfunding platforms like Kickstarter and IndieGogo, noting that many consumers enjoy supporting innovative projects. However, she emphasized: "Consumers should be able to trust their money will actually be spent on the project they funded."

The FTC indicated this action is part of broader oversight efforts regarding emerging financial technologies and consumer protection in digital commerce.

# Council Creates "Wanted" Poster for Fly-Tippers Who Dumped Children's Toys

East Cambridgeshire District Council has taken an unusual approach to tackling illegal dumping by creating a "wanted" poster targeting fly-tippers.

The poster was erected after toys, including a skateboard, bike and buggy, were abandoned on Downham Road in Ely. The sign reads: "Wanted: the person who fly-tipped this waste" as part of the council's mission to "keep our district clean".

Fly-tipping carries serious penalties, with offenders facing fines of up to £50,000 or six-month prison sentences. The council emphasizes the practice is "not only unsightly, inconsiderate, dangerous and expensive to clean up, it is also illegal".

A council spokesperson explained the initiative: "An issue we often have as a local authority is gathering the evidence against those small minority of people who fly-tip. This is why our enforcement officer recently started putting up posters at locations near to where things have been dumped to help get information."

# Ched Evans Rape Conviction Appeal Judgement Reserved

Former Wales international footballer Ched Evans will have to wait until April to learn the outcome of his appeal against his rape conviction.

The 27-year-old striker was jailed in 2012 for raping a 19-year-old woman at a hotel near Rhyl, Denbighshire, and was released in 2014 after serving half of his five-year sentence.

Following a two-day hearing at the Court of Appeal, a panel of three judges reserved their judgement after considering submissions from Evans' legal team and the Crown Prosecution Service.

New evidence was presented during the proceedings, which remain subject to reporting restrictions until the decision is announced.

The court indicated a decision and full reasoning would be delivered "as soon as possible in April".

Since his release from prison, Evans has been unable to secure a contract with any football club, having previously played for Manchester City, Norwich, and Sheffield United.

# Arson Suspected in Belfast House Fire

The Northern Ireland Fire and Rescue Service believes a fire at an unoccupied property on Wyndham Street was started deliberately. Fifteen firefighters responded to the incident on Sunday afternoon.

Assistant Group Commander William Johnston said a neighbouring family was temporarily evacuated whilst crews tackled the blaze. Firefighters successfully prevented the flames from spreading to adjacent properties.

Police are expected to investigate the suspected arson attack.

BBC salary revelations have disclosed that Welsh broadcaster John Humphrys, the host of Mastermind and Today programme, earns between £600,000 and £649,999 annually. 

Several other Welsh stars featured prominently on the corporation's highest earners list. BBC News presenter Huw Edwards, The One Show's Alex Jones, and Radio Wales presenter Jason Mohammad all made the rankings. Rugby analyst Jonathan Davies and journalist Jeremy Bowen each earned over £150,000 yearly.

Former Top Gear presenter Chris Evans dominated the overall list, commanding between £2.2m and £2.25m during the 2016/2017 period, making him the BBC's highest-paid star.

# Scottish League Cup: Rangers Face Motherwell in Revamped Competition

The draw for the revamped Scottish League Cup has produced some intriguing fixtures, with Rangers set to face Motherwell in Group F of the newly-named Betfred Cup.

Cup holders Ross County will take on Raith Rovers, Alloa Athletic, Montrose and Cove Rangers in Group D. The 38 SPFL teams not involved in Europe were included, as well as Cove Rangers from the Highland League and Lowland League side East Stirlingshire.

Teams were drawn into eight groups of five, split into north and south, with the first ties on 16 July.

It will be the first time Motherwell have faced Rangers since the Glasgow outfit, who won the Championship title this season, were denied promotion with a play-off final defeat a year ago. The other sides in Group F are Stranraer, Annan Athletic and East Stirlingshire, who will be involved for the first time as a Lowland League club following their relegation.

Lowland League champions Edinburgh City, who beat Shire in their play-off to win promotion to League Two for the first time, will face Hamilton Academical, St Mirren, Livingston and Ayr United.

Group C features a Fife derby between Dunfermline Athletic and Cowdenbeath, with the other sides being Dundee United, Arbroath and top seeds Inverness Caledonian Thistle.

The revamped competition will result in the group winners and four best runners-up progressing to the second round. European representatives Celtic, Aberdeen, Hearts and Hibernian will also join at that stage. The final will be played at Hampden Park on 27 November.

The first-round groups consist of one top seed, one from the second pot and three unseeded clubs. Each team will play each other once, with games taking place on 16, 20, 23, 27 and 30 July, subject to live TV matches.

Any game ending in a draw will go straight to penalties, with the winner of the penalty shoot-out awarded a bonus point.

Other notable groups include Group A featuring Dundee and Dumbarton, while St Johnstone and Falkirk headline Group B. Partick Thistle face Queen of the South in Group E, and Kilmarnock meet Greenock Morton in Group H.

# New Monitoring Tool to Track Hate Crime Spikes on Social Media After Major Events

Researchers at Cardiff University are developing a sophisticated monitoring tool to help police and government officials combat the surge in hate crimes on social media platforms like Twitter, particularly following significant political events.

The initiative comes in response to alarming statistics showing that hate crime recorded by police in England and Wales jumped 41% in the month following the Brexit referendum vote. Experts have identified "trigger" events, such as last June's referendum result, as catalysts that lead to dramatic spikes in hate-related incidents.

Professor Matthew Williams, from the university's Social Data Science Lab, explained the urgent need for such technology: "The referendum on the UK's future in the European Union has galvanised certain prejudiced opinions held by a minority of people, resulting in a spate of hate crimes."

He added that during the ongoing period of uncertainty surrounding Brexit, "decision makers, particularly those responsible for minimising the risk of social disorder through community reassurance, local policing and online governance, will require near real-time information on the likelihood of escalation of hateful content spread on social media."

The impact has been particularly severe in Wales, where hate crimes increased by 60% during the EU referendum vote period compared with the same timeframe the previous year.

The research team is collecting data over a 12-month period, beginning from 23 June 2016, when the UK voted to leave the European Union. Professor Williams confirmed the lab is collaborating with the UK Head of the Cross-Government Hate Crime Programme at the National Police Chiefs Council.

The university's Social Data Science Lab brings considerable expertise to the project, having previously worked with major law enforcement agencies including the Metropolitan Police, the Ministry of Justice, the Home Office, and the Los Angeles Police Department.

Last July, the UK government published a comprehensive plan to address hate crime in England and Wales, focusing on increasing incident reporting, improving victim support, and reducing the overall scale of the problem.

The funding for this crucial research has been provided by the Economic and Social Research Council, which supports training and study initiatives.

# German University Creates Fake News Site to Test Facebook's Response

Researchers from Hohenheim University in Germany have conducted a revealing experiment that exposed significant vulnerabilities in Facebook's ability to detect and control the spread of fake news on its platform.

The experiment involved setting up four fake profiles on Facebook and creating a bogus news site called "Der Volksbeobachter" – a name deliberately echoing the Nazi propaganda newspaper Völkischer Beobachter (People's Observer). The site even featured an eagle's wings logo reminiscent of Nazi imagery.

## Fake Stories Spread Rapidly

One particularly outrageous false story claimed that a local council was funding free visits to prostitutes for asylum seekers. Despite the absurdity of the claim, the story reached approximately 11,000 people within just four days and was shared more than 150 times, according to German SWR radio.

Many Facebook users reacted with indignation to the fabricated story, with few noticing a critical detail: the location cited in the story, Bad Eulen, does not actually exist.

## The Experimental Method

Professor Wolfgang Schweiger, who led the research team in Stuttgart, designed the experiment to mimic real-world fake news operations. Initially, the researchers spent two weeks posting genuine news stories, but presented them with a far-right editorial slant. They focused on negative coverage of German migration policy and crimes committed by migrants.

To build an audience, the team strategically linked to far-right groups including Alternative for Germany (AfD), Pegida, and the Identitarian Movement. Within two weeks of launching one fake profile, it had attracted 251 Facebook friends.

Additional fabricated stories posted by the site in April included claims that refugees were receiving 50% discounts at German sex shops and that Facebook CEO Mark Zuckerberg had personally apologised to a Syrian refugee falsely accused of rape.

## Troubling Findings

"It was striking that our Facebook profile was never questioned – not by Facebook, that is, the institution itself, nor by other users," Professor Schweiger noted. The fake news blog now displays prominent red warnings labeling it as "fake news," but only after the experiment concluded.

## Growing Concerns in Germany

The experiment comes at a crucial time for Germany, which faces a general election on 24 September. Politicians have warned that Russia might attempt to influence the vote through fake news campaigns, making media manipulation a major national concern.

Facebook, which has an estimated 29 million users in Germany, published full-page advertisements in German newspapers in April advising readers how to identify fake news. The company's tips included checking other reports, verifying evidence, and examining authors' sources.

Facebook is also partnering with Correctiv, a German fact-checking organisation, to combat fake news flagged by users.

## Legal Battles Ahead

However, Facebook has criticised a new German law passed last month that threatens fines up to €50 million (£45 million; $59 million) for social networks failing to delete illegal hate speech or fake news. Facebook argues the threat of substantial penalties would encourage deletion of content "that is not clearly illegal."

Germany's Data Protection Commissioner has supported Facebook's concerns, calling aspects of the new law "vague," particularly regarding powers given to an independent panel that will rule on disputed content.

**Federer Returns from Injury to Claim Victory at Halle**

Roger Federer made a successful return to competitive tennis following a month-long absence due to a back injury that forced him to miss the French Open. The 34-year-old Swiss maestro defeated American Taylor Fritz 6-4 5-7 6-4 in a match that was disrupted by heavy rain and extended into a second day.

The victory was significant for Federer, moving him into a tie with Ivan Lendl for second place on the all-time Open Era wins list with 1,071 victories.

# Treasury Denies Hammond Undermining Brexit Process Amid Cabinet Tensions

Chancellor Philip Hammond has faced accusations from colleagues of attempting to "undermine" Brexit negotiations by delaying key decisions on immigration controls, according to reports in several national newspapers.

However, a Treasury source strongly rejected the claims as "rubbish", while the prime minister's spokeswoman said Mr Hammond's focus remained "on how best to approach" the Brexit negotiations.

The controversy emerged following reports that Mr Hammond was among several voices urging caution at a recent Brexit cabinet committee meeting where new immigration proposals were discussed.

## Visa Regime Proposals

According to the Daily Telegraph, Home Secretary Amber Rudd presented plans for a post-Brexit visa system that would require all EU workers to demonstrate they had secured skilled employment before being permitted entry to the UK.

The newspaper suggested the proposal indicated Britain would leave the single market as part of Brexit - a move Mr Hammond had previously been understood to oppose.

A source quoted by the Telegraph said: "He is arguing from a very Treasury point of view. He is arguing like an accountant seeing the risk of everything rather than the opportunity."

The Telegraph also reported Sunday claims that tensions had escalated to the point where some feared Mr Hammond might resign from his position as chancellor.

Meanwhile, The Times reported that pro-Brexit ministers believed Mr Hammond was "not following Theresa May's instruction that government 'get on' with Brexit".

## Political Reactions

Conservative MP Jacob Rees-Mogg, a Leave campaign supporter, criticized Treasury officials for "negativity" towards Brexit. Speaking on BBC Radio 4's The Westminster Hour, he accused them of "reheating" referendum campaign briefings from former Remain-supporting Chancellor George Osborne.

One Whitehall source told the BBC it was natural for the chancellor to consider the implications of proposals affecting the City of London. However, there was growing consensus that "high-value immigration" beneficial to the financial sector should remain unaffected by Brexit, the source added.

Health Secretary Jeremy Hunt defended the cabinet as "absolutely united" in wanting to reach the right decisions. He told BBC Radio 4's Today programme: "We must go through all the options. This isn't the first time in the history of government where you read reports in the newspapers that may not actually reflect what's happening."

Liberal Democrat Treasury spokeswoman Baroness Kramer criticized the approach of some cabinet members, saying: "You don't have to be an accountant to realise the huge risks of 'hard Brexit' to jobs, wages and our economy. Just because some members of the cabinet wish to hurl us off the economic cliff, doesn't mean everyone else is under some obligation to act like lemmings."

# Council Approval for Compulsory Land Purchase Sparks Concerns in Horley

Reigate and Banstead Borough Council has agreed in principle to use compulsory purchase orders (CPOs) for land off Balcombe Road in Horley, leaving local businesses shocked and worried about their future.

Suresh Mara, manager of Jai Ho restaurant, one of the businesses potentially affected by the development, expressed dismay at the news. "It was a very big shock. We are in a very bad state," he said. Mr Mara said neither he nor his staff were consulted about the plans before Thursday's decision.

"Nobody consulted us and suddenly we are getting this news," he said. "There are 15 or 16 staff whose families will be jeopardised."

The council's executive discussed plans for a business park on the site and expressed willingness to use CPO powers to acquire the land, citing interest from major international businesses wanting to relocate to the area.

However, Green county councillor Jonathan Essex raised environmental concerns, warning that the development would consume green space currently separating Horley from Gatwick Airport. "Horley should be a separate town, not just part of the urban sprawl of Gatwick," he said.

Conservative councillor Natalie Bramhall defended the lack of prior consultation, explaining that information about the plans was "commercially confidential" until the decision was made. She promised future engagement with affected residents, employers and landowners.

"Attracting investment is really important in delivering economic benefits for the borough and jobs for residents," Ms Bramhall said. "We have already had offers from major international businesses that want to move on to this site so we could be providing fantastic jobs for the local residents."

# Murray Ready to Give Everything in French Open Semi-Final Battle

Andy Murray has declared his belief that he can win the French Open as he prepares to face defending champion Stan Wawrinka in Friday's semi-final at Roland Garros.

The 29-year-old British star will take on the Swiss player on Court Philippe Chatrier after 14:00 BST, with a coveted place in Sunday's final just one match away.

"I believe I can win the event. It's possible and only a couple of matches away now," Murray said. "I'll just give everything I've got the next few days."

The semi-final clash represents Murray's fourth appearance in the last four at the French Open, having previously fallen to Rafael Nadal in 2011 and 2014, and to world number one Novak Djokovic in a grueling five-set encounter last year.

Murray faces a challenging task against third seed Wawrinka, who has won their last three encounters, all on clay surfaces. The head-to-head record stands at eight wins for Murray from their 15 previous meetings, but recent history favours the 31-year-old Swiss player.

However, the British number one arrives in Paris with renewed confidence on clay, having defeated Djokovic to claim the Italian Open title in the build-up to Roland Garros.

"Stan is obviously playing great tennis," Murray acknowledged. "It is going to be extremely difficult [but] hopefully I can play my best tennis and reach my first final here."

Wawrinka, who captured the 2015 French Open title and the 2014 Australian Open, remains humble when comparing his career to Murray's, despite both players holding two Grand Slam titles.

"If you were to compare our two careers, he's well ahead of me given all the titles, the finals, number two in the world," Wawrinka said. "He's in the 'Big Four'. His career is very, very impressive."

The statistics support Wawrinka's assessment, with Murray having accumulated 36 career titles compared to the Swiss player's 14.

In the other men's semi-final, Djokovic faces Austria's Dominic Thiem, whilst the women's semi-finals feature Serena Williams against Kiki Bertens and Garbine Muguruza playing Sam Stosur.

# Major Drug Bust in Sydney: Seven Arrested in Record Seizure

Australian authorities have arrested seven people, including four Hong Kong nationals and three Australian residents, following raids in Sydney on Monday that uncovered one of the country's largest drug hauls.

Police seized over half a tonne of illicit drugs, comprising 306kg (674.61lb) of crystal methamphetamine, commonly known as "ice," and 252kg of heroin. The Australian Federal Police (AFP) confirmed this represents the largest seizure of ice and the third largest seizure of heroin in the nation's history.

The drugs have an estimated street value of A$500m (US$526m; £335m), according to the AFP statement.

The operation concluded a year-long investigation that began in August 2011 following intelligence from the US Drug Enforcement Administration. The narcotics were discovered concealed in a shipment of terracotta pots on 19 July.

"Countless lives would have been affected had this seizure made its way to Australian streets," Deputy Commissioner Andrew Colvin told media, adding that investigations remain ongoing with the possibility of further arrests.

The suspects will face drug importation and possession charges in Sydney court.

# Nigel Farage Faces Jeers and Criticism in European Parliament Brexit Debate

UKIP leader Nigel Farage faced a hostile reception in the European Parliament during an emergency debate on Britain's vote to leave the EU, with MEPs jeering and heckling throughout his address.

European Commission President Jean-Claude Juncker directly challenged Mr Farage, asking: "You were fighting for the exit, the British people voted in favour of the exit. Why are you here?" Mr Juncker acknowledged the British vote must be respected but accused the Leave campaign of having "fabricated reality" with some of its claims.

Mr Farage remained defiant, reminding MEPs: "When I came here 17 years ago and said I wanted to lead a campaign to get Britain to leave the European Union, you all laughed at me. Well you're not laughing now."

He called for a "grown up and sensible attitude" to Brexit negotiations but sparked controversy by telling MEPs: "Most of you have never done a proper job in your lives." Parliament President Martin Schulz ruled the comment unacceptable.

The heated exchange saw Mr Schulz criticise heckling MEPs for "acting like UKIP."

Meanwhile, departing UK EU Commissioner Lord Hill received a standing ovation from MEPs after announcing his resignation following the Brexit vote.

The acrimonious debate highlighted the deep divisions and tensions surrounding Britain's historic decision to leave the European Union.

# Police Officers Targeted in Multiple Attacks Across United States

A wave of violence against law enforcement officers swept across the United States on Sunday, leaving one officer dead and several others wounded in what authorities describe as deliberate ambush-style attacks spanning multiple states.

Detective Benjamin Marconi, 50, a twenty-year veteran of the San Antonio Police Department, was killed Sunday morning while writing a traffic ticket outside police headquarters. Authorities say another driver pulled up from behind and fatally shot Marconi as he sat in his patrol car. Police are searching for a male suspect, whose motive remains unclear.

San Antonio Police Chief William McManus said investigators do not believe the gunman knew the motorist who had been pulled over during the initial traffic stop. Texas Governor Greg Abbott condemned the "horrific act of violence."

In St. Louis, Missouri, a 46-year-old police sergeant remains in critical condition after being shot twice while sitting in traffic in a marked police vehicle around 19:30 on Sunday. The married father of three, who has served approximately 20 years with the department, was "ambushed by an individual who pointed a gun at him from inside of his car and shot out the police officer's window," according to Police Chief Sam Dotson. The suspect was later killed in a shootout with police.

Additional attacks occurred in Gladstone, Missouri, near Kansas City, where an officer sustained non-life threatening injuries during a traffic stop that resulted in an exchange of gunfire. The suspect in that incident was fatally shot.

In Sanibel, Florida, a police officer was targeted in a drive-by shooting around 20:00 on Sunday while sitting in his patrol car following a routine traffic stop. The officer received treatment for his injuries and was released, while a suspect was shot and taken into custody.

Sunday's violence recalls the deadly ambushes against police in Texas and Louisiana this past July. In Dallas, a gunman killed five officers in what became the deadliest day for US law enforcement since the September 11 attacks. Days later, three officers were killed in Baton Rouge, Louisiana. Earlier this month, two officers in the Des Moines, Iowa area were also killed in ambush attacks.

The violence underscores a troubling trend: fifty-seven US law enforcement officers have been fatally shot this year, representing a 68% increase compared to the same period in 2015. At least two of Sunday's attacks were confirmed as ambushes, raising concerns about the targeting of police officers nationwide.

# Pigs' Heads Left at Belfast Church Spark Police Investigation

Two pigs' heads discovered at a Belfast church have prompted police to launch an investigation into what they are treating as a "race hate incident."

The disturbing discovery was made at St Luke's Church of Ireland on Northumberland Street on Saturday morning. The incident has been widely condemned by political and religious leaders across Northern Ireland.

According to police reports, anti-Islamic slogans were written on the pigs' heads, making the incident particularly sinister given recent speculation about the building's future use.

The church, which is not currently in use, had been the subject of false social media rumours claiming it had been sold to the Islamic community for conversion into a mosque. However, these claims have been firmly denied by church representatives.

A spokesperson for the Church of Ireland Diocese of Connor clarified: "It is completely untrue that St Luke's has been sold. Any sale would only take place after a process involving the select vestry, diocesan council and representative church body. The highly distasteful act which has taken place is profoundly saddening."

PSNI Assistant Chief Constable Stephen Martin condemned the incident on Twitter, stating: "This is disgusting and must be condemned in the strongest terms. There is no place for race hate." Police have appealed for information from the public.

Political leaders from across the spectrum have united in condemnation of the act. Sinn Féin's Fra McCann noted that the building is used for community events and described the discovery as "gruesome" and "sinister."

DUP assembly member William Humphrey insisted those responsible do not represent the Shankill community, whilst placing partial responsibility on those who spread false rumours about the church's future.

Progressive Unionist Party leader Billy Hutchinson called the incident "absolutely reprehensible," highlighting the dangers of rumour and speculation. He emphasized the need for education to challenge negative attitudes towards people from different backgrounds.

The SDLP's Alex Attwood added: "Hate and intolerance should have no space in our community and those responsible should have no hiding place on our streets."

Police continue to investigate and urge anyone with information to contact them.

# New York Times Corrects 161-Year-Old Error in Solomon Northup Article

The New York Times has issued a correction for a 161-year-old article about Solomon Northup, the subject of the Oscar-winning film "12 Years a Slave."

The original story, published on January 20, 1853, chronicled the kidnapping and enslavement of Northup, a free black man. His name was misspelled twice in the article, appearing as "Northrop" and "Northrup."

The error came to light after a digital copy of the article circulated recently. Rebecca Skloot, author of "The Immortal Life of Henrietta Lacks," drew attention to the mistake by tweeting a link on Monday.

The correction appeared in Tuesday's edition of The New York Times.

The timing coincides with "12 Years a Slave" winning three Academy Awards on Sunday, including Best Picture, Best Adapted Screenplay, and Best Supporting Actress for Lupita Nyong'o.

# Murray Questions Wildcard Decisions as Sharapova Awaits French Open Fate

World number one Andy Murray has questioned the different approaches tennis tournaments take towards awarding wildcards, as Maria Sharapova awaits a decision on whether she will be able to compete at the French Open later this month.

The 30-year-old Russian former world number one needs an invitation to participate in the tournament after her defeat in the Stuttgart Open semi-finals at the weekend. The event marked Sharapova's return to competitive tennis following a 15-month doping ban.

Murray suggested that smaller tournaments have more incentive to award wildcards to high-profile players returning from suspensions than Grand Slam events do.

"Loads and loads of press went there to cover the event - whereas the Slams don't need that coverage," the British player said. "It probably doesn't change their event much either way, so they have a different decision to make."

Sharapova was suspended in 2016 after testing positive for meldonium, a substance added to the banned list that year. The five-time Grand Slam champion has since received wildcards from tournaments in Madrid and Rome for upcoming events.

To qualify automatically for the French Open, Sharapova needed to reach the final in Stuttgart to break into the world's top 200. However, her semi-final loss to Kristina Mladenovic left her ranked at 262, meaning she requires a wildcard to enter either qualifying or the main draw at Roland Garros.

The French tennis federation is expected to announce its decision on 16 May, with the tournament beginning on 28 May.

While Murray acknowledged that the French Open and Wimbledon can "do whatever they want" regarding wildcards, he suggested "there is something to be said for working your way back up" the rankings through regular competition.

However, the 29-year-old Briton was impressed by Sharapova's performance in her comeback tournament. "She's playing at a level where she's capable of winning a tournament like Stuttgart already," Murray said. "To reach the semis in the first tournament back shows that very soon she's going to be back up at the top of the game. It will be a matter of months."

Murray added that he "wouldn't imagine" a player's form would influence a Grand Slam tournament's wildcard decision.

The decision to grant Sharapova wildcards has proven controversial within the tennis community. Canadian player Eugenie Bouchard, the 2014 Wimbledon finalist, branded Sharapova "a cheat" who should not have been allowed to return to professional tennis.

Murray himself is returning from injury, having missed Great Britain's Davis Cup quarter-final defeat to France with an elbow problem. He competed in Monte Carlo before reaching the semi-finals of the Barcelona Open, where he lost to Dominic Thiem.

The world number one will next compete at the Madrid Open, starting Monday, followed by the Italian Open on 15 May as he prepares for the French Open.

Speaking at The Queen's Club, where he will defend his Aegon Championship title next month, Murray discussed his fitness: "My elbow is always sore, so that's nothing to do with the injury - for the last three or four years, it's always been a bit stiff. It was great in Barcelona for the amount of tennis I played."

# NS&I to Cut Premium Bonds Prize Fund as Savings Market Changes
