National Savings and Investments (NS&I) has announced it will reduce the Premium Bonds prize fund, citing the need to balance the interests of savers, taxpayers, and the broader savings sector.

From August, the monthly allocation of £100,000 prizes will drop from five to just three. The overall odds of winning will also decrease, with each £1 Premium Bond number seeing its chances change from 24,000 to one, to 26,000 to one.

Despite the changes, approximately 1.7 million tax-free prizes totalling £49 million will still be distributed monthly, down from the current £57 million. The top prize of £1 million remains unchanged, with other prizes ranging from £25 upwards.

## Market Positioning Drives Decision

NS&I, which is backed by the Treasury, emphasized its responsibility to reflect broader market conditions without becoming overly competitive.

"Rates across the savings market have fallen over recent months, resulting in NS&I savings being increasingly attractive," explained Jane Platt, NS&I chief executive. "In light of our framework to balance the needs of our savers, taxpayers and the stability of the broader financial services sector, we now need to reduce the Premium Bond prize fund rate."

## Premium Bonds Remain Popular

Currently, around £44 billion is invested in Premium Bonds by 21.6 million people. While the number of bondholders has declined by approximately 1.4 million over the past decade, the total amount invested has more than doubled, even excluding inflation.

Premium Bonds work on a unique principle: investors forgo traditional interest payments for the chance to win tax-free prizes in a monthly draw.

## A British Institution

First announced by Harold Macmillan in the 1956 Budget, Premium Bonds were designed to encourage saving and combat inflation. The monthly draw is conducted by Ernie – Electronic Random Number Indicator Equipment – which takes two-and-a-half hours to randomly select winners from a secure location accessible only to a handful of NS&I employees.

In line with modernization efforts, NS&I discontinued over-the-counter Premium Bond sales at Post Offices in April, moving services increasingly online.

The August changes represent a significant adjustment to one of Britain's most recognizable savings products, reflecting the challenging environment facing the savings market.

# Rapist who threatened victim jailed for 12 years

A man who raped a woman and threatened to "bring hell" to her if she reported him to police has been jailed for 12 years.

Lee James Mullen, 28, of Deeside, stuffed a sock in his victim's mouth and wrapped parcel tape around her mouth and head during the attack. He was convicted of rape and sexual assault and was sentenced at Mold Crown Court on Wednesday.

Judge Niclas Parry described it as a sustained attack on the victim, with Mullen out of control through alcohol and cocaine. After raping the woman, he warned her not to call the police, saying that if he went to prison, on his release he would "bring hell to her."

Mullen was found guilty of rape and sexual assault and admitted assault and perverting the course of justice. The judge said he would remain on the sex offenders' register for life.

Following the jury's verdicts, the victim took to the stand to describe the impact of the "horrendous attack" on her. In a statement she read out, she said it had left her with nightmares and in need of sleeping tablets. Her confidence was shaken, she had flashbacks and she had to move away after being assaulted.

She said Mullen knew what he had done but still forced her to endure a trial, adding: "He has got me here to humiliate me."

However, his victim vowed to get her life "back on track" and to not let the attack ruin it. "But I refuse to let him be the end of me," she said. "I will, with the court's help, get my life back on track."

# Nurse Jailed for 19 Years for Raping Three-Year-Old Girl at Party

A nurse who raped a three-year-old girl after being invited to a party at her home has been sentenced to more than 19 years in prison.

George Anderson, 27, repeatedly attacked the child in her bedroom at her mother's home in Torquay, Devon, telling the girl he was a doctor when he entered her room.

Exeter Crown Court heard that Anderson returned to the girl's bedroom seven times throughout the night to abuse her, filming the assaults on his mobile phone. When challenged by the child's mother, he claimed he had gone to check on the girl because she was crying.

Anderson, of no fixed address, admitted 10 charges including rape of a child, two assaults of a child under 13 by penetration, six counts of taking indecent pictures of a child, and one of making indecent pictures of a child.

The court was told that Anderson had downloaded 300 indecent images of children and was "depressed" at the time of the offences, according to defence barrister Paul Dentith.

Sentencing Anderson to a total of 19 years and four months in prison, Mr Justice Dingemans said: "You committed a number of extremely serious assaults on a three-year-old child who was asleep in her bedroom upstairs."

He added that the attacks would have a lifelong effect on the victim.

Anderson had worked as a nurse at Torbay Hospital but has since been dismissed and suspended by the Nursing and Midwifery Council. Devon Partnership NHS Trust Chief Executive Melanie Walker said there was no evidence that people in Anderson's care were at risk during his employment.

In a victim impact statement, the girl's mother said the rape had affected "every aspect" of her life. She said she could not bear to dress or undress her daughter, give her a bath, or take photos of her.

"I feel completely paranoid that anything I do, such as touching her when she is naked will be viewed as inappropriate," she said. "It feels like all the innocence that she once had has now been lost."

The mother added that she did not think she would ever be able to trust another man again.

# Library Cat Jasper Becomes Cambridge University's Purr-fect Stress Reliever

A three-legged ginger cat has become an unlikely hero at Cambridge University, helping stressed students cope with their studies while serving as the official mascot of the Marshall Library of Economics.

Jasper, a five-year-old tom cat, belongs to deputy librarian Simon Frost, who adopted him from a rescue centre after the feline lost his left hind leg in a car accident and was abandoned by his previous owners.

Since being brought to work by Mr Frost, Jasper has become a sensation among students. A recent "tea with Jasper" event drew an impressive 140 cat-lovers, with similar gatherings now planned regularly.

The beloved moggy spends his days at the library browsing shelves and napping on copies of the Financial Times, maintaining impeccable behaviour on university grounds. However, Mr Frost reveals Jasper's more adventurous side at home: "He's bouncy like Tigger, because he has three legs, and he's a bit unstable when he moves slowly - so he goes everywhere at speed."

Librarian Clare Trowell explained Jasper's therapeutic impact: "Students coming to visit and pet Jasper told us just how much he'd calmed them down, and helped relieve any stress. Many of them were missing their own cats or other pets."

Jasper now boasts his own hashtag - #economicscat - and regularly posts library updates on social media. A university "cat club" Facebook group allows pet-missing students to share photos and connect with fellow feline enthusiasts.

# Prison Nurse Banned After Relationship with Inmate at HMP Wealstun

A prison nurse who began an inappropriate relationship with an inmate at a West Yorkshire jail has been banned from practising for 12 months.

Kimberly Hinde, 40, started a relationship with a prisoner while working as a substance misuse nurse at HMP Wealstun, near Wetherby, and continued the contact even after being suspended from her position.

The misconduct came to light in October 2013 when prison security officers discovered evidence during a cell search. Guards found letters indicating a relationship between Hinde and the prisoner, along with a copy of the erotic novel "Fifty Shades of Grey". The inmate had also tattooed Hinde's first name on his arm in code.

Following her suspension in November 2013, Hinde persisted in maintaining contact with the prisoner, writing letters and making phone calls using various aliases. She was subsequently arrested in December 2013 on suspicion of misconduct in a public office.

At Leeds Crown Court in November 2015, Hinde pleaded guilty to the offence. She received a nine-month prison sentence, suspended for two years, and was ordered to complete 200 hours of unpaid work.

The Nursing and Midwifery Council (NMC) panel, which imposed the 12-month ban, stated that "a conviction of this nature strikes at the heart of the nurse and patient relationship, undermines the trust and confidence the public place in nurses and brings the profession into disrepute."

During the hearing, Hinde admitted her wrongdoing, stating: "I accept that I should have removed contact between myself and this prisoner sooner when I realised that we were becoming close."

# Calais 'Jungle' Camp Faces Demolition as Tensions Rise

**CALAIS, FRANCE** — French authorities are preparing to dismantle the notorious migrant camp known as the "Jungle," with thousands of leaflets set to be distributed warning residents they must vacate before bulldozers move in. The announcement comes as tensions escalate, with police firing smoke grenades on Saturday to restore order after clashes with migrants.

The sprawling camp, estimated to house as many as 10,000 people, has become a symbol of Europe's ongoing migration crisis. Most residents will be resettled in reception centres across France starting Monday, according to French officials.

Violence erupted over the weekend when approximately 50 migrants reportedly threw stones at French police, who responded with tear gas and baton charges. The incident highlights growing frustrations as the camp's closure date approaches.

About 10,000 leaflets will be distributed by French authorities instructing residents to report to a designated hangar beginning Sunday morning. From there, buses will transport them to other parts of France, where they will have the opportunity to claim asylum.

However, charity organizations express concern that many migrants may refuse relocation. L'Auberge des Migrants, a French association, estimates up to 2,000 of the camp's 10,000 residents may decline to leave, preferring to remain in Calais in hopes of eventually reaching the United Kingdom.

"The authorities say they do not want to use force, but if there are migrants who refuse to leave the camp, they may have to intervene," officials stated.

Meanwhile, progress has been made in relocating vulnerable populations. The first unaccompanied children without family ties to the UK arrived in Britain under the "Dubs amendment" rules, which prioritize particularly vulnerable minors, including girls and children under 13. This follows Monday's arrival of 39 boys who had UK relatives.

Citizens UK volunteer Esmat Jeraj described the children as understandably traumatized. "Some of them are quite reluctant to talk about their experiences," she said. "They've obviously been through hell and back."

The BBC's Simon Jones, reporting from Calais, notes that amid the camp's mud and squalor, there is growing realization among residents that their time there is ending.

The Jungle has been characterized by squalid conditions and violence, as migrants—mainly from Africa and the Middle East—attempt to board UK-bound lorries, often clashing with drivers and police.

In response to ongoing security concerns, a UK-funded wall measuring 1 kilometer (0.6 miles) is under construction along the main road to the port. The UK government reportedly contributed approximately £1.9 million (€2.2 million) to the project, which began last week and is scheduled for completion by year's end.

The wall aims to deter would-be stowaways from attempting dangerous crossings, though critics question whether physical barriers address the underlying humanitarian crisis.

# Actress Daniele Watts Detained After Refusing to Show ID to LAPD Officers

Actress Daniele Watts, known for her role in Quentin Tarantino's Oscar-winning film "Django Unchained," was briefly detained by Los Angeles police last week after refusing to provide identification to officers investigating a report of lewd conduct.

The incident began when police responded to a complaint from a passer-by who reported seeing a couple engaged in indecent exposure inside a silver Mercedes. When officers arrived at the scene, Watts refused to show identification and walked away from the responding officers.

According to a police statement released over the weekend, Watts was subsequently placed in handcuffs. She later posted a photo on social media showing herself in tears with her hands restrained behind her back. Her boyfriend, chef Brian James Lucas, was not handcuffed during the encounter.

In an interview with CNN on Monday, Watts insisted she and Lucas had been "making out" in the car but were fully clothed, denying any improper behavior had occurred. Audio footage of the encounter obtained by TMZ suggests Watts alleged the police were called because she was black and her boyfriend was white.

The recording captures an officer questioning why she had played "the race card" and explaining his authority to request identification. An LAPD spokesman confirmed that US citizens are required to identify themselves when requested by an officer with reasonable suspicion of a potential offense.

Watts, who also had a recurring role in the television series "Weeds," later told the Associated Press, "I can understand how people would say that I'm being a drama queen. [But] I don't believe I committed any crime where I deserved to be in handcuffs."

# Fatal Bus Crash in Pakistan Kills Dozens

A devastating collision between a passenger bus and a goods vehicle near Khairpur in Sindh province has claimed multiple lives, Pakistani officials report.

The bus was making an overnight journey from Swat in north-western Pakistan to the southern port city of Karachi when the accident occurred early Tuesday morning. According to the BBC's Shahzeb Jillani in Islamabad, the majority of victims were women and children.

At least 15 people sustained injuries, some critical, and have been hospitalized. Medical Superintendent Ghulam Jaffar Soomro of Khairpur district hospital told Geo TV that evidence suggests the bus was travelling at high speed before overturning.

Police confirmed 65 passengers were aboard the bus. Authorities believe dense morning fog blanketing the highway may have contributed to the head-on collision.

Such fatal accidents are unfortunately common across Pakistan's roads, typically attributed to reckless driving, poorly maintained road surfaces, and unsuitable vehicles.

# EU Referendum: Voter Registration Deadline Extended After Website Crash

The deadline for registering to vote in the EU referendum has been extended by two days after the government's registration website crashed just hours before the original cut-off time on Tuesday.

Emergency legislation was rushed through Parliament to allow voters to register until 23:59 BST on Thursday, covering all regions except Northern Ireland, where the online system was not in operation. The referendum on Britain's membership of the European Union is scheduled for 23 June.

However, the extension has sparked controversy, with prominent Leave campaigner Arron Banks indicating he may pursue legal action against the decision. The Leave.EU founder described the move as "unconstitutional" and said his lawyers were examining potential grounds for a judicial review.

"Once you've set the rules you can't really change it halfway through, and Parliament really shouldn't be doing this," Mr Banks told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.

Cabinet Office minister Oliver Letwin explained that the website experienced unprecedented demand in the hour before the crash, with 214,000 registration applications received. He told MPs that Tuesday's surge was "three times as intense a spike as occurred before the general election."

The extension proved highly popular, with 242,000 applications submitted on Wednesday alone - the second highest daily total since a registration campaign launched in mid-May. A further 195,000 applications were received on Thursday, bringing the two-day total to 437,000.

Notably, younger voters dominated the registration figures, with 135,600 of Wednesday's applicants aged under 35. Across both days, 77% of applications came from people under 45.

The demographic breakdown has fuelled concerns among Leave supporters, who believe younger voters are more likely to support remaining in the EU. BBC political correspondent Ross Hawkins reported that many Leave campaigners view the extension as a "fix" designed to benefit the Remain campaign.

The official Vote Leave campaign, which operates separately from Mr Banks's Leave.EU organisation, accused the government of attempting to register as many likely Remain voters as possible, though it stopped short of threatening legal action.

Mr Letwin defended the extension, stating that it would have required a spike "six times as large" to cause another system failure.

# Maria Sharapova Granted Wildcard for Birmingham Tennis Tournament Despite Controversy

Five-time Grand Slam champion Maria Sharapova has been awarded a wildcard entry to compete at the Aegon Classic in Birmingham this June, despite having recently completed a 15-month ban for a doping violation. The decision by the Lawn Tennis Association (LTA) has sparked debate within the tennis community.

The 30-year-old Russian tennis star, who has fallen significantly down the world rankings during her absence from the sport, will not receive an appearance fee for the tournament. LTA chief executive Michael Downey acknowledged the controversial nature of the decision in a statement to staff and senior figures in British tennis.

"This wasn't a decision we took lightly and not everyone will agree with it," Downey said. "Some may question the moral compass of this decision. We do not."

Sharapova received her ban after testing positive for meldonium, a heart disease medication, at the 2016 Australian Open. However, the Court of Arbitration for Sport determined she was not an "intentional doper" when reducing her initial suspension.

The wildcard decision has divided opinion in the tennis world. Men's world number one Andy Murray and several female players have previously stated that athletes returning from drugs bans should not be granted wildcard entries to tournaments.

In his letter to LTA stakeholders, Downey provided a robust defence of the decision: "She made a mistake that we do not condone. She has paid the price through her 15-month ban and now can return to action. We did not take this decision lightly, but - like all other WTA events before ours - have granted her a wildcard so our Birmingham event can benefit British fans who can take in her matches on home soil."

Sharapova, who previously won the Birmingham title in both 2004 and 2005, expressed enthusiasm about her return. "I am really excited to be coming back to Birmingham this year to play on the grass as part of my build-up to Wimbledon and I thank the LTA for this opportunity," she said.

The tournament will feature an impressive field, including British number one Johanna Konta, world number one Angelique Kerber, and other top players such as Garbine Muguruza, Agnieszka Radwanska, and Simona Halep.

BBC tennis correspondent Russell Fuller noted the commercial considerations behind the decision: "From a commercial point of view, this is good business. Sharapova has also signed up for next year without the LTA having to pay appearance fees."

However, Fuller also highlighted the controversy, contrasting the LTA's decision with that of the French Tennis Federation, which chose not to invite Sharapova to Roland Garros, stating it would undermine their anti-doping message.

The decision means another player, possibly British, will miss out on a tournament place. Naomi Broady, who has spent much of the past year in the top 100, was mentioned as a potential beneficiary had the wildcard not been awarded to Sharapova.

The Birmingham event faces stiff competition for attention, running the same week as the ATP tournament at Queen's Club, making Sharapova's star power particularly attractive to organisers hoping to boost ticket sales.

# Suspicious Device Found Behind Bushes in Strabane Estate

A suspicious object discovered behind bushes in the Ballycolman estate on Wednesday has been removed by police for examination.

Detective Inspector Andy Workman condemned the incident, stating: "It is reckless in the extreme to leave such an item in an area near to a community centre which is frequented by all members of the community, including children."

He confirmed the danger has been eliminated and urged anyone with information to come forward.

Meanwhile, in a related incident, police recovered several suspicious objects during a search of open ground at Spout Road in Strabane. These items have also been taken for forensic examination, though authorities have not released further details at this time.

# Polish and German Border Blocks Delay Pro-Kremlin Biker Group's WWII Commemoration Ride

A controversial pro-Kremlin motorcycle group, the Night Wolves, has been prevented from completing its planned journey from Moscow to Berlin after facing border rejections from both Poland and Germany.

The group, which is subject to US sanctions for alleged involvement in Crimea, had intended to ride 6,000km (3,720 miles) following the Red Army's World War Two route. They aimed to reach Berlin in time for Victory Day celebrations in Moscow on Saturday.

Poland initially barred the bikers' entry at its border with Belarus, citing their plans as "provocative." More than 10,000 Poles had protested on Facebook against allowing the Night Wolves into the country. The group's vocal support for Russian President Vladimir Putin's backing of separatist rebels in eastern Ukraine proved particularly controversial in Poland.

Germany's federal police subsequently refused entry over security concerns, though a Berlin court later ruled on Wednesday that insufficient evidence existed to prove they posed a threat to public order, domestic security, or international relations.

Night Wolves leader Aleksandr Zaldostanov criticized Germany's initial decision as "political," telling Russian media the refusal was motivated by politics rather than legitimate security concerns.

The bikers are accused of actively recruiting separatist fighters for Russian-backed rebels in eastern Ukraine's ongoing conflict with the Ukrainian government.

Of the dozens of motorcyclists who departed Moscow on April 25, mainly riding Harley-Davidsons, it remains unclear how many have successfully reached Germany or what alternative routes they may have taken. Their original itinerary included Belarus, Poland, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, and Austria before reaching Berlin.

# Family Raises £425,000 for Boy's Cancer Treatment

A seven-year-old boy with an incurable brain tumour is undergoing pioneering treatment after his family raised hundreds of thousands of pounds.

Ollie Gardiner, from Aston Clinton, Buckinghamshire, was diagnosed in May 2015 and went through 10 cycles of chemotherapy and 34 sessions of radiotherapy before the cancer came back in September 2016.

Doctors said the tumour was "incurable", but the family decided to try and raise money to pay for a new type of treatment.

So far £425,000 has been raised, but the family still needs £15,000 to reach their target.

Ollie and his father, Peter Gardiner, spoke to BBC Three Counties Radio about the fundraising and pioneering treatment.

Peter said: "We're being treated in London on an outpatient basis, which is wonderful because Ollie can be with his friends and can go to school. Maintaining some normality is so important in cancer treatment.

"Friends, family, the wider community and people we don't even know are giving up masses of their free time just to help us, it's an incredible feeling.

"The support has been absolutely fantastic."

Speaking of the treatment he began in October last year, Ollie said: "It's been tough, but it's OK."

# Detective Pikachu Movie in Development Following Pokemon Go Success

A new Pokemon film is in development, focusing on Detective Pikachu, a character recently introduced through a Japanese video game earlier this year.

The announcement comes on the heels of Pokemon Go's massive international success, which has captivated audiences worldwide in recent weeks. The mobile game's extraordinary popularity resulted in a significant 25% increase in shares for Nintendo, which holds partial ownership of the Pokemon brand.

Pokemon first emerged as a video game in 1996, subsequently spawning an animated television series, film franchise, and extensive merchandise including trading cards that became wildly popular in UK schools during the early 2000s.

Legendary Entertainment, the production company behind the project, has previous experience adapting video games for cinema, recently releasing Warcraft, based on World of Warcraft. The media giant's impressive portfolio also includes blockbusters such as Jurassic World, The Dark Knight Rises, and Godzilla.

Follow us on Twitter @BBCNewsEnts, on Instagram, or email entertainment.news@bbc.co.uk.

# Last-Minute Bid Emerges for Struggling BHS as Liquidation Looms

A late bid to rescue department store chain BHS has emerged, led by Greg Tufnell, brother of former England cricketer Phil Tufnell, through his newly formed investment vehicle Richess Group.

The unexpected offer has delayed what administrators hoped would be a swift resolution to find a buyer for the troubled retailer. Other potential bidders, including Matalan founder John Hargreaves, are understood to have withdrawn from the race.

According to sources close to the situation, Friday represents a critical deadline. If no acceptable buyer is secured by then, BHS faces liquidation, threatening the jobs of approximately 11,000 employees across its store network.

The Telegraph has reported that Richess Group is believed to have backing from a wealthy Portuguese family. Tufnell brings considerable retail credentials to the bid, having served as managing director of Mothercare from 1997 to 2000, and holding a similar position at Burton, part of the Arcadia Group, for three years prior. He currently serves as a director of House of Britannia, an investment firm whose portfolio includes prestigious brands such as glovemaker Cornella James, supplier to the Queen.

Tufnell is collaborating with Nick De Scossa, a former investment banker and ex-chief executive of Bristol rugby club, on the rescue attempt.

The bid comes amid ongoing parliamentary scrutiny of BHS's collapse. On Wednesday, MPs from the Business and Work and Pensions select committees are scheduled to question advisers to Retail Acquisitions, which purchased BHS from Sir Philip Green for just £1 last year, along with pension fund trustees.

In Monday's hearing, Goldman Sachs banker Anthony Gutman revealed he had warned Arcadia finance director Paul Budge about Dominic Chappell's bankruptcy history and lack of retail experience before the sale was completed.

# Search Ends for Kayaker Missing in River Since March

Police have called off the search for a man who went missing after his kayak capsized on a river.

Grant Broster, 56, from Guildford, was on his family's kayak on 28 March when it capsized in front of his son. Police said an extensive search of a wide section of the river had taken place over a number of days but Mr Broster had not been found.

Ch Insp Dave Mason said a decision had been taken to end the search. He said information from the agencies involved in the search effort and detailed options had been exhausted.

"This was obviously a very difficult decision and one which we have not taken lightly," he said.

He added that search teams had done everything possible to find Mr Broster, using helicopters, drones, sonar, dogs and divers.

Mr Broster's family have been raising funds for the volunteers who carried out the search and have so far raised £5,623.

# Poets to Be Inspired by Cambridge University's Historic Treasures

Ten of Britain's leading poets are set to find inspiration among some of the world's most remarkable historical artifacts and scientific collections at Cambridge University in an ambitious new literary project.

The initiative, known as Thresholds, will see acclaimed poets including Daljit Nagra, Don Paterson, and Jo Shapcott taking up residencies across various Cambridge University collections and museums. Poet Laureate Carol Ann Duffy, who selected the participants, has described the venture as "an unprecedented initiative."

The collections available to the poets contain extraordinary items of historical and scientific significance. These include Captain Scott's poignant farewell letter to his wife, housed at the Polar Museum, Charles Darwin's zoological specimens at the Museum of Zoology, and Isaac Newton's personal copy of Principia Mathematica at Cambridge University Library.

Each poet will spend two weeks in residence between January and March, during which they will meet with researchers and explore their assigned collections in depth. Following this immersive experience, they will compose a poem inspired by what they have discovered.

"This is a stunning level of commitment to poetry and poets," Duffy said. "These 10 residencies will create a unique collaboration of poets, creating a meeting of minds and disciplines and providing a catalyst for ideas."

Duffy emphasized the caliber of participants, stating: "These 10 poets represent the best of poetry being written at the moment. I wanted to include up-and-coming poets and older poets, as well as representing different cultures and countries, too."

She added that all ten poets were her first choices and accepted immediately without persuasion, calling the project "unheard of" in terms of size and scale.

The complete list of poets and their residencies includes Sean Borodale, Gillian Clarke, Imtiaz Dharker, Ann Gray, Matthew Hollis, Jackie Kay, Daljit Nagra, Don Paterson, Jo Shapcott, and Owen Sheers, each matched with different Cambridge institutions.

Supported by Arts Council England, Thresholds will be officially launched by Duffy on Friday night at the Fitzwilliam Museum as part of the University's Festival of Ideas. An anthology featuring all the newly commissioned poems will be published in March 2013.

# Welsh Government Criticised Over Circuit of Wales Payments

Welsh Conservative leader Andrew RT Davies has raised concerns about payments totalling nearly £1 million made to a consultancy firm owned by Circuit of Wales backer Michael Carrick, questioning whether the project developers were effectively "paying themselves" for advice.

The controversy surrounds the ambitious Circuit of Wales motor racing project in Ebbw Vale, which promises to create up to 6,000 jobs in Blaenau Gwent, one of south Wales's most economically challenged areas. The development plans include a motor racing track, hotels, and industrial units.

During First Minister's Questions on Tuesday, Mr Davies highlighted internal correspondence obtained through Freedom of Information requests that revealed concerns from senior civil servants about the financial arrangements. In an email, civil servant James Price stated that "it appears that our loan guarantee will facilitate a very substantial payment from one company in which Michael Carrick has a significant interest (HOVDC) to another wholly under his control."

Mr Price's email continued: "Consequently I have been resisting allowing these payments to be funded from the guaranteed loan."

The payments in question went to Aventa, Mr Carrick's consultancy firm, for services provided to the Heads of the Valleys Development Company (HOVDC), which is behind the Circuit of Wales project.

Mr Davies questioned why ministers would approve such transactions against civil service advice, particularly when there appeared to be no robust tendering process. "That clearly cannot be right, especially if there hasn't been a robust tendering process and indeed when the civil servants themselves, the director general, is offering such advice to ministers," he said.

First Minister Carwyn Jones defended the Welsh Government's support for project development, though he noted that decisions on specific financial arrangements were made by former Economy Minister Edwina Hart, who is no longer a member of the assembly. He pledged that the government would "seek to ensure that there is prudence in terms of money that's accessed from the public purse."

The Circuit of Wales project has been seeking financial backing for several years, with insurers Aviva named as likely backers. However, HOVDC has been in negotiations with ministers over the taxpayer shouldering some of the project's risk.

In April, Mrs Hart rejected a request for the taxpayer to underwrite the entire project. Her successor, Economy Secretary Ken Skates, stated in July that he wanted the firm to find at least 50% of the budget and underwriting from private sources.

Mr Davies also raised concerns about £9m paid in bank loan guarantees, though he acknowledged the project offered "great opportunity" if executed properly.

Mr Jones responded by accusing Mr Davies of wanting to "have his cake and eat it," arguing that initial public financing was necessary to help businesses reach the next stage of development. However, he emphasised there comes a point where any business must find sufficient private backing rather than relying on "100% guarantee from the taxpayer."

# Giant Airbus A350 Lands at Small Scottish Airport for Training

An Airbus A350, capable of carrying up to 440 passengers, made an unexpected appearance at Stornoway Airport on the Isle of Lewis on Wednesday, arriving from Toulouse, France.

The crew traveled to the remote Scottish island specifically to conduct cross-wind training in the challenging weather conditions frequently experienced there, according to BBC Scotland. Stornoway typically handles much smaller passenger aircraft, making the large jet's presence particularly notable.

The unusual sight sparked humorous speculation on social media that US president-elect Donald Trump might be aboard, given his mother's Lewis heritage.

The flight crew performed "touch-and-go" exercises, making multiple approaches to the runway without fully landing—a standard training procedure.

A spokesperson for Highlands and Islands Airports Limited (Hial), which operates Stornoway Airport, confirmed the training was routine, stating: "Similar training exercises have taken place at Stornoway in the past for a range of aircraft."

The Airbus A350, which made its maiden flight in 2013, is one of the manufacturer's flagship wide-body aircraft, designed for long-haul routes.

# Japanese Crisp Makers Suspend Sales After Devastating Potato Harvest

Japan's leading snack food manufacturers are suspending sales of dozens of crisp products following the country's worst potato harvest in more than three decades.

Both Calbee and Koike-Ya have announced they are halting shipments of 49 potato crisp products after severe weather devastated crops in Hokkaido, Japan's primary potato-growing region. Typhoons and floods struck the area last year, creating a significant shortage of the vegetable.

Calbee, which controls over half of Japan's snack food market, attempted to address the shortfall by increasing potato imports from the United States, but these efforts proved insufficient to meet consumer demand. The company's shares fell more than 1% to a two-month low on Tuesday.

Koike-Ya, Japan's second-largest snack manufacturer, saw its shares drop 3.5% on Tuesday. Neither company would comment on the potential impact on upcoming earnings.

The shortage has pushed retail potato prices sharply higher, with increases of nearly 20% every month since October, according to Japan's Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications. In Tokyo, one kilogram of potatoes now costs 402 yen (£2.95; $3.60), compared with 336 yen during the same period last year.

The agriculture ministry, which has tracked harvest data since 1983, confirmed this marks the worst potato harvest in at least 34 years.

# Bomb Attack Strikes Passenger Bus in Peshawar Ahead of Pakistan Elections

PESHAWAR, Pakistan - A suicide bomber detonated explosives on a busy road in Peshawar, striking a passenger bus after passing a police vehicle, according to media reports. The attack is the latest in a surge of violence targeting Pakistan's electoral process ahead of the May 11 elections.

The bombing comes just a day after Taliban attacks on campaign offices killed at least eight people and injured 23 others on Sunday. The militant group has pledged to continue targeting political parties it considers secular.

Television footage captured the aftermath, showing the mangled bus and motorcycle debris scattered across the scene. Emergency responders transported the wounded to local hospitals.

In a separate incident, a bomb exploded near the home of an Awami National Party (ANP) candidate in Mardan, damaging his compound's wall. No organization has yet claimed responsibility for the Peshawar attack.

The wave of violence has overshadowed what should be a historic moment for Pakistan - the first democratic transition between civilian governments in the nation's history. Correspondents note that the escalating attacks have cast a shadow over the landmark election campaign.

# Police Raid Multiple Properties in Major Human Trafficking Operation

More than 100 police officers conducted simultaneous raids across six cities in a major operation targeting suspected human trafficking and sexual exploitation.

Properties in Nantwich, Crewe, London, Bristol, Stoke and Preston were searched as part of the coordinated effort, according to Cheshire Police. Eight women, believed to be originally from Eastern Europe, were discovered at several of the locations.

Two individuals were arrested in connection with the investigation: a 49-year-old man from Nantwich and a 37-year-old woman from Crewe. Both remain in custody for questioning on suspicion of human trafficking for sexual exploitation purposes.

The operation involved multiple law enforcement agencies, including the Metropolitan Police, Avon and Somerset Police, Staffordshire Police, Lancashire Police, and the National Crime Agency.

Detective Inspector David Brown, leading the operation for Cheshire Police, stated the warrants followed "months of hard work" as part of a broader inquiry. He emphasized that human trafficking and sexual exploitation represent "organised crime" targeting "some of the most vulnerable people in our society."

The women found during the raids are receiving support services.

# Man Cleared of Murder After Fatal Crossbow Shooting in Domestic Dispute

A Cornwall man has been found not guilty of murder and manslaughter after fatally shooting his brother-in-law with a crossbow during a domestic dispute.

Daniel Schofield, 29, was acquitted following a week-long trial at Truro Crown Court. The incident occurred in October last year at a property in Trevallack, outside St Keverne, near Helston, Cornwall, resulting in the death of Roy Hanson, 50.

Throughout the trial, Mr Schofield maintained that Mr Hanson's death was a tragic accident. Police and paramedics were called to the property where they found Mr Hanson with fatal injuries. Despite medical treatment at the scene, the plumber from St Keverne could not be saved.

The court heard that Mr Hanson, who was married to Mr Schofield's sister Julia Hanson, had been violent towards her, prompting her to leave him and stay with her brother. On 25 October, Mr Hanson arrived at Mr Schofield's farm on the Lizard peninsula.

According to evidence presented, Mr Hanson was shot with the crossbow while attacking Mrs Hanson. Mr Schofield told the court he had loaded the weapon hoping to intimidate Mr Hanson into leaving. Under questioning by defence counsel Richard Smith QC, Mr Schofield stated he had no intention of firing when he loaded the crossbow.

The weapon discharged, sending a bolt through Mr Hanson's chest, piercing his heart and a major blood vessel before exiting through his back. Jurors were shown the blood-soaked bolt and the crossbow used in the incident.

In a statement, Mr Hanson's family said: "Roy was a loving, devoted and loyal family man and would have done anything for anyone. How he has been portrayed is not his true character."

After deliberating for nearly five hours, the jury cleared Mr Schofield of all charges.

# Man Dies After Bull Goring at Spanish Festival

A man was fatally gored by a bull at a festival in Coria, Spain, despite standing behind what was supposed to be a protective barrier.

The incident occurred on Wednesday when the bull unexpectedly charged at the man, who was positioned behind a fence at the bullring. In a tragic turn, one of the animal's horns penetrated between the barrier bars, piercing the victim's abdomen and chest.

The man, a resident of a nearby village, was immediately evacuated from the scene and rushed to hospital for emergency medical treatment. However, he died from his injuries.

Bull-running festivals remain popular throughout Spain, though they face increasing criticism over safety concerns from both critics and enthusiasts alike. Video footage of the fatal goring has circulated on multiple Spanish news platforms.

This marks Coria's first bull-related fatality since 2007, according to Spanish news outlet hoy.

# Northern Ireland Human Trafficking Bill Aims to Lead UK Legislation

**A proposed bill in Northern Ireland could make the region a leader in UK human trafficking law while criminalizing the purchase of sexual services.**

The Human Trafficking and Exploitation Bill, put forward by the Democratic Unionist Party's Lord Morrow, is currently under public consultation until 18 October. If passed, the legislation would significantly strengthen protections for trafficking victims while making it illegal to pay for sex from prostitutes.

Currently, buying or selling sex is legal throughout the UK, though related activities such as kerb crawling, operating brothels, and pimping remain criminal offences. Lord Morrow emphasized that while paying for sex from someone who has been coerced is already illegal in Northern Ireland, stronger measures are needed.

"The majority of rescued victims of trafficking in Northern Ireland are those brought here for sexual exploitation and I believe that we can do better," Lord Morrow stated. He pointed to Sweden's zero-tolerance approach to purchasing sex as a successful model that has clearly impacted trafficking rates.

The comprehensive bill includes several key provisions beyond criminalizing the purchase of sexual services. It would expand the definition of exploitation to include forced begging and establish clear definitions for trafficking victims. The legislation proposes streamlined compensation procedures and allows courts to consider aggravating factors during sentencing.

Child protection measures feature prominently, including the provision of legal advocates to guide child victims through criminal proceedings, immigration matters, and compensation claims. The bill also ensures special measures for trafficking victims serving as witnesses and prohibits prosecution of victims for crimes committed as a direct result of being trafficked.

Additional provisions call for mandatory training for police and prosecutors, and require the Department of Justice to produce annual strategies for raising awareness and reducing trafficking.

The proposal comes as the Republic of Ireland conducts its own public consultation on prostitution legislation, scheduled for committee review later this month. Irish Justice Minister Alan Shatter acknowledged the consensus on combating child prostitution and sex trafficking, while noting "differing and genuinely held views" exist regarding the broader legal treatment of prostitution.

The Northern Ireland bill represents a potentially significant shift in UK trafficking legislation and victim support services.

**McIlroy Offers Masters Advice to Scottish Teen Neil Ahead of Augusta Debut**

Scottish amateur golfer Jack Neil received some invaluable guidance from Rory McIlroy during a practice round at Augusta National ahead of his Masters debut this week. The 19-year-old revealed that the Northern Irish star advised him against rushing into the professional ranks, despite believing his game is already good enough to compete at the highest level.

"He said to me there's no rush," revealed Neil, who admits he may turn professional before September's Walker Cup. "He said my game is good enough to come out here and do well, so there's no rush and just wait until I feel comfortable."

The pair had arranged the practice round after meeting at last year's Ryder Cup, with their paths crossing again recently as Neil experienced his first taste of practising at Augusta ahead of the prestigious tournament.

Neil revealed that their conversation ranged beyond golf, discussing "girls and football" between shots. In a humorous twist, the Scottish teenager once again demonstrated his skill on the par-five second hole, much to McIlroy's amusement.

"I holed out from about 90 yards and he couldn't stop laughing because the day we met here I did the exact same thing and he was on the third tee," said Neil. "I'll remember that round for a long time to come."

The reigning Amateur Championship winner, who claimed his title at Royal Portrush last year, expressed his appreciation for the unique experience of playing alongside one of golf's biggest stars.

"Just getting the chance to play here is memorable, but to get to play with Rory McIlroy just adds to the experience," Neil said. "Rory always gets a crowd and the fact that I got to taste that was great. I doubt I'll play in front of a crowd like that during the rest of the week. It's going to be easier now."

Neil praised McIlroy's approachable nature, saying: "He's a really nice guy and made me feel really comfortable. He's only six years older than me, but if I was to even get to where he's at in 15 years, I'd be happy."

Meanwhile, fellow Scot Stephen Gallacher, who finished tied for 34th on his own Masters debut last year, offered his own words of wisdom to his young compatriot. The 40-year-old, who qualified through being in the top 50 of the world rankings, emphasized the importance of staying relaxed.

"Just to keep a smile on his face," Gallacher advised. "No matter what happens, just play with no stress. Just go round, take it all in and hopefully, when he comes back as a pro, he'll be better off for it."

Gallacher reflected on his own learning experience from last year, noting: "There are certain things I did wrong last year and you learn not to get too aggressive at certain times. There's holes where you've just got to get your fours and get pars and have a go at the fives."

Mirroring his preparations from 2014, Gallacher played a practice round with Miguel Angel Jimenez and former Masters champion Jose Maria Olazabal, praising the Spaniard's strategic approach to the course.

"The course is in awesome condition," Gallacher concluded. "You've just got to hit it in the right spots."

# 300 Jobs to be Created by Intelling Limited in Northern Ireland

Intelling Limited, a customer services support provider for major companies including TalkTalk and O2, has announced the creation of 300 new jobs in Northern Ireland.

The posts will be established over the next three years, offering average annual salaries of £16,000. The company has already filled 45 positions, with Invest NI contributing £1 million towards the project.

Enterprise Minister Jonathan Bell welcomed the investment as "positive news" for the local economy, praising Intelling as "an ambitious, young company."

"It creates much-needed jobs that offer flexible employment and the opportunity to develop transferable skills," Mr Bell said.

Phil Morgan, chief executive of Intelling Ltd, explained the decision: "The availability of talent here and cost competitive environment, along with Invest NI support, made Northern Ireland the best choice for Intelling over alternative locations."

# Antony Gormley Sculpture Finds Permanent Home on Scottish Coast

A life-sized sculpture by renowned artist Antony Gormley will remain permanently on the Kintyre coast after being purchased by an anonymous donor for the Landmark Trust.

The abstract human form looks out over the Kilbrannan Sound to Arran from the rocks below Saddell Castle in Kintyre. Gormley, who is most famous for the Angel of the North, made the sculpture in 2015 to celebrate 50 years of the Landmark Trust. It was one of five placed at trust properties around the UK.

The life-sized figures, together known as Land, were originally to have remained in place until May 2016. The other four were removed as planned last year. They have been returned to the artist who will use them for future projects.

The Kintyre sculpture, called Grip, is the only one to get a permanent home. It has been purchased for the trust by an anonymous private donor for an undisclosed sum. It has been granted planning permission by Argyll and Bute Council.

Gormley said: "There is an excitement about making a sculpture that can live out here amongst the waves and the wind, the rain and snow, in night and day. The sculpture is like a standing stone, a marker in space and time, linking with a specific place and its history but also looking out towards the horizon, having a conversation with a future that hasn't yet happened."

Caroline Stanford, who managed the Land installation, said: "Grip's human scale and magical setting make it a deeply moving work by one of this generation's finest artists. We are so grateful to our wonderful donor for enabling it to stay in Scotland for good."

The Landmark Trust has owned Saddell Bay since 1975. It has restored each of the six buildings on the bay and they are available for self-catering holidays.

# Human Head Found at Cambridgeshire Quarry Believed to Have Traveled 40 Miles

A grim discovery at a Cambridgeshire quarry has launched a multi-agency investigation after a human head was found by a worker on Monday.

The remains were discovered at Mepal, Cambridgeshire, and forensic analysis suggests the head originated from a site approximately 40 miles away in Sharnbrook, Bedfordshire. Authorities believe the victim died before 2015.

Cambridgeshire Police confirmed they have not yet determined whether the remains belong to a man or woman. The National Crime Agency's Missing Person's Bureau has been enlisted to assist with identification efforts.

An NCA spokeswoman explained their comprehensive approach: "Our Missing team has been in touch with the force. In cases like this, the bureau will conduct searches and checks to see if there are any other partial remains that could be linked to the incident, or any missing persons."

The agency will gather crucial evidence including DNA samples and dental records. "Depending on the outcome of enquiries, we would also recommend a forensic artist is engaged to create an impression of what the person may look like in order to aid identification," the spokeswoman added.

The Mepal site operates as a multifunctional facility, handling landfill, recycling, and aggregate supply including limestone and gravel, as well as concrete mixing operations.

Investigators are working to determine how the remains traveled between the two locations and the circumstances surrounding the death.

# Gurkhas Memorial Unveiled in Nuneaton to Honor War Dead

A stone memorial commemorating 43,000 Gurkhas who died in World Wars One and Two has been dedicated in Riversley Park, Nuneaton.

The monument honors soldiers from the Queen's Gurkha Signals regiment, which is based in the town. Local residents raised £40,000 for the memorial in just three months.

The dedication ceremony featured a march by veteran soldiers.

Warwickshire County Councillor Bob Hicks said the Gurkhas have long ties with the borough, making Nuneaton a fitting location for the monument.

# Swimmer Found Dead Off Brighton Coast After Rough Seas Search

A 22-year-old man from Redhill, Surrey, has been found dead after going missing while swimming in rough seas near Brighton's Palace Pier on Saturday.

The swimmer was last seen east of the pier before a search operation was launched at 07:45 BST. Coastguards located him approximately one kilometre from the pier and pulled him from the water, but he was pronounced dead at the scene.

Sussex Police have informed the coroner of the incident.

# BBC to Open Weather Forecasting Contract to Competition, Ending Met Office's 94-Year Partnership

The BBC has announced it will put its weather forecasting contract out to tender, potentially ending a partnership with the Met Office that has lasted nearly a century.

The UK's weather service has provided the data used for BBC forecasts since the corporation's first radio weather bulletin on 14 November 1922. The BBC said it was legally required to secure the best value for money for licence fee payers and would tender the contract to outside competition.

The Met Office said it was disappointed by the decision. A replacement is expected to take over next year.

Steve Noyes, Met Office operations and customer services director, said: "Nobody knows Britain's weather better and, during our long relationship with the BBC, we've revolutionised weather communication to make it an integral part of British daily life.

"This is disappointing news, but we will be working to make sure that vital Met Office advice continues to be a part of BBC output."

Former BBC Weather presenter Bill Giles told BBC Radio 5 Live that he was "absolutely shattered by it (the news)".

"We have one of the best Met offices in the world.... there won't be any more accurate (service) from anyone else, far less."

The Met Office also provides many of the presenters who read the weather on the BBC and said it would be supporting them to "ensure clarity on their future".

But a BBC spokesman said they didn't anticipate significant changes to the on-air presenting team, which includes Strictly Come Dancing contestant Carol Kirkwood.

The spokesman said: "Our viewers get the highest standard of weather service and that won't change.

"We are legally required to go through an open tender process and take forward the strongest bids to make sure we secure both the best possible service and value for money for the licence fee payer."

The new provider will be announced later this year. The spokesman said the Met Office's severe weather warnings would still be used by the BBC.

# Convicted Murderer Shaun Walmsley Escapes Custody in Armed Ambush Outside Liverpool Hospital

A convicted murderer serving a life sentence escaped from custody after armed men ambushed prison officers outside a Liverpool hospital, sparking calls for an immediate investigation into the security breach.

Shaun Walmsley, 28, described by authorities as "highly dangerous," was being escorted by prison officers and was getting into a taxi when two masked men, armed with a gun and knife, threatened the guards and forced them to release him near Liverpool's Aintree University Hospital on Tuesday.

The 28-year-old is one of four men serving life sentences for the "vicious and savage" fatal stabbing of Anthony Duffy in 2014. He was facing a 30-year sentence at the time of his escape.

Liverpool Mayor Joe Anderson expressed outrage over the incident, calling it a "serious security breach" and demanding a full inquiry. "I am angry and incredibly shocked," Anderson said, adding that he is awaiting a complete briefing on the circumstances surrounding the escape.

According to police, the getaway vehicle—a gold-colored Volvo with registration number MW02 XHE—had been strategically positioned in the area. Officers believe the car was parked on Adlam Crescent in Fazakerley from approximately 12:00 GMT before moving to Aintree University Hospital around 13:30. The vehicle was later recovered on Adlam Crescent at 20:00 Tuesday evening and is currently being examined by forensic teams.

The Prison Officers' Association has raised serious concerns about the security arrangements. Mark Fairhurst, who sits on the POA national executive and is based at HMP Liverpool where Walmsley was held, questioned why the prisoner was not classified as Category A given his "gangland connections" and serious conviction.

"This incident put our officers' lives—and that of the taxi driver—at risk," Fairhurst said. He revealed that while the prison had recognized Walmsley as "more dangerous than others" and assigned a third officer to the escort, the guards "had no deterrent capability—just extendable batons."

During the ambush, one officer had a gun held to his head and was left "very shaken," while another had a knife pressed to his throat. All three officers were also threatened with CS gas. Fairhurst praised the officers for doing "the right thing" by releasing the handcuffs and immediately contacting police.

Andy Darken, Deputy General Secretary of the POA, defended the use of taxis for transporting non-Category A prisoners, stating it is "fairly common" following appropriate risk assessments. However, he acknowledged that "there's not a lot of difference if they are held up by armed gunmen in a secure van or a taxi."

A Ministry of Justice spokeswoman declined to comment on specific details but confirmed they are "working closely with the police and are urgently investigating the matter."

Wales flanker Dan Lydiate has been ruled out of the summer tour to New Zealand after suffering a shoulder injury in Saturday's England defeat.

He has been replaced in the Welsh squad by Cardiff Blues' uncapped 23-year-old open-side Ellis Jenkins. Wales play the first of three Tests against the world champion All Blacks on 11 June.

"It's hard for Dan because his tour is already over," said Wales head coach Warren Gatland.

Lydiate, who was captaining Wales in the absence of Sam Warburton, was taken off the field during the first half of the 27-13 defeat at Twickenham.

The 28-year-old also filled in for Warburton at open-side flanker, with Ross Moriarty taking Lydiate's place at six.

Jenkins' call-up means there is now natural open-side cover for his regional team-mate Warburton in the Wales squad.

The two have played together for the Blues this season, with Jenkins often wearing seven and Warburton switching to the blind-side.

The other back-rowers in the Wales squad to face New Zealand are Taulupe Faletau, Ross Moriarty, James King and Josh Turnbull.

**Ramirez Joins Sampdoria After Middlesbrough Spell**

Gastón Ramirez has completed a move to Italian side Sampdoria after leaving Middlesbrough. The 26-year-old Uruguay international scored nine goals in 44 appearances for the Championship club following his January 2016 transfer from Southampton.

Sampdoria have not revealed contract details for their new signing. Meanwhile, Middlesbrough begin their Championship campaign on Saturday with a trip to Wolves.

# Liberation: French paper's editor quits after journalists' revolt

Nicolas Demorand, the editor of French left-wing newspaper Liberation, has resigned following a bitter dispute with journalists over plans to restructure the ailing publication.

Mr Demorand's restructuring plan was denounced by the paper's journalists in a front-page story at the weekend. He had already suffered four votes of no confidence from its editorial board. Mr Demorand had led the paper since March 2011.

In an interview with another newspaper, Le Monde, he said he hoped his departure would help "revive the dialogue needed to take the newspaper out of the crisis".

The dispute has caused turmoil at the paper, which was co-founded in 1973 by French philosopher Jean-Paul Sartre.

Under the restructuring plan, the paper would have been transformed into a social network, providing content for multimedia platforms. The paper's headquarters would have become a cultural centre, with a bar, a restaurant, a TV studio and a start-up hub.

Key shareholders defended the plan as the only viable future for the struggling 40-year-old paper, which saw its sales slide 15% last year.

But journalists accused the management of wanting to turn Liberation into a brand and said the plan involved doing everything but journalism. After staging a one-day strike, the journalists used Saturday's edition to publicly attack the plan.

# Computer Algorithm Uses Sound Echoes to Map Rooms in 3D

Researchers have developed a groundbreaking computer algorithm that can map a room in three dimensions using only sound echoes, mimicking the echolocation abilities of bats and dolphins.

The innovative technology, detailed in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), uses just four microphones to record echoes bouncing off walls and constructs a complete 3D image of a space. The team behind the development believes the technology could eventually have applications in crime-solving and audio forensics.

Echolocation, the ability to use sounds to navigate the world, is naturally employed by dolphins and bats. While some blind individuals have also developed this remarkable skill, it remains rare in humans. Now, scientists have harnessed the power of computer algorithms to interpret the echoes from chirp-like sounds to reveal the shape and dimensions of a room.

The algorithm works by distinguishing between stronger and weaker echoes and determining whether sound waves have bounced once or multiple times around the room. Interestingly, the system doesn't rely on amplitude variations caused by different wall materials. Instead, it analyzes the differing arrival times between echoes, meaning any sound could theoretically be used to achieve the same results.

"Our software can build a 3D map of a simple, convex room with a precision of a few millimetres," explained Ivan Dokmanic, lead author of the study from the Ecole Polytechnique Federale de Lausanne in Switzerland (EPFL).

The process works by having each microphone pick up both the direct sound from the source and the echoes arriving from various walls. "The algorithm then compares the signal from each microphone," Mr Dokmanic said. "The infinitesimal lags that appear in the signals are used to calculate not only the distance between the microphones, but also the distance from each microphone to the walls and the sound source."

The potential applications for this research are numerous and varied. In architecture, for example, designers building concert halls could use the algorithm to work backwards from desired acoustics. By "plugging" specific echoes into the computer, they could determine "the kind of space needed to produce those echoes."

Virtual reality technology could also benefit significantly. Mr Dokmanic explained that when visual and audio information don't correspond, "your brain is confused and disorientated." The algorithm could help create virtual spaces that are acoustically realistic, enhancing the overall immersive experience.

Perhaps most intriguingly, the technology shows promise in audio forensics. A sound recording made in an unknown location could potentially provide clues about the space where it was recorded, which could prove valuable in criminal investigations.

However, Mr Dokmanic acknowledges that further research is needed to fully realize these forensic applications. The researcher confirmed he is continuing to develop the technology to unlock its full potential.

# Fusilier Lee Rigby Memorial Unveiled at St George's Chapel in Woolwich

A memorial plaque honouring Fusilier Lee Rigby and 10 other service personnel and civilians from Greenwich has been unveiled at St George's Chapel, close to where the soldier was murdered.

The 25-year-old was off-duty when he was hit by a car outside the army barracks and then hacked to death. His is one of 11 names on a plaque at St George's Chapel, near the barracks, to honour service personnel and civilians local to Greenwich.

Fusilier Rigby's mother Lyn, his widow Rebecca and son Jack were among those at a private unveiling earlier. The chapel is about 700m (765yds) from where Lee Rigby was murdered in south-east London in May 2013.

The Royal Borough of Greenwich council said the memorial had been an "emotive issue" and to reach this point it had needed to consider competing interests about how Fusilier Rigby, who was from Middleton, Greater Manchester, should be commemorated.

"It has been widely and wrongly reported that we were concerned about right wing extremists or Islamist extremists attacking the site," a spokesman added. The Met has not commented on whether it has security concerns about the memorial.

In a statement the Ministry of Defence said it supported Greenwich council's marking of Armistice Day with a new memorial dedicated to service men and women who lived or worked in the borough and lost their lives while serving their country.

"It is right that we pay tribute to those courageous individuals who have worked to keep Britain safe, both at home and abroad."

Fusilier Rigby joined the Army in 2006 and was posted to the Second Battalion, The Royal Regiment of Fusiliers based in Woolwich. He served in Cyprus, Afghanistan and Germany.

Two men, Michael Adebolajo and Michael Adebowale were jailed last year for his murder.

Those listed on the plaque died in Iraq, Afghanistan, and Woolwich as a result of conflict post-September 1945. The names surround a marble memorial featuring the borough's crest and the words: "At the going down of the sun and in the morning, We will remember them".

An online book of remembrance can be viewed at the council's website. There is also one at the town hall in Woolwich.

The chapel, which is owned by the Heritage of London Trust, will be open to the public every Sunday from January when renovation works have finished.

# Bob Bradley Vows to Win Over Swansea Fans After Historic Premier League Appointment

Bob Bradley has insisted he is a "football manager" rather than an "American manager" as he prepares to make history as the first American to manage in the Premier League.

The 58-year-old was appointed Swansea City manager on Monday, replacing Francesco Guidolin with the Welsh club hovering just one point above the Premier League relegation zone.

Bradley acknowledged he faces a challenge to win over Swansea's passionate fanbase, but says he is ready to earn their respect through hard work and results.

"There's not one person in Swansea who could care less about America," Bradley said. "I am here to give everything for the fans and the club."

The former United States national team coach understands that some supporters may be unhappy with the managerial change, particularly given Guidolin's departure.

"If they're angry right now I get it. I have full respect for Francesco and I will do anything to earn their respect," he said.

Bradley drew on his previous experience when taking his first professional head coaching role at Chicago Fire, emphasizing the importance of connecting with the local community.

"The first thing I said was we needed to have a connection with the city. When you have that you have something," he explained. "I know it's more important than anywhere here."

The American manager is under no illusions about the challenge facing him in the Premier League, acknowledging that respect must be earned rather than given.

"If you come to the Premier League you have to earn respect. No-one gets it on a plate. You get tested," Bradley said. "In everything I've done in life, I've fully understood you have to earn respect."

Analyzing Swansea's difficult start to the season, Bradley pointed to a challenging fixture list and a subsequent loss of confidence as contributing factors to their struggles.

"We had a very difficult list of fixtures at the start of the season, it's had some bad luck and lost a bit of confidence," he said. "I'm not coming in with a new book, but we have to be honest that certain things have to be better."

Bradley was particularly enthusiastic about Swansea's unique ownership structure, with the Supporters' Trust holding a 21% stake in the club.

"I already know enough about Swansea City Football Club," he said. "I know I'm at a club with a soul, that has real passion and real fans. That for me is special."

The new manager expressed his excitement about the opportunity, saying: "I could not be more excited to get the chance."

# Driver Jailed for Seven Years After Fatal Pavement Collision

A driver who killed a young man after mounting a pavement while under the influence of alcohol has been sentenced to seven years in prison.

Constantin Radu, 32, of Salt Hill Way, Slough, pleaded guilty to causing death by dangerous driving following the incident on Wexham Road in September last year. His Rover 45 struck two pedestrians after leaving the road, fatally injuring 20-year-old Jacob Chapman-Pickett, who died the following day. A second man was also injured and required hospital treatment.

Tragically, Mr Chapman-Pickett was scheduled to begin university on the day of the collision. His father, Keith Pickett, paid tribute to his son: "His honesty, loyalty and sense of fairness, along with his sense of humour, cheeky grin and willingness to help anybody, were things that made this world a better place. A part of me died with Jacob and there will always be a part of myself missing."

At Reading Crown Court on Thursday, Radu received an additional four-month concurrent sentence for driving with excess alcohol. He has been disqualified from driving for 13 years and three months.

The court heard that Radu had no insurance or UK driving licence and had a previous conviction for drink-driving in Romania.

PC Victoria Jones described it as "a tragic and unnecessary loss of life caused by the reckless behaviour of a driver who had been drinking."

# Man charged over death of traffic controller in west London

A man has been charged with causing death by dangerous driving after a traffic controller was killed while directing vehicles around his broken-down van in west London.

The victim is thought to have been directing traffic around his broken-down van in Pembridge Villas, Notting Hill when he was hit on Thursday.

George Claudia Albu, 31, of Porchester Road, Paddington, will appear at West London Magistrates' Court on Monday. He is also charged with failing to stop at the scene.

Police were called to the scene shortly before midnight on Thursday. The van driver was pronounced dead just over an hour later.

Police said Mr Albu has also been charged with causing death by driving a vehicle not in accordance with a licence and causing death by driving a vehicle while uninsured.

The victim worked for Kensington and Chelsea Council's grounds maintenance contractors Quadron.

# Four Teenagers Injured After Police Chase Ends in Crash

Four teenagers were seriously injured when their car crashed into barriers in Langworth, Lincolnshire, following a police pursuit on Thursday.

The vehicle failed to stop for police before smashing into the barriers. The driver was airlifted to hospital with serious injuries.

Three passengers were arrested at the scene: an 18-year-old man and two women aged 18 and 19.

A 16-year-old boy remains in serious condition at Queens Medical Centre in Nottingham, while a 15-year-old boy is receiving treatment at Lincoln County Hospital.

Lincolnshire Police confirmed the incident has been referred to the Independent Police Complaints Commission (IPCC) due to police involvement in the pursuit.

# Burkina Faso Coach Rohr Recalls Star Winger Pitroipa for World Cup Qualifier

Burkina Faso manager Gernot Rohr has handed Jonathan Pitroipa a recall to the national team squad for their upcoming 2018 World Cup qualifier against Botswana, marking a potential return for the talismanic winger who has been absent from international duty since the German coach took charge.

Pitroipa, who was named player of the tournament when Burkina Faso reached the final of the 2013 Africa Cup of Nations, has not featured for the Stallions since Rohr's appointment. However, the 62-year-old coach has now included the experienced winger in his 24-man squad for the crucial Group D encounter scheduled for 5 September.

Speaking to local media, Rohr expressed optimism about Pitroipa's potential contribution to the team while emphasizing that the decision ultimately rests with the player himself.

"He's been unavailable for different reasons like club engagements and injury but I'd be hoping [to have him for the qualifiers] because he brings a lot to the team," Rohr explained. "It is no secret that a fully fit and motivated Pitroipa is every coach's joy and only a few managers would deny that."

The coach added: "I'm sure we'll see him playing for his country again which will be exciting, but right now the ball is in his court."

Pitroipa currently plies his trade with Al Nasr in the United Arab Emirates and would bring valuable experience to a squad that has already made a positive start to their World Cup qualification campaign.

The squad features several notable inclusions, including Chelsea's Bertrand Traore, despite the young forward yet to make an appearance for the Premier League champions this season. His brother Alain Traore, who plays for French side Lorient, is also included in the selection.

Algeria-based midfielder Patrick Malo receives his first call-up to the national team, while veteran defender Paul Koulibaly, currently with Guinea's Horoya AC, has been recalled to the squad.

Rohr has organized a comprehensive preparation schedule, with the squad set to gather for a three-day training camp in Paris beginning 29 August. The team will then fly to Johannesburg, South Africa, on 2 September before making the journey by road to Botswana's capital Gaborone, and finally to the match venue in Lobatse.

Burkina Faso opened their Group D campaign impressively with a 2-0 victory over Comoros Islands in Ouagadougou last June, putting them in a strong position as they continue their quest to reach the 2018 World Cup finals in Russia.

# Prost Apologises After Last-Lap Crash Hands Di Grassi Formula E Victory in Beijing

**Nicolas Prost has apologised for a last-lap collision that denied Nick Heidfeld victory in the Beijing Formula E race on Saturday.**

The Frenchman turned sharply into Heidfeld as they battled on the final lap, allowing Audi Sport's Lucas Di Grassi to triumph.

"I feel very bad about the incident.... I understand that I am responsible," Prost wrote on Twitter.

Prost has been handed a 10-place grid penalty for the next round in Malaysia.

Pole-sitter Prost initially accused ex-F1 driver Heidfeld of making a "suicide move" but backtracked after watching a video of the incident.

"I just did not see him. I feel very bad," Prost added.

"The most important thing is that my friend Nick Heidfield is OK, sorry again Nick, you know I would never do something like this."

Venturi driver Heidfield welcomed Prost's apology, adding that he accepted his rival would not "drive anybody off on purpose".

The two drivers are team-mates at Rebellion Racing in the World Endurance Championship and are due to compete together at the next round of that series in Austin next week.

The crash paved the way for Brazilian Di Grassi to come through for an unexpected win.

Frank Montagny was runner-up for the Andretti team, while Britain's Sam Bird finished third for Virgin Racing.

There was disappointment for Bruno Senna - nephew of the late Ayrton Senna, the great rival of Nicolas Prost's father Alain - who failed to record a lap in qualifying after battery problems.

Forced to start from near the back of the grid, he collided with another car during the opening lap.

Another son of an F1 great, Nelson Piquet Jnr, came eighth.

Di Grassi, meanwhile, was left to reflect on his good fortune after being gifted the win on a circuit located just outside the Bird's Nest Stadium, site of the 2008 Olympics.

"When I realised that they were off it was like a dream come true," he said.

"I was alone and have won the race, and I am really, really really happy to be in this position."

The 10-race season concludes in London's Battersea Park next June.

**Former West Ham goalkeeper joins Southend United**

A 22-year-old former Scotland Under-21 international has signed for Southend United after being released by West Ham United this summer. The goalkeeper previously had a loan spell with the Shrimpers in 2016, making five appearances for the club.

He failed to make a senior appearance for West Ham after joining from Hamilton in 2015. "I came here on loan for a short spell and it's a great club, I can't wait to start playing," the player said.

# Former Church of England Curate Jailed for Historical Child Sex Abuse

A retired Church of England curate has been convicted of historical sexual abuse crimes against a young girl.

Graham Gregory, 79, of Brockfield Park Drive, Huntington, York, was a curate in Wandsworth when he indecently assaulted the girl, then aged under 13. Police were contacted by the victim in 2012 who said she had been abused by him between 1969 and 1971.

Gregory was found guilty of two counts of indecent assault by a jury at Kingston Crown Court.

As well as working as a curate in Southfields, Wandsworth, Gregory also held positions in Hastings, Chichester, York and the Isle of Man as a vicar.

Det Con Aaron Vardy, of the Met's Sexual Offences Exploitation and Child Abuse Command, said: "Gregory abused his position as a figure of trust and authority."

He added: "I would urge anyone else who may have been a victim of Gregory's abuse to make contact with the police."

# New Railway Station Proposed for Inverness Retail Park

A new railway station could be built on the Inverness to Aberdeen line to serve shoppers, workers, and students in the city.

The proposed stop would provide access to a busy retail park and the nearby Inverness College UHI campus. Highlands and Islands public transport body, Hitrans, has begun investigating the feasibility and costs associated with the project.

This proposal follows similar plans by Hitrans for a station near Inverness Airport at Dalcross, demonstrating a broader strategy to improve regional connectivity.

Stewart Nicol, chief executive of Inverness Chamber of Commerce, expressed strong support for the initiative. "We have got to continue to develop all forms of public transport across the Highlands," he said.

Mr Nicol highlighted the diverse potential user base: "Part of the attractiveness of this is that there is a wide range of possible users. There are people who live and work in that part of the city, those who use the shopping park, the leisure facilities and the university campus."
