The railway station proposal comes as the retail park itself undergoes significant development. Highland councillors approved plans for a comprehensive revamp of the shopping area earlier this year, suggesting the location's growing importance to the local economy.

# Irish Golf Legend Christy O'Connor Senior Dies

**Galway native and Ryder Cup icon Christy O'Connor Senior has passed away, marking another devastating loss for Irish golf following his nephew's death earlier this year.**

The legendary golfer from Galway dominated the Irish and British circuits throughout his illustrious career, claiming victory in more than 20 tournaments. O'Connor's consistency at golf's most prestigious event was remarkable, finishing in the top 10 at The Open Championship on 10 separate occasions.

His Ryder Cup career spanned nearly two decades, competing in every tournament between 1955 and 1973. This outstanding contribution to the sport earned him induction into the World Golf Hall of Fame in 2009.

O'Connor's trophy cabinet includes British Masters titles in 1956 and 1959, whilst his closest brush with major championship glory came at Royal Birkdale in 1965, where he finished tied-second at The Open, just two strokes behind winner Peter Thomson. The golfer often reflected that his major championship opportunities were limited by financial constraints that prevented regular travel to the United States.

His international achievements included 15 World Cup appearances, highlighted by victory in 1958 alongside Harry Bradshaw. He later dominated senior golf, capturing six PGA Senior Championships between 1976 and 1983.

Current Ryder Cup captain Darren Clarke expressed his profound sadness, calling O'Connor "the father of Irish golf." Clarke noted that Ireland has now lost two Ryder Cup legends within five months, with O'Connor Junior having passed away in January aged 67.

"Irish golf in particular and golf in general has lost one of its greatest heroes," Clarke concluded.

# Kenyan Town Orders Nappies for Donkeys to Keep New Road Clean

Officials in the Kenyan town of Wajir have issued an unusual directive requiring donkey-cart owners to fit their animals with nappies to protect the area's newly constructed tarmac road.

A letter from local authorities instructed cart owners to manage their animal's faeces "to avoid poop all over the tarmac road creating nuisance." The notice, issued on Monday and enforced from Thursday, states that no donkey will be permitted in town without a poop-collecting bag.

According to BBC Monitoring's Abdullahi Yusuf Osman in Kenya, cart owners are complying with the order, with some sharing practical advice on social media about attaching nappy sacks to their animals.

Donkey carts remain a common sight in Wajir's town centre, playing a vital role in local transportation and commerce. The authorities are believed to be particularly protective of the new 27-kilometre road, completed last year after decades of waiting for such infrastructure development.

The county government acknowledged the economic contribution of donkey-cart operators whilst emphasising cleanliness standards. "The town must be kept clean at all times," the notice stated.

This isn't Kenya's first such initiative. A similar nappy order was issued in Limuru, near Nairobi, in 2007, though it was never implemented. Wajir, located more than 600 kilometres north-east of the capital, appears more determined to enforce the measure.

# RAF Mildenhall to Receive Major US Military Expansion with Osprey Aircraft

RAF Mildenhall is set to undergo a significant expansion as the United States Air Force prepares to deploy advanced military aircraft to the Suffolk base.

The base will receive 10 CV-22 Osprey tilt-rotor aircraft and 12 MC-130J Commando II fixed-wing planes as part of a major modernization initiative. The expansion will bring approximately 900 additional personnel and their family members to the area, with the first aircraft arriving this month and all 22 expected to be operational by 2018.

The CV-22 Osprey represents cutting-edge military technology, capable of vertical take-off and landing like a helicopter before tilting its rotors to fly as a conventional aircraft. The aircraft provides crucial ground troop transport capabilities, while the MC-130J Commando II specializes in mid-air refueling operations.

The expansion involves the USAF's 352nd Special Operations Group, which will add approximately 380 serving personnel to its ranks. Colonel Christopher Ireland, the group's commander, emphasized the significance of the development: "It's been almost six years since we've had vertical lift-off in Europe and this modernisation of the force improves our efficiency and effectiveness."

The enhanced capabilities will enable better operational support and improved training opportunities. While the base has recently upgraded its schools and housing facilities, some service families are expected to settle in surrounding communities to accommodate the increased population.

# Cheshire East Council Waived Rules for Contracts Given to Former Leader's Physiotherapist

Cheshire East Council bypassed its own procurement regulations when awarding three contracts to Core Fit Ltd, a company owned by Amanda Morris, the physiotherapist of former council leader Michael Jones.

The contracts, collectively valued at £156,000, were granted to Core Fit Ltd, which operates fitness classes in schools throughout the area.

A police investigation into misconduct in a public office is currently underway. Cheshire Police confirmed investigators will examine the contract awarding process and "the involvement of all relevant individuals." A spokeswoman stated: "The purpose of the investigation is to establish what happened and who was involved."

Mr Jones, who stood down from his position on 8 December, denied any wrongdoing at the time of his resignation. He cited preventing infighting within the Conservative group as his reason for stepping down. He was unavailable for comment regarding the investigation.

**Rochdale Sign Young Defender on Permanent Deal**

Rochdale have completed the permanent signing of 22-year-old defender Liam Kitching on an 18-month contract, days after his initial loan arrival from Middlesbrough.

Kitching made his debut for Dale in Saturday's 4-0 FA Cup fourth-round defeat against Championship side Huddersfield Town at Spotland.

The defender joined Middlesbrough in July 2013 and made two appearances for Boro in the EFL Trophy this season before securing his move to the League One club.

# Alanis Morissette's Former Business Manager Admits to $4.8m Fraud

Jonathan Schwartz, the former business manager of Canadian singer Alanis Morissette, has pleaded guilty to charges of wire fraud after admitting he embezzled $4.8 million from the Grammy-winning artist.

The fraud occurred between 2009 and 2016, when Mr Schwartz was responsible for managing Morissette's finances, including collecting revenue, managing accounts, and organizing bill payments. When initially confronted about the missing funds, Schwartz fabricated a story, claiming he had invested the money in an illegal marijuana growing operation.

Appearing at federal court in Los Angeles on Wednesday, Mr Schwartz admitted to stealing not only from Morissette but also from other unnamed celebrity clients, from whom he embezzled more than $2 million. His attorney, Nathan Hochman, stated that his client has fully cooperated with investigators and accepted responsibility for his actions. If convicted on criminal charges, Schwartz faces a prison sentence of between four and six years.

The theft was discovered after Morissette hired a new manager who identified significant discrepancies in her financial accounts. Last year, the "Ironic" singer filed a civil lawsuit against Schwartz and his former company GSO, seeking $15 million in damages. The company expressed shock upon learning that Schwartz had been using the stolen funds to finance a lavish lifestyle.

The lawsuit was subsequently dropped after a settlement was reached between the parties. Mr Schwartz is scheduled to appear in court on the criminal charges on 1 February.

# Donald Trump Faces Criticism Over Social Media Comments on Russian Hacking Claims

Donald Trump has found himself at the centre of controversy this week following comments he made on social media about the US presidential election.

Since winning the election, the president-elect has frequently used social media platforms to share his views with the public. However, his recent tweets have sparked widespread criticism from political opponents and security experts.

The controversy centres on Trump's response to claims made by US intelligence agencies. American spies have stated that Russia interfered with the presidential election in an attempt to help Trump secure victory. According to intelligence officials, Russia hacked into email accounts belonging to Hillary Clinton's campaign team and released embarrassing information designed to damage her electoral chances.

Despite these findings from his own intelligence services, Donald Trump has taken to Twitter to express his doubts about their conclusions. He has publicly stated that he does not believe the American spies have reached the correct assessment.

Many critics have argued that Trump's social media behaviour is inappropriate for someone about to assume the presidency. Current Vice-President Joe Biden, who serves as second in command to President Barack Obama, told reporters in an interview that Trump needs to "grow up".

Political analysts have noted that it is highly unusual for an incoming US president to openly contradict his own intelligence agencies in such a public manner.

However, Trump's supporters maintain that his unconventional approach represents a refreshing change from traditional politicians, arguing that his willingness to challenge established institutions is exactly what voters wanted.

# Bangladesh MP Manjurul Islam Shot Dead in Gaibandha District

A member of parliament for Bangladesh's ruling Awami League has been shot dead in the northern district of Gaibandha.

Manjurul Islam was attacked by three unidentified gunmen who fired multiple shots before fleeing the scene on a motorbike, according to police officials.

The MP was rushed to hospital but succumbed to his injuries. Prof Bimal Chandra Roy of Rangpur Medical College Hospital confirmed that Mr Islam had been shot five times at close range.

The assailants remain at large and their identities are still unknown.

Local residents have staged protests following the killing.

Mr Islam had previously been arrested in October 2015 on charges of shooting a schoolboy, though he was subsequently released on bail.

# Mourinho Receives Suspended Ban for Comments About Match Officials

Jose Mourinho has been handed a suspended one-match stadium ban and fined £50,000 after criticizing match officials following Chelsea's defeat to Southampton.

The Chelsea manager had claimed officials were "afraid" to award his team penalties after Robert Madley denied Chelsea a spot-kick in a 3-1 loss to Southampton. The FA charged that his comments "imply bias on the part of a match official". Mourinho's ban will only be enforced if he repeats the offence within a year.

The home defeat by Southampton was Chelsea's fourth loss in the defending champions' opening eight Premier League games of the season and left them 10 points behind leaders Manchester City and four points above the relegation zone.

Speaking after the game, Mourinho had said the Blues were "always punished" by officials because "there is always a question mark" from the media. "If the Football Association wants to punish me they can. They don't punish other managers," he added.

A Chelsea spokesperson told BBC Sport the club would wait to read the FA's full reasoning before making any comment on the verdict.

Mourinho was charged hours after the Blues said the Portuguese retained their "full support" following back-to-back defeats. His side return to Premier League action at home to Aston Villa - four points and two places below them - on Saturday.

# Gay Couple Sparks Kiss-In Protest at London Sainsbury's After Complaint

A kiss-in protest was held at a Sainsbury's supermarket in Hackney, east London, after a gay couple were confronted by security over a complaint about their behaviour.

Thomas Rees, 32, and Joshua Bradwell, 25, were shopping at the Sainsbury's on Hackney Road on Monday evening when a security guard approached them after they had paid for their groceries. The guard informed them that a woman had complained about their behaviour in the store.

Mr Rees said they had simply been holding hands and he may have put his arm around his partner's waist while shopping for food. "It knocked me for six," he said, adding that the incident left him "analysing how I'm perceived."

Following the confrontation, the couple's story spread rapidly on social media, prompting an outpouring of support from around the world. On Saturday night, protesters gathered outside the Hackney Road store to demonstrate solidarity with the couple, dancing outside before moving inside to kiss in the aisles.

Mr Bradwell described the turnout as "absolutely insane," expressing gratitude for the community response. Despite one person shouting at protesters to "get off my street," the demonstration continued peacefully.

Sainsbury's has apologised for the incident and offered the couple a £10 voucher. The supermarket provided biscuits and water for protesters and issued a statement acknowledging: "We do our best to make sure everyone feels welcome in our stores but occasionally we make mistakes."

The company is conducting an investigation and says it is "working hard to make sure lessons are learnt."

This incident echoes a similar protest held two years ago at a Brighton Sainsbury's, where a lesbian couple were asked to leave after sharing a kiss on the cheek.

# China's Top Security Chief Visits Afghanistan in Historic Trip

China's domestic security chief Zhou Yongkang has made a landmark visit to Afghanistan, becoming the most senior Chinese official to travel to the country in nearly half a century. The visit, which was kept secret for security reasons until his departure, signals Beijing's growing interest in the war-torn nation ahead of the 2014 withdrawal of US-led forces.

During his visit on Saturday, Mr Zhou met with Afghan President Hamid Karzai and signed several agreements aimed at deepening bilateral cooperation. Among the key deals is a security partnership that will see China help train Afghanistan's police force, with approximately 300 Afghan officers set to receive training in China over the next four years, according to Afghan foreign ministry officials.

The BBC's Ethirajan Anbarasan reports from Kabul that the visit reflects China's strategic interest in expanding its influence in Afghanistan, particularly as neighboring countries position themselves ahead of the Western troop withdrawal. Analysts suggest China is keen to protect its growing economic investments in the region.

China has been actively pursuing Afghanistan's vast mineral wealth for several years. A Chinese state-owned company has already invested heavily in a copper mine in Logar province, though excavation of a 7th-century Buddhist site has delayed operations. Last year, China also secured rights for oil exploration in the Amu Darya river basin.

The visit follows a June decision by both nations to upgrade their relationship to a strategic and cooperative partnership during a regional conference in Beijing.

# Rural Scottish GP Surgery to Close After Years of Challenges

A branch surgery in Cockburnspath, Scottish Borders, is set to close in August, affecting more than 200 patients, following longstanding operational difficulties cited by Eyemouth Medical Practice.

The practice has attributed the closure to multiple factors, including problematic building design, concerns over lone working conditions, unreliable IT infrastructure, and the broader challenge of GP shortages in rural areas. The decision has prompted concern from local representatives, with MSP Iain Lamont describing it as part of an "ongoing trend" of declining GP surgery numbers in rural Scotland.

Dr Kirsty Robinson, the practice's administration partner, sought to reassure affected patients about continuity of care. "We wish to reassure patients that the medical practice will continue to provide you with the usual general medical services from our other two premises in Coldingham and the newly refurbished Eyemouth Health Centre," she said.

Both alternative locations are accessible via public transport, and the practice has confirmed that home visits will continue for eligible patients where clinically appropriate. The surgery has also maintained an existing arrangement with a local shop in Cockburnspath to distribute prescription medications, which will continue on a weekly basis following the closure.

NHS Borders medical director Dr Cliff Sharp expressed support for the decision, citing "practical, safety and quality of care reasons." Registered patients have been sent letters advising them of the closure and inviting them to discuss concerns with NHS Borders by 21 July.

However, Mr Lamont criticized the short notice period. "This is a really disappointing decision which will make it more difficult for some to access GP care," he said. "To announce a closure with only a month's notice is far from ideal and the priority must be to ensure that patients are properly supported during this time."

The closure highlights ongoing pressures facing rural healthcare provision in Scotland.

# Town Appoints First Official Jester in 700 Years

Erwyd le Fol, also known as Russell Erwood, 34, has been officially appointed as town jester in a historic naming ceremony held in the town square.

The medieval-themed event featured a birds of prey demonstration, traditional games, and a colourful parade to mark the occasion.

# Jobcentre Plus Offices in Glasgow Face Closure Under DWP Review

The Department of Work and Pensions (DWP) announced on Wednesday plans to close several Jobcentre Plus offices in Glasgow as part of a comprehensive estate review, prompting concerns from Scottish government officials.

Scottish Employability Minister Jamie Hepburn has written to the department seeking clarity on the proposed closures. The DWP has committed to public consultation on any closures that would increase travel distances by more than three miles for claimants.

Denise Horsfall, DWP work services director for Scotland, told BBC Radio's Good Morning Scotland programme that three locations – Maryhill, Castlemilk and Bridgton – would see travel distances increase to up to four miles. These offices could remain open depending on consultation outcomes. Meanwhile, Jobcentre Plus offices in Govan, Drumchapel and Laurieston will not be affected by the proposals.

Minister Hepburn expressed frustration that discussions had not taken place with the Scottish Government, particularly given ongoing collaboration on transferring new employability support powers. "My first concern is to understand how DWP have assessed the impact of these proposed changes on their customers at a time when they are increasing the level of Jobcentre Plus-based support in favour of reducing funding for devolved employment provision," he said.

He also demanded clarification on whether further closures are planned across the wider Jobcentre Plus network.

A final decision is expected within six months, with completion scheduled for 31 March 2018.

# Parents Mistakenly Believe Tanning is Healthy for Children, Survey Reveals

A concerning new survey has revealed that approximately one-third of parents in the UK mistakenly believe that getting a tan is beneficial for their children's health, with a quarter actively encouraging their offspring to develop a suntan.

The findings, based on interviews with 1,000 parents of children aged 11 and younger, have raised alarm bells among health professionals, particularly as the UK experiences its hottest June day since the summer of 1976.

Perhaps most worryingly, some parents admitted to allowing their children to use sunbeds, despite well-documented health risks. One in ten parents said they had instructed their child to remove their top in the sun specifically "so they don't get tan lines." Additionally, more than one in five parents (21%) stated they would only consider applying sunscreen if their child's skin started to turn red and burn.

Medical experts are quick to dispel the myth that tanning is healthy. A tan does not protect against the sun's harmful rays – in fact, it's actually a sign that skin damage has already occurred. When skin is exposed to sunlight, cells called melanocytes produce more dark pigment, known as melanin, in an attempt to absorb further UV radiation. This darkening process is the skin's defensive response to damage, not a sign of health.

Repeated sun exposure, particularly during childhood, can significantly increase the risk of developing skin cancer in later life. Children and babies have considerably more sensitive skin than adults, making protection even more critical. Health guidelines recommend that infants under six months should be kept out of direct strong sunlight entirely.

From March to October in the UK, children should be protected with appropriate clothing, sunscreen with adequate SPF, and kept in the shade during peak UV hours. Many parents don't realise that UV radiation cannot be felt, making it easy to get sunburnt even on overcast days when temperatures aren't particularly warm.

Clare Nasir, Met Office presenter and meteorologist, emphasized that "protecting against skin cancer isn't something parents should leave to chance." She noted that UV levels are typically highest between May and September, and that clouds don't always block harmful UV rays. Parents can check daily UV forecasts on the Met Office website or app.

Dr Nigel Acheson from NHS England acknowledged that some sun exposure is beneficial for vitamin D production but cautioned against overdoing it. "We typically recommend that people spend no more than 10 to 15 minutes in the UK summer sun, unprotected, several times a week," he explained. Anyone spending longer than 15 minutes in the sun should apply sun protection factor 15 or higher.

Nicola Smith from Cancer Research UK was unequivocal: "There's no such thing as a safe tan, from the sun or sunbeds. A suntan is your skin's way of trying to protect itself from too much sun. And a sunburn is a clear sign that your skin has been damaged."

For more guidance on sun safety, parents are encouraged to follow NHS England's skin cancer campaign #CoverUpMate on Twitter.

# Venezuelan Woman Killed as Gunmen Attack Symbolic Opposition Vote

A woman was shot dead and three others wounded when gunmen on motorcycles opened fire on voters participating in an unofficial referendum in Venezuela on Sunday, escalating tensions in a country already gripped by months of deadly political violence.

The victim, identified by prosecutors as Xiomara Soledad Scott, died minutes after arriving at hospital following the attack in Catia, a traditionally pro-government neighbourhood in the capital, Caracas. The opposition quickly blamed "paramilitary" gangs for the shooting.

Video footage from the scene captured panicked voters fleeing as gunshots rang out, with many seeking refuge in a nearby church. Opposition spokesman Carlos Ocariz expressed deep sorrow over the incident, saying: "We lament this very much, with great pain." Prosecutors announced they would investigate the deadly attack.

The shooting occurred as millions of Venezuelans participated in a symbolic vote organized by opposition politicians to reject President Nicolas Maduro's plans for a new constituent assembly. The unofficial referendum, held at improvised polling stations including theatres, sports grounds and roundabouts across Venezuela and in more than 100 countries worldwide, asked citizens three key questions: whether they opposed the new assembly, wanted early elections before Maduro's term ends in 2018, and whether the armed forces should defend the current constitution.

Despite long queues and a generally festive atmosphere at most polling sites, President Maduro dismissed the exercise as "meaningless," calling it an internal opposition consultation conducted "without electoral rulebooks, without prior verification."

The violence underscored the deepening crisis in Venezuela, where more than 100 people have died in political clashes since April. In a separate incident on Sunday, journalist Luis Olavarrieta was kidnapped, robbed and beaten by a group of attackers before managing to escape. Images later emerged showing him receiving medical treatment.

The opposition organized the unofficial vote to demonstrate public rejection of Maduro's plans for an official election on July 30 to create a new constituent assembly. This body would have sweeping powers to rewrite the constitution and dissolve existing state institutions, leading critics to warn it could pave the way for dictatorship.

President Maduro argues the constituent assembly is necessary to resolve Venezuela's severe economic and political crisis. He claims a new constitution would "neutralize" the opposition and defeat "coup-plotters," thereby promoting peace. However, opposition leaders fear the process would delay scheduled regional and presidential elections while further weakening the National Assembly, the country's opposition-controlled legislative body.

The BBC's South America correspondent Katy Watson noted that while Sunday's vote was purely symbolic, the opposition hoped a strong turnout would increase pressure on the government to abandon its constituent assembly plans.

# Nazi-Era Machine Gun Seized in Australian Traffic Stop

CENTRAL COAST, NSW - Police have seized a World War II-era Nazi machine gun during a routine traffic stop on Australia's Central Coast, authorities announced Monday.

Officers discovered an MP40 sub-machine gun along with 60 rounds of ammunition while searching a vehicle on Sunday night. The weapon, developed in Nazi Germany with more than a million produced during the war, was found to be missing its barrel, though initial examinations suggest it remained operational.

A 40-year-old male passenger was arrested and charged with possessing a prohibited firearm. He was refused bail and appeared at Wyong Local Court on Monday. Police will conduct a forensic examination to determine if the weapon is linked to any shooting incidents.

The arrest comes just days after Australia launched a national gun amnesty in response to growing terrorism threats and an influx of illegal weapons. Authorities estimate approximately 260,000 illicit firearms are currently circulating in the country, despite strict gun control laws requiring all firearms to be registered and licensed.

Those caught with prohibited weapons during the amnesty period face severe penalties: fines up to A$280,000 ($212,730; £166,480) or imprisonment for up to 14 years.

Australia's last major gun amnesty followed the 1996 Port Arthur massacre in Tasmania, where 35 people were killed. That program resulted in the destruction of approximately 650,000 firearms and contributed to a significant decline in gun-related crimes nationwide.

# Children Help Clean Cemetery After Vandalism Attack

More than 20 schoolchildren rolled up their sleeves to help restore a Welsh cemetery after vandals caused heartbreaking damage to the historic site.

Seven graves in Ferndale Cemetery were deliberately toppled in January and rubbish left strewn across the site. The senseless act of vandalism shocked the local community and left grieving families devastated.

More than 20 children from nearby Ferndale Community School took part in the litter pick on Tuesday, determined to restore dignity to the resting place. The children collected more than 20 bags of rubbish including a broken bicycle and several traffic cones that had been discarded across the grounds.

PC Steve Davies, who organized the community clean-up, said he noticed the rubbish when examining the area. "I have a little son who passed away. I know the price, I know the cost implications and the emotional impact it would have on someone to come and visit a grave and seeing that their headstone has been damaged or destroyed," he told the BBC.

"It's just getting people together in response to what's happened to the headstones to build the respect up amongst the community," he added.

Among the pupils helping was Rachel, 14, who said she found the experience upsetting. "My ancestors' gravestones haven't been damaged and I'm quite grateful but when I see the others, it makes me wonder how their relatives must feel," she said. "It's upsetting, it's left me quite distraught to be honest."

A local stonemason has agreed to repair the headstones and South Wales Police is still investigating.

# Police Search for Missing Driver After M6 Crash

Police are growing increasingly concerned for a motorist who disappeared after a crash on the M6 motorway.

Zahid Mirza, 40, from Chelmsley Wood, crashed on the M6 between junctions 4A and 5 on 15 January. His family has had no contact with him since the incident.

Detective Superintendent Tom Chisholm said: "We have now learned that Mr Mirza's family have had no contact with him since then, so we are very concerned for his safety."

Officers fear Mr Mirza may have come to harm and are conducting searches near the motorway.

"At the time of the collision a search was made of the immediate area, but there was no trace of the driver," Det Supt Chisholm added.

Mr Mirza is described as 5ft 9ins tall with a stocky build, short dark hair, and wears glasses.

West Midlands Police have urged anyone with information to come forward.

# Harris Reflects on Lean Years After Career-Best Match Figures at Lord's

Middlesex seamer James Harris has spoken candidly about the struggles he faced following his high-profile move from Glamorgan, after recording career-best match figures against his former county.

The 24-year-old, who moved to Lord's from Glamorgan at the end of 2012, took 9-34 in the second innings to finish with match figures of 13-103.

"I've had two very lean years which has hurt me," he told BBC London 94.9. "I came here as a fairly big signing and expected to be doing these sort of things from the off. I am there to perform and I wasn't doing it."

The right-arm seamer added: "I came on a decent contract and wasn't performing so I was getting some criticism, and rightly so."

Harris took 21 wickets at an average of 38.33 in his first season at Middlesex but his second year in north London was more difficult, following a change in his action. He took just 12 wickets at 55.50 in his seven appearances and returned to Glamorgan on loan in order to find form.

"We changed last year to be better - you want to be better and you want to improve," he said. "Many things have been said that if I was half a yard quicker I'd be that much closer to hopefully getting an England call-up. That's what we went searching for.

"You could argue that we probably found it, but it was at the detriment to what I did naturally. I lost my height, I wasn't hitting the seam and I wasn't causing problems."

Harris has now re-modified his bowling action over the winter, culminating in his best bowling figures since his second first-class match for Glamorgan in 2007, aged just 17.

"We made a choice to go back. This is the type of bowler I have always been," he said. "I was never going to be express but I'm hopefully bowling at a decent enough pace and doing a bit with it.

"I said all the way through the summer so far that I had been bowling quite nicely but there was still something to click. I got in a nice rhythm and I'm thrilled. It has been a long wait to get another 10-for."

# Taliban Execute Woman in Public in Afghanistan's Jowzjan Province

A video showing the public execution of a woman by the Taliban has emerged on social media, officials confirmed on Wednesday. The footage, filmed one to two months ago in Jowzjan Province, shows a woman in a burqa sitting on the ground as a crowd listens to the verdict being read before she is shot in the back of the head.

The Taliban have not issued any statement regarding the incident, though similar killings in previous years have drawn widespread international condemnation.

Public executions of women were common practice during Taliban rule in the 1990s, when the group frequently carried out such punishments, typically for alleged adultery, in Kabul's main stadium.

These brutal practices have persisted in various forms since then. In 2012, a young woman was stoned to death in central Afghanistan's Ghor province on adultery charges. The previous year, both a woman and the man she had eloped with were stoned to death in Kunduz province's Dashte Archi district.

A Taliban spokesman defended the 2011 stoning at the time, stating that such punishment was prescribed in Islamic law and the Koran, dismissing critics as attempting to impose "foreign thinking" on Afghanistan.

Extrajudicial killings remain a serious problem throughout Afghanistan. In a high-profile case last March, Farkhunda Malikzada was brutally beaten and burned alive in downtown Kabul after being falsely accused of desecrating the Koran. Her murder sparked nationwide protests and international outrage over violence against Afghan women.

# Man Shot Dead in "Cold-Blooded Execution" at West Belfast Home

A father of one was killed in what police have described as a "cold-blooded, summary execution" at his home in west Belfast on Thursday evening.

Joe Reilly, 43, was shot multiple times in the chest and died at the scene at Glenwood Court in Poleglass. Two other people who were in the house at the time were forced to lie on the kitchen floor while the fatal shooting took place.

The incident, reported to police at approximately 20:15 BST on Thursday, marks the second shooting in the area in less than a week.

Detective Chief Inspector Peter Montgomery said the killing was almost beyond description. "It's really difficult to know how to describe what happened last night, the adjectives brutal, senseless and barbaric are inadequate," he said.

"This was a cold-blooded, summary execution of a man in his own house. At this early stage of my investigation I have no motive for Joe Reilly's murder and I will keep a completely open mind as to why has been killed."

DCI Montgomery confirmed that Mr Reilly was known to police and had a criminal record. He appealed for information about three children who were reportedly seen in the area as the gunmen fled the scene.

Neighbours who rushed to help on Thursday night described Mr Reilly as a quiet man who rarely left his home.

Sinn Féin MLA Jennifer McCann described "distressing scenes" as family members arrived at the police cordon. "This brutal killing has achieved nothing other than plunging another family into grief and despair," she said. "This is a good community and there's no support for this."

SDLP MLA Alex Attwood told Good Morning Ulster: "A gunman or gunmen turned up at a house and at least two shots were fired. The result is that one man is dead. His family are in deep distress and the community is tangibly shocked and shaken." He accused those responsible of "brutally undermining the rule of law."

Alliance MLA Trevor Lunn offered his "deepest condolences" to the family, adding: "This follows another shooting in the same area last week and has now left a family without a loved one through the evil actions of others."

People Before Profit Councillor Matt Collins said he was "deeply disturbed by this senseless and unjustifiable attack."

The murder follows a pattern of violence in the area. Last Sunday, a man was shot several times in the leg in a paramilitary-style attack in nearby Glenwood Drive. On Wednesday, another man was shot in the leg in Dungiven, County Londonderry.

Police have appealed for witnesses to come forward.

# Deadly Green Mamba Snake Euthanised After Discovery on Ship at Scottish Port

A highly venomous western green mamba snake discovered on a ship that had docked from west Africa on Wednesday has been destroyed due to health and safety concerns.

Workers aboard the vessel discovered the deadly reptile and secured it in a box before contacting animal welfare authorities. The snake was transported under police escort to a Scottish SPCA animal centre in Drumoak, Aberdeenshire.

Despite the safe capture, the SSPCA made the difficult decision to euthanise the snake after determining the nearest available anti-venom was located in London, posing significant risk to handlers and the public.

The western green mamba, native to coastal tropical rainforests of west Africa, preys on small animals and rodents. According to experts, its venomous bite can prove fatal to humans in as little as 30 minutes.

# Motorcyclist Dies After Collision in Penkridge

A motorcyclist has died following a collision between a Kawasaki motorbike and a Toyota Land Cruiser in Teddesley Road, Penkridge, at 17:40 BST on Monday.

Despite efforts by police officers, paramedics and doctors, the motorcyclist was confirmed dead after arriving at hospital by air ambulance, Staffordshire Police said.

The Toyota driver escaped injury in the crash, which closed the road for three hours.

Police have appealed for witnesses to come forward.

# Blackburn Rovers: Tommie Hoban Set for February Return from Injury

Blackburn Rovers manager Owen Coyle is hopeful that on-loan defender Tommie Hoban will return to action later this month.

The 22-year-old, who arrived from Watford in August, has been sidelined since mid-October after dislocating his shoulder during a training session, having made just 10 appearances for the club.

"He's got a meeting with the surgeon that did his operation and then hopefully he can get the all-clear," Coyle told the club website.

"To my mind I would love to have Tommie available from the middle of February towards the end of the month because that would add a real quality player."

Rovers currently sit 22nd in the Championship table, one point from safety, making Hoban's return potentially crucial to their survival bid.

# Franz Ferdinand to Headline Belladrum Festival in Scottish Highlands

Scottish rock band Franz Ferdinand will make their debut performance at the Belladrum Tartan Heart Festival, marking a significant moment for the Highland event.

The three-day festival, scheduled for 3-5 August 2017 near Beauly in the Scottish Highlands, has announced an impressive lineup. Franz Ferdinand will headline the closing night, supported by fellow Scottish artist KT Tunstall.

Adding to the star-studded bill, disco icons Sister Sledge will headline Thursday's opening night.

Festival promoter Joe Gibbs expressed his enthusiasm: "This is the first time Franz Ferdinand has played Bella and we are totally delighted to welcome them to our stage. I couldn't think of a better act to close out the festival."

Regarding Tunstall's return, Gibbs noted she previously appeared as an unannounced special guest but is now officially confirmed on the programme.

# Amber Heard and Johnny Depp Restraining Order Hearing Delayed

A Los Angeles judge has ruled that a hearing regarding actress Amber Heard's restraining order against Johnny Depp will begin on 17 August, two days later than originally scheduled, after determining the proceedings could take up to five days to complete.

Heard filed for divorce from Depp on 23 May and subsequently obtained a temporary restraining order after accusing the actor of repeatedly hitting her. If the court rules in her favour, the restraining order could be extended for up to five years.

Los Angeles Superior Court Judge Carl H Moor ruled on Tuesday that Heard should sit for a deposition on Friday, with Depp providing sworn testimony on Saturday. The judge determined that Depp—who has denied the abuse allegations through his lawyer—will not be permitted to attend Heard's deposition.

The couple met while co-starring in the 2011 film The Rum Diary and married in February 2015. Depp, 53, was ordered to maintain no contact with Heard, 30, and remain 100 yards away from her following her allegations that he struck her and threw a mobile phone during an argument in May.

# Airports Commission Extends Runway Consultation Over Air Pollution Concerns

Sir Howard Davies, chairman of the Airports Commission, has announced an extension to take additional evidence on air pollution issues before finalizing runway expansion recommendations.

The decision follows a Supreme Court ruling in April that mandated stronger UK action on air quality improvements.

The commission has already shortlisted three runway options: expansion at Heathrow or Gatwick airports. An immediate consultation period will run until Friday, 29 May.

The final report, originally scheduled for next month, faces potential delays due to this additional review process.

The Airports Commission launched its comprehensive inquiry three years ago, with publication deliberately postponed until after the general election to avoid politicization of the infrastructure decision.

# Quitongo Clinches Victory as Morton Edge Past Dunfermline

**Morton secured a dramatic 2-1 victory over Dunfermline Athletic in a hard-fought Scottish Championship encounter, with Jai Quitongo's spectacular late strike proving to be the decisive moment.**

The home side took an early lead through Gary Oliver, who displayed excellent individual skill to skip past a couple of challenges before driving a low shot past the Dunfermline goalkeeper. The opener gave Morton confidence and control in the opening exchanges at Cappielow Park.

However, Dunfermline showed their resilience and pulled level on the half-hour mark through somewhat fortunate circumstances. Callum Fordyce's shot was heading towards goal when Nicky Clark's deflection wrong-footed the Morton keeper and found the back of the net, restoring parity to the contest.

The match became increasingly fractious in the second half, with referee officials having to reach for their cards on multiple occasions. Ben Richards-Everton, Joe Cardle, Nicky Clark, Jamie McDonagh, Lewis Martin, and match-winner Quitongo all found their names in the book as tensions rose and challenges flew in.

Both managers made tactical changes in an attempt to find a winner. Dunfermline boss introduced Kallum Higginbotham and Farid El Alagui from the bench, replacing Michael Paton and Gavin Reilly respectively, while Morton brought on Scott Tiffoney for Aidan Nesbitt before late substitute Thomas Orr replaced the impressive Gary Oliver.

The Pars pushed forward in search of a winner, with Lee Ashcroft coming close with a header from a corner that missed the target. Goalkeeper Andy McNeil was also called into action to preserve Morton's chances of claiming all three points.

With time running out and a draw looking the likely outcome, Quitongo produced a moment of individual brilliance that settled the contest. Receiving the ball outside the box from Tiffoney, the Morton forward unleashed a powerful right-footed effort that crashed off the underside of the crossbar and into the net, sending the home fans into raptures.

Despite late pressure from the visitors, Morton held firm to secure all three points. The victory will provide a significant boost to their league ambitions, while Dunfermline will rue their inability to hold onto their equalizer and their failure to convert chances in the second period.

Gary Oliver's late effort that sailed high and wide summed up Morton's desperation to add a third, but Quitongo's stunning strike proved sufficient to seal a memorable victory for the Greenock side.

# Woodford Fund Scraps Bonuses in City Pay Shake-up

Star fund manager Neil Woodford has abolished bonuses at his investment firm, in an unusual move that challenges the City of London's long-held belief that performance-related pay is essential for motivating staff.

The 35 employees at Woodford Investment Management will instead receive increases to their basic salaries and benefits package to compensate for the loss of bonus payments.

Mr Woodford, who manages £14bn in assets, earned his reputation as one of Britain's most successful stock-pickers during his time at Invesco Perpetual. After launching his own boutique fund management business in 2014, he rapidly attracted significant investment from those hoping he would continue delivering the above-average returns that marked his Invesco career.

Craig Newman, chief executive and co-founder of Woodford Investment Management, explained the rationale behind the decision: "While bonuses are an established feature of the financial sector, Neil and I wanted to take the opportunity to do something different that supports the firm's culture and ethos of challenging the status quo."

Mr Newman cited extensive academic research suggesting bonuses fail as motivational tools, with employees coming to expect them as standard. "There is little correlation between bonus and performance," he said. "Many studies conclude that bonuses don't work as a motivator, as expectation is already built in. Behavioural studies also suggest that bonuses can lead to short-term decision making and wrong behaviours."

The financial crisis intensified scrutiny of City pay practices, particularly the link between remuneration and performance. Top fund managers can earn millions in performance-related bonuses.

However, critics of the no-bonus approach argue such incentives are crucial for retaining talented staff who might otherwise seek opportunities elsewhere. They also note that higher fixed salaries make it more difficult for firms to reduce costs during economic downturns.

The firm referenced research from The Journal of Corporation Law, which concluded: "Financial incentives are often counterproductive as they encourage gaming, fraud and other dysfunctional behaviours that damage the reputation and culture of the organisation."

# Philip Larkin's Hidden Talent: Poet's Photography Collection on Display at Hull University

An exhibition showcasing the photographic work of renowned poet Philip Larkin has opened at the University of Hull's Brynmor Jones Library, where he served as librarian for three decades.

The display reveals Larkin as an accomplished amateur photographer who captured nearly 6,000 images throughout his lifetime. The collection includes intimate portraits of female companions, friends, and self-portraits, alongside family photographs from his childhood and portraits of literary contemporaries.

The exhibition also features familiar scenes of Hull and the East Riding countryside, as well as various landscapes that inspired the celebrated poet's work.

University Librarian Dr Richard Heseltine described the collection as "a unique glimpse into Larkin's life, his interests and even subjects which informed some of his poems."

The exhibition, running until 23 December, coincides with the publication of a new book by Richard Bedford examining Larkin's photographic portfolio.

"It is an unmissable opportunity to come along to see another side of one of the most celebrated poets of our time," Dr Heseltine added, highlighting Larkin's significance to the university's cultural heritage.

# Welsh Drug Services Call for Action as Deaths Rise 50%

Drug support services in Wales are calling for urgent action after new figures revealed a dramatic 50% increase in drug-related deaths during 2015, reversing a five-year downward trend.

Drugaid Cymru has warned that all agencies involved must "get to grips" with the escalating problem, which comes amid concerns about increased heroin availability and purity on Welsh streets.

Ifor Glyn, regional director of Drugaid Cymru covering mid and south Wales, described the situation as a "massive issue" for both service providers and the Welsh Government.

"Deaths are likely to go up as there is a lot more heroin around, the purity of heroin has been stronger and there's a lot more people who are not known to the services," Mr Glyn explained. "We weren't able to engage with them. It's something that agencies like ourselves and across Wales have got to get to grips with."

Among the solutions proposed, Mr Glyn suggested recruiting drug users as informers to help services reach vulnerable individuals. More controversially, he renewed calls for introducing supervised "fix rooms" where users could take drugs under medical supervision.

The proposal follows approval in October for Britain's first such facility in Glasgow.

"Allowing people to inject in a room is highly controversial," Mr Glyn acknowledged. "I don't want to see people taking drugs but you've got to be pragmatic. There's tonnes of evidence supporting injecting rooms."

The Welsh Government currently allocates £50 million annually to its substance misuse delivery plan and is examining options to address the rising death toll between 2016 and 2018.

A government spokesman stated their priority was returning to falling death rates: "We are working closely with partners to evaluate the reasons behind the increase and to take action to address it.

"This includes working with the substance misuse area planning boards so that everything possible is done to reach those individuals currently not in touch with substance misuse services."

# Ivanka Trump Sparks Controversy After Briefly Sitting in for Father at G20 Summit

Ivanka Trump has faced widespread criticism after briefly taking her father's seat at a G20 summit table during a meeting with world leaders.

The US president had stepped away for a meeting with the Indonesian leader during the G20 meeting. Ms Trump is an adviser to her father, but a leader's absence is usually covered by high-ranking officials.

A BBC correspondent at the summit said he could recall no similar precedent.

There has been widespread criticism on social media.

## What Happened?

Mr Trump returned a short while later to retake his seat between the British prime minister and the Chinese president.

Ms Trump did not seem to make any major contribution to the session on African migration and health during her father's absence.

A photograph of her presence was tweeted by a Russian attendee, but later deleted.

## Social Media Backlash

Some users highlighted that Ms Trump is unelected, or questioned her credentials - as a fashion brand owner - to sit at such a senior diplomatic meeting.

Others lampooned her appearance among the world's most powerful leaders after her claim in an interview two weeks ago that she tries to "stay out of politics".

But her brother appeared to suggest there was nothing wrong and asked the "outraged left" if they would rather he sat in instead.

## Earlier G20 Appearance

Ms Trump had joined her father for an earlier G20 event on Saturday on women's entrepreneurship and finance, along with German Chancellor Angela Merkel and Christine Lagarde, director of the International Monetary Fund.

All three women had previously appeared together on a panel during the G20 women's summit in Berlin in April.

At that appearance she defended her father as a "tremendous champion of supporting families and enabling them to thrive".

Earlier on Saturday, Donald Trump said having him for a father was the only "bad thing" in Ms Trump's life.

"I'm very proud of my daughter, Ivanka - always have been, from day one," he told world leaders at the panel on female entrepreneurs. "If she weren't my daughter, it would be so much easier for her. Might be the only bad thing she has going, if you want to know the truth."

## Background

While her siblings, Donald Jr and Eric, took over the family business, Ms Trump put her own fashion brand assets in a trust in order to take an unpaid White House position, a move criticised as nepotism.

After a brief modelling career as a teenager, Ms Trump was given a job in her father's company. There, she expanded the Trump hotel brand and became an executive vice-president of development, alongside her siblings.

Ms Trump is married to Jared Kushner, who also plays in influential role in Donald Trump's White House.

# Monks Fear "Catastrophe" as New A96 Route Threatens Abbey Peace

Monks at Pluscarden Abbey near Elgin have expressed alarm over preliminary proposals for a new stretch of the A96 road between Forres and Fochabers, warning that routing the highway close to their centuries-old retreat would be disastrous for their contemplative way of life.

Brother Michael de Klerk described the community's shock at discovering the potential route. "We couldn't quite believe it, it seemed extraordinary," he told BBC Scotland. "If we are actually living by it, we would find it hard to absorb it, the noise would be day and night."

The monk emphasized the abbey's current tranquility: "The valley is quiet - you can hear a cow lowing. You would just hear a constant whirr of traffic."

Father Giles, a resident of over 40 years, cited European examples where transportation infrastructure has damaged monastic communities. "There are a lot of monasteries on the continent where they got railways running through and it has just destroyed the place," he said. "People come here for peace. Why destroy the peace here, it's just daft."

Transport Scotland stated it is in the early stages of route assessment and won't finalize the corridor option for two years. The agency plans community engagement throughout the process. The A96 upgrade aims to improve journey times and safety between Aberdeen and Inverness by 2030.

# Chisora Fined and Given Suspended Ban After Table-Throwing Incident

Dereck Chisora has been fined £25,000 and handed a two-year suspended ban following his shocking actions at Wednesday's press conference, where he threw a table at rival Derick Whyte.

The British Boxing Board of Control has imposed strict sanctions on the 32-year-old heavyweight, who must also pay £5,000 in costs. The two-year ban will only be activated if Chisora commits another offence during that period.

# Scottish League Cup Final to be Held at Celtic Park

The Scottish Professional Football League has confirmed that Celtic Park will host the League Cup final between Aberdeen and Inverness Caledonian Thistle on 16 March, with SPFL chief executive Neil Doncaster citing Rangers' fixture the previous day as the decisive factor in the venue selection.

With Hampden Park unavailable due to preparations for the Commonwealth Games, organisers faced a choice between Scotland's two other major stadiums. However, Rangers' scheduled match against Dunfermline at Ibrox on 15 March proved to be the "key determining factor" in ruling out that venue.

"Certainly with it being the first major final that Aberdeen have been in for some years and the first ever in Inverness's history, we're certainly expecting big interest from both teams," he said.

"Hopefully, there'll be many thousands of fans travelling from the north to enjoy it," he added.

Doncaster acknowledged that Glasgow is "blessed" with three stadia capable of holding over 50,000 spectators, though Hampden's unavailability limited options for this year's final.

Celtic Park will also host the Scottish Cup final in May, continuing its role as a major venue for Scottish football's showpiece occasions.

In a separate matter, Doncaster confirmed that Hearts are reviewing CCTV footage relating to an incident that led to Celtic manager Neil Lennon leaving Aberdeen's semi-final victory early at Tynecastle Stadium on Saturday.

# Abuse Inquiry: Ex-Derry care home resident tells of 'Taliban-like' treatment

A former resident of a Catholic children's home in Londonderry has described the treatment he received there as equivalent to being "reared by the Taliban".

The witness lived at St Joseph's in Termonbacca, Londonderry, in the 1950s. He said he became a zombie, introverted and fearing the next beating.

The Historical Abuse Inquiry is investigating abuse claims against children's residential institutions from 1922 to 1995. Termonbacca and another Derry home, Nazareth House, were run by the Sisters of Nazareth.

The former Termonbacca resident said he lay soaked in urine at night in an attempt to dissuade any sexual abusers.

The man, now 65, said he was never told he had brothers in the same home and sisters in another nearby.

He said he witnessed an eight-year-old boy being sexually abused, a 10-year-old boy being raped and that he had been hit on the head with a steel industrial ladle.

He said he complained about his treatment to a priest after leaving the home. The response was: "You must never speak about this, you must understand.... you and the other orphans are bastards. You are the product of an evil and satanic relationship. You never had a chance."

The witness said: "That was the day I left the Catholic Church."

He added: "The truth is setting me free today more than this commission knows. I have come here to tell the truth and as I am reaching out, I am reaching out in healing and trying to forgive, but at this moment I cannot.

"I have waited 65 years to say this. When I was reared by the Sisters of the Congregation of Nazareth it was equivalent to being reared by the Taliban, such was their sadism, their lack of empathy, their fundamentalism, their lack of dignity to the little helpless boy."

He said he ran away but was brought back time after time. One nun smirked and said: "Welcome back, your majesty," the witness said. "Then the beatings would start."

The inquiry, being held in Banbridge, County Down, is chaired by retired judge Sir Anthony Hart and is considering cases in 13 residential institutions.

Public hearings are due to finish in June 2015, with the inquiry team to report to the Northern Ireland Executive by the start of 2016.

# Kellingley Colliery: Miners Vote for Phased Closure of Yorkshire Pit

Miners at Kellingley Colliery have voted overwhelmingly in favour of an 18-month phased closure plan, the National Union of Mineworkers (NUM) has announced.

The ballot saw 79.9% of workers support the managed closure scheme, which was backed by a £10m government loan to UK Coal. The decision means the North Yorkshire pit will avoid an immediate shutdown that could have happened "within days" had workers rejected the proposal.

Chris Kitchen of the NUM acknowledged the difficulty of the decision, saying: "At least the men will not be made a scapegoat for closing Kellingley early. The men had hoped to keep the pit open for a longer term future. It's been a tough decision, it's not a nice thing to vote to put yourself or your workmates on the dole."

The ballot results showed 719 papers were issued with 658 returned. Of those, 575 voted for the scheme, 81 against, and two were spoiled. UK Coal counted non-returned and spoiled papers as "No" votes, making the final split approximately 80-20 in favour of closure.

The managed closure plan also affects Thoresby Colliery in Nottinghamshire. Business minister Michael Fallon had previously stated that both pits had no long-term future.

Andrew Mackintosh of UK Coal welcomed the result, saying: "The vote has been a great hurdle jumped over today, a good result I think. We were nervous before we went into it but the alternative to this was closure within a few days. So, difficult as this has been, it is the best option."

UK Coal will now report the ballot outcome to investors, including the government, to seek their acceptance of the result. Mr Mackintosh described it as "a significant vote, that's what the investors were looking for."

The phased closure will allow workers time to seek alternative employment and provides a more orderly wind-down than an immediate shutdown.

# Sri Lanka Elections: UNP Wins Majority as Rajapaksa's Comeback Bid Fails

Sri Lanka's United National Party (UNP) secured a decisive victory in Monday's parliamentary elections, winning 106 seats and effectively blocking former President Mahinda Rajapaksa's attempted political comeback.

While Mr Rajapaksa successfully won his parliamentary seat, the election results confine him to the opposition benches, dashing his hopes of leveraging electoral support to force President Maithripala Sirisena into naming him prime minister.

The political dynamic is complicated by the fact that both Mr Rajapaksa and Mr Sirisena belong to the UPFA, though they lead rival factions within the alliance. Mr Sirisena's supporters are expected to join the UNP in forming a national unity government.

The UNP is also expected to secure support from smaller parties, including the Tamil National Alliance, which won 16 seats, and the leftist JVP, which secured six seats.

# Iranians Celebrate Nuclear Deal as Historic Agreement Emerges

The Iranian capital experienced an unusual quiet Thursday night as news of a breakthrough nuclear agreement began to surface, according to Thomas Erdbrink of the New York Times. # British Victim of Tunisia Beach Attack Named as Stuart Cullen

A British man killed in the terrorist attack at a Tunisian beach resort has been identified as Stuart Cullen, 52, from the Lowestoft area in Suffolk.

# "Black Widow" Serial Killer Sentenced to Death in Japan

**SAITAMA, Japan** — A Japanese court has sentenced Kanae Kijima, 37, to death for the murders of three men she met through internet dating sites, in a case that has captivated the nation.

## Varoufakis Reveals Contingency Plans

The talks come as it emerged former finance minister Yanis Varoufakis told a group of investors in London that a five-man team under his leadership worked on a contingency plan to create euro liquidity if the European Central Bank (ECB) cut off emergency funding to the Greek financial system.

Greek newspaper Kathimerini reported Mr Varoufakis as saying in a phone call that a small team in the governing Syriza party had prepared plans to secretly copy online tax codes. It said the "Plan B" was devised to allow the government to introduce a parallel payment system if the banking system was closed down, which would have seen the return of the drachma.

Mr Varoufakis said passwords used by Greeks to access their online tax accounts were to have been copied secretly and used to issue new Pin numbers for every taxpayer to be used in transactions with the state.

"This would have created a parallel banking system, which would have given us some breathing space, while the banks would have been shut due to the ECB's aggressive policy," Mr Varoufakis was quoted as saying.

In the same phone call, Mr Varoufakis accused German Finance Minister Wolfgang Schaeuble of being "hell-bent" on ensuring Greece left the eurozone.

He added that while the government had a Plan B, the difficulty was "to go from the five people who were planning it to the 1,000 people that would have to implement it".

# Syrian Refugees Stranded at Jordan Border with Limited Aid Access, Rights Group Reports

AMMAN — Hundreds of Syrian refugees remain trapped in makeshift camps just inside Jordan's border with severely restricted access to food, water, and medical assistance, according to a new report by Human Rights Watch (HRW).

The international rights organization acknowledged that Jordan has made significant efforts to assist Syrians fleeing their country's brutal civil war, but emphasized that "this is no excuse to abandon newer arrivals" in remote border locations.

The Jordanian government has maintained that it "continues to adopt an open-border policy," even as it hosts approximately 630,000 of the nearly four million Syrians registered as refugees with the United Nations. Jordanian officials say the actual number of Syrians in the country totals 1.4 million, including those who arrived before the 2011 uprising against President Bashar al-Assad.

According to HRW, Jordanian authorities have progressively tightened entry restrictions over the past two years. Two informal desert crossings in eastern Jordan—Rukban and Hadalat—have become the primary entry points for most Syrian refugees. However, Jordan has heavily restricted access at these crossings since July 2014.

Recent satellite imagery analyzed by HRW revealed approximately 175 makeshift tent shelters at Rukban and 68 at Hadalat, suggesting the presence of hundreds of refugees. Aid agencies estimated that roughly 2,500 people were stranded at these locations in mid-April, though an international aid worker reported this number had decreased to about 1,000 by late May after Jordanian border guards permitted some to leave the border zone.

"Jordan has gone to great lengths to meet the needs of Syrian refugees," said Nadim Houry, HRW's deputy Middle East and North Africa director. "But that is no excuse to abandon newer arrivals in remote border areas for weeks without effective protection and regular aid access."

The report also documented at least one case of immediate deportation, with a Syrian taken to the Raba Sarhan registration center and returned to Syria without being registered. HRW warned that such summary returns could constitute refoulement, violating international law prohibiting the return of individuals to areas where they face persecution risks.

A Jordanian government spokesman responded by reaffirming the country's commitment to maintaining open-border procedures coordinated with international organizations.

# Ding Junhui Makes 147 Break Despite Loss to Neil Robertson

Chinese snooker star Ding Junhui produced a magnificent maximum 147 break during his quarter-final defeat to Neil Robertson at a ranking event, setting a new personal milestone despite ultimately losing the match 5-2.
