# Belfast Giants Dominate Edinburgh Capitals with Emphatic Victory

The Belfast Giants delivered a commanding performance at Murrayfield Ice Rink, overwhelming the Edinburgh Capitals in a one-sided contest that saw them net six goals in a devastating opening period.

Colin Shields led the onslaught with an impressive hat-trick completed within the first 14 minutes. Dustin Whitecotton contributed two goals in the opening frame, with Jeff Mason also finding the net before the period concluded.

The Giants had already established a 4-0 lead when Curtis Leinweber managed Edinburgh's consolation goal in the 13th minute. Jade Portwood scored the only goal of the second period, but the match was effectively decided. Whitecotton sealed his own hat-trick with a final-period strike.

The victory, combined with Dundee Stars' 5-6 home defeat to Sheffield Steelers, extends Belfast's league lead to 17 points. Sheffield now sits level with Dundee and Braehead on 41 points following the latter's 3-0 win over Hull.

The triumph caps a perfect weekend for Paul Adey's side, following Saturday's 3-1 victory in Sheffield.

# Saoirse Ronan Wins Big at British Independent Film Awards for Brooklyn

Irish actress Saoirse Ronan cemented her status as a leading Oscar contender after winning best actress at the British Independent Film Awards (Bifas) for her performance in Brooklyn.

The Irish actress, who plays a young Irish immigrant, is widely tipped to get an Oscar nomination next year. Picking up the award at Sunday night's ceremony in London, Ronan revealed that she had met the film's producers at the same awards two years ago.

"Brooklyn began at the Bifas for me," she said.

In the film she plays Eilis Lacey, a young woman from rural Ireland in the 1950s, who has to leave her home to find job opportunities and a future in the US.

For Ronan herself the film was particularly personal. Her parents were migrants to the US in the 1980s and she was later born in New York.

"I got an amazing role to play. I was given the opportunity to honour a journey and a story that's very close to me," she said during her acceptance speech.

Ronan beat Carey Mulligan, Marion Cotillard, Charlotte Rampling and Alicia Vikander to win the best actress prize.

Speaking backstage, she said the film had achieved a "universality" since its release. "A lot of people related to it because everyone's left home and felt that way."

She added that Irish actors and directors were having a great year. "It's really important to represent home for me. I think we've got a nation of really terrific storytellers, we always have done, and that's kind of our culture and our roots."

## Other Winners

Other acting winners included Tom Hardy who won best actor for his dual role as Ronnie and Reggie Kray in Legend. Olivia Colman won her third Bifa for her best supporting actress performance in The Lobster.

Brendan Gleeson won best supporting actor for Suffragette, having won last year's best actor prize for Calvary. Gleeson's prize was picked up in his absence by his son Domhnall, who was nominated in the same category for his role in Brooklyn.

Sci-fi thriller Ex Machina was the big winner of the night with four awards, including best British independent film. It also won best director and best screenplay for Alex Garland and outstanding achievement in craft for its visual effects.

Ex Machina producer Andrew Macdonald told the BBC backstage that the technology and the visual effects had allowed the film-makers to tell "a human story."

Kidnap drama Room was named best international independent film. Jacob Tremblay, the nine-year-old star of the film, collected the award with director Lenny Abrahamson.

As previously announced, Kate Winslet received the Variety Award for helping "to focus the international spotlight on the UK". Picking up the award, the Oscar-winning actress said: "In spite of some Titanic moments, independent film is where I have learnt the most and laughed the most."

The Richard Harris Award for outstanding contribution to British film was presented to Chiwetel Ejiofor.

The full list of winners is on the Bifas website.

# Two New Dinosaur Species Discovered in Montana

Paleontologists have announced the discovery of two new dinosaur species, with one nicknamed "Judith" after the Judith River rock formation in Montana where it was found.

The dinosaur's official name is Spiclypeus shipporum. Experts believe Judith measured approximately 4.5 metres long and featured distinctive large horns protruding sideways over its eyes, along with spikes pointing in various directions at the back of its head.

The second discovery, Machairoceratops, was nearly twice Judith's size. This dinosaur possessed two prominent spikes extending from the back of its head, horns above its eyes, and possibly a nose horn.

Both species were relatives of the famous Triceratops and were four-legged, herbivorous creatures. Scientists estimate these magnificent beasts roamed the Earth over 75 million years ago.

# Paulton Honors WWI Hero with Victoria Cross Commemoration

A Somerset village is preparing to honor its most distinguished military hero, Lance Sergeant Oliver Brooks, who was awarded the Victoria Cross for extraordinary bravery during World War One.

The commemoration will take place in Paulton, where Brooks was born, marking his courageous actions at the Battle of Loos, France, on 8 October 1915. The event will include a church service and the laying of a commemorative plaque near the village's war memorial.

Paulton Parish Council chairman Les Wild emphasized the local significance of the honor: "Oliver Brooks was the only person in the Bath and North East Somerset area to get a Victoria Cross."

More than 50 of Brooks' relatives are traveling from across the country to attend the ceremony, which will also involve local schoolchildren. Mr Wild stressed the importance of preserving this history: "We shouldn't allow future generations to forget what happened and I think it's important we're involving school children as well and local people so they almost see a bit of history that went on in Paulton."

Lance Sergeant Brooks served with the 3rd Battalion, Coldstream Guards. His Victoria Cross citation described how he single-handedly led a bombing party to recapture 200 yards of trenches seized by German forces. The citation praised his "absolute fearlessness, presence of mind and promptitude" during the assault conducted under heavy enemy fire.

The plaque is part of a nationwide initiative honoring World War One Victoria Cross recipients. Following the ceremony, a civic reception will be held for attending family members, ensuring Brooks' legacy of courage continues to inspire future generations.

# Leicester Tigers: Richard Cockerill Signs New Five-Year Deal as Director of Rugby

Leicester Tigers director of rugby Richard Cockerill has committed his future to the club by signing a new five-year contract, despite reported interest from French club Clermont Auvergne.

Cockerill, 42, was strongly linked with a move to France with Clermont Auvergne reportedly keen for him to replace Vern Cotter, who is becoming Scotland coach at the end of the season.

He told BBC Radio Leicester: "There has been interest from other places. But for me it's about security for myself and my family."

He added: "I talk about loyalty the whole time to players and other coaches and staff here. It's all right for me to preach that but it's important that I practice that as well."

The former England hooker emphasized that his decision was not financially motivated: "It's not always about finances. It's about where you are happy, it's about what you are as a person and all those things and the emotional attachment to what you do."

Cockerill joined Leicester Tigers in 1992 and played 262 games, winning five league titles, two domestic cups and two Heineken Cups. The 42-year-old won 27 caps for England during his playing career.

Cockerill left Welford Road to play in France in 2002 but returned as an academy coach in 2005. He has been in charge since 2009 following two separate spells as acting head coach and has led Tigers to three Premiership titles, five Premiership finals and a Heineken Cup final.

Despite only signing a three-year contract last summer, Cockerill is thrilled to be extending his stay at Welford Road.

"The club have been very supportive," he said. "They were comfortable with what I was doing and I am happy to stay. My record speaks for itself. I care about what I do. I get paid to do a job but it's something I would do anyway.

"I am grateful for their support. That stability is great because it keeps everybody on an even keel."

Reflecting on his journey with the club, Cockerill added: "I think I have proved I am the right person. I came through as a player and started as an academy coach and I have ended up as director of rugby. But I have had to prove myself on the way. It's been a great eight or nine years and hopefully that will continue for another five."

# Visa delays threaten Llangollen International Music Eisteddfod performers

The renowned Llangollen International Music Eisteddfod is facing significant challenges after being inadvertently excluded from a crucial Home Office list of permit-free festivals, causing severe delays in visa processing for international performers.

The administrative oversight means competitors must undergo lengthier visa application procedures, with several participants from China, Algeria, Tanzania and Ivory Coast already facing rejection. Over 100 dancers and musicians from multiple countries remain uncertain about their participation in this year's festival, scheduled for 7 July.

Clwyd South MP Susan Elan Jones has intervened, writing directly to the home secretary requesting urgent government assistance. She confirmed that Home Office officials have acknowledged the error in correspondence with eisteddfod organisers.

Merle Hunt, the eisteddfod's competitors liaison officer, explained that inclusion on the permit-free list is vital as it "confirms they're coming for bona fide reasons," streamlining the visa process considerably.

The annual celebration, first established in Llangollen in 1947, traditionally welcomes performers from approximately 50 nations. Currently awaiting visa decisions are two groups from India, five from Morocco, 14 dancers from Ghana and five from Nepal, among others.

The Home Office has been approached for comment on the matter.

# Rare Welsh Whisky Bottles Fetch Over £14,000 at Auction

Two exceptionally rare bottles of Welsh whisky have sold for a combined total of more than £14,000 at a Carmarthen auction house, far exceeding expectations.

The bottles from the historic Welsh Whisky Distillery Company were auctioned by Peter Francis Auctioneers, selling for £7,300 and £7,200 respectively to private collectors. Both bottles date back to approximately 1900.

Auctioneer Charles Hampshire expressed delight at the results: "We're thrilled that a lot of people got involved in it - the sale has done exceptionally well." The bottles had been estimated to fetch around £3,000 each, but Mr Hampshire acknowledged the difficulty in valuation, noting "it was almost impossible to put a figure on it because there's nothing to compare it to."

The Welsh Whisky Distillery Company operated in Frongoch, Bala, Gwynedd, from its founding in 1889 until closure in the early 20th Century. The distillery site later served as a World War One prison camp and, more notably, an internment camp following the Easter Rising in Ireland.

These particular bottles were purchased by a Fishguard wine merchant in the 1960s for just £5 each, having been in the original family's possession since 1914.

Only a handful of these bottles are known to exist today, with examples on display at Penderyn Distillery and Cardiff's St Fagans National History Museum. Another was previously auctioned in Cardiff in 2001.

Mr Hampshire revealed that one bottle will return to Wales near the original distillery location, calling it "a nice finish, particularly for one of them."

# Wales Coach Gatland Challenges North to Reach Full Potential Despite Impressive Career

Northampton Saint George North will be 23 years and 138 days old when he takes the field at Dublin's Aviva Stadium, carrying the weight of immense expectations alongside his impressive rugby resume. With 22 international tries and three Lions Test appearances already to his name, the Welsh wing has achieved more than most players accomplish in an entire career. Yet Wales coach Warren Gatland believes North's best rugby still lies ahead.

North's upcoming appearance marks his return after a five-month absence due to concussion recovery. His last outing in a Wales jersey showcased his undeniable talent—a hat-trick against Italy in the 2015 Six Nations. He also impressed during the 2013 British and Irish Lions tour to Australia, scoring twice in the Test series.

Despite these highlights, Gatland has identified areas requiring improvement, particularly North's tendency to drift out of matches. "Players of that ability need to get their hands on the ball," the coach explained. "He probably went through a couple of campaigns where his touches weren't enough, and he made some defensive errors."

Gatland, who first selected North for international duty as an 18-year-old against South Africa in 2010, remains deeply impressed by his protégé's achievements. # Church of England Appoints Eighth Female Bishop for Sherborne Diocese

The Church of England has announced Archdeacon Gorham as the new Bishop of Sherborne, becoming the eighth female bishop in the denomination's history.

The Bishop of Sherborne serves within the Diocese of Salisbury, primarily overseeing parishes throughout Dorset. Archdeacon Gorham expressed gratitude for her time serving the church in Buckinghamshire and working in the Diocese of Oxford, calling it "a real privilege."

She succeeds the Right Reverend Graham Kings, who departed the position in July. Looking ahead, Archdeacon Gorham said: "I now look forward to getting to know the people and places of Dorset, an area I have loved since childhood holidays."

The Bishop of Salisbury, the Right Reverend Nicholas Holtam, praised the appointment, stating that Archdeacon Gorham "emerged as the right person for this post from a company of excellent men and women considered equally."

The consecration ceremony will take place on 24 February at Westminster Abbey, marking another milestone for women's leadership in the Church of England.

# Historic Wedgwood Vase Campaign Receives Major Boost as Deadline Extended

A campaign to save an historic Wedgwood vase for Stoke-on-Trent has received a significant boost with a £90,000 grant from Art Fund, extending the fundraising deadline.

The First Day's Vase, created on the opening day of Josiah Wedgwood's Etruria factory in the 18th Century, had been on long-term loan to The Potteries Museum & Art Gallery. However, its owner withdrew the piece and sold it to an overseas buyer at auction last year, prompting urgent action from the city council.

The Friends of the Potteries Museum & Art Gallery are leading efforts to raise £482,500 to purchase the vase and secure its permanent display in the city. The campaign has already gathered momentum, with £83,000 raised including a £60,000 grant from Arts Council England.

Art Fund's £90,000 contribution has proved crucial, enabling an extension of the original Tuesday deadline to 14 July. This follows a temporary export ban placed on the vase by the government in December, which has also been extended.

The vase holds exceptional historical significance as one of only four surviving pieces made by Wedgwood on Etruria's first day of operation. The Victoria and Albert Museum owns two of the other vases, whilst the fourth remains with the Wedgwood family.

Campaigners continue their efforts to keep this important piece of local heritage in Stoke-on-Trent.

# US Spy Allegations Rock Brazil and Mexico as NSA Surveillance Exposed

Brazil and Mexico are demanding answers following explosive allegations that the United States National Security Agency (NSA) spied on their presidents' communications, according to reports broadcast on Brazilian television.

Rio-based American journalist Glenn Greenwald made the startling revelations during a programme on TV Globo on Sunday evening, citing secret documents obtained from former US intelligence contractor Edward Snowden. The claims have sparked diplomatic tensions and raised serious questions about US surveillance activities in Latin America.

According to the report, the NSA not only intercepted communications between aides of Brazilian President Dilma Rousseff but also deployed sophisticated programmes to monitor all internet content accessed by the president herself. The allegations suggest extensive and intrusive surveillance of Brazil's highest office.

Mr Greenwald, who writes for the British Guardian newspaper, told the Fantastico news programme that classified documents revealed systematic spying on Brazilian government communications. The report also alleges that Mexican President Enrique Pena Nieto was targeted by US intelligence, with his emails reportedly being read even before his election in July 2012, according to documents dating from June of that year.

Brazil's response was swift, with US Ambassador to Brazil Thomas Shannon summoned briefly to the Brazilian foreign ministry to explain the allegations. The ambassador declined to speak to reporters following the meeting, and the foreign ministry has yet to issue an official statement.

Brazilian Justice Minister Jose Eduardo Cardozo expressed strong concern over the allegations, stating: "If these facts prove to be true, it would be unacceptable and could be called an attack on our country's sovereignty." President Rousseff's office confirmed she was meeting with top ministers to discuss the situation.

A spokesman for the Mexican foreign ministry acknowledged seeing the report but offered no immediate comment. The BBC's Julia Carneiro in Sao Paulo suggests the suspected motivation for the alleged surveillance relates to Brazil's significant economic influence and substantial commercial interests at stake.

The revelations come as Mr Greenwald continues to publish stories based on documents leaked by Edward Snowden, who was granted temporary asylum in Russia after exposing secret US and UK surveillance programmes. Mr Greenwald was the first journalist to publish Snowden's leaked documents on 6 June.

The case has already generated international controversy, particularly following the nine-hour detention of Mr Greenwald's partner, David Miranda, at London's Heathrow Airport last month. Mr Greenwald condemned the detention as "bullying" and an attempt at "intimidation" against those working on the NSA revelations.

The British government defended the detention, stating police were right to act when they believed someone possessed "highly sensitive stolen information."

# Alton Towers Crash Victim Shares Hopeful Photo After Amputation

The teenager was seated on the front row when the ride collided with an empty carriage on 2 June, leaving 16 passengers trapped for up to four-and-a-half hours. In addition to losing her leg above the knee, Miss Washington also suffered a fractured hand.

Her recent photograph, showing herself surrounded by 15 supporters, received hundreds of likes from well-wishers on social media.

The teenager attended the theme park with her 18-year-old boyfriend Joe Pugh, who sustained shattered knees and hand injuries.

Merlin Entertainment Group, Alton Towers' parent company, has confirmed that all 16 passengers will receive compensation. Legal representatives for eight victims revealed that interim payments were distributed in late June to support rehabilitation efforts.

# Why do people willingly pay for pain? Study examines Tough Mudder phenomenon

Cardiff University academics have investigated why millions voluntarily subject themselves to the grueling Tough Mudder obstacle course, despite its deliberately painful design and serious injury risks.

The extreme endurance event, which features obstacles including electric wires delivering 10,000-volt shocks, has attracted 2.5 million participants worldwide—even though injuries have ranged from strokes and heart attacks to fatalities.

Dr. Rebecca Scott of Cardiff Business School highlighted a striking paradox: "Consumers spend billions of dollars every year on pain relief, while exhausting and painful experiences such as obstacle races and ultra-marathons are gaining in popularity."

The international research collaboration, involving Cardiff, Singapore's Nanyang Business School, and France's Kedge Business School, uncovered several motivations behind this trend. Researchers found that pain helps office workers combat physical inactivity and allows participants to "rediscover the nature of their body."

Additionally, the study revealed that pain "facilitates escape" from modern life pressures, providing "temporary relief from the burdens of self-awareness."

Professor Bernard Cova of Kedge Business School explained: "Electric shocks and ice-cold water may be painful but they also allow participants to escape from the demands and anxieties of modern life."

He added that these experiences help people create "the story of a fulfilled life spent exploring the limits of the body," with marks and wounds serving as tangible reminders of achievement.

# South Sudan Hold Sudan to Draw, Move Closer to Quarter-Finals

South Sudan's defensive tactics paid dividends as they held on for a point against their northern neighbors Sudan in the CECAFA Cup on Wednesday. After beating Djibouti 2-0 in their opening Group C game on Monday, the result puts South Sudan in a strong position to qualify for the quarter-finals of the tournament.

The draw leaves Sudan in third place behind their southern neighbors with just a single point so far, after they lost 2-1 to Malawi in their first match.

Guest team Malawi top the group and have already qualified for the last eight after brushing aside Djibouti 3-0. Yaboh Idriss Moussa missed several chances for Djibouti before Gerald Phiri converted a penalty for Malawi, with John Banda and Chiukepo Msowoya securing the victory.

In other Wednesday fixtures, defending champions Kenya and Burundi settled for a 1-1 draw, while hosts Ethiopia recovered from their opening loss to Rwanda by beating Somalia 2-0 in front of a capacity crowd.

# Fatal Stabbing at Dublin Flat Complex Under Investigation

A man has died following a stabbing at the Oliver Bond flat complex in Dublin 8 on Sunday morning, police have confirmed.

The victim was initially transported to St James's Hospital for emergency treatment but succumbed to his injuries. A post-mortem examination is scheduled for later Sunday to determine the exact cause of death.

The incident is part of a violent weekend in Dublin. Separately, a man remains in critical condition after being stabbed at a bonfire on Dromheath Drive, Mulhuddart, on Saturday night.

In another attack on Sunday morning, a man was hospitalized in serious condition following a stabbing on Templeview Avenue, Clarehall. Two additional men sustained minor injuries in that incident.

Police investigations are ongoing.

# UK Government Confirms Driverless Lorry Trials Following Budget Announcement

The government has officially confirmed that "lorry platooning" trials will proceed on UK motorways, following speculation earlier in March about tests on a quiet stretch of the M6 in Cumbria.

The innovative scheme involves convoys of heavy goods vehicles travelling in formation, with only the lead lorry requiring a driver. The announcement, made in Wednesday's Budget, forms part of the government's ambition to establish the UK as "a global centre for excellence in connected and autonomous vehicles".

Additionally, the government revealed plans for driverless car trials on British roads by 2017, joining companies like Ford and Google who have been testing autonomous vehicles, primarily in California.

However, the proposals have attracted criticism from motoring experts. Edmund King, president of the AA, raised concerns about the UK's motorway infrastructure. "The problem with the UK motorway network is that we have more entrances and exits of our motorways than any other motorways in Europe or indeed the world," he stated.

King questioned how a 44-tonne, 10-lorry platoon would operate practically, noting that "other vehicles need to get past the platoon to enter or exit the road."

The Budget also included various other technology-related initiatives as the government pushes forward with its autonomous vehicle strategy.

# Youth Reoffending Falls to Lowest Level in 15 Years, New Report Shows

A comprehensive report on criminal reconviction rates has revealed encouraging trends, with reoffending among young offenders dropping significantly over the past decade.

The study shows that a third of criminals under 21 went on to commit further offences in 2012-13, representing a 9.4% decrease from peak levels recorded in 1997-98. Among 21 to 25-year-olds, there was an even more dramatic fall of 28% in reconviction rates over the past ten years.

The overall reconviction rate has fallen by one percentage point for 2012-13, with the report noting: "Between 2003-04 and 2012-13, the reconviction rate has fallen by 4.1 percentage points from 32.7 to 28.6, and the average number of reconvictions has fallen by 18% from 0.62 to 0.51."

The data revealed that people convicted of dishonesty crimes were most likely to reoffend, while those who committed sexual offences had the lowest reconviction rates. These reductions coincide with falling crime numbers recorded by police since 2004-05.

However, the report highlighted concerning patterns in short-term imprisonment effectiveness. People imprisoned for three months or less had a 60% reconviction rate, compared to just 10.1% for those serving more than four years. Those given drug treatment and testing orders (DTTOs) showed the highest average number of reconvictions.

"Those that commit relatively low-level crimes but in high volumes are more likely to be reconvicted, and are more likely to get short custodial sentences," the report explained.

Offenders under 21 had the highest reconviction rate at 33% in 2012-13. Men were more likely to reoffend than women, and just under a third of people given community payback orders went on to commit further offences.

# Trump Opens DC Hotel as Celebrity Chef Campaigns Against Him

Donald Trump mixed business with politics Wednesday at the ribbon-cutting ceremony for his Trump International Hotel in Washington DC, but one name was conspicuously absent from the glittering affair – celebrity chef Jose Andres, who was instead campaigning for Hillary Clinton in Florida.

The Democratic nominee enjoyed multiple celebrations throughout the day. "Donald Trump has changed us, we're different as a result." He noted that the newspaper had been forced to use the word "liar" in a headline for the first time.

# AC/DC Guitarist Malcolm Young Diagnosed with Dementia

Malcolm Young, the legendary rhythm guitarist and co-founder of rock band AC/DC, has been diagnosed with dementia, his family has confirmed. His nephew, Stevie Young, will replace him on rhythm guitar for both the new recordings and the planned world tour next year.

# Ex-Rotherham Mayor Barry Dodson Faces Historical Sex Assault Trial

A former mayor of Rotherham is on trial accused of sexually assaulting a 13-year-old girl nearly three decades ago.

The trial continues.

# Nick Clegg Loses Sheffield Hallam Seat in Major Election Upset

In one of the most stunning results of Thursday's general election, Nick Clegg has lost his Sheffield Hallam constituency to Labour's Jared O'Mara, ending the former deputy prime minister's 12-year tenure representing the area.

Mr Clegg, who had held the seat since 2005 with a majority of 2,353 in the 2015 election, was defeated by first-time MP Mr O'Mara in what represents a significant personal blow to the former Liberal Democrat leader.

The loss comes as exit polls suggest the Liberal Democrats will secure 14 seats overall - an improvement on the eight seats won in 2015, but still far below their historical strength. Mr Clegg led the party into coalition government with the Conservatives in 2010, becoming deputy prime minister to David Cameron when the Lib Dems held 57 seats. That arrangement proved electorally disastrous, with the party's representation collapsing to just eight MPs in 2015.

With Thursday's election producing another hung parliament and the Conservatives emerging as the largest party without a majority, senior Liberal Democrat figures have been quick to rule out any repeat of the coalition arrangement. The party's press office tweeted emphatically that there would be "no coalition" and "no deals."

Former leader Sir Menzies Campbell told the BBC he would be "astonished" if current leader Tim Farron joined with the Tories for a second coalition or formed a "progressive alliance" with Labour. He explained the harsh lessons learned from the previous coalition: "The major party gets the credit for everything that is done and the junior party takes the blame for the things people don't like."

Sir Menzies argued that Theresa May's commitment to a hard Brexit made any alliance impossible, saying Mr Farron "could not take the party with him, nor any of the over 100,000 membership" in supporting such a position. However, he was equally critical of Jeremy Corbyn's Brexit approach, which he said "frankly almost defies definition."

Former Lib Dem leader Paddy Ashdown observed that Britain "is more polarised than ever in my lifetime" and declared it "REALLY time now for the centre to get its act together." He also told ITV News that Mrs May had "lost all credibility" during the election campaign.

Baroness Lynne Featherstone warned on Sky News: "If the exit poll is right we'll have a government of chaos."

# McKibbin Wins by Two Strokes at Palm Beach Gardens

# Kiddisave Customers Left Without Prams Despite Paying Hundreds

Dozens of customers who paid for baby equipment from Kiddisave have been left empty-handed after the company ceased trading, leaving families devastated just weeks before Christmas.

Kay Possard, of WP Mayfield insolvency practitioners, confirmed she expected to be formally appointed as liquidator at a directors' meeting scheduled for 3 December. The firm has remained unavailable for comment regarding the situation.

Among those affected is Chloe Khan, 27, from Dudley, who paid an £878 deposit towards goods totalling £1,756, including a double buggy for twins she is expecting within the next fortnight. The mother of an 18-month-old son said she has received nothing and feels "devastated" by the situation.

Now facing the imminent arrival of her twins, Miss Khan finds herself with "no money and no pram."

# Welsh Farmer Convicted in Landmark DNA Case Over Stolen Sheep

A Welsh farmer has been convicted of sheep theft in a groundbreaking case that used DNA testing to prove his guilt, marking the first time such evidence has been employed in Wales for livestock crime.

Andrew Thomas, 39, from Garnant, pleaded guilty at Swansea Crown Court after DNA tests revealed that lambs born to stolen ewes had been fathered by rams belonging to the victim, Alan Price of Derwydd near Llandybie.

The case began when approximately 50 sheep were stolen from Mr Price's land in Carmarthenshire. Two weeks later, Thomas attempted to sell 18 sheep at Llanybydder market, but mart officials and local farmers grew suspicious after noticing the animals' earmarks had been tampered with.

Judge Geraint Walters praised the farming community for pulling together "to defeat those who seek to deceive it." He sentenced Thomas to eight months imprisonment, suspended for two years, and ordered him to pay £1,000 compensation.

The judge told Thomas he had "caused a great deal of hurt" by stealing from those he worked alongside, warning it would be "a long time before they forgave him."

Dyfed-Powys Police confirmed this landmark prosecution demonstrates the force's commitment to tackling rural crime using cutting-edge forensic techniques.

# Warrington Wolves' Ben Currie Faces Nine-Month Injury Layoff After ACL Tear

Warrington Wolves forward Ben Currie is facing up to nine months on the sidelines after suffering a severe knee injury during Friday's Super League match against Wigan Warriors.

The 22-year-old tore his anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) off the bone while scoring a try in Warrington's 35-28 home defeat. He was immediately sent to London for surgical repair, which will involve grafting the ligament back onto the bone.

The injury is particularly disappointing timing for Currie, whose impressive form this season had him widely tipped for England selection in the upcoming Four Nations tournament.

# Pig on M62 Causes Hour-Long Closure Near Leeds

A seven-week-old piglet brought traffic to a standstill on the M62 motorway after escaping from a moving vehicle on Tuesday evening.

Highways England reported the unusual incident occurred between junctions 28 and 29, south of Leeds, at approximately 19:00 BST near Tingley. Both carriageways were closed at 19:20 while authorities worked to recover the wandering animal.

The West Yorkshire Police Dogs unit was deployed to assist in capturing the porcine escapee. The operation resulted in significant disruption, with a 3.5-mile queue forming eastbound and a 1.8-mile tailback westbound.

After more than an hour of closure, the motorway reopened at around 20:30 BST. West Yorkshire Police Road Policing Unit later confirmed via Twitter that the piglet had been safely reunited with its owner.

# Top IS Aide Reportedly Killed in Iraq Air Strike

Iraq's defence ministry has announced the death of a senior aide to Islamic State leader Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi in an air strike on Mosul, though the claim remains unconfirmed. The development comes as IS fighters reportedly kidnapped 40 men from a northern Iraqi town.

According to Iraqiya TV, defence officials confirmed that Abu Alaa al-Iraqi, head of the IS military council in Tal Afar, was killed in the air strike. Initial reports on social media had suggested al-Baghdadi himself was the target of a separate strike on Mosul, but the defence ministry later clarified that intelligence indicated a senior aide was killed instead.

The strikes come amid ongoing military operations against IS positions that began in August when US forces started conducting air strikes after the group seized several northern Iraqi cities. It remains unclear whether the latest strikes were carried out by US or Iraqi forces.

The Islamic State has taken control of vast territories across Iraq and Syria in recent months. Amnesty International has accused the group of "systematic ethnic cleansing," including mass killings of ethnic and religious minorities. Human Rights Watch has also reported discovering new sites of mass killings in Tikrit.

The situation escalated further when President Barack Obama vowed to destroy IS following the release of a video showing the beheading of American journalist Steven Sotloff. The group has carried out multiple beheadings, including that of US journalist James Foley and several Kurdish fighters.

Iraqi security forces, supported by Kurdish and Shia fighters, have recently launched offensives against IS-controlled towns. While they have successfully pushed IS out of several areas, the group maintains control over large swathes of territory across the region.

# Circuit of Wales: Economy Secretary Demands Progress on Ebbw Vale Racing Project

**Welsh Government minister Ken Skates has issued an ultimatum to developers behind the troubled Circuit of Wales motorsport project, demanding they provide proof of private investment within two weeks.**

The Economy Secretary has told the Heads of the Valleys Development Company (HOVDC) that they must make "faster progress" with the ambitious scheme planned for Ebbw Vale. The proposed motorsport and technology hub is claimed to have the potential to create up to 6,000 jobs in the area.

A spokesman for the Circuit of Wales said the company welcomed Mr Skates' "desire for a speedy resolution."

The project has been mired in uncertainty over funding arrangements. In July 2016, Mr Skates informed the firm it would need to secure at least 50% of the project's budget and underwriting from private sources before the Welsh Government would consider supporting it.

On Wednesday, the Economy Secretary expressed his concerns to Assembly Members about the long-running saga. "The project has been publicly debated for many years" without sufficient private finance being found, he said.

"The people of Ebbw Vale deserve to know if this project is going ahead and crucially if so when," Mr Skates added.

The minister's frustration is evident in his latest statement. "I am keen to avoid more opportunity costs associated with a project that does not have a final date," he said. "I have therefore written to the Heads of Valleys Development Company today asking them to make faster progress on this project and asking for evidence to be provided to me of named investor term sheets within the next two weeks."

The Circuit of Wales initially requested the Welsh Government underwrite the entire £400 million-plus project with taxpayer funds. Ministers rejected this approach and suggested they might potentially underwrite half the costs, but only if substantial private investment could be demonstrated.

BBC Wales business correspondent Brian Meechan described the move as "very significant," noting it represents "the latest sign of growing frustration from the Welsh Government about how this company has been approaching this project."

Sources suggest ministers still haven't received concrete information about the identity of investors or confirmation that funding is in place, despite the company bringing in a merchant bank to secure additional investment.

The development's backers claim it could attract 750,000 visitors annually and inject approximately £50m into the Welsh economy each year. While insurers Aviva have been named as likely financial backers, negotiations with government over risk-sharing have continued.

Earlier this year, HOVDC announced Extreme Sports Company as a new business partner for the venture.

# Homes Evacuated After Suspicious Device Found in Northern Ireland

Approximately 20 houses in Gelvin Gardens were evacuated on Sunday evening following the discovery of a suspicious object, believed to be a pipe bomb.

The evacuation began at 17:00 GMT, with residents permitted to return to their homes four hours later. Army bomb disposal experts are currently examining the device.

Police have stated that the incident is not believed to be sectarian in nature and is not connected to recent attacks elsewhere in Northern Ireland.

Community worker Geraldine Doherty described the palpable anger among residents during the alert.

"You have to condemn attacks like this at all times," she stated.

# Head Teachers Reject Grammar School Expansion Plans

The National Association of Head Teachers (NAHT) has formally backed moves to reject the government's proposed expansion of grammar schools, citing a lack of evidence that selective education improves social mobility for disadvantaged children.

At their annual conference in Telford, delegates heard strong criticism of Conservative plans to increase the number of grammar schools across England, with speakers warning that the policy would add further pressure to an already strained education system.

Prime Minister Theresa May has consistently defended grammar schools, arguing they provide valuable opportunities for bright children from poorer backgrounds to access high-quality education. However, this stance faces opposition from Labour, the Liberal Democrats, and now the nation's head teachers.

The NAHT argues that investment in early-years education represents a far more effective approach to closing the achievement gap between rich and poor pupils. According to the union, by the time children complete primary school, the educational advantages enjoyed by wealthier students have already become firmly established.

Robert Campbell, proposing the motion at the conference, criticized the government's approach: "The government is fixated with delivering a policy for the few at the expense of the many."

However, the practical mechanisms through which head teachers might actively oppose the planned expansion remain unclear.

## A "Perfect Storm" Facing Secondary Schools

The union used the conference platform to warn of what it describes as a "perfect storm" of challenges confronting secondary schools this summer, which could have "dire consequences for pupils and standards."

These pressures include the implementation of a new secondary examination system, ongoing difficulties with teacher recruitment and retention, and projected real-term cuts of £3bn to school budgets by 2020.

NAHT General Secretary Russell Hobby expressed frustration that concerns from head teachers, teachers, and parents about school funding were being ignored by ministers. He announced the union's intention to make education funding a key general election issue.

"We need to make sure that all our parliamentary constituencies are asking questions on school funding," Mr. Hobby said.

## Schools Filling Public Service Gaps

Conference delegates highlighted how schools are increasingly being required to compensate for underfunded public services as local government finances become progressively stretched.

Past NAHT president Kim Johnson revealed that schools in Medway were being asked to part-fund police officers working in schools despite lacking adequate resources. He disclosed that his special school, Bradfields Academy, was spending £200,000 from its £6m budget on social care and health support—including two social workers, three therapists, and counsellors—services that should be provided by frontline public agencies.

The government maintains that schools are receiving record levels of funding.

# Jordanian Security Forces Kill Three Suspects in Raid After Deadly Karak Attack

Jordanian security forces have killed three people in a raid on a house in the northern city of Irbid, according to official sources.

The operation targeted suspected militants believed to be hiding in the residence, security sources confirmed. A security official told the state-run Petra news agency that Tuesday's raid was not connected to Sunday's deadly shootings in the historic city of Karak that claimed 10 lives.

A statement distributed Tuesday through the Telegram messaging app stated that "four soldiers of the caliphate" had targeted Jordanian security forces and citizens of countries participating in the US-led coalition fighting IS in neighboring Iraq and Syria.

Jordanian authorities have not verified the attackers' identities or confirmed any IS affiliation, referring to them only as "terrorist outlaws."

Sunday's violence began when police responded to reports of a fire in Qatraneh village, approximately 32 kilometers east of Karak. Officers came under fire from the house, with two wounded before the assailants escaped toward Karak castle, a popular tourist destination overlooking the town.

Interior Minister Salameh Hammad said tourists were inside the castle during the incident but denied they were held hostage, explaining they took shelter during the hours-long standoff between gunmen and security forces.

Minister Hammad revealed that five or six explosive belts were recovered from the attackers, suggesting additional targets may have been planned. "I don't think the target was only Karak castle," he stated. "Maybe there were more targets, but Allah helped us discover this cell before more attacks took place."

The assault killed seven Jordanian security personnel, two local civilians, and Canadian tourist Linda Vatcher, a 62-year-old retired teacher from Newfoundland visiting her son Chris, who was among 34 people injured.

Jordan remains a key partner in international efforts against Islamic State militants in the region.

# Scottish Business Leaders Demand Voice in New Powers Debate

The chief executive of Scottish Chambers of Commerce has called for businesses to have a central role in shaping Scotland's constitutional future, warning that tax changes could have far-reaching consequences for the economy.

Liz Cameron acknowledged that 2014 had brought "great advances" for Scottish business but expressed concern that many recommendations from the Smith Commission, particularly regarding taxation powers, carried significant implications for the commercial sector.

"Scottish businesses have been extraordinarily patient over a protracted period that has seen political attention dominated by constitutional politics," Ms Cameron said in her New Year message. "While the political battle raged, little attention was paid to the daily endeavours and achievements of business."

She criticised the referendum campaign period, claiming that "lip service was paid to the business sector" and insisted this approach must change going forward.

Ms Cameron emphasised the urgency of securing "clarity, resolution and speed" on Smith Commission recommendations concerning additional powers for the Scottish Parliament. She stressed that Scotland needs not only to create more businesses but to "grow our medium-sized businesses into tomorrow's corporate giants."

Highlighting the crucial link between business prosperity and social progress, she warned: "Truly, without a thriving business sector, our chances of economic and social improvement are slim indeed."

The business leader called for "full and extensive consultation" with businesses and business organisations as Smith Commission proposals advance toward legislation. She particularly cautioned that taxation changes must not "prejudice the ability of Scottish companies to attract skills and talent from across the UK and overseas as well as within Scotland."

Ms Cameron insisted it was "vitally important" that business voices are not just heard but listened to during this critical phase of constitutional change.

# Justin Thomas Sets PGA Tour Records at Sony Open

Justin Thomas continued his extraordinary form at the Sony Open in Hawaii, carding a third-round 65 to establish a new 54-hole scoring record on the PGA Tour.

The 23-year-old American has been rewriting the record books for three consecutive days at Waialae Country Club. After opening with a remarkable 59 on Thursday - becoming the youngest player to break 60 on the PGA Tour - Thomas followed up with a 64 on Friday, setting the lowest 36-hole total in tour history.

On Saturday, Thomas extended his commanding lead with another impressive round. Starting five shots clear, he played cautiously through the front nine, making eight consecutive pars before finally recording his first birdie at the par-five ninth hole. He added further birdies at the 10th, 14th, 16th and 18th holes to complete a bogey-free 65.

His three-round total of 188 (22 under par) matches the 54-hole record previously set by Steve Stricker at the 2010 John Deere Classic.

Two-time major champion Zach Johnson sits in second place after matching Thomas's 65, while England's Justin Rose is part of a group on 14 under par. Scotland's Russell Knox and American Kevin Kisner, who narrowly missed a 59 after failing to convert a nine-foot eagle putt on the final hole, are one shot further back.

Thomas needs a final round of 65 or better to break the all-time 72-hole PGA Tour record of 254.

# North Devon Families Told to Remove Tributes from Cemetery Graves

North Devon Council has sparked controversy after ordering families to remove personal tributes from graves at Bear Street cemetery in Barnstaple, with some relatives accusing the authority of acting like "dictators."

The council said people were breaking cemetery rules by spreading photographs, messages, lights and other items along the length of graves, making it difficult to maintain the grounds and reopen burial plots for relatives.

Families have been given a 90-day deadline to remove the items. While some have complied, 27 families have yet to clear the graves.

Peter Hull, who has been told to remove flowers from his brother-in-law's grave, expressed frustration at the decision. "For my wife it's very upsetting, for me it is more annoying that a council do not want to listen," he said. "We live in a world of democracy but they're making me feel like they're dictators."

North Devon Council insisted it had tried to deal "sympathetically and tactfully" with affected families. Mark Drummond, representing the authority, explained that most graves were designed for two burials. # Google Street View Captures Pembrokeshire Coast Path

The Pembrokeshire Coast Path has been captured on Google Street View, offering virtual access to one of Wales' most scenic routes.

The route covers 186 miles (299 km) from Amroth to St Dogmaels and passes cliff tops, beaches and estuaries. It took 28 days between April and June 2016 to film after Google loaned the authority a backpack-mounted camera.

Rights of way manager Anthony Richards said it "shows the national park at its absolute best".

People can access the route on their mobile phone, computer or tablet. In total, Google plans to make 15 national trails available on street view.

# School Meals Investigation After Gluten Found in "Free-From" Products

A county council has launched an investigation after discovering gluten in shepherd's pie and beef bolognese meals that were labeled as gluten-free and served to schoolchildren.

The authority's nutritionists identified the contamination during routine ingredient monitoring of food supplied to schools across the county. The gluten was traced to a gravy powder used in both dishes.

Twenty pupils registered with gluten intolerance or coeliac disease could have been affected, though the council confirmed no children have reported adverse reactions.

Councillor Andrew Grant stated: "Our nutritionists regularly monitor the ingredients used by our suppliers in the food we provide and it was as a result of these checks that we picked up the discrepancy between the labelling and the actual ingredients."

He added: "While the quantity of gluten a child may have consumed is quite small, it is nevertheless completely unacceptable for a child with allergies to be exposed to this risk."

The council has requested a full investigation into how the mislabeling occurred and believes the issue is limited to these two specific meals.

Gluten, a wheat protein, triggers an auto-immune response in intolerant individuals, causing inflammation and damage to the small intestine's lining, which impairs nutrient absorption. The condition requires strict dietary management to prevent health complications.

# Nobel Prize Winner John Nash and Wife Alicia Killed in New Jersey Taxi Crash

John Nash, the brilliant mathematician whose life story inspired the Oscar-winning film "A Beautiful Mind," has died alongside his wife Alicia in a taxi accident in New Jersey. Nash was 86, and his wife was 82.

The couple were killed when their taxi crashed on Saturday, according to police reports. Authorities stated that both John and Alicia Nash were ejected from the vehicle during the accident, with media reports suggesting they may not have been wearing seatbelts at the time. The taxi driver and a passenger in another vehicle involved in the crash also sustained injuries.

Nash was internationally renowned for his groundbreaking work in game theory, which earned him the Nobel Prize for Economics in 1994. His life, marked by both extraordinary mathematical achievements and a devastating battle with schizophrenia, became the subject of the acclaimed 2001 film "A Beautiful Mind," starring Russell Crowe.

Crowe expressed his shock and sadness on Twitter, writing: "Stunned.... My heart goes out to John & Alicia & family. An amazing partnership. Beautiful minds, beautiful hearts." Director Ron Howard also paid tribute to the "brilliant" mathematician and his "remarkable" wife.

Born in Bluefield, West Virginia, Nash began his academic career in Pittsburgh before moving to Princeton University. His recommendation letter famously contained just one sentence: "This man is a genius." He married Alicia Larde in 1957, shortly after publishing some of his most important works in game theory—the mathematical study of decision-making and strategic interaction.

However, Nash's life took a difficult turn when he developed severe schizophrenia. "I was disturbed in this way for a very long period of time, like 25 years," Nash said in an interview on the Nobel Prize website. Alicia had him committed for psychiatric care on several occasions, and the couple divorced in 1962.

Despite the divorce, the two remained close. As Nash's condition gradually improved during the 1980s, their relationship strengthened, and they remarried in 2001. Together, they became prominent advocates for mental health awareness.

Nash's contributions to mathematics continued to be recognized until his final days. Just this week, he received the Abel Prize, another prestigious honour in mathematics.

Christopher Eisgruber, President of Princeton University, said he was "stunned and saddened" by the news. "John's remarkable achievements inspired generations of mathematicians, economists and scientists who were influenced by his brilliant, groundbreaking work in game theory," he stated.

Nash's famous Nash Equilibrium has been applied across numerous fields, including computing, evolutionary biology, artificial intelligence, and studies of economic corruption, cementing his legacy as one of the most influential mathematicians of the modern era.

# Abortion Case: Charges Dropped After Warnings Issued to Belfast Pair

Charges have been withdrawn against two people in a high-profile abortion case after they received formal warnings last week.

A judge imposed reporting restrictions preventing identification of a 21-year-old woman involved in the case, citing a significantly elevated suicide risk associated with any media coverage. The woman had been charged with using poison to procure her own abortion.

The alleged offence centred on the administration of Mifepristone and Misoprostol, drugs commonly used for medical abortions. Her co-defendant, aged 22, faced charges of supplying a poison with intent to procure a miscarriage. The incidents allegedly occurred in Belfast during 2015.

Unlike the rest of the United Kingdom, Northern Ireland has never adopted the 1967 Abortion Act. Current legislation permits terminations only when a woman's life or long-term health faces serious risk.

Defence lawyers presented the woman as vulnerable and immature, highlighting three previous self-harm episodes. A consultant forensic psychiatrist's assessment warned that prosecution and media attention would substantially increase suicide risk.

The judge granted anonymity to protect the woman's right to life under human rights legislation.

Prosecutors confirmed they re-evaluated the case following expert medical testimony. Both defendants received formal cautions on 13 January, effectively concluding the proceedings without trial.

The case has reignited debate about Northern Ireland's restrictive abortion laws.

# NHS Introduces Nursing Apprenticeships as Alternative Route to Degree

The NHS is launching a new apprenticeship scheme that will allow up to 1,000 staff members to train as nurses without attending university through the conventional route, Health Secretary Jeremy Hunt has announced.

Starting in September 2017, the nursing degree apprenticeship programme will provide an alternative pathway into the profession, working alongside the nursing associate role that was introduced a year earlier. Both initiatives are designed to offer more flexible entry routes into nursing across England.

The announcement comes at a time when the government is planning significant changes to nursing education funding. Currently, student nurses receive bursaries ranging from £4,500 to £5,500 for those living in London, plus an additional £1,000 annual grant throughout their course, with tuition fees fully covered. However, ministers intend to scrap these bursaries in September 2017, introducing university fees to align health staff training with other students. Some NHS financial support will remain available for expenses such as travel costs during placements.

Under the new apprenticeship scheme, trainees will typically receive funding from the NHS trust employing them. Participants can join at various stages depending on their existing qualifications and experience, and crucially, they can continue working while learning. The training pathway usually takes five years to complete and results in a full nursing degree.

This differs from the nursing associate route, where trainees also receive paid training while working but would need additional qualifications to become registered nurses. The apprenticeship scheme therefore offers a direct route to full nurse registration.

The Royal College of Nursing welcomed the expansion of training opportunities but urged caution. Chief executive Janet Davies said: "Nursing has progressed over many years, we must be careful to learn from the lessons of the past when student nurses were often seen as nursing on the cheap. We must be careful we do not create a two-tier system which reduces equality of opportunity."

She emphasised the importance of attracting people from all ages and diverse backgrounds into the profession whilst ensuring new courses meet educational standards.

Mr Hunt defended the initiative, saying: "Nurses are the lifeblood of our NHS, but the routes to a nursing degree currently shut out some of the most caring, compassionate staff in our country. Not everyone wants to take time off to study full time at university, so by creating hundreds of new apprentice nurses, we can help healthcare assistants and others reach their potential as a fully trained nurse."

Chief nursing officer Professor Jane Cummings added that the programme offers "a new, exciting route into nursing that is open to more people whether they are working within the NHS already or would like to pursue a career in nursing."

# Protestors Disrupt James Bulger Memorial Event at Liverpool Hotel

A charity event in memory of James Bulger was disrupted by protestors who broke windows and kicked doors at Liverpool's Titanic Hotel on Friday night.

He praised the people of Merseyside for their continued support of the family, adding: "Denise adores the people of Merseyside, who have always stood by her and helped her in James's name."

Merseyside Police confirmed that about 12 members of the group entered the hotel's reception area, causing damage to several items.

A spokeswoman for Love Activists claimed the protest was peaceful and alleged that security staff assaulted group members. She insisted they were unaware the event was connected to James Bulger.
