When asked about apologising to the family, the spokeswoman said: "We regret any upset caused."

# Mike Leigh to Direct Film About 1819 Peterloo Massacre

British director Mike Leigh is set to helm a film about the Peterloo Massacre, a pivotal moment in British history when government forces violently dispersed a peaceful pro-democracy gathering in Manchester in 1819.

The incident saw approximately 15 people killed and hundreds injured when troops charged into a crowd of 60,000 who had assembled to demand political reform. Leigh told Screen International the project holds "personal resonance" for him as a native of Manchester and Salford.

The film, reportedly Leigh's biggest-budget production to date, is scheduled to shoot in 2017. The director will reunite with cinematographer Dick Pope, who earned an Oscar nomination for their previous collaboration on Mr Turner.

That 2014 biographical drama garnered four Academy Award nominations and has grossed over £6.4 million in the UK alone, despite Leigh and star Timothy Spall missing out on hoped-for wins.

Leigh emphasized the Peterloo Massacre's "universal political significance," noting that the historic event was a defining moment in British political history and led to the founding of the Guardian newspaper.

Currently, Leigh is rehearsing with the English National Opera for their production of Gilbert and Sullivan's Pirates of Penzance, opening May 9th. He previously explored the famous duo in his 1999 film Topsy-Turvy.

# NI Water Customers Face Service Interruptions Due to Industrial Action

Customers across Northern Ireland are facing the prospect of significant water supply interruptions as industrial action by trade unions continues to affect NI Water services.

The disruption is being caused by ongoing industrial action by three trade unions - Nipsa, Unite and GMB - whose members voted last month for a work-to-rule and withdrawal of on-call services and overtime.

Regional Development Minister Danny Kennedy met with union representatives on Wednesday in an attempt to resolve the dispute. However, he made it clear that any resolution would have to be within the Northern Ireland Executive's current pay and pensions policy.

NI Water chief executive Sara Venning expressed regret on Friday that the industrial action was preventing customers from receiving an "essential public service". She said she believed the proposals in the latest offer presented to the unions "could be acceptable" and appealed for measures to be put in place to protect public drinking water while the proposals were being considered.

"We are working round the clock from an operational perspective to minimise the impact on customers," Ms Venning said. "We have been talking to the unions almost daily. We are working late into the night to try and find a proposal and a common ground that would enable the unions to withdraw and to suspend this action."

Since Wednesday's meeting, NI Water said "intensive negotiations" had been ongoing. The company has made a third formal offer to unions "which includes movement on pension issues as well as the potential for a two-year pay settlement".

While this offer is being considered, NI Water sought a re-instatement of the Christmas arrangement to protect public health and critical customers, but this request was declined.

"The result of this is that customers across Northern Ireland now face the prospect of supply interruptions on a scale greater than those which affected Fermanagh and Tyrone during the week," the company said in a statement.

NI Water emphasised that while it had sought to end the dispute by putting forward numerous proposals, "the key demand from unions that pension reform be deferred is not something that NI Water management have in their power to deliver."

The company said the major incident regime which has been in place since before Christmas would continue over the weekend. This regime has largely allowed services to be maintained across the province, but without the emergency cover that has been withdrawn, customers will suffer.

"Unfortunately the extent and exact location is something which we cannot predict in advance," the company warned.

Where customers are off supply for more than 24 hours, NI Water said it will seek to provide alternative water supplies, though the company acknowledged that its ability to provide these alternatives will also be impacted by the ongoing industrial action.

# Chibok Schoolgirl Rescued by Nigerian Troops After Boko Haram Abduction

A 15-year-old Nigerian schoolgirl has been rescued by government troops after being abducted by Boko Haram militants, according to presidential spokesman Femi Adesina. While the girl attended the same school in Chibok as the 276 girls kidnapped in 2014, she was taken in a separate incident.

The teenager was found by security forces as she attempted to escape from her captors in north-eastern Nigeria, where the militant group has been waging an eight-year insurgency aimed at establishing an Islamic caliphate.

Three years after the mass abduction that shocked the world, 113 of the original Chibok girls remain in Boko Haram captivity. However, 103 have been released, including 82 freed earlier this month in a prisoner exchange involving five Boko Haram commanders. These 82 girls met with President Muhammadu Buhari on 7 May and are expected to reunite with their families this week.

President Buhari has stated that the government remains "in constant touch through negotiations, through local intelligence, to secure the release of the remaining girls and other abducted persons unharmed."

Aid organisations emphasize that while the Chibok case received international attention, thousands of others abducted by Boko Haram have received little media coverage or support. The conflict has killed more than 30,000 people and displaced hundreds of thousands, according to government figures. Aid agencies are now warning of potential famine in the region, as residents have been unable to farm for several years.

# Church Break-in: Vandals Urinate in Holy Water at Northampton Catholic Church

Would-be thieves who broke into a Northampton Catholic church caused extensive damage and desecrated holy water by urinating in it, police have confirmed.

The perpetrators smashed through a window at St Mary's Roman Catholic Church on Bridge Street before using fire extinguishers to break down internal doors during Thursday's break-in.

Father Marc Lyden-Smith expressed shock at the discovery, saying he found it "incredible" that anyone could commit such an act. A police officer detected the contamination of the holy water stoup during the investigation.

Despite the vandalism, nothing was reported stolen from the church. Cleaning volunteers discovered the damage Thursday morning.

The holy water stoup, typically positioned near the church entrance for Catholics to make the sign of the cross upon entering, has since been cleaned.

Father Lyden-Smith responded philosophically to the incident: "It is disappointing but it is the year of mercy and we have to keep that in our thoughts."

# Guernsey Honors Canadian Military Hero Gen Isaac Brock on 200th Anniversary

A series of commemorative events were held in Guernsey, Channel Islands, marking the 200th anniversary of the death of General Sir Isaac Brock, the celebrated "Hero of Upper Canada."

The day's ceremonies began at 08:45 BST when Colonel Paul Keddy, the Canadian Defence Attache, raised the Canadian flag on the memorial mast, honoring the military commander born on this British island.

General Brock earned his legendary status in 1812 when he led a combined force of British, Canadian and First Nation troops to victory against an invading American army during the War of 1812. He was killed at the Battle of Queenston Heights in Ontario on October 13, 1812.

A formal parade followed the flag-raising ceremony, featuring veterans and standard bearers from local emergency services, armed forces groups, and volunteer and charity organizations. The procession marched from the memorial mast to Boots, which now occupies the site of Sir Isaac's former family home.

Wreaths were solemnly laid outside the shop before participants continued to the Town Church for a commemoration service. A 15-gun salute was fired precisely at midday Guernsey time, corresponding exactly to 07:00 Canadian time—marking 200 years to the moment when General Brock fell in battle.

Plans to unveil a specially commissioned bust were postponed due to the sculptor's illness. The Brock Memorial Foundation, established by one of the general's descendants, aims to "provide support for projects that celebrate the legacy of Sir Isaac Brock," including plans to erect identical statues in both Guernsey and Canada.

Richard Collas, the Bailiff of Guernsey, shared a letter from Canadian Prime Minister Stephen Harper, who wrote: "His leadership and bravery at the Battle of Queenston Heights earned him iconic status as the 'Hero of Upper Canada.' Though he died in defence of the colony, his sacrifice was not in vain. Brock's thwarting of the American assault was a key victory in the War of 1812 and a step towards forging a strong and united Canada."

# Paramount Pulls Out of Planned Kent Theme Park Resort

A major theme park development near Dartford has lost its headline partner after Paramount Pictures withdrew from the ambitious project.

The London Resort Company Holdings (LRCH) confirmed it has ended its agreement with the Hollywood studio, though the company insists the massive entertainment complex will still proceed as planned.

The resort, set for the Swanscombe Peninsula, is envisioned to be twice the size of London's Olympic Park. Plans include 5,000 hotel rooms, a water park, and more than 50 rides and attractions across a 900-acre brownfield site.

Originally, attractions were to be based on Paramount's extensive catalogue of films and television programmes. However, chief executive Humphrey Percy said the split actually provides greater flexibility.

"What it means is we won't have the name Paramount above the door," Percy explained. "We are not looking for a new studio."

He emphasized that the Paramount deal had restricted the park from collaborating with other entertainment companies. "It just gives us the freedom to work with other partners," Percy said.

LRCH plans to submit its planning application in November, with the park scheduled to open in 2022 pending government approval of a Development Consent Order.

Despite losing its flagship brand, Percy stressed: "We are committed to going ahead - nothing has changed on that score."

# DX Group Acquires City Link Assets for £1.125m Following Courier Firm's Collapse

DX Group has announced the acquisition of assets from the collapsed courier company City Link for £1.125 million, purchasing scanners, cages, and certain intellectual property rights from the failed business.

The deal comes as administrators continue to wind down City Link's operations following its dramatic collapse over the Christmas period. DX, which floated on the London Stock Exchange's Alternative Investment Market (AIM) last year with a valuation of £175 million, is led by former City Link managing director Petar Cvetkovic, who left the courier firm in 2009.

Commenting on the acquisition, Mr Cvetkovic expressed sympathy for those affected by City Link's failure. "It is very sad that City Link has been unable to continue as a going concern, particularly for its employees and contractors," he said. "The administrators are now proceeding with an orderly sale of assets and we have made a limited investment to acquire certain assets."

The DX chief executive added that his company was committed to helping former City Link staff, stating: "We are also doing all we can to provide opportunities for former City Link employees and contractors and to offer solutions to customers who may need a new carrier."

City Link's administrators announced 2,356 job losses on New Year's Eve after rejecting a last-minute rescue bid from an unnamed consortium, which "offered no money up front and significantly undervalued the assets to be acquired."

The Coventry-based company, founded in 1969 and employing 2,727 people, had suffered sustained losses. It was acquired by Better Capital for £1 in April 2013, with the investment firm subsequently injecting £40 million. However, administrators Ernst & Young concluded this investment proved insufficient to save the business.

Business Secretary Vince Cable confirmed government support measures were in place to assist affected workers in finding new employment.

# Delhi Brings Back Odd-Even Car Scheme to Combat Pollution

Delhi has reintroduced its controversial odd-even car rationing scheme in a bid to tackle the Indian capital's severe air pollution crisis.

Private cars with even and odd number plates will only be allowed on alternate days from 15 to 30 April, Chief Minister Arvind Kejriwal announced. The scheme means vehicles with registration numbers ending in odd digits can drive on odd-numbered dates, while even-numbered plates are permitted on even dates.

This marks the second phase of the experimental program, following a fortnight-long trial from 1 January that took more than a third of the city's three million private cars off the road, significantly easing traffic congestion. However, it remains unclear whether the initiative actually helped reduce pollution levels.

The local government has described this second phase as "decisive" in determining the scheme's effectiveness as a pollution control measure and whether it should be implemented monthly going forward.

The scheme will be enforced by 2,000 traffic personnel, 580 enforcement officials, and more than 5,000 civil defence volunteers. Violators face fines of 2,000 rupees (£21; $30), and a special task force has been appointed to investigate complaints.

As with the January trial, emergency vehicles including ambulances, police cars, fire engines, and taxis are exempt. Single women drivers and two-wheelers are also allowed daily access.

While January's trial successfully reduced traffic congestion, its impact on air pollution remains disputed. Authorities claimed a "more than 50% drop in air pollution primarily caused by vehicular traffic," but the state-run System of Air Quality Weather Forecasting and Research showed PM 2.5 particulate levels hovering between "very poor" and "severe," well above WHO safe limits.

Delhi faces mounting pollution challenges with 8.5 million vehicles on its roads and approximately 1,400 new cars added daily to the capital's already congested streets.

# Lincoln Christmas Market Makes Just £4,000 Profit After £100,000 Loss

Lincoln's Christmas Market generated a meagre profit of just £4,000 in 2013, prompting concerns about its financial viability following a £100,000 loss the previous year.

The City of Lincoln Council has attributed the disappointing figures to a significant decline in coach parties and reduced stallholder numbers. Coach visits dropped dramatically from 438 in 2012 to just 314 last Christmas, while the number of stalls fell from 243 to 199. The unavailability of parts of Lincoln Castle also impacted the event.

Despite the financial challenges, the council insists the market's future remains secure. However, it has proposed a controversial 12% increase in pitch fees, raising the maximum charge to £1,411.

Council leader Ric Metcalfe defended the decision, arguing that stallholders making "a significant amount of money" should contribute more towards running costs. "Given there are very significant overhead costs falling on the council primarily but other public authorities as well, it's only fair that those businesses should share the infrastructure costs of maintaining the event," he said.

The proposed increase has drawn criticism from local business leaders. Linda Wardale, chairman of the Bailgate Traders' Group, warned that traders may struggle to afford the higher fees. "There will not be the variety of stalls there and it could be a potential flop," she cautioned.

The 2012 market was heavily criticised after organisers introduced a controversial one-way system to manage overcrowding. A council report now acknowledges that "a fundamental review of the business plan is required" to ensure the event's sustainability.

# National Theatre Makes Rare Move into Film Production with London Road

The National Theatre has ventured into film production for the first time with London Road, though artistic director Rufus Norris insists this doesn't signal a permanent shift in the institution's focus.

"We're not opening up a film slate because that's not what we're given public money to do," Norris told the BBC. "We are a theatre, but occasionally things come up where you think, 'Why not? Let's give it a go.'"

The NT acquired the film rights to the musical London Road last year, marking its first foray into production. While there have been successful adaptations of NT plays previously—including Amadeus, The Madness of King George, The History Boys and War Horse—the theatre had no financial or creative stake in those films.

The theatre has been expanding its reach through live cinema broadcasts of shows including Macbeth, The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time, Frankenstein and The Audience, but producing a standalone film represents new territory.

Norris admitted making a feature film was "not something that we set out to do," though he's eager to "see how it goes in the next few weeks and months." While the theatre won't open a full-time film division, he added: "I wouldn't be surprised if another little idea popped up sooner or later. I would never say we'd never do it again."

Norris directed both the stage and screen versions of London Road, which documents the arrest of Steve Wright, an Ipswich man convicted of murdering five sex workers in 2008. The production uses real dialogue from rural townsfolk whose lives were disrupted when they discovered a serial killer had been living in their community.

The cast includes Olivia Colman, Anita Dobson and Tom Hardy, who had a "get-out clause" written into his contract over concerns about his singing ability.

"He said from the beginning, 'I'm going to keep the back door open until the last minute, so you've got to have a Plan B,'" Norris revealed. "But there was no Plan B. I knew that Tom wouldn't give up."

# Lukashenko: Leaders Ate Omelettes During Marathon Minsk Peace Talks

Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko has revealed details about the grueling 16-hour peace negotiations that produced a ceasefire agreement for eastern Ukraine on Thursday.

Speaking to Belarus news agency Belta, Lukashenko described how world leaders sustained themselves during the marathon talks in Minsk. "They ate omelettes, cheese, dairy produce, drank several buckets of coffee," he said, adding that his role was "to provide the ammunition on time."

The Belarusian leader emphasized that only Belarusian and Russian products were served—a pointed reference to Russia's ban on EU food imports imposed in response to Western sanctions over the Ukraine conflict.

The talks brought together Russian President Vladimir Putin, French President Francois Hollande, German Chancellor Angela Merkel, and Ukrainian President Petro Poroshenko. Their expert advisers "slept in shifts - in order to keep clear heads," Lukashenko noted.

Lukashenko, often called "Europe's last dictator," has ruled Belarus in authoritarian style since 1994, maintaining tight state control and suppressing dissent in the former Soviet republic.

# Lions Tours Must Continue Despite Club Concerns, Says Gavin Hastings

The British and Irish Lions remains the pinnacle of rugby despite mounting pressure from club owners, according to former captain Gavin Hastings, who has called for stakeholders to prioritize the historic touring tradition over domestic interests.

Hastings, speaking to BBC 5 live, delivered a pointed message to Premiership club owners who have expressed dissatisfaction with the current Lions model: "You have to say 'guys, the Lions is bigger than your clubs'. Let's look at what's best for British and Irish rugby - that's the Lions."

The debate over the Lions' future has intensified, with plans to shorten tours from 2021 onwards amid concerns from club rugby directors. The current New Zealand tour has particularly highlighted tensions, with the squad arriving just three days after the domestic season concluded and before embarking on a 10-game itinerary that some club directors have labelled "ludicrous."

Hastings, who captained the 1993 Lions tour of New Zealand and led the side to victory in the second Test in Wellington, witnessed history repeat itself on Saturday. The former Scotland full-back was in attendance at the Westpac Stadium to watch the current Lions square the series with a 24-21 victory - ending his 24-year reign as the last Lions captain to defeat the All Blacks in a Test match.

"That final whistle will be a moment that will live with everyone who was there for a very long time," said Hastings, who described himself as "delighted" to share the distinction. "We are all supporters. To share in that joy of victory was amazing, and it will show the Lions has to stay."

Despite the ever-growing popularity of the Lions brand, the future of the tours hangs in the balance. While some parties advocate for condensed schedules, Lions organisers maintain that anything shorter than the current format would prove damaging.

Hastings acknowledges the ongoing dispute but insists a compromise must be reached. "It just goes on and on," he said. "For people who have been with the Lions and are as passionate as I am, we feel there is no debate - the Lions should continue."

# West Way Shopping Development Unveils Video Plans

Developer Doric Properties has released a "walk-through" video showcasing proposed plans for the West Way shopping area in Botley, following a request from North Hinksey Parish Council.

The development, submitted to Vale of White Horse District Council in December 2013, features restaurants, a hotel, and student accommodation.

Proponents claim the project will generate 600 construction jobs and 480 permanent positions once operational.

However, the plans have faced opposition from residents concerned about the development's size relative to the site. Critics have also raised issues regarding potential increases in traffic and congestion in the area.

The district council continues to review the application.

# Smart Meters Will Save Consumers Little Money, MPs Warn

The government's ambitious smart meter rollout programme will deliver only modest savings on household energy bills, a parliamentary committee has warned.

The Science and Technology Committee said ministers must make a stronger case for the wider benefits of the technology, including creating a more efficient energy grid and reducing pollution, rather than focusing primarily on cost savings for consumers.

The government has pledged that every home and business in the country will be offered a smart meter by the end of 2020, requiring the installation of 53 million meters across more than 30 million premises over the next four years.

Smart meters automatically measure gas and electricity consumption and send readings directly to energy suppliers, eliminating the need for manual meter readings. However, the massive installation programme has encountered significant problems.

The committee highlighted that the communication system linking meters to suppliers has been delayed. More significantly, there is an "unresolved" issue with early meters installed during the initial rollout phase losing their smart functionality when customers switch energy suppliers.

Interim committee chairwoman Tania Mathias criticised the government's handling of the problem. "The government has known for years that early smart meters can lose their smartness if the customer switches supplier," she said. "Ministers merely have an 'ambition' to fix this by 2020. Taxpayers will be unimpressed with this situation, and timely action is needed."

Ms Mathias emphasised that consumers need personalised advice on maximising the benefits of smart meters. "The 'smartness' comes from what customers can do with them - fit and forget would be a wasted opportunity," she said.

The committee also called on the government to reassure customers about cybersecurity concerns surrounding the technology.

A spokeswoman for the Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy defended the programme, stating: "Smart meters will bring Britain's energy infrastructure into the 21st century - as the committee has made clear."

Sacha Deshmukh, chief executive of Smart Energy GB, which is managing the rollout campaign, highlighted "the transformative effect smart meters will have, not only on how we buy and use energy as individual consumers, but on Britain's energy infrastructure as a whole."

# Primark Opens 16 New Stores as Owner AB Foods Reports Strong Performance

Associated British Foods (AB Foods) has announced the opening of 16 new Primark outlets across the UK, Europe and the United States last year, as the discount fashion retailer continues its expansion despite economic uncertainties.

The company predicts total sales for Primark will increase by 11% in the six months to March 4, with no evidence that UK consumers are cutting back on spending. Finance director John Bason emphasized the resilience of the British consumer, stating: "The consumer in the UK has got more disposable income this year than they had a year ago - fact."

Primark's UK operations are performing particularly well, with like-for-like sales expected to rise by 2% for the six-month period, though remaining flat for the overall business. The chain plans to open additional stores in London, Belgium, Spain and the US over the coming three months.

However, AB Foods cautioned that the weakened pound could put pressure on Primark's profit margins. The retailer, which accounts for approximately half of the group's profits, faces increased costs as sterling has fallen 16% against the US dollar and 10% against the euro since last June's EU referendum, making imports more expensive.

Industry analysts suggest Primark's competitive pricing offers some protection, but the retailer faces growing competition. Kate Ormrod, senior analyst at GlobalData, warned: "Ensuring product ranges remain fashionable and relevant will be imperative to retain appeal. This is particularly important as emerging players such as boohoo.com and Missguided continue to encroach on Primark's fast fashion USP."

Beyond Primark, AB Foods' other divisions are performing strongly. Twinings tea and Ovaltine reported revenues well ahead of last year, with Twinings gaining market share in the US, Australia, France and the UK. Ovaltine showed good growth in Vietnam and Brazil.

The company's sugar business also benefited from higher prices and increased African production.

AB Foods expects "excellent progress" in group profits, with its full-year outlook unchanged. Shares traded flat at £26.09 in afternoon London trading, though they have declined more than 20% over the past year.

# Cardiff Student Jailed for Planning to Join Islamic State in Syria

A Cardiff college student who saved £3,000 to travel to Syria and join Islamic State has been sentenced to more than three years in a young offenders' institution after admitting preparation of terrorist acts.

The Old Bailey heard the only reason 19-year-old Syed Choudhury did not go was because he could not find someone to travel with. The Cardiff and Vale College student admitted to engaging in conduct in preparation of terrorist acts. He will serve three years, four months at a young offenders' institution.

Originally from Bradford, Choudhury was living with his aunt in Cardiff. The court heard he had been radicalised by people he regarded as elders after he left home to study in Cardiff.

## Chilling Custody Rant

His extreme views were revealed when he ranted to officers about Sharia law, saying he wanted to be the one to bring it to the UK while in custody.

"The bluntness of what you said on that occasion is chilling. It reveals your dangerousness," Judge Peter Rook QC said.

"However I do accept you are immature. You are impressionable to indoctrination.

"You now say 'I'm lucky I came to prison, I'm lucky I got stopped'.

"You have shown some awareness of how misguided your earlier extremist position was."

## Gaza Protest Brought Attention

The court heard how in July 2014, Choudhury took part in a demonstration in Cardiff protesting about the conflict in Gaza. He carried a banner proclaiming his support for Islamic State which brought him to the attention of anti-terrorism officers.

Prosecutor Sarah Whitehouse QC said in the weeks following the demonstration, Choudhury accessed websites about travelling to Syria and another one that was entitled "10 reasons to join ISIS".

Ms Whitehouse said he also downloaded images that showed his active interest in extremism and had conversations on social media about travelling to Turkey and Syria to fight.

## £3,000 Saved for Jihadi Travel

Choudhury was arrested last December and during interview he repeatedly said he supported IS and that he would be happy to kill non-believers under Islamic State rule.

The court also heard throughout 2014 he was downloading extremist ideology and had saved £3,000 working in a fast food restaurant to fund his jihadi travel.

He was due to go on trial on Wednesday at the Old Bailey, but changed his plea after the jury had been sworn in.

Abdul Iqbal QC, defending, said the evidence showed Choudhury's enthusiasm to travel to Turkey or Syria, but said that Choudhury had not got further than making inquiries.

"There are no direct links with anyone in the area of Turkey or Syria who could assist him," he said.

"Naivety, immaturity and lack of insight are the hallmarks of his character," Mr Iqbal said.

Choudhury was vulnerable and was targeted by older individuals in the Cardiff area who indoctrinated him in extremist views, he added.

## Police Statement

Following the sentence, South Wales Police Assistant Chief Constable Nikki Holland said: "Cardiff is a multi-cultural city and local policing teams, together with partner agencies, work hard to ensure that the people who live there can do so in a safe and peaceful environment.

"It is therefore vital that those who wish to support violent and murderous actions against others are identified both through rigorous policing and the support of communities who can report suspicious actions and behaviour."

# MPs Clash Over Swansea Bay Tidal Lagoon Funding Concerns

A heated exchange erupted in Westminster as MPs debated the future of the Swansea Bay Tidal Lagoon project, with politicians crossing party lines over concerns about government commitment to the groundbreaking renewable energy scheme.

Conservative MP Craig Williams accused Labour colleagues of jeopardizing the project by publicly questioning the government's dedication, claiming their comments were "shaking" potential investors during crucial price negotiations.

The dispute arose during a Westminster Hall debate on Tuesday following the Autumn Statement, when Neath Labour MP Christina Rees expressed concern that the "vital" lagoon received no mention in Chancellor George Osborne's Spending Review.

"In light of the landmark agreement reached in Paris this last weekend, we know that projects like the tidal lagoon are essential if this country is to meet its international obligations to combat climate change," Ms Rees said, referring to the recent UN climate change conference.

Cardiff North Conservative Mr Williams sharply intervened, warning: "Investors around the world are being shaken by what you and mainly members of the Labour party are saying about the tidal lagoon at a very critical point when we're negotiating the strike price. You are endangering lagoons, not just Swansea."

Ms Rees firmly rejected the accusation, responding: "We're not giving the uncertainty - the government are."

The £1bn Swansea Bay project has faced delays, with Tidal Lagoon Power announcing in October that construction would be postponed until 2017 while negotiations continue with UK government ministers over energy pricing.

Ms Rees emphasized the project's importance to south Wales, highlighting potential investment and up to 1,900 construction jobs. "It will be a travesty if the UK government were to fail to deliver this opportunity," she concluded.

# Everton Sign Striker Oumar Niasse from Lokomotiv Moscow

Everton have completed the signing of Senegalese striker Oumar Niasse from Russian side Lokomotiv Moscow on a four-and-a-half-year contract.

The 25-year-old forward has been in impressive form this season, netting 13 goals in 23 appearances for the Russian club before making the move to Goodison Park.

Everton manager Roberto Martinez expressed his satisfaction with the acquisition: "We're delighted as Oumar is a player we've been following for a long time. He brings a real hunger and desire to be successful into what is already a strong squad."

The signing comes after Everton's attempts to secure their primary target, Dynamo Kiev's Andriy Yarmolenko, proved unsuccessful. The move also follows recent departures, with Steven Naismith joining Norwich and Aiden McGeady moving to Sheffield Wednesday on loan.

Niasse revealed he had been monitoring Everton since October after learning of their interest. "I was interested to see how they play. If you see players who are aged 20 or 21 and see them perform like that, you know you have a good coach," the striker said.

The transfer represents Everton's efforts to strengthen their attacking options for the remainder of the season.

# Philippines' Duterte Threatens to Drop US Arms Deal Over Human Rights Concerns

Philippines President Rodrigo Duterte said Monday he would seek alternative weapons suppliers after a US senator moved to block a rifle sale over human rights concerns related to his controversial drug war.

According to Reuters, a US senator had planned to block the arms purchase over concerns about human rights violations. The decision came as thousands have been killed as part of Mr Duterte's bloody crackdown on drugs since he took office.

In a televised speech on Monday, Mr Duterte said: "We will not insist on buying expensive arms from the United States. We don't need them. We will just have to look for another source that is cheaper and maybe as durable and as good as those made in the place we are ordering them."

The Philippine leader, who once promised to kill 100,000 criminals, has consistently brushed off criticism from the UN, which said the killings could be crimes under international law, as well as from the US and numerous human rights bodies.

Last week, Mr Duterte accused his American counterparts of "rude" treatment and said he could alternatively source rifles from Russia or China. "Look at these monkeys, the 26,000 firearms we wanted to buy, they don't want to sell. These American fools," he said.

The US State Department declined to comment on the sale of rifles to the Philippines, but spokesman John Kirby said Mr Duterte's rhetoric was "inexplicably at odds" with US-Philippine relations.

Philippine police chief Ronald dela Rosa supported the president's position, saying the US had lost out on the rifle sale.

# Historic Fareham School Faces Closure After a Century

**Wykeham House School in Fareham could close at the end of the Autumn term after being open for 100 years.**

The independent school, which was founded in 1913 as a girls' school, announced it is facing closure due to mounting financial pressures affecting both its boys' and girls' sites.

In a statement, the school confirmed: "Due to increasing financial pressure, Wykeham House School in Fareham is facing the prospect of closure at the end of the Autumn term."

The Board of Trustees has assured families that the school will continue operating until at least the end of term. Staff are actively working with parents to help secure alternative school placements for affected pupils.

The announcement affects both the boys' and girls' schools, which operate on separate sites with independent teaching but function under the same organizational structure.

"Although they are on separate sites and are taught separately, they are part of the same organisation so this news applies to both sites," the statement added.

The potential closure marks the end of an era for the century-old institution.

# UK's Syrian Refugee Programme to Cost Nearly £1.2bn Over Five Years

The UK government's plan to resettle 20,000 Syrian refugees over five years will cost approximately £1.2 billion, ministers have revealed, raising concerns about transparency and funding.

Syrian refugee minister Richard Harrington estimated the figure would be £589m. Home Affairs Committee chairman Keith Vaz said the cost was "huge". The UK has already accepted more than 1,000 Syrian refugees, as part of the government's Vulnerable Persons Relocation (VPR) scheme.

The figures came to light in a written response to a parliamentary question from Labour's Coventry MP Jim Cunningham. Mr Harrington's reply confirmed that the first year of the VPR scheme will be paid for through the UK's overseas aid budget, and that the government had already allocated £129m to help local authorities with costs for the remaining years. But it is unclear where the remainder of the money will come from.

Mr Harrington said the scheme would cost approximately £1.2 billion over its five-year duration, though the precise breakdown of annual costs was not provided.

Mr Vaz said he had written to the prime minister for clarification. "This is a huge figure," he added. "As the Home Office refuses to provide regular updates on the numbers being resettled, or where they are being placed, there is an unacceptable lack of transparency in the use of these significant funds."

So far 1,194 Syrians have been resettled in the UK under the scheme, including 605 under-18s, according to government figures. Local authorities can volunteer to take part in the VPR scheme and as of the beginning of December, 55 had signed up.

The government has previously signalled that the refugees getting resettled in the UK will be taken from established refugee camps. Syria has been embroiled in a bloody armed conflict for nearly five years. More than 250,000 Syrians have been killed, and 11 million displaced from their homes - more than four million have already left the country.

Earlier in the year, the prime minister was criticised by a group of 27 charities - including Oxfam and Amnesty International - which said the UK should take a "proportionate" share of refugees.

# New Tolkien Book 'Beren and Lúthien' Published on Anniversary

A new book by JRR Tolkien, edited by his son Christopher, has been published, featuring a deeply personal story inspired by the author's experiences in World War One.

Beren and Lúthien has been described as a "very personal story" that the Oxford professor thought up after returning from the Battle of the Somme. It was edited by his son Christopher Tolkien and contains versions of a tale that became part of The Silmarillion. The book features illustrations by Alan Lee, who won an Academy Award for his work on Peter Jackson's film trilogy.

More on this and other stories from across the south of England.

It is being published on Thursday by HarperCollins on the 10th anniversary of the last Middle Earth book, The Children of Húrin.

Tolkien specialist John Garth, who wrote Tolkien And The Great War, said the Hobbit author used his writing like an "exorcism" of the horrors he witnessed in World War One.

He said: "When he came back from the trenches, with trench fever, he spent the winter [of 1916-1917] convalescing. "He'd lost two of his dearest friends on the Somme and you can imagine he must have been inside as much of a wreck as he was physically."

Mr Garth said on a walk in an East Yorkshire wood Tolkien's wife Edith danced in a glade filled with white flowers, which became the key scene in Beren and Lúthien.

He said: "Mr Tolkien felt the kind of joy he must have felt at times he would never feel again."

The names Beren and Lúthien are carved on the gravestone Tolkien and his wife share in Wolvercote cemetery in Oxford.

The story is about the fate of lovers Beren and Lúthien, a mortal man and an immortal elf who together try to steal from the greatest of all evil beings, Melkor.

For the new book Christopher Tolkien, now aged 92, has kept his father's story in the original form in which it was written and has also shown how the narrative changed to become part of The Silmarillion.

Published in 1954, The Lord of the Rings was the sequel to The Hobbit and is one of the most successful novels ever written, having sold more than 150 million copies.

The film adaptation, released from 2001 to 2003, is one of the highest-grossing series of all time, with the final movie also winning 11 Academy Awards, tied for the most ever with Ben Hur.
