# Former US Air Force Mechanic Convicted of Attempting to Join Islamic State

A former US Air Force mechanic has been convicted of attempting to join the Islamic State (IS) militant group in Syria, marking a significant victory for prosecutors in the fight against IS sympathizers.

Tairod Pugh, 48, who converted to Islam, was found guilty of attempting to cross into Syria from Turkey just weeks after being dismissed from his mechanic position in Egypt. Turkish authorities denied him entry and subsequently extradited him back to the United States, where he now faces up to 35 years in prison.

This case represents the US government's first trial victory among more than 75 prosecutions related to IS sympathizers since 2014, highlighting the ongoing legal battle against domestic extremism.

According to prosecutors, Pugh had immersed himself in violent IS propaganda before purchasing a one-way ticket from Egypt to Turkey. Investigators discovered a letter on his computer addressed to his Egyptian wife, stating he faced "victory or martyr" as his only options.

When traveling to Istanbul, Pugh carried suspicious materials including a black face mask and maps showing IS strongholds and border crossings between Turkey and Syria.

Pugh served as an avionics specialist in the Air Force from 1986 to 1990 and later worked as an Army contractor in Iraq between 2009 and 2010.

Only one other IS-related prosecution has reached trial in the US, with Abdul Malik Abdul Kareem currently facing charges in Phoenix.

# Two Teenagers Dead After Car Crash in Morley, West Yorkshire

Two teenage boys have died following a devastating car crash in Morley, West Yorkshire, while two other 14-year-olds remain in critical condition in hospital.

The tragic incident occurred on Saturday afternoon when a blue Peugeot carrying four teenage boys crashed on Gelderd Road at 13:50 GMT. The vehicle, driven by a 21-year-old man, left the road and collided with a tree while traveling in the direction of Gildersome.

According to West Yorkshire Police, one 13-year-old passenger was killed instantly at the scene, while another boy subsequently died in hospital on Saturday night. The two other 14-year-old passengers suffered life-threatening injuries and remained in critical condition in hospital on Sunday morning. The 21-year-old driver was also hospitalized and is in a serious but stable condition.

Superintendent Sam Millar of Leeds Police described the incident as "a terrible tragedy for two young boys who had their whole lives ahead of them." He revealed that investigators believe the driver picked up the four boys from their homes without their parents' permission.

The deceased boys were from the local area and attended Bruntcliffe School and Morley Academy respectively. Specially trained officers are providing support to both schools and the victims' families during this difficult time.

Police are investigating the exact circumstances of the crash and have appealed for witnesses who may have seen how the vehicle was being driven before the incident. It is believed the car overtook another vehicle at speed shortly before leaving the road, though no other vehicles are thought to have been involved in the collision itself.

Authorities are particularly interested in speaking with anyone who saw the blue Peugeot's movements that day, especially near the Tesco Express store in Churwell.

Superintendent Millar praised members of the public who stopped to help at the scene, describing their actions as "absolutely commendable." He said: "As you can imagine it must have been one of the most horrendous scenes to come across and yet members of the public gave immediate support and first aid to these boys."

The Major Collision and Inquiry Team is leading the investigation. Anyone with information is urged to contact West Yorkshire Police on 101.

Superintendent Millar added: "This is an absolute tragedy for these boys, their families and for the community and for our local community schools."

# Plymouth Argyle Frustrated as Barnet Secure Comfortable Away Victory

**Plymouth Argyle 0-2 Barnet**

Plymouth Argyle's struggles continued at home as Barnet secured a convincing 2-0 victory, leaving the hosts frustrated after a string of missed opportunities and controversial moments at Home Park.

The visitors took the lead through an unmarked Bira Dembele, who capitalized on poor Plymouth defending from a corner kick. The midfielder rose unchallenged to send a looping header beyond the reach of home goalkeeper Jamie Stephens, giving Barnet an early advantage that would prove decisive.

Plymouth showed signs of fighting back when midfielder David Fox tested the Barnet goal with a fierce strike from the edge of the penalty area, only to see his effort crash against the crossbar. The home side's frustrations mounted further when striker Jake Jervis went down in the box under what appeared to be significant contact, but the referee waved away strong penalty appeals from the Plymouth players and supporters.

The match was effectively put beyond Plymouth's reach when Barnet's prolific striker John Akinde added a second goal. The division's leading scorer demonstrated his predatory instincts by timing his run perfectly to beat the offside trap before coolly slotting the ball past Stephens to double the visitors' advantage.

Despite trailing by two goals, Plymouth continued to press forward in search of a way back into the contest. Visiting goalkeeper Jamie Stephens proved to be an insurmountable barrier, producing two exceptional saves to preserve Barnet's clean sheet. First, he denied Jervis with a smart stop from close range, then showcased his athleticism by keeping out a powerful header from defender Sonny Bradley.

The second half saw Plymouth manager make tactical adjustments, introducing Craig Tanner and Jordan Slew in an attempt to inject fresh impetus into the home side's attack. Barnet responded by bringing on Sam Togwell and Alex Nicholls to help see out the victory.

The match became increasingly scrappy as Plymouth's desperation grew, with both Ryan Watson and Connor Smith receiving yellow cards during a heated exchange. Paul Garita had two attempts from distance saved, while substitute Craig Tanner saw his difficult header from the left saved in the top corner.

Barnet comfortably managed the closing stages, with John Akinde continuing to pose problems for the Plymouth defence despite being largely isolated up front. The Bees' defensive organization frustrated the home side, who struggled to create clear-cut chances despite dominating possession for long periods.

The defeat leaves Plymouth with questions to answer about their home form and ability to convert territorial dominance into goals. For Barnet, the victory represents an impressive away performance, built on defensive solidity and clinical finishing when opportunities arose. John Akinde's goal further enhances his credentials as the division's most feared striker, while Bira Dembele's opening goal highlighted Plymouth's vulnerability from set-pieces.

# Teacher Paid £13,000 to Man After Sexual Activity with Pupil, Panel Hears

A former teacher has been found to have engaged in an inappropriate sexual relationship with a sixth-form pupil and paid a man £13,000 in an alleged attempt to keep the relationship secret, a professional misconduct hearing has concluded.

Francoise Jenkins, 45, was working as a teacher at Danum Academy in Doncaster when her relationship with the Year 13 student began in 2007. A National College for Teaching and Leadership disciplinary panel heard disturbing allegations about the extent of the inappropriate conduct, including an incident where the pupil engaged in sexual activity with Ms Jenkins and two men at the teacher's home.

The hearing was told that Ms Jenkins befriended the pupil in April 2007, meeting her both inside and outside of school. She had obtained the student's mobile phone number from the school's database, which she claimed was solely for the purpose of study intervention. However, the pupil's partner at the time commented that the text messages appeared inappropriate.

The relationship escalated on the night of the school prom, when the two drank alcohol together. The panel heard that Ms Jenkins and the pupil shared a bed and engaged in sexual activity at the teacher's home. In a statement given to the school in December 2015, the former pupil described multiple incidents of sexual activity involving Ms Jenkins and other individuals.

In one particularly distressing account, the pupil said she had been invited to Ms Jenkins' house with a friend, referred to as individual A, where she engaged in sexual activity with Ms Jenkins, individual A, and a third person, individual C. The pupil told the panel she had sex with individual A but became upset and asked for it to stop, saying she did not want to have sex with a man.

The panel found it proven that Ms Jenkins paid individual C £13,000 to prevent him from reporting her relationship with the pupil. Ms Jenkins denied this was to silence him, claiming instead that the payment was to buy him out of his share of her home. The panel rejected this explanation.

Ms Jenkins also denied engaging in sexual activity with the pupil while she was still enrolled at the school. Some allegations, including sexual activity with a fifth person and kissing the pupil in a classroom store cupboard, were found "not proven" by the panel.

The relationship, which began in April 2007, continued until around December 2008. The former pupil reported the relationship to authorities in October 2015 while at university, after being advised to do so by someone she had confided in. She explained that she had felt mentally unable to report it earlier.

Ms Jenkins had begun teaching at Danum Academy in February 2007 and left in July 2015. She was teaching at another institution when the relationship emerged but was subsequently suspended from teaching.

# Deadly Drone Strike Hits Al-Qaeda Stronghold in Yemen

A deadly attack occurred near Radda in Yemen's al-Bayda province, a recognized stronghold of al-Qaeda militants. Local witnesses reported the strike appeared to be carried out by a drone aircraft, though the specific aircraft type remains unconfirmed.

The United States, which provides support for Yemen's counter-terrorism operations, has admitted to using drone technology in the region but maintains its policy of not commenting on individual strikes. # Demolition Delay Leaves Merseyside Residents Unable to Return Home

Two vacant high-rise buildings in Seaforth, Merseyside, were scheduled for simultaneous demolition at 10:00 BST, but the controlled explosion failed to bring down either tower initially.

Churchill House eventually collapsed unexpectedly after the botched attempt, while Montgomery House remained standing. Residents within the exclusion zone have been prevented from returning to their homes until the remaining tower is safely demolished.

One Vision Housing, owner of the properties, confirmed that Widnes-based demolition contractor J. Bryan (Victoria) Ltd is investigating the failure.

A company spokesperson addressed concerned spectators and displaced residents, acknowledging they had "experienced delays" while working to "get as many people safely back into their homes as possible."

# Microsoft Cuts Jobs as Windows Phone Business Struggles

Microsoft has confirmed it is cutting hundreds of jobs in its struggling smartphone division, marking another setback for the tech giant's mobile ambitions.

The US software giant paid $7.2bn (£5.5bn) for Nokia's handset business in 2014, but failed to make a success of new devices. In May, Windows-powered smartphones accounted for fewer than 1% of global smartphone sales.

One industry analyst suggested the firm was too late to the market.

"They spent all that money because they recognised that the smartphone market was important," said Eddie Murphy, telecoms analyst at Priory Consulting. "They were right - but just too late. Apple and Android devices have dominated the space and Windows hasn't made an impact."

One of the problems Microsoft faced was the so-called "app gap" - a shortage of popular titles appearing on its smartphones. The problem also blighted Blackberry's BB10 operating system.

"It was a tremendous problem," said Mr Murphy. "I have a lot of sympathy because I have a Windows phone and the number of apps is very small in comparison to Android. That was a real disadvantage for Microsoft."

The job losses were initially announced in May as part of a plan to close 1,850 posts in Microsoft's smartphone business.

The firm's latest operating system Windows 10 can still be used to power smartphones and in February computing giant HP announced a smartphone running Windows 10 that could transform into a desktop PC.

"I think they have looked at what Google did with Android. The dominance of the Android platform is because it is open and other companies can use it," said Mr Murphy.

"One of the things Microsoft has done is introduce the common Windows 10 platform, that allows apps to work across desktop, tablet and mobile. It's a good idea and hopefully one that will generate some new apps for the platform.

"I hope we haven't seen the last of Windows Phones. Having more platforms in the market is in the best interests of consumers."

# NSA Official Suggests Amnesty for Snowden, But Director Dismisses Idea

The official leading the National Security Agency's damage assessment of Edward Snowden's leaks has suggested he would be open to discussing an amnesty deal for the former intelligence contractor, even as the agency's director firmly rejected the possibility.

Richard Ledgett, who is in charge of evaluating the impact of Mr. Snowden's disclosures, told CBS television that a conversation about amnesty could be worthwhile under certain conditions.

"So my personal view is, yes it's worth having a conversation about," Mr. Ledgett said. "I would need assurances that the remainder of the data could be secured, and my bar for those assurances would be very high, would be more than just an assertion on his part."

However, NSA Director General Keith Alexander quickly dismissed the idea, using a stark analogy to explain his opposition.

"This is analogous to a hostage taker taking 50 people hostage, shooting 10, and then say, 'if you give me full amnesty, I'll let the other 40 go'. What do you do?" Gen Alexander said in his interview with CBS.

The contrasting positions highlight the NSA's difficult situation as it grapples with the fallout from Mr. Snowden's revelations about the extent of the agency's surveillance activities.

According to the BBC's Washington correspondent Jonny Dymond, while an amnesty for Edward Snowden is an intriguing prospect, it faces significant obstacles. Much of Congress would likely be "apoplectic" at such a proposal, making it "an unimaginably hard-sell politically." Many lawmakers have expressed fierce opposition to Mr. Snowden since the leaks began.

The discussion of amnesty suggests the NSA harbors deep concerns about what Mr. Ledgett called "the keys to the kingdom" – potentially devastating classified information that Mr. Snowden may possess but has not yet released. In an earlier interview with Reuters, Mr. Ledgett expressed serious worry about highly classified documents among the estimated 1.7 million files Mr. Snowden is believed to have accessed.

Mr. Ledgett described Mr. Snowden's disclosures as "cataclysmic" for the agency. Authoritative reports indicate the NSA is struggling to determine exactly what Mr. Snowden did and did not take.

Earlier this month, a UK newspaper editor informed British MPs that only 1% of the files leaked by Mr. Snowden have been published.

The State Department has maintained that its position remains unchanged: Mr. Snowden must return to the United States to face criminal charges. He has been charged with theft of government property, unauthorized communication of national defense information, and willful communication of classified communications intelligence. Each charge carries a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison.

Gen Alexander, who is retiring early next year, made his comments during a weekend in which the NSA took unprecedented steps toward transparency, allowing a CBS television crew into its headquarters for the first time in the agency's history in an effort to be more open about its data collection activities.

The BBC's Suzanne Kianpour reports that despite Mr. Ledgett's comments, there has been no change in the official US government position on Mr. Snowden.

# Body Found in Sheffield River Believed to Be Missing Student Caroline Everest

A body discovered in a Sheffield river is believed to be that of missing student Caroline Everest, 18, South Yorkshire Police have confirmed.

South Yorkshire Police are working to "establish the circumstances surrounding her death." Officers have been observed searching undergrowth near the recovery site and have appealed for anyone who may have seen Ms Everest after she left the nightclub to come forward.

The discovery was made in an area of modern office buildings and car dealerships, situated between the city centre and Eccleshall Road, where many students reside. The location is approximately half a mile from the Corporation nightclub and near Sheffield's inner ring road.

Charlton Athletic have completed the signings of defender Zakarya Bergdich and midfielder Cristian Ceballos as they continue to strengthen their squad for the Championship campaign.

# Judge Orders Uber to Return Waymo Trade Secrets in Self-Driving Car Dispute

A San Francisco federal judge has dealt a significant blow to Uber in its ongoing legal battle with Waymo, ordering the ride-hailing company to return thousands of confidential documents and barring a key engineer from working on critical aspects of its autonomous driving project.

District Judge William Alsup ruled Monday that Waymo "has shown compelling evidence that its former star engineer" Anthony Levandowski "pilfered" approximately 14,000 confidential files from the Google-owned company before joining Uber. The documents allegedly contained proprietary information related to Lidar technology, a crucial sensor system used in self-driving vehicles.

"The bottom line is the evidence indicates that Uber hired Levandowski even though it knew or should have known that he possessed over 14,000 confidential Waymo files likely containing Waymo's intellectual property," Judge Alsup wrote in his ruling, which was unsealed Monday.

Under the court order, Uber must return all stolen documents to either Waymo or the court by month's end. Additionally, Mr. Levandowski has been prohibited from working on any Lidar-related projects at Uber, directly targeting the technology at the heart of the lawsuit.

Waymo spokesman Johnny Luu praised the decision, stating: "Competition should be fuelled by innovation in the labs and on the roads, not through unlawful actions."

However, the ruling offered Uber some relief. Judge Alsup noted that "few" of Waymo's alleged trade secrets have actually been traced to Uber's self-driving car technology. He also determined that not all of Waymo's 121 asserted trade secrets qualify for legal protection as trade secrets.

Significantly, the judge stopped short of shutting down Uber's entire autonomous vehicle division—a worst-case scenario for the company, which views self-driving technology as essential to its future business model.

"We are pleased with the court's ruling that Uber can continue building and utilizing all of its self-driving technology, including our innovation around Lidar," said Uber spokeswoman Chelsea Kohler.

The ruling comes as Waymo announced a partnership with Lyft, Uber's primary US competitor, to test self-driving technology.

# Ferrari Dealer Smashes Record with £518,000 Number Plate Purchase

A Ferrari dealer has broken the DVLA's record for the most expensive number plate ever sold in the UK, paying an eye-watering £518,000 for the registration "25 O."

John Collins secured the prestigious plate at an auction held at the Vale Resort near Cardiff, outbidding several determined competitors in what he described as "very fierce bidding."

The millionaire dealer revealed the number plate will adorn a Ferrari 250 SWB that once belonged to rock legend Eric Clapton and is currently valued at £10 million.

"I was determined to get the number," Collins told Newsbeat. "It's just the perfect number plate for a 250."

Despite the record-breaking price, Collins had been prepared to go even further. He'd anticipated paying around £300,000 but admitted he would have bid up to £1 million to secure the plate.

## Sound Investment Strategy

Collins remains confident about the purchase, viewing it as a solid investment rather than an extravagant expense.

"If you put a half a million number plate on some cars you'd get an extra million for the car," he explained. "I could sell it tomorrow for a profit to somebody, but it's not for sale."

The bidding war intensified as it reached six figures, with approximately four serious contenders remaining. Collins believes he recognized some of his competitors, describing the finale as a test of "who had the biggest cheque book on the day and the biggest resolve."

## Celebrity Congratulations

Following his victory, Collins received congratulatory messages, including one from television presenter Chris Evans, who texted: "Well done."

However, his daughter offered a more practical perspective, pointing out: "You could buy six houses dad!"

Collins, who prefers number plates that relate to the vehicles they adorn rather than personal vanity plates, has a history of collecting distinctive registrations. He previously owned HDT 1, which he thought resembled "HOT 1."

The DVLA auction demonstrates the continuing appetite among collectors for prestigious number plates that complement luxury vehicles.

# Historic Aberfan Chapel Destroyed in Deliberate Fire

South Wales Police investigations concluded the fire was started intentionally.

# British Woman Found Dead in Finnish Lapland as Boyfriend Arrested After Dog Sled Chase

A 26-year-old British woman, believed to be from Scotland, has been found dead in the remote Finnish village of Kuttanen in Lapland, prompting a dramatic manhunt in sub-zero temperatures.

Lapland Police confirmed that the woman's 36-year-old Czech boyfriend fled the scene on a dog sled following the incident on Saturday. Authorities immediately launched a search operation involving snow scooters and a helicopter to locate the suspect in the harsh Arctic wilderness.

The man was discovered several hours later in temperatures plummeting to -30C and was transported to hospital for treatment. Following medical care, he was taken into police custody on suspicion of murder.

Both individuals were seasonal workers in the area, which sits near the Swedish border. The victim, whose name has not been released, was employed by Santa Safari, a company that partners with Oxford-based tour operator Transun Travel to organize Christmas-themed excursions in Lapland.

In a statement, Santa Safari expressed their grief: "We are deeply saddened to confirm that a member of the Santa Safari team was discovered dead on the 3rd December. We are all in shock from this tragic news and our thoughts go out to her family."

Police Scotland confirmed they have been contacted by the Foreign and Commonwealth Office regarding the death and will continue to provide assistance as required. A Foreign Office spokeswoman stated: "We are supporting the family of a British national who died in Finland on 3 December."

Transun Travel posted on Facebook warning that some tours may face disruption due to the police investigation. The company extended condolences to the victim's family, friends, and the Santa Safari team, pledging full support during this difficult period.

The investigation into the woman's death continues.

# Essex Care Homes Challenge Council Over "Unsustainable" Funding Rates

Care England, a body representing adult care providers, has expressed deep concerns about the viability of the care home market in Essex, launching judicial review proceedings against Essex County Council over the rates it pays for residential care.

The dispute centres on what providers describe as inadequate funding levels that threaten the sustainability of care services across the county.

Sean Watson, director of St Michael Homes Ltd in Brentwood, highlighted the stark disparity in payment rates. The council currently pays £483 per week per resident, while private residents pay £650 weekly for the same care.

"Lots of care homes who depend on council-funded residents are closing down or providing a poor service and you can't really blame them because they haven't got funding to back them," Mr Watson said.

He explained that whilst the issue emerged in the early 1990s, the situation has deteriorated significantly. "It's much worse now with increasing demand on services for the elderly, and rates the council pays us not going up for years or increasing in line with inflation," he added.

Care England's judicial review seeks to "challenge the lawfulness of the council's fee setting decision", arguing the authority has breached its responsibilities under the Care Act 2014.

Mr Watson warned the funding crisis could have serious consequences for vulnerable residents. "Care homes can't sustain the low fees with all the increases in wages and the Care Quality Commission demanding ever more of the service with no increase in fees," he said, suggesting homes may refuse council-funded residents in future.

An Essex County Council spokesman said the authority could not comment on specific legal proceedings but confirmed it takes its Care Act 2014 obligations "extremely seriously" and remains committed to "a sustainable social care market".

# Safety Checks Ground North Sea Helicopters

Helicopter operators in the North Sea have been ordered to conduct immediate safety inspections following a recent incident on an offshore platform.

The checks, issued overnight by manufacturer Sikorsky, focus on tail rotors and are expected to take several hours per aircraft, disrupting flights throughout the day.

The Air Accidents Investigation Branch is investigating an incident last month on the West Franklin Platform, where an S92 helicopter experienced a technical fault during landing, leaving "significant gouge marks" on the platform deck.

All operators have been instructed to carry out the precautionary checks immediately, affecting offshore operations for the remainder of the day.

# Scotland House Opens in London as Business Hub for Scottish Companies

Scotland has officially opened a new business hub in the heart of London, designed to help Scottish companies expand their reach in one of the world's leading financial centres.

Scotland House, located on Victoria Embankment near the Houses of Parliament at Westminster, was officially opened by First Minister Nicola Sturgeon on Tuesday evening. The facility serves as an investment and innovation centre, similar to one previously opened in Dublin, with additional hubs planned for Brussels and Berlin.

The centre is intended as a membership-based space where Scottish businesses can showcase their products, meet with customers, and connect with investors from across the UK and international markets. According to Ms Sturgeon, more than 450 companies have already expressed interest in becoming members.

"London is a very important trading market and a meeting place for the world's business leaders, but for Scottish businesses it can be challenging and costly to try and break into these markets," the First Minister said. "The new hub will play a critical role in attracting investment to Scotland, helping businesses trade internationally and raising Scotland's international profile."

Scotland House will provide Scottish companies with affordable access to London's business community, offering a base to build partnerships without the substantial costs typically associated with establishing a London presence.

The facility will also serve as offices for Scottish government officials and staff from Scottish Enterprise, Highlands and Islands Enterprise, and VisitScotland, creating a consolidated Scottish presence in the capital.

Malcolm Roughead, chief executive of VisitScotland, emphasized London's importance as Scotland's most significant trading partner. "If Scottish tourism is to continue punching above its weight on the world stage, we need to keep attracting new investment, events, airlines and ultimately, visitors," he said.

Lena Wilson, chief executive of Scottish Enterprise, described the opening as "the start of an exciting new phase of growth and collaboration between Scotland and London." She noted that Scotland and London together form "a formidable force for tourism, trade, investment and collaboration."

The phenomenal initial response, with hundreds of businesses seeking to utilize the facility, suggests strong demand for such a platform among Scotland's business community.

Maria Sharapova withdrew from the Bank of the West Classic in Stanford before her scheduled second-round match against Ukraine's Lesia Tsurenko, dealing another setback to the Russian's comeback efforts.

Meanwhile, newly-crowned Wimbledon champion Garbine Muguruza made a dominant return to action, thrashing American Kayla Day 6-2, 6-0. The Spanish world number four adopted a measured approach to her recent triumph.

"[Wimbledon] is just another tournament," Muguruza insisted. # Birmingham City Boss Harry Redknapp Confirms Shotton Deal But Awaits Replacement

Birmingham City manager Harry Redknapp has confirmed that defender Ryan Shotton has agreed terms with Championship rivals Middlesbrough, but insists the player will remain at St Andrew's until a replacement is secured.

Veteran Paul Robinson remains an option, having been on the bench for the past two matches following his suspension.

"We now have five players out injured," Redknapp said. "We could have only one [available] centre-half on our books, which is not a good position to be in at this stage of the season.

# Crown Dependencies Face Uncertain Future After Being Denied EU Referendum Vote

Residents of the Crown dependencies - the Isle of Man, Jersey and Guernsey - were excluded from voting in the EU referendum as they are not part of the European Union. In contrast, Gibraltar, a British overseas territory, was granted voting rights and voted decisively to remain.

Isle of Man Chief Minister Mr Bell described the referendum outcome as the "start of a journey into the unknown for both the UK and the Isle of Man," calling the situation "without precedent." He warned that Britain's withdrawal from the EU "will have a significant impact" on the island.

The Isle of Man now faces the challenge of replacing its Protocol 3 arrangement with the EU, which currently enables free trade in manufactured goods and agricultural products. While Mr Bell stated the island was "well-prepared," he emphasized the importance of working closely with UK politicians to understand their plans and ensure the island's interests "are not overlooked."

The exclusion sparked controversy earlier this year when Isle of Man resident and Lord of the Rings actor John Rhys-Davies, 71, launched a petition demanding voting rights for Crown dependency residents. He described the referendum as "one of the most important [and] constitutionally significant events in recent times."

The dependencies must now navigate complex negotiations to protect their economic interests in the post-Brexit landscape.

# Fatal Road Collision in Moira Claims One Life

A man has died following a single-vehicle collision on Moira Road shortly after 10:00 BST. The victim was driving a black Skoda when the incident occurred.

Police have launched an investigation and are appealing for witnesses to come forward with information. The road remains closed at its junction with Carnkilly Road while inquiries continue.

Motorists are being advised to follow diversions and avoid the area until further notice.

# Blizzard Warns Players After Security Breach Exposes Battle.net Account Data

Gaming giant Blizzard Entertainment has urged millions of players to change their passwords after discovering unauthorized access to its internal network and the theft of sensitive account information from its Battle.net service.

The company revealed details of the security breach in a message posted to its Battle.net account management service, with CEO Mike Morhaime announcing that the intrusion was discovered on August 4th. The breach affected players using North American servers, including users in the United States, Canada, Latin America, Australia, New Zealand, and Southeast Asia.

According to Blizzard's investigation, hackers gained access to a comprehensive list of email addresses for all Battle.net users outside China. Battle.net serves as the central account management and login platform for Blizzard's popular gaming titles, including World of Warcraft, StarCraft 2, and Diablo 3.

The stolen data also included information about security questions and account authenticators used by players on North American servers. Perhaps most concerningly, attackers obtained a cryptographically scrambled list of passwords for North American Battle.net accounts. However, Mr. Morhaime emphasized that the encryption technique used by Blizzard makes these passwords extremely difficult to unscramble.

Despite the sophisticated security measures, Blizzard is taking no chances. The company has initiated an automatic process to force affected players to change their security questions and update their authenticator devices. Players are being strongly encouraged to change their passwords immediately, particularly if they use the same credentials on other online services.

In what may provide some relief to concerned users, Blizzard stated it has found "no evidence" that financial information was compromised. Credit card numbers, billing addresses, and real names appear to have remained secure during the breach.

"We are truly sorry that this has happened," Mr. Morhaime said in the company's statement.

Security expert Paul Ducklin from Sophos described the breach as "painful but probably not too bad," praising Blizzard's "sensible" approach to storing and managing login credentials, which should help minimize the impact.

However, the incident has reignited criticism of Blizzard's controversial decision to require constant online connectivity for traditionally offline games. Gaming journalist Nathan Grayson of Rock Paper Shotgun noted that players seeking single-player experiences are likely "the angriest of all" about this breach, as they're forced to maintain online accounts even when not playing multiplayer modes.

The company continues to investigate the breach while implementing additional security measures to protect its user base.

# Liverpool Vicar Sentenced for £70,000 Theft from Funeral Fees

A Liverpool vicar who stole approximately £70,000 in funeral fees over eight years has been given a suspended prison sentence after admitting to what a judge described as "an enormous breach of trust".

Michael John Fry, 57, of Aigburth Vale, Liverpool, pleaded guilty at Liverpool Crown Court to committing eight offences spanning from late 2005 to 1 January 2014. The court heard that Fry misled Liverpool diocese about the number of funerals he had conducted and illegally retained fees from 1,250 parochial funerals.

Judge Elizabeth Nicholls told the court that what began as an administrative failing had evolved into outright "dishonesty". However, she added that "the good you have done in the community outweighs the harm" and sentenced Fry to 20 months in jail, suspended for two years.

The vicar spent the stolen money on alcohol, books, and travel. The thefts began modestly with £1,751 between December 2005 and January 2007, but escalated significantly, reaching £20,049 between December 2011 and January 2013. Fry was required to send any fees exceeding his £22,000 annual stipend to the diocese but failed to do so.

Defence lawyer Martine Snowdon argued that the theft resulted from a failure to act rather than a premeditated scheme, though she acknowledged her client was "deeply remorseful" about betraying his peers and society.

The court heard that Liverpool diocese had initially been relaxed about Fry's accounts due to the "expectation of honesty and integrity of one of their own". The stolen funds could have supported four full-time clergy posts.

The Archdeacon of Liverpool, Venerable Ricky Panter, described the "scale of the fraud" as "staggering" but expressed that he was "pleased" with the suspended sentence. He said he felt "immensely sad and let down" but acknowledged the personal struggles Fry had faced, adding that he hoped for Fry's return to "some kind of ministry in the future".

Fry, who was a member of the St Luke in the City Team serving three parish churches, resigned from his position in early 2014.

# Ireland Miss Out on World Cup Semi-Final Spot After Narrow Loss to Spain

Ireland's hopes of reaching the World League semi-finals were dashed following a narrow 2-1 defeat to Spain in a tightly contested quarter-final match.

All three goals came in a dramatic third quarter that proved decisive for both teams' tournament futures. Spain's Ricardo Sanchez opened the scoring, before Alan Sothern equalized for Ireland with a powerful drag flick. However, Alvaro Iglesias struck the winner just a minute later to send Spain through to the semi-finals.

The result means Ireland will now compete in the fifth to eighth place play-offs, with their next fixture against France scheduled for Friday. Finishing fifth would guarantee automatic qualification for the World Cup, making Friday's match crucial for Irish hockey's ambitions. Should they fail to secure a top-five position, Ireland must anxiously await results from continental championships to determine their World Cup fate.

Ireland dominated possession in the first half, accumulating 10 penalty corners, but found Spanish goalkeeper Quico Cortes in inspired form. Eugene Magee came agonizingly close when his reverse shot skimmed past the post, while Cortes repeatedly denied Irish attacks.

Spain emerged with renewed intensity after halftime, forcing Irish goalkeeper Davy Harte into several smart saves. Drama unfolded in the 37th minute when Johnny McKee bravely blocked a Spanish penalty corner shot but landed heavily on his shoulder, requiring a stretcher to remove the young Banbridge player from the field.

Despite Harte's heroics in making two consecutive saves from the resulting penalty corner, Sanchez managed to flick the rebound into the net in the 43rd minute. Ireland's response was immediate, with Sothern leveling the scores just a minute later. However, Spain regained the lead almost instantly when a mis-trapped penalty corner was crashed back into the circle, allowing the unmarked Iglesias to sweep home at the back post.

Ireland pressed frantically for an equalizer, with fine efforts from Magee and Jeremy Duncan calling Cortes into action once more, but the Spanish goalkeeper stood firm.

Ireland head coach Craig Fulton remained philosophical despite the disappointment. "We're happy with our performance, but they took their chances on the day and we didn't," he said. "It was a good game and it could have gone either way. We know the chances we created and on another day we'll definitely finish those."

The team will now regroup ahead of Friday's crucial encounter with France, a side they defeated on penalties in the World League 2 final in Belfast last March.

# Kenya Faces Possible Ban from International Competition Over Anti-Doping Non-Compliance

Kenya is on the brink of being declared non-compliant with global anti-doping rules, potentially leading to a ban from international athletic competitions including the Rio Olympics.

The World Anti-Doping Agency's (Wada) compliance review committee is meeting in Montreal on Tuesday and is expected to recommend that the East African nation be declared non-compliant. Wada's board is then scheduled to approve the recommendation on 12 May.

As previously reported by BBC Sport, Kenya failed to meet an 11 February deadline to pass legislation establishing a new national anti-doping agency. Following this failure, Wada placed Kenya on a 'watch-list' of countries at risk of breaching its code and extended the deadline to 5 April to demonstrate progress in combating doping.

While Kenyan lawmakers have conducted a preliminary reading of a bill that would criminalise sports doping, two additional hearings and presidential approval are still required. Complicating matters further, the country's parliament entered a month-long recess last week without approving the legislation or allocating additional funding, guaranteeing the latest deadline would be missed.

Once a country is declared Wada non-compliant, the International Olympic Committee and international federations such as the IAAF have the authority to ban it from international competition. IAAF president Lord Coe has stated his readiness to ban Kenya if it receives the non-compliant designation.

Kenya, which dominates distance running and topped the medal table at the 2015 World Championships in Beijing with seven gold medals, has become embroiled in doping and bribery controversies. Since 2011, more than 40 Kenyan athletes have failed drug tests.

Additionally, three senior officials at Kenya Athletics have been suspended amid accusations of corruption related to Doha's successful bid for the 2019 World Championships. Both the officials and Qatar's campaign team deny any wrongdoing.

In February, the Kenyan government assured the BBC it was taking doping threats "very seriously" and stated its newly established national anti-doping organisation would soon be operational.

# Former High Court Judge Sir Nicholas Wall Dies at 71

Sir Nicholas Wall, the former president of the High Court's Family Division, has died at the age of 71 after a battle with a rare neurological condition, his family has announced.

The distinguished judge had been suffering from fronto temporal lobe dementia, a degenerative brain disease that was only recently diagnosed. According to a death notice published in the Times, Sir Nicholas "died by his own hand on 17th February 2017."

In a statement, his family said he "took his own life having suffered for several years" from the disease, which had significantly impacted his quality of life.

Sir Nicholas had a distinguished legal career spanning more than four decades. Called to the Bar in 1969, he became a recorder in 1990 and was appointed as a judge of the High Court Family Division in 1993. He assumed the role of president of the Family Division in 2010 but was forced to retire in 2012 due to declining health.

The Family Law Bar Association paid tribute, describing him as "a compassionate judge who cared deeply about the outcome of his cases." Throughout his career, Sir Nicholas also served at the Employment Appeal Tribunal, the Administrative Court, and the Court of Appeal.

Sir Nicholas was known for his progressive views on family law. In 2011, he advocated for a "live-in lovers" law to protect women in long-term relationships from losing their homes and income after separation. The following year, he championed no-fault divorce, stating he could "see no good arguments against" it.

His successor, Sir James Munby, praised Sir Nicholas for speaking "with passion, and in plain language, about the importance of family life" and for being "appropriately outspoken about the plight of children caught up in the midst of parental conflict."

# Wang Claims Third European Tour Title in Qatar Play-off Thriller

South Korean golfer Wang secured his third European Tour victory in dramatic fashion, winning a three-way play-off at the Qatar Masters in Doha.

The 21-year-old Wang, who had taken a three-stroke lead into the final day, was caught at 16 under par by Sweden's Joakim Lagergren and South Africa's Jaco van Zyl after regulation play. However, Wang displayed nerves of steel by firing the only birdie on the par-five first extra hole to claim victory.

Wang, who won consecutive tournaments in Morocco and Mauritius last May, nearly sealed the win on the 72nd hole but left a birdie putt agonisingly short. In the play-off, Van Zyl three-putted for par whilst Lagergren failed to get up and down from a greenside bunker, allowing Wang to capitalise.

The young Korean becomes the third youngest player to win three European Tour titles, behind only Italy's Matteo Manassero (19) and Spain's legendary Seve Ballesteros (20).

England's Jordan Smith finished strongly with a final-round six under to claim sixth place, two strokes behind the leaders. Wales' Bradley Dredge, who had led after day one, finished tied for 21st on nine under.

# Westminster Attack: Welsh MPs Call for Unity and Resources in Commons Debate

Welsh MPs took part in an emotional House of Commons debate following Wednesday's terror attack in Westminster that claimed four lives, with calls for adequate security resources and warnings against responses that could fuel further extremism.

Gower MP Byron Davies, drawing on his experience serving under counter-terrorist command in London during the 1980s, emphasized the critical need for proper resourcing of security forces. The Conservative MP, who is a member of the home affairs committee, told fellow parliamentarians that he understood "only too well the challenge that's faced by police" having previously tackled Irish and Middle Eastern terrorism.

Mr Davies stressed the importance of ensuring that all police and security forces fighting terrorism should "want for nothing," reinforcing concerns about adequate resources for those on the front line of protecting the public.

Plaid Cymru MP Liz Saville Roberts struck a cautionary note, warning against inappropriate reactions to the attack. She told the House that MPs' return to the Commons on Thursday was "not a show of defiance" but rather "a show of respect for the dead and the injured." In a direct question to Prime Minister Theresa May, she asked: "Do you agree with me that we must not react to such a warped ideology with unworthy responses?"

Mrs May responded by praising the "absolutely appropriate" response of MPs, highlighting three key elements of the parliamentary reaction. "It has shown gratitude for the bravery of the police and our emergency services," she said. "It has shown respect and concern for those who have been the victims of the terrible attacks that took place but also it has shown normality. I think that is what is important as we defy the terrorists and as we work to defeat them."

Rhondda MP Chris Bryant made an emotional appeal for a shield to be unveiled in the Commons chamber to honour PC Keith Palmer, who was stabbed to death by the suspected terrorist. The Labour member referenced the custom of honouring murdered MPs such as Ian Gow and Airey Neave with similar memorials. "He was our shield and defender yesterday," Mr Bryant said of the fallen officer.

Meanwhile, arrests have been made in Birmingham and London, with related police activity also taking place at a location in Wales.

Former Pontypriod MP Kim Howells, who previously served as chairman of Parliament's security and intelligence committee, acknowledged the inherent challenges of preventing such attacks. "We don't live in a police state and as a consequence of course there's a very good chance that someone will always get through," he told BBC Wales.

Lord Carlile, the UK government's former independent reviewer of terrorism legislation and former Welsh Liberal Democrat leader, said the security services possessed sufficient powers to address terrorist threats. However, he suggested that consideration might need to be given to whether all police should be armed around major public buildings.

Welsh Assembly committees met as scheduled on Thursday, with chairmen pausing proceedings at 0933 GMT to observe a minute's silence following Wednesday's suspension of Senedd proceedings.

# Wales Eye Fiji Victory to Pile Pressure on England at Rugby World Cup

Wales coach Warren Gatland believes his team can seize control of their Rugby World Cup pool by defeating Fiji on Thursday, following their dramatic 28-25 victory over England at Twickenham.

The win puts Wales in a commanding position, and Gatland is eyeing another crucial result against the Pacific Islanders. "If we beat Fiji we'll put quite a bit of pressure on England I suppose because they'll have to beat Australia," said the coach.

However, Wales face the challenge with three fresh injury concerns. Centre Scott Williams suffered a knee injury, while wing Hallam Amos sustained a shoulder problem – both appearing set to miss the remainder of the tournament. Full-back Liam Williams was concussed following a blow to the head and is unlikely to feature against Fiji.

The injuries occurred during a passage of play when Wales trailed 25-18 to England. Despite having three backs playing out of position, Wales rallied impressively to secure victory.

Australia's 65-3 thrashing of Uruguay on Sunday sees them join Wales on nine points at the pool's summit. Fiji, meanwhile, have lost both opening matches – 35-11 to England and 28-13 against Australia – though Gatland believes the Pacific Islanders have been unfortunate.

"It's massive for us," Gatland said. "We've spoken that if we could win today and win against Fiji then that game England v Australia becomes huge and the pool could be over by that stage."

The New Zealander insists Wales won't underestimate their opponents. "I think they've been pretty unlucky and we have to make sure we respect them. But I think we can take a lot of confidence out of this performance."

Gatland revealed extensive preparation has gone into managing the short turnaround between matches, with various scenarios meticulously planned.

# Campaigners Fight to Save Highland Heartbeat Centre Amid Closure Plans

Campaigners have mounted a strong defence of the Highland Heartbeat Centre, criticising NHS Highland's decision to close the facility and questioning the health board's handling of the situation.

NHS Highland is preparing to transition from the dedicated centre to a clinic-based model combining joint physiotherapy and specialist nurse patient assessments, with the changeover scheduled for early June 2017. The health board is currently recruiting additional cardiac rehabilitation specialist nurses to support the new arrangements.

Under the proposed system, cardiac rehabilitation would be delivered as an outreach service throughout the health board's region, with some sessions taking place in local leisure centres. NHS Highland has assured the public that the Highland Heartbeat Centre at Raigmore Hospital will remain operational until alternative arrangements are fully established.

The health board stated it needs the centre's space for other clinical services that require a hospital location. The building, which opened 12 years ago following substantial fundraising efforts, has become a focal point in the controversy.

Charlie Bloe, clinical ward manager for coronary care at Raigmore, acknowledged public concerns whilst defending the decision. Speaking to BBC Radio Scotland, he said: "We have been very sympathetic to the views of the various charities that contributed to the development of the Highland Heartbeat Centre."

He explained that cardiac care has evolved significantly, stating: "Cardiology and cardiac nursing is a fast evolving specialism and the way in which you deliver modern-day cardiac rehabilitation has changed significantly in the last 10 years."

Mr Bloe emphasised continuity of care: "The assurances I want to give them is that patients will continue to benefit from an improved cardiac rehabilitation service, albeit it won't be in the Highland Heartbeat Centre."

The centre opened in 2005 after hundreds of thousands of pounds were raised through public donations, with additional funding provided by the British Heart Foundation.

Inverness Bravehearts, a charity instrumental in establishing the centre, has strongly opposed the closure plans. A spokeswoman said: "These proposals do not in any way represent the NHS's previously promised equitable solution, equivalent to the specialist facility of the current Highland Heartbeat Centre and the services it provides."

The charity added that the proposals "do not respect and reflect the Highland public's commitment and £1m investment in the centre and its dedicated cardiac rehab programme."

The campaign group We All Need the Heartbeat went further, calling it "laughable" for NHS Highland to describe the new arrangements as an improvement. The group accused the health board of being "motivated by a property-grab" on a publicly-funded building.

# Tougher Penalties Planned for Laser Attacks on Aircraft and Transport

The Department for Transport has announced new legislation that will significantly increase penalties for people who shine lasers at aircraft, trains, buses and taxis, with offenders facing fines of thousands of pounds or imprisonment.

The move comes as attacks on aircraft have remained persistently high, with approximately 1,500 incidents reported annually since 2009. While a 2010 law introduced protections specifically for pilots, the new legislation will widen these protections to include other transport operators whilst simultaneously increasing penalties.

Under current regulations outlined in the Air Navigation Order, individuals convicted of "shining a light at an aircraft in flight so as to dazzle or distract the pilot" face maximum fines of £2,500. In cases where the distraction is considered serious, offenders may be prosecuted for reckless endangerment, which carries a prison sentence.

Crucially, the new law will ease the burden of proof for police. A Department for Transport spokesman explained that current legislation requires authorities to prove a person endangered an aircraft when committing the offence. The updated law will only require proof that the laser was shone at the vehicle.

Transport Secretary Chris Grayling emphasised the severity of the issue: "Shining a laser pointer at pilots or drivers is incredibly dangerous and could have fatal consequences. Whilst we know laser pens can be fun and many users have good intentions, some are not aware of the risks of dazzling drivers or pilots putting public safety at risk."

The problem has escalated dramatically since the first reported laser attack on an aircraft in 2004, which saw over 200 incidents by 2008. Recent years have witnessed a substantial increase in such attacks, with similar incidents targeting train and bus drivers.

Steve Landells, flight safety specialist at the British Airline Pilots Association, welcomed the announcement: "Any move to give the police and authorities more powers to tackle this real and growing threat to flight safety is a good thing."

The urgency of the issue was highlighted in February 2016 when a New York-bound aircraft was forced to return to Heathrow Airport after a laser beam struck the cockpit, causing a medical issue for one pilot. This incident prompted calls from both the British Airline Pilots Association and Civil Aviation Authority to classify laser pointers as offensive weapons.

The Department for Transport confirmed that details of the new powers and penalties will be outlined in forthcoming legislation.

# Eugene Laverty Finishes Tenth at Czech Republic MotoGP

Northern Ireland's Eugene Laverty secured a tenth-place finish at the Czech Republic MotoGP in Brno on Sunday.

Crutchlow's hard tyres suited the testing conditions in Brno and he worked his way from 10th on the grid to take the lead with seven laps to go. He is the first Briton to win an elite-class GP since Barry Sheene in 1981.

The next race is the British GP at Silverstone on 4 September.

# Obama: US-Led Coalition Making Progress Against Islamic State

President Barack Obama has delivered a strong message about progress in the fight against the Islamic State group, speaking at the Pentagon after a National Security Council meeting.

November saw more airstrikes launched against the group than in any previous month, he said. He said the US had killed a number of its leaders and attacked oil facilities it relies on for cash. He has been seeking to reassure the public following an attack in California at the hands of militants.

# Mock Firearms Incident Exercise Held at Royal Shakespeare Company

A major multi-agency emergency exercise was conducted at the Royal Shakespeare Company (RSC) in Stratford-upon-Avon to test response capabilities to a simulated firearms incident.

Exercise Titus, which had been planned for three months, involved personnel from Warwickshire Fire Service, Warwickshire and West Mercia police forces, and West Midlands Ambulance Service. # Cyclists Stage Rush-Hour Protest at Bank Junction After Latest London Deaths

Cyclists brought central London to a standstill during Wednesday morning's rush hour in protest over road safety, following two cycling deaths in just two days.

The 15-minute protest from 08:30 BST brought traffic to a halt on all six arms of Bank junction. Ying Tao, 26, died in a collision with a lorry while she was cycling to work at PricewaterhouseCoopers on Monday. The London Cycling Campaign (LCC) is calling for segregated space for cyclists on London's roads.

The campaign group, which organised the demonstration, also wants the removal of dangerous lorries from streets. A minute's silence was also held in memory of Ms Tao and 60-year-old Clifton James, who was killed in a collision with a car in Harrow, north west London on Sunday.

Neil Hampson, a partner at PricewaterhouseCooper, said the company was "shocked" by the news of their employee's death and sent their condolences to her family. "Ying was a bright and popular colleague with a promising career in front of her," he said. "She excelled at everything she did, with a passion for life, for work and for the friendships she made. During Prime Minister's Questions, David Cameron said a lot had been done to try to make cycling safer in London and money had been invested in cycling lanes. However, he added: "The number of fatalities is still very high and extremely depressing [that] young lives [are] being snuffed out in this way."

Of the eight fatalities on the capital's roads this year, seven have involved heavy goods vehicles.

# Turkish President Erdogan Supporters Charged Over Washington Brawl

Two supporters of Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan have been charged with assault following a violent brawl outside the Turkish ambassador's residence in Washington last month.

Eyup Yildirim of New Jersey and Sinan Narin of Virginia face charges in connection with what police described as a "brutal attack on peaceful protesters" during President Erdogan's visit to the United States.

According to a detailed New York Times investigation, both men had travelled to Washington specifically to support the Turkish president, though their formal connection to his security detail remains unclear.

# Northern Ireland Teacher Describes Stockholm Terror Attack Scene

A science teacher from Northern Ireland has described the chaotic scenes he witnessed during a suspected terror attack in Stockholm that has left at least four people dead.

Dr. Jonathan Lappin, from Enniskillen, County Fermanagh, was having coffee with a colleague across from the affected area when the incident unfolded on Friday afternoon. What began as seemingly innocent excitement quickly descended into mass panic.

"I thought they were chasing a celebrity," Dr. Lappin told the BBC, describing how he initially saw people running with their phones out. "People started to mass panic, and run into the coffee shop and crowd the back of it."

The confusion in the café was immediate, with conflicting messages from staff telling customers not to worry while others fled. Moments later, police arrived on scene, shouting at people to evacuate the area.

After waiting several minutes, Dr. Lappin and his colleague decided to leave. Upon stepping outside, they immediately "could smell the burning and the smoke," though the full extent of what had happened remained unclear.

"I jumped to the conclusion that it must be a terrorist attack and wanted out of there, so we started to run as fast as we could down the street," Dr. Lappin said.

He praised the swift response of Swedish authorities, noting that riot police with shields and helicopters arrived promptly. However, the size of Stockholm created additional challenges. "It's such a spread out city, there's a lot of confusion," he explained, with much of the area now in lockdown.

Swedish Prime Minister Stefan Lofven has stated that all evidence points toward an act of terrorism. Police have confirmed one arrest has been made in connection with the attack.

# Manslaughter Trial Over Thomas Orchard Police Custody Death Halted

A manslaughter trial involving three custody staff has been stopped after 11 weeks, with the judge announcing his intention to order a retrial.

Thomas Orchard, 32, who had schizophrenia, died in October 2012 after being arrested in Exeter. Custody sergeant Jan Kingshott, 44, and civilian detention officers Simon Tansley, 38, and Michael Marsden, 55, were on trial for manslaughter at Bristol Crown Court.

Mr Justice King told the jury of seven men and four women: "I have decided this trial cannot continue. I appreciate this may be a disappointment to you given the number of weeks you have sat. Given there may be a re-trial we cannot say anymore."

Mr Orchard suffered a heart attack at Heavitree Road Police Station and died later in hospital.

Julian Evans, representing the Crown, confirmed the prosecution intended to pursue a retrial. The Independent Police Complaints Commission (IPCC) stated it would await the retrial decision before addressing "disciplinary matters."

Tom Milsom, associate commissioner of the IPCC, said: "I appreciate the trial has been a difficult experience for everybody involved, in particular Mr Orchard's family who have listened with dignity and strength to painful details about his tragic and untimely death."

# Bromyard Celebrates Rich Motoring Heritage with Inaugural Festival of Speed

Hundreds of car enthusiasts gathered in Bromyard this weekend for the town's first Festival of Speed, celebrating its significant contributions to British automotive history.

The Herefordshire market town has deep roots in the motor industry, having been home to the chairmen of Austin, Bean and Morgan motor companies. Notably, parts for the iconic Morgan three-wheelers were manufactured locally, establishing Bromyard's place in motoring heritage.

Approximately 120 vintage and historic vehicles paraded through the town streets, with the star attraction being a Sunbeam Bluebird. This legendary car was driven by Sir Malcolm Campbell to set a world speed record in 1924, exceeding 140 mph.

Organisers highlighted that automotive engineering in Bromyard began with the Pettifer family, who manufactured chassis components for Morgan Three Wheelers from 1910, before Morgan established its Malvern factories.

For the inaugural festival, Morgan Motor Company was featured prominently, recognizing its special association with the area. Founded by HFS Morgan in 1909, the company began producing three-wheelers in 1910 and remains the UK's last privately owned motor manufacturer.

"The town and its immediate locality has been linked to the British motor industry since the birth of the motor car," organizers stated, promising this celebration of Bromyard's automotive legacy will become an annual tradition.

The company continues its reputation for hand-built small sports cars today.

# Carnivorous Plant Found to Selectively Devour Invasive Asian Hornets in France

A botanical garden director in western France has made a remarkable discovery that could help combat the invasive Asian hornet population threatening European beehives.

Romaric Perrocheau, head of the botanical garden in Nantes, recently found a stem of the carnivorous pitcher plant Sarracenia completely filled with dead Asian hornets. What makes this discovery particularly extraordinary is the plant's apparent selectivity – it devours Asian hornets whilst leaving European hornets, bees, and wasps unharmed.

"Sarracenia had invented a very selective trap" for the aggressive Asian hornets, Mr Perrocheau told AFP news agency. The insects are lured by the plant's nectar and pheromones on its tubular leaves. Once a hornet crawls inside the rim, it easily slips and plunges into the pitcher, where it is digested by the plant's juices.

Interestingly, this appears to be a European adaptation, as Asian hornets do not exist in Sarracenia's native Massachusetts in the eastern United States. The plant grows easily in Europe and poses no threat to native flora.

Mr Perrocheau and an entomologist now plan to study the contents of 200 pitchers, hoping to identify the chemical secret behind their attraction for Asian hornets specifically.

Asian hornets, catalogued as Vespa velutina nigrithorax, pose a significant threat to honeybees across France, Portugal, Spain, Italy, Germany, and Belgium. First spotted in France in 2004, their native habitat is China's Shanghai region. In some cases, hornet stings have proven fatal to humans due to allergic reactions.

Each Sarracenia plant possesses up to 15 pitchers and can attract as many as 50 hornets. However, with typical hornet nests housing 4,000 insects, the plants alone cannot solve the problem entirely.

The Independent reported in April that Asian hornets had not yet reached the UK, though plans exist to destroy any nests should they cross the English Channel. These nests prove notoriously difficult to locate and destroy, often hidden high in trees or underground hollows.

# Adlington backs Peaty to handle Olympic pressure after European test

# Scottish Economy Shows Further Signs of Slowdown as Business Activity Contracts

Scotland's private sector experienced a contraction in business activity during September, according to the latest Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) report from the Bank of Scotland, adding to concerns about the country's economic performance.

The bank's PMI fell from 50.8 in August to 49.0 in September, dropping below the critical 50 threshold that separates economic expansion from contraction. The report revealed that new business declined "at a marginal pace" while backlogs of work also fell. Particularly concerning was the continuation of declining export orders, which have now fallen for eight consecutive months.

Manufacturing firms bore the brunt of the downturn, reporting a sharp fall in new orders from both domestic and international markets. This led to deterioration in production across the sector. The service sector also experienced contraction in activity during September, despite a modest rise in incoming new business, though this increase was the weakest recorded in seven months.

However, there were some positive indicators within the report. Workforce numbers expanded "at an accelerated rate," with the service sector leading employment growth. Manufacturing companies also registered modest increases in staffing levels, suggesting businesses remain cautiously optimistic about future prospects.

Price pressures presented a mixed picture. Service sector companies reported higher input costs, while manufacturing firms experienced sharp reductions in prices. Overall, input prices softened, and output prices fell again during the month.

Bank of Scotland chief economist Donald MacRae commented: "September's PMI showed a broad-based decline in economic activity across both service and manufacturing sectors. The slowdown in the Scottish economy identified in summer has taken further hold in the month of September but employment intentions suggest a return to moderate growth in coming months."

The PMI data follows national statistics released last week showing Scotland's economic growth slowed to just 0.1% in the second quarter of 2024, down from 0.4% in the previous quarter. This compares unfavourably with the UK economy as a whole, which expanded by 0.7% during the same period.

The figures raise questions about Scotland's economic trajectory as businesses face continued challenges from weak demand and uncertain export markets.

# Hundreds Attend Funeral of Arthur Jones After Crete Tragedy

# Elderly People Targeted in Third of Fraud Cases, Charity Warns

Over-65s are being disproportionately targeted by fraudsters, making up more than a third of all fraud referrals to a leading victims' charity despite representing less than a fifth of the population, new figures reveal.

Victim Support received 39,272 fraud referrals in England and Wales in the year to September, with people aged 65 and over accounting for 35% of cases. This is nearly double their 18% share of the population. Even more concerning, those aged 75 and over represented 22% of victims despite making up just 8% of the population, the analysis showed.

Lucy Hastings, director of Victim Support, described the targeting of older people as "disturbing and despicable." She warned that many other cases were likely going unreported. "We need to take away the stigma, so that victims of fraud have the confidence to report it, knowing that they are not alone and will be taken seriously," she said.

Caroline Abrahams, charity director at Age UK, said elderly people could be scammed through multiple channels – on the doorstep, by phone, online or by post. "Figures like this aren't surprising to us as time and time again we're seeing stats that highlight this horrible problem and as scams become more sophisticated the risks they pose to older people are growing," she said.

"To most of us it's unbelievable that anyone would target an older person to defraud them but unfortunately it happens and we know that older people can be especially vulnerable if they are lonely and isolated or suffer with dementia."

## Real-life victims speak out

Pat Bottomley from Hull lost her entire £8,500 life savings after falling victim to fraudsters impersonating police officers. The 76-year-old widow received a call from a fake officer claiming a teenager with her son's name had been arrested in possession of her bank card.

"The police officer assured me he was genuine and needed my assistance," Pat recalled. "He even gave me the name and phone number of a real policeman, which I looked up - so I thought he was being honest."

A second fraudster then convinced her to transfer money into a savings account, supposedly to help catch international criminals. She only realised it was a scam when her son returned home.

"I was totally drawn in and I felt absolutely gutted," Mrs Bottomley said. "The experience made me totally lose my confidence. I felt very stupid. It wasn't about the money - it was about how I was made to feel. I didn't want to answer the phone to anyone or go out anymore."

## Growing problem

Last month, fraudsters posing as bank staff tricked 65-year-old Nargess Sadjady from west London into handing over her £12,000 savings.

In March, Cormac McGuckin, 29, from County Londonderry, was sentenced to 20 months in prison after stealing more than £17,000 from a pensioner to pay gambling and wedding debts. He had befriended the elderly man and persuaded him to write blank cheques.

Concerns have also been raised about the vulnerability of those approaching retirement under new pension rules, which make it easier to access money in pension pots. The Financial Conduct Authority has warned that con-artists have been keen to take advantage of the change.

# Trump Calls House Healthcare Bill "Mean" After Previously Praising It

Sources present at the White House lunch meeting told Politico that Mr Trump said senators needed to "pass a bill that Republicans are able to more easily defend".

"That may be adding additional money into it," he reportedly said.

Mr Trump's remarks on the "mean" House bill are in stark contrast to his previous public position. Although the bill gave Mr Trump his first legislative win, it was criticised by both Democrats and Senate Republicans.

It was passed before being fully assessed - and a later assessment from the non-partisan Congressional Budget Office concluded some 23 million people would lose health insurance over the next decade.

One Republican Senator, Bob Corker, said at the time the bill had "zero" chance in the Senate. Instead, Senators decided to "start fresh" on drafting their own legislation.

That new bill is being crafted in private by the Senate's Republicans. The 13 senators invited to lunch at the White House were a mix of conservative and moderate Republicans.

One attendee, Finance Committee Chairman Orrin Hatch, told Reuters news agency that there still was a lot of work to do before legislation can be unveiled. "The total bill hasn't been resolved," he said.

While Mr Trump's Republican party has a majority in both the House and Senate, his margin in the Senate is considerably smaller - just three Republicans voting against the bill would prevent it from passing.

Sources at the meeting told Politico that Republicans "risk getting savaged in the 2018 midterms" if they failed to repeal Obamacare, after campaigning against it for seven years.

During his election campaign, Mr Trump consistently criticised President Obama's healthcare policy, vowing to "repeal and replace" the legislation.

The president first attempted to push through a bill in March, but withdrew it at the last minute when House Speaker Paul Ryan told him he would not have the minimum 215 votes needed. The debacle was seen as a major defeat for the new president, who blamed Democrats for not supporting his bill.

The failure led to a new version of the bill allowing states to opt out of several of its provisions, and allow higher premiums for some patients.

# Indian School Warden Suspended After Forcing Students to Strip During Menstruation Inspection

# Major Internet Companies Stage 'Internet Slowdown' Protest Over Net Neutrality Rules

Dozens of major internet companies are preparing to stage a coordinated protest on Wednesday against proposed Federal Communications Commission regulations that they fear could fundamentally alter how the internet operates, potentially forcing content providers to pay extra fees for fast access to consumers.

The protest, dubbed "Internet Slowdown," will see participating websites displaying a spinning wheel icon—the familiar symbol of slow loading speeds that frustrates internet users worldwide. However, the sites themselves will continue to function normally, with the icon serving as a symbolic reminder of what could happen if net neutrality protections are weakened.

Netflix, the streaming video giant, signaled its participation by posting an animation of the loading wheel on its US Twitter account Monday. The company urged other firms to join the campaign, with the icon linking to information about how users can take action to defend net neutrality principles.

According to Free Press, one of the protest organizers, participants include some of the internet's most popular platforms: Reddit, Mozilla, Kickstarter, Upworthy, Automattic (which operates WordPress), Digg, Vimeo, Boing Boing, Thunderclap, Urban Dictionary, Foursquare, and Cheezburger. The American Civil Liberties Union has also confirmed its participation.

Twitter, while supporting the cause, said it would participate "in other ways" rather than adding a banner to its homepage, though a spokesman declined to provide specific details about the form its protest would take.

The controversy stems from FCC proposals introduced following a January ruling by the US Court of Appeals that found broadband providers were not obligated to treat all internet traffic equally. The FCC's new rules would require telecom providers to ensure users have access to internet service that is "sufficiently robust, fast and effectively usable."

However, critics argue the proposals contain a critical flaw: while providers would be banned from blocking legal content, they would be allowed to charge for "prioritized" data delivery. This has raised concerns about the creation of internet "fast lanes" where companies that can afford to pay receive better service, potentially disadvantaging smaller competitors and startups.

"The cause of net neutrality is important to us as a business. It's important to our visitors, and it's important for our democracy. We're proud to take part in the Internet Slowdown and encourage others to join with us," said Erik Martin, general manager of Reddit.

Paul Sieminski, general counsel of Automattic, emphasized the broader implications: "The free and open internet has been central to the economy and to global free expression. Everyone has to step up now and do everything they can to protect it."

More than 100 technology companies, including Microsoft, Google, Facebook, and Twitter, have already written to the FCC expressing their concerns. In their letter, they warned that the proposed rules "would enable phone and cable internet service providers to discriminate both technically and financially against internet companies and to impose new tolls on them."

Craig Aaron, president of the Free Press Action Fund, framed the issue as a David versus Goliath battle: "We need our leaders to stand up to the cabal of cable and phone giants that have called the shots in Washington for too long."

The companies concluded their letter with a stark warning: "This represents a grave threat to the internet."
