# Cyclist Celebrates Victory One Lap Too Early at Giro d'Italia

A premature celebration left Slovenian cyclist Luka Pibernik red-faced during stage five of the Giro d'Italia on Wednesday, as he mistakenly thought he had won the race in Messina.

Pibernik punched the air in triumph as he crossed what he believed was the finish line. However, the route looped back for another lap, and his celebration turned to embarrassment as the peloton swept past him moments later.

Colombia's Fernando Gaviria actually claimed the stage victory, finishing the 159km route from Pescara in 3 hours, 40 minutes and 11 seconds. This was Gaviria's second stage win of this year's race, having also triumphed on Sunday's stage three. Italy's Jakub Mareczko finished second, with Ireland's Sam Bennett taking third place.

Pibernik eventually crossed the genuine finish line in 148th position, 20 seconds behind the winner.

In the overall standings, Luxembourg's Bob Jungels retained the pink jersey as race leader. Welsh cyclist Geraint Thomas of Team Sky remains in second place, just six seconds behind, while fellow Briton Adam Yates sits third, 10 seconds off the pace.

Yates shares his time with defending champion Vincenzo Nibali and 2014 winner Nairo Quintana, setting up an intriguing battle for the podium positions.

Thursday's sixth stage presents a challenging 217km ride from Reggio Calabria to Terme Luigiane, featuring both category-three and category-four climbs that could shake up the general classification.

# South Korea Heads to Polls as Moon Jae-in Leads Presidential Race

South Koreans are voting today in a presidential election that comes at a critical time for the nation, facing economic challenges and escalating tensions with North Korea.

Left-leaning candidate Moon Jae-in enters election day as the clear front-runner, with centrist Ahn Cheol-soo his nearest challenger. The vote takes place against the backdrop of unprecedented political upheaval following the impeachment of former President Park Geun-hye.

On the final day of campaigning, Mr. Moon called for an "overwhelming victory," arguing it would help heal the national divide caused by Ms. Park's downfall and impeachment. Meanwhile, Mr. Ahn, campaigning in swing states, expressed confidence he could still secure victory.

The election follows the dramatic removal of Park Geun-hye in March, who became the first South Korean president to be impeached. She is currently standing trial on charges of bribery and abuse of power, though she denies wrongdoing and has repeatedly apologized.

**North Korea Policy a Key Divider**

Mr. Moon, who narrowly lost to Ms. Park in 2012, proposes a markedly different approach to North Korea than his conservative predecessor. While Ms. Park cut almost all ties with Pyongyang, Mr. Moon advocates for increased contact and dialogue.

He has criticized previous conservative administrations for failing to stop North Korea's weapons development and favors a two-track approach combining increased dialogue with sanctions to encourage change.

BBC Korea correspondent Stephen Evans notes this approach could create tensions with Washington, particularly if US President Donald Trump pursues a harder line against North Korea, especially following any potential nuclear tests.

**Domestic Issues Drive Voters**

Beyond foreign policy, domestic concerns feature prominently in voters' minds. All candidates have promised to protect South Korea's fragile economic recovery—the fourth largest in Asia—and tackle stubbornly high youth unemployment.

Candidates are also pledging to reform the family-run conglomerates, or chaebols, that dominate the domestic economy and address perceptions of elitism in political society.

Observers expect high turnout, boosted by younger voters. Polls close at 20:00 local time (11:00 GMT), with results expected soon after.

**Warnock Demands Desire as Cardiff Face Championship Leaders Brighton**

Cardiff City manager Neil Warnock has warned he will not tolerate players lacking commitment when his side travels to face Championship leaders Brighton on Friday.

After his team again conceded late to draw at Brentford on Boxing Day, Warnock accused some of his players of lacking "desire" and vowed to make changes for the crucial encounter.

"I can't pick anyone who is going to drift in that game because Brighton are a good side," said Warnock, clearly frustrated by his team's recent performances.

The Bluebirds boss has been particularly disappointed by his side's inability to see out games when in winning positions. At Brentford, Cardiff appeared to have secured all three points when Kenneth Zohore scored in the 89th minute, only for Sullay Kaikai to grab his second goal in added time to level the match.

It was a familiar pattern for Cardiff, who had similarly surrendered a late lead in their previous fixture against Barnsley in the Welsh capital.

Now they face a Brighton side sitting top of the Championship following their victory over QPR, which was aided by Newcastle's defeat to Sheffield Wednesday.

"We have to stand up and be counted. It's good to be going down there. They are as good a team in the league as there is," Warnock acknowledged.

The manager may be forced into changes regardless, with midfielder Peter Whittingham—who scored from the penalty spot at Brentford—doubtful after being substituted at half-time with a hamstring problem.

"He felt a little bit tight and he'd been booked as well so we thought we would be careful," Warnock explained.

# Sainsbury's Apologises for Seeking Unpaid Artist to Refurbish Store Canteen

Supermarket giant Sainsbury's has issued an apology after facing a social media backlash over an advertisement seeking an unpaid artist to redecorate a staff canteen.

The store in Camden Road took out an advert for "an ambitious artist" to "voluntarily refurbish" the facility. The company was shamed on social media by people who pointed out the successful supermarket chain should pay its way.

Artist Conor Collins attacked the supermarket's attempt to hire someone for free and suggested the store deducted some money from its bosses' salaries to "pay someone to do work for you so that the concept of 'starving artist' wouldn't have to be a thing."

He wrote on Twitter: "Dear Sainsbury's, I am looking for a company worth £150,000,000 to feed all of my artist friends in Manchester."

Other social media users expressed similar outrage. One tweet read: "@Sainsbury's Awful. You can afford to pay an artist their worth." Another said: "So @sainsburys let me get this straight. You turnover £26bn yet want an artist to voluntarily decorate your canteen?"

A spokesman for the company said the advert was an "error of judgement". Sainsbury's told the BBC it was discussing the matter with the store in Camden, adding: "It is not our policy to hire volunteers and we are sorry for this error of judgement."

# Former Flint Emergency Managers Charged in Water Crisis

Two former state-appointed emergency managers and two city employees face felony charges for their roles in the Flint water crisis that exposed thousands of residents to lead-contaminated drinking water.

Michigan Attorney General Bill Schuette announced charges Tuesday against Darnell Earley and Gerald Ambrose, who served as emergency managers during the critical period when Flint's water supply became dangerously contaminated with lead in 2014.

Mr. Earley and Mr. Ambrose each face charges of false pretenses, conspiracy to commit false pretenses, misconduct in office, and willful neglect of duty in office. The charges carry a combined maximum sentence of 46 years in prison.

"The tragedy that we know of as the Flint water crisis did not occur by accident," Mr. Schuette said at a press conference. "Flint was a casualty of arrogance, disdain and failure of management, an absence of accountability."

Also charged were two former city employees: Howard Croft, a public works superintendent, and Daugherty Johnson, a utilities manager. Both face conspiracy charges for allegedly operating a water treatment plant that was not properly equipped to treat water from the Flint River. They face up to 40 years in prison.

Mr. Johnson's attorney, Edwar Zeineh, told the Associated Press his client will plead not guilty. The other defendants and their lawyers could not immediately be reached for comment.

The water crisis began in April 2014 when Mr. Earley, serving as emergency manager, decided to switch the city's water source from Lake Huron to the Flint River as a cost-saving measure. The acidic river water corroded aging pipes throughout the city, causing lead to leach into the drinking water supply.

Tests later revealed high levels of lead in blood samples from children in the majority African-American city of approximately 100,000 residents. Lead exposure can cause serious developmental problems in children and other health complications.

Flint switched back to its previous water system in October 2015. Federal regulators now say filtered tap water is safe to drink, though they still recommend bottled water for young children and pregnant women.

The charges bring the total number of people facing criminal counts related to the investigation to 13. Previous charges have been filed against state regulators, health officials, and environmental workers accused of concealing data about elevated lead levels in children's blood.

The announcement comes one day after a Reuters report identified nearly 3,000 areas nationwide with lead poisoning rates twice as high as Flint's during the peak of its crisis, highlighting the scope of lead contamination problems across the United States.

**Blackburn's Jordan Rhodes Set for Middlesbrough Talks**

Blackburn Rovers have granted permission for striker Jordan Rhodes to discuss a potential move to Middlesbrough. The 25-year-old Scotland international, who joined Rovers from Huddersfield for £8m in 2012, has been prolific at Ewood Park with 83 goals in 169 appearances, including 11 this season.

"The player has expressed his desire to talk to the Teesside club and will travel for discussions," Blackburn confirmed in a statement.

# Doll's House Listed on Rightmove Attracts Genuine Buyer Interest in Charity Fundraiser

A miniature Georgian doll's house has been listed on property website Rightmove in an unusual fundraising effort for a Warwickshire hospice charity, prompting at least one potential buyer to request a viewing of what they believed was a real property.

The 75cm (30in) high toy house belongs to Shipston Home Nursing, a hospice charity supporting terminally-ill patients in south Warwickshire. The charity is hoping to raise funds through the sale to continue its vital care services.

The listing was placed on Rightmove "as a joke" by Peter Clarke Estate Agents, which is supporting the charity's fundraising efforts, according to the Warwick Courier. However, the elaborate description and professional photographs proved convincing enough to confuse at least one prospective homebuyer.

The property is described on the website as a "classic Georgian house" featuring four bedrooms, a drawing room, and "potential for further accommodation" in a "quiet location situated in a popular village in south Warwickshire."

The listing highlights traditional features including a fireplace, an Aga, exposed wood floors, and "charming period features." It notes that "a unique feature of the property is the roof and front elevations swing open to reveal beautiful accommodation set on three floors and it is part furnished."

Sally Coombs, branch manager at Peter Clarke Estate Agents, recounted the confusion: "We put it on Rightmove as a joke but we actually had somebody who wanted to view it, thinking it was a proper house. We said to the caller that if they looked at it properly, they would see it was a doll's house."

Rebecca Mawle, the hospice's fundraising co-ordinator, explained that the house was created as a "labour of love" by a charity supporter. The charity is accepting bids until 7 September and hopes offers will be "as high as possible."

"It's beautifully made," Ms Mawle said, adding that she found the buyer confusion "hilarious." "Looking at it on the pictures, it really does look like a charming property."

Rightmove's housing expert, Miles Shipside, acknowledged the unusual listing: "We wouldn't normally allow listings like this but as it's captured the attention of so many and it's for the agent's local charity, we've let it stay on Rightmove to help them get as many offers as possible."

# Hannah Mills Eyes Tokyo Gold in New Olympic Sailing Class

Britain's Olympic sailing champion Hannah Mills is embarking on an exciting new challenge as she aims to become the nation's most successful female Olympic sailor.

The 29-year-old Welsh athlete, who claimed gold at the Rio Olympics and silver in London alongside Saskia Clark in the 470 dinghy class, is switching to the 49er FX skiff for the Tokyo Games. With Clark's retirement following Rio, Mills has chosen to pursue this demanding new discipline.

"The FX to me just presents such a new and exciting shift. Every day I go sailing I'm scared, I'm excited, I'm laughing so much," Mills explained enthusiastically.

After a decade competing in the 470 class, Mills felt the need for a fresh challenge to rekindle her passion for the sport. "For me it was about finding the love of sailing again. It's an amazing sport, I love the 470 and the racing is awesome," she said. "But having done something for ten years, at some point in time I think you have to step away. And I didn't want to step away and not sail."

The 49er FX, which made its Olympic debut in Rio, presents a significant challenge for the decorated sailor. However, Mills remains realistic about her prospects.

"It's a big challenge, that's for sure. I'm not deluded that I'm stepping into the FX and everything will be rosy. But I think that challenge is really positive for me," she acknowledged.

"Obviously it is all about winning a gold medal in Tokyo," Mills added. "To me right now I'm fully committed to the FX and I'm going to be giving that as good a shot as I can."

# Carli Lloyd Hat-Trick Fires USA to World Cup Glory

Carli Lloyd scored a stunning hat-trick, including a remarkable long-range strike, as the United States defeated Japan 5-2 to win the Women's World Cup final in Vancouver.

The 32-year-old midfielder netted three times within the opening 16 minutes, with her third goal - a spectacular shot from the halfway line - becoming one of the most memorable moments in World Cup history.

"I did it once in training but very rarely do you wind up and hit it like that," said Lloyd, who had suffered penalty heartbreak in the 2011 final defeat to Japan. "You train and train and train and I dreamed of scoring a shot like that."

Lloyd opened the scoring after just three minutes before doubling the lead two minutes later. After Lauren Holiday's volley made it 3-0, the Houston Dash player completed her hat-trick with an audacious strike that beat Japanese goalkeeper Ayumi Kaihori from distance. Tobin Heath added a fifth goal as the USA became the first nation to win the tournament three times, adding to their 1991 and 1999 triumphs.

"When you're feeling good mentally and physically, those plays are instinctive," Lloyd explained. The midfielder, who had scored in each of her side's previous three matches, revealed she uses visualization techniques as part of her preparation.

"I was at home with my headphones on but I was on the field and I was running and doing sprints," she said. "I completely zoned out and dreamed of playing in a World Cup final and scoring four goals. It sounds funny but that's what it is all about. I feel like I blacked out for the first 30 minutes of the game. It was crazy."

Despite trailing 4-0 after 16 minutes, Japan showed resilience by pulling two goals back through Yuki Ogimi and a Julie Johnston own goal before Heath's strike sealed victory for the Americans.

Lloyd's hat-trick brought her tournament total to six goals, matching Germany's Celia Sasic for the Golden Boot. "I've had people believe in me," she said. "Fitness was definitely an issue for me but I've turned that into a strength and the mental side of the game is a huge thing. I'm just really proud of everyone. It's a surreal moment, we made history."

The victory came under English-born coach Jill Ellis, who took charge just 14 months ago following Tom Sermanni's dismissal. The 48-year-old, born in Portsmouth, defended her team's journey despite criticism during the build-up and group stages.

"I told the players they had to continue to believe in the process," Ellis said. "There have been some growing pains but it's not vindication, it just feels really good and I could not be more proud of the players and the staff because I knew they had it in them."

# Hallam Amos Returns from Injury in Time for Six Nations Consideration

Dragons wing Hallam Amos has returned from a shoulder injury at what could prove to be a crucial time for his international ambitions, with Wales head coach Warren Gatland set to name his Six Nations squad on Tuesday.

The 21-year-old medical student, who sustained the injury during Wales' memorable World Cup victory over England in October, marked his comeback with a try after just 50 seconds in Dragons' 31-18 European Challenge Cup Pool Two victory over Castres.

"I've come back at a good time. There are exciting matches coming in the next few weeks," Amos told BBC Wales Sport, though he remained cautious about his international prospects.

"I'm not sure, it's a tough one because I'm only just back from injury and there are other boys playing really well at the moment," he said. "I haven't thought too much about it, I just wanted to get back on the pitch with the Dragons, and whatever happens, happens."

Amos, who has five international caps, faces stiff competition for a place in Gatland's squad. He will be vying for selection alongside established names like Northampton's George North and Cardiff Blues' Alex Cuthbert, with the Ospreys' Eli Walker and Blues' Tom James also in contention.

The wing returned to action ahead of schedule, having originally targeted a return around this time but managing to come back a couple of weeks early. His first touch could hardly have gone better, finishing off a move involving Sarel Pretorius and Jason Tovey.

"You think about it the night before and that's exactly what you want," Amos said. "In rugby you will pick up injuries, though it's been tough watching the boys. But I can't ask for much more than that with my first touch back after three months."

Amos will now focus on helping Dragons secure a home quarter-final in the Challenge Cup when they face Sale Sharks away on Thursday.

# Northern Ireland Politicians Divided on Brexit Vote Following High Court Ruling

Political tensions have intensified in Northern Ireland following a landmark High Court ruling in London that determined the UK government cannot trigger Article 50 of the Lisbon Treaty without parliamentary approval.

The ruling means MPs must vote before formal exit negotiations with the European Union can begin, sparking contrasting responses from Northern Ireland's political parties.

The Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP) has pledged to vote against triggering Article 50 when the matter comes before parliament. SDLP representative Mr Durkan, speaking on the Sunday Politics programme, emphasized his party's commitment to reflecting the wishes of Northern Ireland voters.

"If we get to a situation where parliament will be voting on the terms, I want to make one thing clear, we will be voting against Article 50 because that is our position and that is the position that the people of Northern Ireland have voted for," Mr Durkan stated.

In contrast, the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) plans to leverage their parliamentary position differently. DUP MP Nigel Dodds indicated his party would work to secure favorable terms for Northern Ireland during the Brexit process, stating he expects "a deal which is in the mutual interests of the Irish Republic, of the other member EU states, of the United Kingdom and Northern Ireland."

The division reflects Northern Ireland's unique position on Brexit. While the overall UK electorate voted to leave the EU, 56% of Northern Ireland voters opted to remain, creating ongoing political friction.

Prime Minister Theresa May had argued that the referendum result and existing ministerial powers eliminated the need for a parliamentary vote, but campaigners successfully challenged this position as unconstitutional.

The Westminster government plans to appeal Thursday's ruling at the Supreme Court, with a further hearing expected next month.

# Stonehenge Bluestones May Have Been Chosen for Their Musical Properties

A groundbreaking study has revealed that the ancient bluestones of Stonehenge may have been selected for their unique acoustic qualities, offering a fascinating new perspective on one of archaeology's greatest mysteries.

Researchers from London's Royal College of Art have discovered that rocks in the Preseli Hills of Pembrokeshire possess remarkable sonic properties, ringing like bells when struck. The investigation, part of the Landscape and Perception Project, aimed to understand what "Stone Age eyes and ears" would have experienced in a prehistoric landscape.

"It hasn't been considered until now that sound might have been a factor," said Paul Devereux, the project's principal investigator. The team tested thousands of stones along the Carn Menyn ridge and found an unusually high proportion produced clear, resonant tones when struck.

"The percentage of the rocks on the Carn Menyn ridge are ringing rocks, they ring just like a bell," Mr Devereux explained. "And there's lots of different tones, you could play a tune. In fact, we have had percussionists who have played proper percussion pieces off the rocks."

Since the 1920s, archaeologists have known that Stonehenge's bluestones were transported 199 miles (320 km) from Mynydd Preseli to Wiltshire, but the reason for selecting these particular stones has remained elusive. The monument, constructed between 3,000 BC and 1,600 BC, has puzzled researchers for generations.

"There had to be something special about these rocks," Mr Devereux said. "Why else would they take them from here all the way to Stonehenge?"

Prof Tim Darvill, who has conducted hundreds of excavations at Stonehenge, supports the theory that prehistoric peoples had different relationships with stone than modern society. "We don't know of course that they moved them because they rang but ringing rocks are a prominent part of many cultures," he noted.

"You can almost see them as a pre-historic glockenspiel, if you like and you could knock them and hear these tunes," Prof Darvill added. "And soundscapes of pre-history are something we're really just beginning to explore."

This discovery opens new avenues for understanding how ancient peoples interacted with their environment and selected materials for sacred monuments.

# Bristol bridge approval 'begins new era' for UK masonry arch construction

A pedestrian and cyclist bridge approved for construction over Bridge Valley Road in Bristol marks a significant milestone in British engineering, according to experts.

The bridge will complete a missing link in the circular route around the Downs, addressing longstanding safety concerns at what has been described as a "busy and dangerous junction".

Dr Adrienn Tomor, from the University of the West of England, who proposed the scheme alongside the Friends of the Downs and Avon Gorge group (FODAG), expressed her delight at the approval. "This is the first time thatadelical stone bridge has been approved for construction during the past 100 years," she said.

Dr Tomor believes the project "represents a new era for masonry arch bridge construction in the UK and Europe" and will "provide great improvements for pedestrians and cyclists".

Before construction can begin, planning conditions must be finalised and an independent charity established to oversee fundraising efforts.

Jack Penrose from FODAG welcomed the city council's decision, stating: "It'll be infinitely safer than what's on offer at the moment."

# Derby County Edge Nottingham Forest in Hard-Fought East Midlands Derby

Martin Olsson's late strike was enough to secure a 1-0 victory for Derby County over Nottingham Forest in an East Midlands derby that was long on effort but desperately short on quality at the iPro Stadium.

The Swedish defender curled home a superb 79th-minute effort past Dorus de Vries to settle a tense encounter that had promised much but delivered little in terms of genuine goalmouth action until that decisive moment.

Forest, under the interim stewardship of Paul Williams, had actually enjoyed the better of a scrappy first half, their high-tempo pressing game causing the Rams all sorts of problems in the opening exchanges. The visitors' energetic approach forced numerous errors from the hosts, leaving the home supporters increasingly frustrated as their side struggled to find any rhythm.

However, the introduction of Derby's new football adviser Harry Redknapp's influence at half-time proved pivotal. The experienced coach had trudged down from his seat in the directors' box towards the dressing room at the interval, and whatever words of wisdom he and head coach Darren Wassall imparted clearly had the desired effect.

Derby emerged a transformed side after the break, finally beginning to assert themselves in midfield and looking far more threatening in attack. Tom Ince started to cause problems with his pace and trickery, producing a couple of surging runs and a fierce low strike that De Vries dealt with comfortably – remarkably, it was the first effort on target in the match.

The breakthrough eventually arrived eleven minutes from time when Ince turned provider, slipping a pass to Olsson who demonstrated excellent technique to curl a first-time shot beyond the helpless De Vries and into the net.

The reality was that this derby match, while full of committed tackles, passion and intensity, offered precious little in the way of genuine quality or entertainment. Bone-crunching challenges, blocked shots, misplaced passes and a succession of free-kicks dominated proceedings, but clear-cut chances remained conspicuous by their absence.

Forest had looked relatively comfortable for long periods and managed a couple of speculative long-range efforts, but they too were disappointingly toothless in the final third and had no answer once Olsson had broken the deadlock.

The victory ensures Derby remain firmly in the promotion race, staying fifth in the Championship table. For Forest, the search for goals continues to be their Achilles heel.

Derby head coach Darren Wassall was quick to praise Redknapp's contribution: "I wanted Harry in the dressing room before the game, at half-time and at full-time. His input is just as much as anyone else's and I welcome that because if he can improve us in our promotion push by three or four per cent we will be delighted."

Forest's Williams remained philosophical despite the defeat: "For the majority of the game I was very pleased with how the players performed. The pressure is on me now as to how we are going to create and score goals."

# Netflix Identifies Popcorn Time as Major Piracy Threat

Netflix has publicly acknowledged a growing concern over illegal streaming services, specifically calling out Popcorn Time as a significant competitor in a recent letter to shareholders. The streaming giant's admission highlights how digital piracy continues to challenge legitimate subscription services.

Popcorn Time operates as an application that streams films and television programmes using torrent technology. The app has gained substantial traction, particularly in the United Kingdom, where it has been installed on hundreds of thousands of computers, according to TorrentFreak, a website specializing in copyright and privacy news.

The founder of TorrentFreak, identified only as "Ernesto," explains that Popcorn Time poses a unique threat because "its easy-to-use user interface appeals to a mainstream audience." This accessibility makes it particularly dangerous for legitimate streaming services, as it lowers the technical barrier that typically prevents casual users from engaging with piracy.

Despite its user-friendly design, Popcorn Time remains entirely illegal. Copyright holders have repeatedly attempted to shut down the service, with major movie studios successfully pressuring the original developers to close their project. However, because the application's code is open source, it was quickly revived by other developers, allowing the service to persist and grow.

Ernesto reports that Popcorn Time now boasts millions of users worldwide. This claim is supported by Google search data cited by Netflix, which shows a dramatic increase in searches for the app in the Netherlands. Netflix described these findings as "sobering," underscoring the scale of the piracy challenge.

In response to such threats, Netflix has been investing heavily in original content production, including high-profile series like House of Cards starring Kevin Spacey. The company also identified other legitimate competitors in their shareholder letter, including HBO Go, Hulu, and Amazon Prime.

The piracy problem is compounded by geographical content restrictions. Some Netflix subscribers attempt to use workarounds to access the US version of the service, which offers a different content library. While Netflix is working to close these loopholes, they remain unresolved.

Popcorn Time maintains an advantage over legitimate services by operating without rights agreements with studios and producers, allowing them to offer unrestricted content regardless of users' locations. This fundamental difference continues to make piracy an attractive, albeit illegal, option for many viewers worldwide.

# German Teen Gets Six Years for IS-Ordered Knife Attack on Police

A German court has sentenced a teenage girl to six years in youth detention for stabbing a police officer in what prosecutors say was an attack ordered and supervised by the Islamic State group.

Safia S, who was 15 at the time of the incident, stabbed and seriously wounded a police officer in the neck at Hanover's central station on 26 February last year. The Celle regional court convicted her of attempted murder and helping a terrorist organisation, as well as grievous bodily harm.

The German Moroccan teenager had previously travelled to Istanbul with the intention of joining IS in Syria, but was brought back by her mother. Despite returning to Germany, she maintained contact with the jihadist group via the internet.

Judge cited phone messages as evidence that the attack was carried out in support of IS. In one text to an acquaintance after the November 2015 Paris attacks, she wrote: "Allah bless our lions who carried out an operation in Paris yesterday."

Security camera footage from Hanover station captured the moment she approached two police officers. When they asked to see her identification, she lunged at the 34-year-old policeman with a knife.

In a related case, 20-year-old Mohamad Hasan K was sentenced to two and a half years in prison on Thursday for failing to alert authorities about the planned attack despite having knowledge of it.

The teenager later apologised to the wounded officer both in writing and during the trial. Her defence team had called for acquittal on some charges and a reduced sentence. They have announced plans to appeal the verdict.

Her lawyer, Mutlu Guenal, argued that authorities bore responsibility, noting that Safia S's family had warned police about her radicalisation. "The real failure lay with police," he stated.

The trial was held behind closed doors due to the defendant's age. Under German privacy laws, only surnames' initials are released publicly.

This case comes amid heightened security concerns in Germany, with Hanover police also investigating a suspected jihadist plot targeting an international football friendly match.

# Birmingham City's Gianfranco Zola Under Pressure After Heavy Home Defeat

Birmingham City manager Gianfranco Zola admits he needs to discuss his future with the club's owners following a humiliating 4-1 home defeat to Queens Park Rangers on Saturday.

The loss at St Andrew's was the heaviest of nine defeats Blues have suffered in 14 games since Zola replaced Gary Rowett as manager in December. It also represented their worst home performance since an 8-0 thrashing by Bournemouth in October 2014.

"Obviously I need to have a chat with the owners," said Zola. "As long as they trust me I am willing to try and do my best at St Andrew's."

Since the Italian's appointment, Birmingham have collected just six points from a possible 36 in the Championship, plummeting to 14th in the table and now sitting 18 points adrift of the play-off places.

The decline has been stark. When Rowett's side won their final match under his stewardship - a 2-1 victory over Ipswich Town on 13 December - Blues were seventh and level on points with sixth-placed Sheffield Wednesday. Rowett was controversially dismissed the following day by Trillion Trophy Asia Ltd, owned by Hong Kong businessman Paul Suen Cho Hung, who had already secured Zola as his replacement.

"At the moment, I am feeling very low," admitted Zola. "But I take full responsibility. I am probably not giving enough and it is making me upset. I have committed myself to the club and I am doing it with a lot of passion. We do not like where we are at the present time, but I really care about this club and I want to help them."

QPR manager Ian Holloway was sympathetic but direct about his counterpart's predicament: "Birmingham have got to get on with it. The fans do not know what to think. I do not know where Zola will go after this game. It is up to him to work out."

# GAA Unveils Scaled-Back Plans for Casement Park Stadium in Belfast

The GAA has announced revised plans for Casement Park stadium in west Belfast, reducing its proposed capacity to 34,500 - a decrease of 3,500 seats from the original design.

The organization stated it aims to complete the project within the initial £76 million budget, with the stadium expected to open by 2019 ahead of the 2020 Ulster finals. The GAA emphasized the revised plan demonstrates its willingness to "engage and listen" to community concerns.

The new design features reduced height, scale, and capacity compared to the previous proposal, addressing issues raised by local residents and safety experts.

Tom Daly, chairman of the Casement Park Project Board, highlighted the GAA's commitment to delivering a "travel culture change." The updated plans incorporate coach travel options, park and ride facilities, and integrated travel arrangements linked to ticket sales.

"This strategy is good for ease of access to and from the stadium, is cognisant of the needs and views of the local community and is good for the wider environment," Daly said.

Ulster GAA president Michael Hasson expressed optimism about the project's future: "GAA members and supporters, as well as people across the local community, are looking forward to an exciting new beginning for Antrim and a provincial stadium for Ulster."

He added: "We want to create a positive sporting legacy and iconic stadium that will be a beacon to inspire young GAA players throughout west Belfast, Antrim and across Ulster."

The multi-million pound project has faced significant challenges since its inception. Planning permission was overturned in 2014 following objections from local residents. Additionally, safety expert Paul Scott claimed he experienced bullying after raising concerns about emergency evacuation procedures under the initial stadium plans.

# Italy Edge Zambia in Dramatic Extra-Time Thriller to Reach U-20 World Cup Semi-Finals

**Suwon, South Korea** - Italy survived a dramatic quarter-final encounter against Zambia at the U-20 World Cup, prevailing 3-2 in extra-time after a pulsating match at the Suwon World Cup Stadium.

Luca Vido emerged as Italy's hero, scoring the decisive goal in the second period of extra-time after being afforded far too much space in the Zambian penalty area. The strike completed a remarkable comeback for the Italians, who spent more than half the match playing with ten men.

Zambia will rue their missed opportunity after Giuseppe Pezzella received a straight red card for a professional foul on Edward Chilufya just before half-time. In a dramatic twist, the referee initially awarded a penalty before reversing the decision following a video assistant referee consultation, though the dismissal stood.

The African champions had started perfectly when Patson Daka fired them ahead after just three minutes, converting Emmanuel Banda's exquisite pass from close range. Zambia should have extended their lead when Banda's 14th-minute free-kick was saved, but both Chilufya and Fashion Sakala failed to capitalize on the rebound.

Italy equalized early in the second half through Riccardo Orsolini's header - his fourth tournament goal. Fashion Sakala appeared to have sealed victory for Zambia with his fourth goal of the campaign six minutes from time, but Federico Dimarco's brilliant free-kick four minutes later forced extra-time.

With penalties seemingly inevitable, Vido's late intervention broke Zambian hearts and secured Italy's place in the semi-finals, where they will face England, who defeated Mexico 1-0 in their quarter-final clash.

# Syrian Army Announces Major Offensive on Rebel-Held Eastern Aleppo

The Syrian army has announced the start of a new offensive to retake rebel-held areas of the divided city of Aleppo, escalating a devastating conflict that has already claimed thousands of lives.

US Secretary of State John Kerry said Washington could not be the only one trying to hold open the door to peace. The US wants Russia to press the Syrian government to ground its warplanes. Mr Kerry added that he would hold further consultations with the Russian team on Friday.

Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said that would amount to a "unilateral pause". Some had attempted to present the ceasefire as if only the Syrian government should be taking steps, he said, but the opposition also needed to stop fighting.

The UN envoy for Syria, Staffan de Mistura, described the meeting as "long, painful and disappointing".

This feels like a very serious breakdown, with little obvious room left for dialogue until the major powers find new space for compromise, the BBC's diplomatic correspondent, James Robbins, reports from New York. The week in New York is heading towards disastrous diplomatic failure, he adds.

## Devastating Air Strikes Continue

Announcing the new offensive, Syrian state media quoted army officials as saying there were exit points for anyone, including rebels, who wanted to flee eastern Aleppo.

Women and children are believed to be among those killed in the latest bombing. Some reports put the death toll as high as 45.

An AFP news agency journalist reports that his entire street in the southern Bustan al-Qasr district was left burning after warplanes dropped incendiary bombs.

The Syrian Observatory for Human Rights (SOHR), a UK-based group which documents casualties in the conflict, said 14 air strikes had hit Bustan al-Qasr and the neighbouring Kallasa district, starting "massive fires", as rebels and troops clashed.

SOHR director Rami Abdul Rahman described them as "the most intense strikes in months" on the two areas, with three women and three children among the dead.

The pro-rebel Aleppo Media Centre said the fires had been caused by "incendiary phosphorus bombs". Video footage posted by it and another pro-opposition activist group, Thiqa, showed intense blazes lighting up the night sky.

Aleppo, once Syria's commercial and industrial hub, has been divided roughly in two since 2012, with the government controlling the west and rebels the east.

# V&A Launches £5m Campaign to Secure Cardinal Wolsey's Lost Angels

The Victoria and Albert Museum is racing to raise £5 million to permanently acquire four bronze angel figurines originally designed for Cardinal Wolsey's tomb, with £2.5 million still needed.

The rare 16th-century sculptures have caught the attention of acclaimed historical novelist Hilary Mantel, author of the Booker Prize-winning *Wolf Hall*, who described them as a tangible connection to "one of our liveliest eras of history." Cardinal Wolsey, who features prominently in Mantel's work, was the powerful advisor to King Henry VIII during the Tudor period.

The bronze figures were commissioned in 1524 from Florentine sculptor Benedetto da Rovezzano to adorn the corners of Wolsey's elaborate tomb, intended to reflect his considerable stature and influence. However, the tomb was never completed, and the angels were sold off during the English Civil War, subsequently separated and lost to history.

The pieces have only recently re-emerged through various sales and are now reunited at the V&A for the first time in centuries during the museum's fundraising campaign.

The National Heritage Memorial Fund has committed £2 million toward the purchase, with the Art Fund contributing an additional £500,000. The museum is appealing to the public to donate the remaining funds online, via text message, or in person at the gallery.

V&A director Martin Roth emphasized the angels' significance as "a vital part of our national history and artistic heritage," expressing his determination to acquire them for permanent preservation.

Cardinal Wolsey fell from royal favour in his final years after failing to secure a Papal annulment for Henry VIII's marriage to Catherine of Aragon. He died in 1530. Henry VIII later intended to appropriate the tomb for himself, but work remained incomplete at his death in 1547.

The angels vanished from public view until 1994, when two surfaced at auction but went unrecognized as the Wolsey bronzes.
