# Brexit Negotiating Team Now 40% Women, Says David Davis

Brexit Secretary David Davis has defended the gender balance of the UK's EU negotiating team after facing criticism from parliamentary committee members who described earlier photographs of the predominantly male delegation as "a disgrace."

In a letter to the House of Lords EU Committee, Mr Davis revealed that 40% of his team in last month's round of talks were women, a significant increase from previous rounds. The committee had previously expressed concern about images showing a largely male line-up representing Britain in the crucial Brexit negotiations.

Mr Davis emphasised that the government is committed to making the civil service "representative of modern-day Britain." He explained that personnel would "vary from round to round as we deploy the best available staff for each issue under negotiation."

The Brexit Secretary also noted that 52% of all staff at his Department for Exiting the EU (DExEU) are women. "I will continue to work for the best possible deal for the UK during these negotiations, and that means using the best expertise we have available, regardless of gender or any other factor," he stated.

The gender balance issue came to prominence last month when Labour's Baroness Kennedy questioned Mr Davis about female representation during a committee appearance. Subsequently, Labour MPs wrote to Prime Minister Theresa May, warning that the talks risked becoming "just another job for the boys."

Meanwhile, controversy erupted when Mr Davis's former chief of staff, James Chapman, described Brexit as the "biggest calamity" facing Britain since World War Two. In a series of tweets, Chapman urged "sensible" MPs to reverse the Brexit process, possibly by forming a new party, warning that businesses would "flee" the UK.

Former UKIP leader Nigel Farage questioned Chapman's loyalty, asking: "Which side was Mr Chapman really working for in the Brexit department?"

Brexit negotiations continue, with the UK scheduled to leave the EU in March 2019.

# Historic Crystal Palace Fireplace Returns to Cliffe Castle Museum

A remarkable malachite fireplace that was once showcased at London's Crystal Palace Exhibition in 1851 has found its way home to Cliffe Castle Museum in Keighley.

The ornate fire surround, crafted in St Petersburg from malachite—a distinctive green copper mineral—was purchased at auction in 1880 by Henry Isaac Butterfield, a wealthy textile manufacturer who built Cliffe Castle in the late 19th Century.

The chimneypiece was relocated to another property in the 1950s when Cliffe Castle was converted into a museum. Following the recent death of its latest owner, the historic piece was bequeathed back to the museum.

According to Cliffe Castle, only one similar malachite fireplace is known to survive, housed at the Kremlin Palace in Moscow, making this returned treasure extraordinarily rare.

**Swansea City Secure Premier League Survival as Hull City are Relegated**

Swansea City manager Paul Clement has expressed his pride after his side secured their Premier League status for another season, avoiding relegation on a dramatic final day of fixtures.

The Swans' 2-0 victory over Sunderland, combined with Hull City's 4-0 defeat at Crystal Palace on Sunday, confirmed Swansea's survival in the top flight. Hull needed just a point to keep their hopes alive, but Palace's comprehensive win sealed their fate and brought relief to the Liberty Stadium.

"Credit to the players for showing the form they have over the last four games to pick up 10 points from a possible 12," Clement told Swansea's official website. "They deserve to be where they are - playing in the Premier League again."

The turnaround has been remarkable for the Welsh club. When Clement arrived in January, Swansea were bottom of the table with a mere 12 points from 19 games, seemingly destined for the Championship.

"I am very proud of what we have achieved in the second half of the season, especially when you put into context where we were when I arrived," Clement added. "It's been a collective effort from everyone connected to the club; so congratulations to the players, backroom staff, club staff and definitely our supporters."

Clement admitted he expected the survival battle to go down to the wire. "I honestly thought it would go down to the last game of the season," he said. "I'm not complaining it hasn't gone to the last game as I predicted."

Swansea will conclude their campaign at home to West Bromwich Albion on Sunday, 21 May, with Clement targeting 41 points to finish the season.

"Our supporters have been amazing," Clement said. "I'm looking forward to enjoying the last game of the season with them at the Liberty on Sunday. It should be a fantastic atmosphere."

# Prankster's Galaxy Note 7 Wi-Fi Name Causes Alarm on Virgin America Flight

A passenger's attempt at humor nearly resulted in an emergency landing when they renamed their Wi-Fi hotspot to mimic the banned Samsung Galaxy Note 7 smartphone.

Lucas Wojciechowski was aboard Virgin America flight 358 traveling from San Francisco to Boston when he noticed an unusual Wi-Fi network name on his laptop: "Samsung Galaxy Note 7_1097." What seemed like a harmless observation quickly escalated into a serious situation aboard the late-night flight.

The Samsung Galaxy Note 7 had been banned from all U.S. aircraft by the Department of Transportation after several devices caught fire due to battery defects. The ban made any presence of the device on a flight a matter of significant safety concern.

After Wojciechowski alerted the crew, flight attendants made an urgent announcement requesting any passenger with a Note 7 to press their call button. When no one responded, the situation intensified.

"This isn't a joke. We're going to turn on the lights (it's 11pm) and search everyone's bag until we find it," the crew announced, according to Wojciechowski's tweets from the flight.

The captain then warned passengers of potential consequences: "Apparently the plane is going to have to get diverted and searched if nobody fesses up soon."

Eventually, the owner of the Wi-Fi hotspot came forward, confessing they had simply renamed their wireless device to "Samsung Galaxy Note 7_1097" as a prank. The flight crew announced the resolution: "Ladies and gentlemen, we found the device. Luckily only the name of the device was changed to 'Galaxy Note 7'. It was not a GN7."

The incident had wider repercussions. Serenity Caldwell, managing editor of iMore, was waiting to board a subsequent flight at the destination airport when she discovered a massive line at the gate counter. A 9am flight had been cancelled, and it took approximately two hours to sort out passenger itineraries.

Caldwell later overheard crew members discussing the real reason for the cancellation: the Galaxy Note 7 scare from the previous flight. "The plane was mid-flight when an attendant noticed a wi-fi hotspot. A Galaxy Note 7 wi-fi hotspot," the crew member explained.

According to Wojciechowski, no further action was taken against the passenger responsible for the prank.

Virgin America responded to the incident, stating: "The U.S. Department of Transportation has banned the transport of the Samsung Galaxy Note 7 onboard all U.S. aircraft, and Virgin America actively informs guests that they should not bring these devices onboard. As such, when our InFlight Teammates see potential evidence of this device onboard, they take it seriously. In this case, there was no such device - and no flights were cancelled or delayed as a result."

The airline's statement contradicted passenger accounts regarding flight cancellations.

# England Euro 2016 Squad Announcement Delayed

England manager Roy Hodgson has postponed the announcement of his 23-man squad for Euro 2016, which was originally scheduled for Thursday. The official deadline for the Football Association to submit the squad to Uefa is 31 May.

England are preparing for the tournament with warm-up fixtures against Turkey, Australia and Portugal before the finals commence in France from 10 June to 10 July.

Arsenal's Danny Welbeck faces exclusion after sustaining a right knee injury during Sunday's 2-2 draw with Manchester City. Fellow Gunner Alex Oxlade-Chamberlain, 22, has already been ruled out.

Midfielder Jack Wilshere's fitness remains uncertain despite returning to Arsenal's first team following a 10-month absence due to a broken leg. Liverpool captain Jordan Henderson, 25, is recovering from knee ligament damage sustained last month, though manager Jurgen Klopp has expressed confidence he will be fit for the tournament.

# Business Leaders Urge Government Action on Heathrow Expansion

The head of Britain's leading business lobby group has called on the government to stop delaying and move forward with building a third runway at Heathrow Airport.

CBI president Paul Drechsler will deliver a strong message to ministers at the organization's annual conference on Monday, urging them to "get on" with the controversial infrastructure project.

His intervention comes after the Airports Commission published a landmark report in July recommending Heathrow expansion. The commission's findings suggested that a third runway would deliver significant economic benefits, adding £147bn to the UK economy and creating 70,000 jobs by 2050.

The government has promised to make a final decision on the matter by the end of the year, though the project has faced years of political disagreement and delays.

**Infrastructure Investment Priority**

Mr Drechsler will also praise Chancellor George Osborne's decision to establish the National Infrastructure Commission, which will oversee £100bn in infrastructure spending across the country.

"The commission is a chance to end the cycle of politicisation and procrastination that has plagued British infrastructure for decades," he will tell the conference.

However, he will stress that the commission cannot be used as an excuse to postpone urgent decisions. "On airport capacity, we need strong political leadership and decisive action from government. Britain needs that new runway, so let's get it built," he will say.

**Political Opposition and Controversy**

Heathrow expansion has remained politically divisive for years. Prime Minister David Cameron famously opposed it whilst in opposition in 2009, declaring "no ifs, no buts" against expansion.

The proposal faces opposition from multiple quarters, including rival airport Gatwick, London Mayor Boris Johnson—who advocates for an entirely new airport—as well as environmental groups and local residents concerned about noise and pollution.

Reports emerged earlier this month that Sir Jeremy Heywood, the UK's most senior civil servant, wrote to ministers before party conference season warning them against publicly discussing the issue.

**European Union Membership**

Addressing the 1,000 delegates in London, Mr Drechsler will also discuss Europe, expressing hope that Britain remains in a reformed EU, noting that most CBI members believe membership advantages outweigh disadvantages.

**Charlton striker Nicky Ajose rejoins Bury on loan**

Charlton Athletic striker Nicky Ajose has returned to Bury on loan for a third spell with the League One club.

The 25-year-old joined the Addicks from Swindon Town in June 2016 and scored seven goals in 28 appearances. Ex-Manchester United trainee Ajose has had two previous loan spells with his hometown club, in 2010-11 and 2013.

"I sat down with him and he said this was something he wanted, so I told him I wasn't going to stand in his way," Charlton boss Karl Robinson said.

# Libyan Rights Activist Salwa Bughaighis Shot Dead After Voting

**BENGHAZI, Libya** — Prominent Libyan human rights activist and lawyer Salwa Bughaighis was shot dead in her Benghazi home on Wednesday, just hours after she cast her vote in the country's parliamentary elections and urged others to do the same despite ongoing violence.

Armed men fought their way into Ms. Bughaighis' house before shooting her in what witnesses described as a targeted assassination. A medical source at a Benghazi hospital confirmed she died from a gunshot wound to the head. An eyewitness reported that she was attacked by five armed men, four of whom wore masks.

Her husband, Issam, has disappeared following the attack, and relatives believe he has been kidnapped. The couple's whereabouts during the assault and Issam's current location remain unknown.

Ms. Bughaighis was an outspoken critic of many of the armed groups which still control much of Libya. The killing is the latest in a string of attacks on politicians, activists, and journalists who have spoken out against the actions of certain militias operating with impunity across the country.

The BBC's Rana Jawad in Tripoli reflected on Ms. Bughaighis' significance to Libya's political landscape. "It is not just Salwa Bughaighis' family and friends who are mourning her but many across Libya," Jawad said. "In 2011, in the early days of the uprising against Col Gaddafi, she was one of the few who kept me up-to-date on the deadly crackdown on protestors."

Ms. Bughaighis was heavily involved in recent moves to establish a National Dialogue to address Libya's numerous problems. As a civil and women's rights activist, she frequently spoke bluntly about the dangers posed by Islamist groups and the failures since Gaddafi was ousted. As a lawyer, she championed the urgent need for the rule of law in post-revolutionary Libya.

In a chilling final act of civic duty, Ms. Bughaighis gave a live television interview just hours before being killed. Despite a battle raging outside her home and the audible crackle of gunfire during the interview, she urged Benghazi residents to participate in the elections.

Ms. Bughaighis had also been a strong critic of Muammar Gaddafi and joined some of the first protests against him in 2011. She later became an adviser to Libya's National Transitional Council, which governed the country during and directly after the uprising. She leaves behind three sons.

U.S. Ambassador to Libya Deborah Jones called the killing "heartbreaking," describing it as a "cowardly, despicable, shameful act against a courageous woman and true Libyan patriot."

The assassination follows the killing of a parliamentary candidate in the southern city of Sabha earlier this week, according to local media reports.

Libya has suffered from persistent instability and violence since the downfall of Gaddafi in 2011. The government has struggled to disarm the various armed groups that remained from the war, leading to a security vacuum that has enabled targeted killings and lawlessness to flourish.

# Fatal Incident in Cork: Woman Found Dead, Man Arrested

Police were called to a residence on Murmount Avenue in Montenotte, Cork city, at 08:00 GMT on Monday, where they discovered a woman's body. A man in his 60s was transported to Mercy University Hospital Cork with non-life-threatening injuries.

A man in his mid-20s was arrested at the scene and is currently being detained at Mayfield Police Station. According to RTE reports, the woman had been stabbed.

The scene has been preserved for technical examination as investigators work to establish the circumstances surrounding the incident.

# Pussy Riot's Tolokonnikova 'Disappears' During Prison Transfer

The husband of jailed Pussy Riot member Nadezhda Tolokonnikova says he has lost contact with his wife, whose whereabouts remain unknown as she is being transferred between Russian prisons.

Pyotr Verzilov told US news website Buzzfeed that he had received no information about her current location, which authorities are keeping secret. He last knew her precise whereabouts on 21 October, when prison guards placed her on a train bound for a different facility.

Ms Tolokonnikova was briefly sighted by a fellow passenger on 24 October as the train arrived in Chelyabinsk, a city in the Ural Mountains. Since then, there has been no further news.

The 24-year-old activist had been serving her sentence at a penal colony in Mordovia, a region approximately 445km (275 miles) east of Moscow, home to labour camps dating from Joseph Stalin's notorious Gulag system. She recently staged hunger strikes to protest alleged abuses by prison staff.

"They want to cut her off from the outside world," Mr Verzilov said, claiming the transfer order came from Moscow authorities. He added that his wife remains weak from two hunger strikes and accused officials of punishing her for speaking out.

Ms Tolokonnikova and another Pussy Riot member were sentenced to two years' imprisonment for performing a crude protest song in a Moscow cathedral in February 2012. Their prosecution sparked international condemnation, though many Russians considered the act blasphemous. A third band member was released on appeal.

# England's James Vince Opts Out of IPL to Focus on County Cricket and Test Ambitions

England batsman James Vince has decided not to enter the Indian Premier League auction as he prioritizes his Hampshire captaincy and Test cricket aspirations, according to county director of cricket Giles White.

The 24-year-old, who has represented England in both one-day and Twenty20 formats, averaged 28.57 in the 2015 County Championship. Despite his limited-overs success, including topping the T20 Blast run charts and impressing during England's T20 series against Pakistan in the UAE last November, Vince is keeping his focus closer to home.

"James is very much in the space that he wants to play Test cricket," White told BBC Radio Solent. "I think that if he were to go to the IPL auction, for him at the moment, it might narrow that opportunity."

White praised Vince's mature approach: "His head's screwed on. James is looking at it broadly and can see what's ahead of him right now."

The right-hander took over Hampshire's captaincy from Jimmy Adams last season and believes performing well in early-season county cricket will strengthen his Test credentials.

Vince is currently featuring for Karachi Kings in the inaugural Pakistan Super League and awaits England's T20 World Cup squad announcement on Monday.

# Kenyan Bus Attack Hero Salah Farah Dies from Injuries

Salah Farah, hailed as a hero for protecting Christian passengers during an al-Shabab attack in Kenya, has died from his injuries nearly a month after the incident.

Mr Farah was travelling on a bus through Mandera in December when militants from the Somalia-based extremist group al-Shabab ambushed the vehicle. The attackers ordered passengers to separate into Muslims and Christians, a tactic used in previous attacks where Christians were executed while Muslims were spared.

However, Mr Farah and fellow Muslim passengers refused to comply with the gunmen's demands. "They told us if you are a Muslim, we are safe," Mr Farah told the BBC's Bashkas Jugsodaay shortly after the attack. "We asked them to kill all of us or leave us alone."

The attackers opened fire, and a bullet struck Mr Farah. He was transported to hospital in Nairobi, where he fought for his life before succumbing to his injuries.

In interviews following the attack, Mr Farah explained his courageous stance: "People should live peacefully together. We are brothers. It's only the religion that is the difference."

Inspector General of Police Joseph Boinnet praised Mr Farah as "a true hero" following news of his death. His brother Rashid expressed hope that the tragedy would promote religious harmony in Kenya.

Mr Farah's selfless act of solidarity has resonated across Kenya, symbolizing unity in the face of terrorism that seeks to divide communities along religious lines. His sacrifice serves as a powerful reminder of the bonds that transcend faith.

British sailor Alex Thomson is closing in on race leader Armel Le Cleac'h in the Vendee Globe round-the-world yacht race, narrowing the gap to just 77 miles with fewer than 3,000 miles remaining.

# National Teaching Service Scrapped After Pilot Fails to Meet Targets

The government has scrapped plans for a National Teaching Service that was meant to deploy 1,500 outstanding teachers to struggling schools across England by 2020, after a pilot scheme failed to attract sufficient applicants.

The initiative was announced with fanfare by then Education Secretary Nicky Morgan in 2015, promising to send "the country's best teachers and leaders to underperforming schools that struggle to attract and retain the professionals they need."

A Department for Education spokesman confirmed that "following a review of the outcomes, we can confirm that we will not be progressing" with the scheme beyond its initial pilot phase in the North West.

The National Teaching Service was designed to tackle educational inequality by deploying elite teaching staff to areas where schools struggled to recruit quality educators. In a speech to the Policy Exchange think-tank in November 2015, Mrs Morgan outlined the vision as part of a broader government commitment "to give every child an excellent education."

"Too many places are lagging behind, meaning young people in these areas are not being given a fair shot," the government stated at the time.

Under the original plan, NTS staff would work with schools for up to three years to drive up standards. The pilot, launched in September 2016, aimed to recruit up to 100 teachers and leaders for primary and secondary schools in the North West.

However, according to the Times Educational Supplement, just 54 teachers were recruited after only 116 applied – falling significantly short of expectations.

Despite the disappointing figures, the Department for Education maintained a positive tone about the pilot, saying officials were "pleased with the level of interest in the pilot and the calibre of the successful candidates."

The spokesman added: "We recognise that it is vitally important that schools, particularly in challenging areas, can recruit and retain excellent teachers, and we are determined to continue to support them to do this. We will use the lessons learnt from the pilot to secure a better understanding of to support schools in the future, and will set out future plans in due course."

The announcement comes as Thursday's Ofsted annual report highlighted serious problems in recruiting teachers and school leaders, particularly in northern England. School heads reported an "auction" for teachers in some areas.

Labour's shadow education secretary, Angela Rayner, described Ofsted's verdict as "damning," adding: "We now learn that they're scrapping the much lauded National Teaching Service after just a year. Last week, we learnt that the Tories have missed their recruitment target for the fifth year in a row. And last year, the highest number of teachers left the profession in a decade.

"The chronic teacher shortage continues to threaten standards under the Tories, and they are completely failing to take this crisis seriously."

**Connacht Secure Fifth Consecutive Victory with Bonus-Point Win Over Treviso**

Connacht achieved a significant milestone by securing their fifth consecutive league victory for the first time since 2002, defeating Benetton Treviso in an entertaining Pro12 encounter at the Sportsground.

The Irish province showcased their attacking prowess with second-half tries from Robbie Henshaw, Tom McCartney, and Matt Healy, though they ultimately fell short of claiming the bonus point they desperately sought in the closing stages.

Craig Ronaldson's boot kept Connacht in control during the first half, landing three penalties to give the hosts a 9-5 lead at the interval. The opening 40 minutes saw two Ronaldson penalties establish an early 6-0 advantage before Treviso responded through Jayden Hayward's opening try after 26 minutes, showcasing his pace with a clear sprint to the try line.

The second half belonged predominantly to Connacht. World Cup star Henshaw, making his first appearance for the province since the tournament and operating at full-back, crossed in the corner just two minutes after the restart to extend the lead.

Despite Hayward claiming his second try to keep Treviso in contention, replacement hooker Tom McCartney powered over following an effective line-out move in the 51st minute. Matt Healy added Connacht's third try with five minutes remaining, setting up a frantic finish.

Desperately chasing the fourth try needed for a bonus point, Connacht pushed forward in the dying moments but lost possession. Italy scrum-half Edoardo Gori capitalized on the turnover to grab a late consolation try for the visitors.

The victory maintains Connacht's impressive form and marks a historic achievement for the Galway-based side, matching their best winning streak in two decades. Referee Ian Davies oversaw the contest, which demonstrated both sides' commitment to attacking rugby.

# Asda Reports Decline in Sales as Supermarket Struggles Continue

UK supermarket chain Asda has reported a 2.8% fall in like-for-like sales for the three months ending in March, highlighting ongoing challenges for the country's third-largest grocer as it battles to regain market share from discount rivals.

While the figures represent a sequential improvement from previous quarters, analysts have cautioned that significant work remains for the struggling retailer to return to growth. The results stand in stark contrast to parent company Walmart's performance in the United States, where the retail giant posted a 1.4% rise in comparable sales during the same period.

Asda's latest decline, though concerning, marks a considerable improvement from the devastating 7.5% quarterly sales drop reported in August last year. The results also showed marginal progress compared to the 2.9% decline recorded in the final quarter of 2016.

Chief Executive Sean Clarke acknowledged the challenges ahead while expressing cautious optimism. "We're pleased that the momentum of Q4 has continued into the New Year with a third consecutive quarter of improvement," he said. "Despite this progress we are in no way complacent and there is still much for us to do."

The supermarket experienced a 2% decrease in customer footfall during the period, while the average transaction value also fell by 0.8%, indicating both declining visitor numbers and reduced basket sizes.

Asda has been hit harder than its fellow Big Four competitors—Tesco, Sainsbury's, and Morrisons—all of which have shown signs of recovery over the past year. The primary challenge comes from German discount chains Aldi and Lidl, which have aggressively expanded their UK presence, though their rapid growth has recently moderated.

Tom Berry, associate retail analyst at GlobalData, explained Asda's particular vulnerability: "Asda's position as the main UK discounter prior to Aldi and Lidl's arrival, means they will suffer greatest in terms of losses in market share."

Meanwhile, Walmart reported what it called a "solid first quarter" in the US, with sales reaching $117.5bn, meeting analyst expectations. The American retail giant has been investing heavily in e-commerce acquisitions to compete with Amazon, particularly as the online behemoth expands its grocery delivery operations.

Industry observers note that Asda, once considered Walmart's crown jewel, has suffered from a strategic emphasis on profit margins over sales volume, contributing to its recent market share losses.

# Health Officials Consider Withdrawing Consultant-Led Maternity Care Amid Staffing Crisis

Health officials have suggested withdrawing consultant-led care at one of the region's three district hospitals due to a staffing shortage, sparking growing concern across North Wales.

A protest was held in Rhyl this week to defend the maternity unit at nearby Glan Clwyd Hospital, with support now growing for the service at Wrexham Maelor Hospital. The other service at risk is at Ysbyty Gwynedd in Bangor.

Prestatyn GP Dr Eamonn Jessup, chairman of the North Wales Local Medical Committee, expressed strong opposition to any changes. "We have to have three fully staffed maternity and obstetric units in north Wales," he said. "Any change to that particular system is going to increase risk for mothers and babies."

The health board, still consulting on various proposals including retaining all services, emphasized that the quality and safety of maternity services was hugely important and said it looked forward to hearing feedback from the meeting.

A public meeting is being held at the Catrin Finch Centre at Glyndwr University from 19:00 BST.

# Chinese Fishing Vessel Crew Face Charges in Galapagos Marine Reserve

The crew of a Chinese fishing vessel intercepted in Ecuador's protected Galapagos waters are facing potential prison sentences after authorities discovered an illegal catch of endangered sharks.

The Fu Yuan Yu Leng 999 was discovered on Sunday within the Galapagos archipelago, a UNESCO World Heritage Site and marine reserve, carrying approximately 300 tonnes of fish. Most significantly, the majority of the catch consisted of sharks, including protected species such as hammerheads.

Ecuador's environment minister Tarsicio Granizo announced Tuesday that a judge on San Cristobal island had ordered around 20 crew members to remain in custody pending trial. If convicted of trafficking protected species, they could face up to three years in prison.

"Not necessarily all of the catch came from the marine reserve, but the fact that it included young sharks, even baby sharks, indicates that they could have been caught inside the reserve," Granizo told AFP news agency.

Walter Bustos, director of Galapagos National Park, confirmed the vessel was the largest ever captured operating illegally within the marine reserve.

The incident highlights ongoing conservation challenges in the region. In 2015, Ecuadorian authorities seized approximately 200,000 shark fins destined for Asian markets, where shark fin soup remains a prized delicacy at banquets.

Conservation groups warn that continued demand for shark fins is driving endangered species toward extinction while fuelling illegal wildlife trafficking networks.

# Justice Secretary Defends Feltham Prison Regime Despite Rule Breaches

The Justice Secretary has acknowledged that prison regulations were breached at Feltham Young Offenders Institution, but disputes claims that conditions amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment, the High Court has heard.

Liz Truss is contesting legal action brought by the mother of a teenage boy with mental health problems, known as AB, who was confined to his cell for 23-and-a-half hours daily. Her lawyer, Tom Weisselberg QC, admitted the isolation regime was "unlawful" but argued it was necessary due to the boy's "challenging" behaviour.

Mr Weisselberg told the court that AB had a "history of assaulting staff" and had directed "rude, racist and threatening language" towards prison officers and fellow inmates. The teenager's racist remarks to Muslim and black inmates had inflamed tensions at the facility, making him a target within the prison population.

The court heard that AB's "removal from association" breached Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which protects the right to private and family life, and violated prison regulations. Additionally, the boy did not receive the statutory minimum of 15 hours' education per week, constituting another breach of prison rules.

However, Mr Weisselberg insisted that AB's behaviour required "very careful management" and defended the prison's response. "The prison has not sat on its hands," he said, arguing that staff were actively managing a difficult situation.

The hearing continues as judges consider whether the isolation regime crossed the threshold into inhuman or degrading treatment.

# Carlton Cole on Trial at Celtic as Bhoys Seek Striking Options

Carlton Cole is training with Celtic as manager Ronny Deila considers adding the experienced striker to his squad. The 31-year-old former England international became a free agent after departing West Ham United at the end of last season.

Deila expressed cautious optimism about Cole's potential arrival at Parkhead. "We have a good squad but we are always looking to improve," the Celtic boss stated. "We are happy he is here."

The Norwegian manager acknowledged Cole's qualities as a target man but stressed the need for patience. "He's been good in the two exercises I've seen him doing but he needs more time. He hasn't trained for a while," Deila explained.

The Celtic manager remained non-committal about the duration of Cole's trial period, saying only "we will see how it comes."

Cole brings substantial experience, having earned seven England caps and scored 85 goals across 380-plus senior appearances for Chelsea, Aston Villa, and West Ham United.

# Song Byeong-hun Holds Off Jordan Spieth to Win Singapore Open

South Korea's Song Byeong-hun held his nerve on Monday morning to claim his maiden professional title at the Singapore Open, finishing one shot ahead of three-time major champion Jordan Spieth.

The duo were among 13 players who had to finish their final rounds on Monday after Sunday's play at Sentosa Golf Club was curtailed by thunderstorms. American Spieth sank a five-foot birdie putt on the last hole for a five-under-par 66 to finish 11 under.

Song, resuming on 12 under, parred his remaining three holes for a one-under 70 and victory by one shot. The world number 204 began the day with a testing 12-foot putt at the 16th, but a simple tap-in at the last secured his first professional victory after two second-place finishes on the Japan Tour.

Song, 24, led from the second round and was five in front of Spieth heading into the final round.

# Bigg Boss Tamil Faces Backlash Over "Insensitive" Mental Health Task

A popular Indian reality show has come under fire for making contestants imitate mental health patients in what experts have condemned as an offensive and stigmatizing segment.

Bigg Boss Tamil, which airs in Tamil Nadu, told contestants to act as if they were in a mental health facility. The contestants, in what looked like green hospital scrubs, started clapping their hands wildly and jumping around.

Their display has been criticised as exaggerated, inaccurate and insensitive by experts.

Dr Achal Bhagat, a Delhi-based psychologist, told the BBC that the episode was "outrageous".

"It sustains the stigma that already exists against mental health patients in Indian society," he said. "Widely held perceptions that people who suffer from mental illness have no capacity and are dangerous have to be challenged."

Dr Bhagat said the episode was indicative of a problem not just in the entertainment industry but in society as a whole. The word "mental" was often used as an insult and assumptions that people with mental health issues were dangerous were widespread.

"This urgently needs to change," he said.

Adding to the controversy, one of the contestants, Helen "Oviya" Nelson, who also participated in the episode, left the show soon afterwards, citing mental health issues.

Bigg Boss Tamil, which airs every Saturday and Sunday, is one of the most popular shows in the southern state.

Tamil actor Kamal Haasan who hosts the show, criticised the task and threatened to resign, saying it was "not in good taste".

"I'm actually angry about it," he said in the following episode. "If it happens again, this show is not important to me."

The show's legal consultant, C Rajasekar, told BBC Tamil's Pramila Krishnan that Bigg Boss Tamil follows "norms prescribed by the Information and Broadcasting Ministry".

Asked about the widely-criticised episode, S Shekher, a member of Tamil Nadu's censor board, told BBC Tamil that imitating and mocking those with mental health issues "should have been avoided".

The state censor board however does not have the authority to review entertainment shows produced for television. However, the Broadcasting Content Complaints Council (BCCC) advises against the use of "humour", "undesirable depiction of persons with disabilities" and "derisive and disparaging" references to their disabilities.

# Arthur Simpson-Kent Arrives in UK After Arrest in Ghana

Arthur Simpson-Kent has been arrested at Heathrow Airport following his arrival in the United Kingdom on a flight from Ghana. He has been taken to a west London police station for questioning.

# Roger Moore Praises Sam Smith's Bond Theme as Twitter Divides Over "Writing's On the Wall"

Former James Bond actor Sir Roger Moore has praised Sam Smith's new theme song for the upcoming 007 film Spectre, calling "Writing's On the Wall" "very haunting and wonderfully orchestrated". However, the track's release has sparked fierce debate among fans and critics on social media.

Speaking on BBC Breakfast, Paterson suggested the song tells the story of "a man deciding to quit it all for love". He compared its melody to Michael Jackson's 1995 single "Earth Song" and noted it was vastly superior to Madonna's much-criticised "Die Another Day" from the 2002 Bond film.

The reaction from celebrities has been equally mixed. Comedian David Schneider greeted the release with the quip: "The name is Bland. James Bland." However, fellow comic Omid Djalili, who appeared in 1999's "The World is Not Enough", was far more enthusiastic, tweeting that the song had left him "in a broken heap" and declaring: "If you're not moved by this song you don't have a pulse."

Smith makes history as the first solo male British artist to perform a Bond theme since Tom Jones sang "Thunderball" in 1964. The previous Bond theme, Adele's "Skyfall" from 2012, reached number two in the UK singles chart. Remarkably, no Bond song has ever topped the UK chart, and opinion remains divided on whether Smith's track will break that streak.

Currently, Canadian pop star Justin Bieber holds the number one position and is expected to retain it when this week's chart is announced on Friday.

Smith and his songwriting partner Jimmy Napes have stated they aimed to create something "timelessly classic". In a promotional video, Smith emphasised: "This isn't about me, about my life. I just hope people listen to it and think, 'That's Bond'."

# EU Launches Legal Action Against Poland, Hungary and Czech Republic Over Refugee Quotas

The European Commission has initiated legal proceedings against Poland, Hungary, and the Czech Republic for refusing to accept refugees under the EU's mandatory relocation scheme.

Migration Commissioner Dimitris Avramopoulos said the three countries had ignored "repeated calls" from the EU's executive to take their share. Only 20,869 of the 160,000 refugees have so far been relocated in the EU.

The three states could be referred to the European Court of Justice (ECJ) and eventually face heavy fines.

The relocation plan was conceived in response to the large influx of migrants and refugees in 2015, in an attempt to relieve pressure on frontline states, mainly Greece and Italy, where the vast majority of migrants were arriving.

EU countries agreed to relocate 160,000 asylum-seekers between them - though Romania, the Czech Republic, Slovakia and Hungary voted against accepting mandatory quotas. Hungary and Slovakia challenged the quota last month in the ECJ.

While the UK and Ireland were exempt from the original 2015 proposal, Poland's previous government backed the plan, although its current Eurosceptic administration has since rejected it.

The Czech Republic has accepted only 12 of the 2,000 it had been designated, while Hungary and Poland have received none.

"I regret to see that despite our repeated calls to pledge to relocate, the Czech Republic, Hungary, and Poland have not yet taken the necessary action," Mr Avramopoulos told journalists.

"For this reason, the Commission has decided to launch infringement procedures against these three member states. I sincerely hope that these member states can still reconsider their position and contribute fairly."

But Poland has already signalled it will not fall into line with the quota. "Each decision to relocate groups of migrants encourages thousands or millions more at the borders of Europe, to come to Europe, to get on boats and pontoons and risk their lives to reach the European continent," said Polish government spokesman Rafal Bochenek.

Czech Prime Minister Bohuslav Sobotka stressed that his country too would not take part either, "with regard to the worsened security situation in Europe and dysfunctionality of the quota system".

The quotas were based on the size and wealth of each country, but Austria and Denmark have so far not taken in any refugees either. Despite the small number of refugees relocated from Italy and Greece, the European Commission says the pace has quickened since January.

# Wales Defense Coach Shaun Edwards Backs Under-Fire Rob Howley

Wales defense coach Shaun Edwards has leapt to the defense of interim head coach Rob Howley, praising his "attention to detail" and coaching abilities amid growing criticism of Wales' autumn performances.

Howley is leading Wales through the 2016-17 season while regular boss Warren Gatland prepares for next year's British and Irish Lions tour to New Zealand. Lock Bradley Davies has been released back to the Ospreys to continue his injury rehabilitation.

# Google Reverses Ad Ban on 9to5Google After Trademark Dispute

# Record Number of Red-Necked Phalaropes Breed in Scottish Islands

Red-necked phalaropes, which migrate to Scotland's Western Isles, Orkney and Shetland during summer, have achieved record breeding numbers this year.

RSPB Scotland reported that thirty-six breeding males were counted at their Fetlar reserve in Shetland, matching the highest number ever recorded at the site. The success extends beyond Shetland, with a pair breeding at Balranald reserve in North Uist for the first time in 31 years.

# Brighton 1-0 Nottingham Forest: LuaLua strikes to secure opening-day victory

Brighton & Hove Albion began their Championship campaign with a hard-fought 1-0 victory over Nottingham Forest at the Amex Stadium, with winger Kazenga LuaLua's second-half strike proving to be the difference between the two sides.

**Gabrielle Giffords Launches Gun Control Initiative on Anniversary of Shooting**

Former Arizona Congresswoman Gabrielle Giffords has launched a new political action committee aimed at curbing gun violence, marking the second anniversary of the shooting that nearly claimed her life with a direct challenge to the powerful gun lobby.

The initiative, Americans for Responsible Solutions, was unveiled Tuesday as Ms. Giffords and her husband, former astronaut Mark Kelly, pledged to match the financial and political muscle of pro-gun groups like the National Rifle Association. The announcement comes amid renewed national debate over gun control following last month's elementary school massacre in Newtown, Connecticut, that left 20 children and six adults dead.

"In response to a horrific series of shootings, Congress has done something quite extraordinary - nothing at all," Ms. Giffords and Mr. Kelly wrote in an opinion piece published in USA Today. The couple, both gun owners themselves, criticized lawmakers for failing to act despite mounting gun violence across the nation.

The new organization aims to counter the NRA's influence on Capitol Hill, where the gun rights group spent more on lobbying in 2011 than all gun control organizations combined. "Until now, the gun lobby's political contributions, advertising and lobbying have dwarfed spending from anti-gun violence groups. No longer," Ms. Giffords declared.

The couple emphasized they do not seek to disarm responsible gun owners but rather to achieve "reforms to reduce gun violence and prevent mass shootings." This will require "matching gun lobbyists in their reach and resources," they wrote.

In a television interview with ABC News, Mr. Kelly did most of the speaking as his wife continues her recovery from the January 8, 2011, shooting in Tucson, Arizona, where she was meeting with constituents. The gunman killed six people and wounded 13 others, including Ms. Giffords, who suffered a severe brain injury.

The initiative's launch coincides with ongoing discussions at the White House about potential gun control measures. Vice President Joe Biden, leading the administration's gun violence task force, is scheduled to meet with gun safety organizations and victims' groups on Wednesday. He will also hold talks later this week with the NRA and other gun-owner representatives, as well as members of the entertainment and video game industries.

President Barack Obama has called on Congress to reinstate a ban on assault weapons, limit high-capacity ammunition magazines, and close loopholes that allow some gun purchases to proceed without background checks. The White House has promised to present specific proposals by the end of January.

Last Friday, Ms. Giffords visited Newtown to meet with families affected by the Sandy Hook Elementary School shooting. The visit sparked controversy when Connecticut State Representative DebraLee Hovey, who represents Newtown, wrote on Facebook: "Gabby Gifford [sic] stay out of my towns!!" The politician later apologized for the comment.

While some pro-gun lawmakers have indicated they are reconsidering their positions following the Newtown tragedy, political observers note that attention to gun control may have waned as Congress focused on reaching a fiscal cliff deal to avert automatic tax increases and spending cuts. Another round of budget deadlines looms at the end of March, potentially overshadowing the gun debate once again.

Ms. Giffords and Mr. Kelly have also consulted with New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg, a prominent gun control advocate, as they develop their strategy to challenge what observers call one of America's most powerful special interest groups.

# Jersey Care Inquiry Hears Testimony of Harsh Treatment in Post-War Years

A former resident of Jersey's care system has told a public inquiry how his treatment deteriorated dramatically after World War Two, transforming his experience from relatively bearable to "hell."

Giffard Aubin, 79, testified before the Independent Jersey Care Inquiry about his experiences between 1943 and 1951, describing severe punishments, psychological abuse, and rampant bullying. Speaking emotionally, Mr Aubin expressed bitterness and anger over his treatment, saying he hoped such abuse would never be repeated.

The inquiry, which has cost £6.5 million, is examining abuse within Jersey's care system from 1945 to the present day.

Mr Aubin's testimony revealed a stark contrast between wartime and post-war care. During the German occupation, he described conditions as austere but relatively stable. German soldiers even made Christmas presents for the boys and escorted them to beaches that were otherwise prohibited to islanders.

However, following liberation, despite improvements in diet and clothing, recreational outings ceased and conditions worsened significantly. Mr Aubin said certain boys were targeted for mistreatment by the matron, while insufficient staffing allowed older boys to bully younger residents with impunity.

"I remember having darts thrown at you - they were different to the darts you get today, much heavier - and if you moved you were hit with an armoury stick, which would cut you," Mr Aubin recalled. He also described being subjected to electric shocks from generator wires applied to his wet legs.

Fear of reprisals prevented him from complaining. So profound was his trauma that Mr Aubin said he still refuses to celebrate Liberation Day because he "did not feel liberated."

The panel also heard from Violet Renouf, who entered the Jersey Home for Girls in 1942 aged six. She described having stinging nettles placed in her bed as punishment for bed-wetting and being locked in isolation for three weeks after a false accusation of theft.

Mrs Renouf said her care experience had lasting effects on her relationships with her own children.
