The blaze, which broke out near St Mary's High School, was reported at approximately 20:50 BST and required crews to battle the inferno for more than five hours before it was finally extinguished at 02:00 BST. The incident was among 161 emergency calls that fire crews responded to since 18:00 BST on Friday.

Local residents gathered to watch the dramatic scene unfold, with some moved to tears as the flames advanced perilously close to their properties, located just a mile from the city centre. Northern Ireland Fire and Rescue Service (NIFRS) Group Commander Brian Stanfield confirmed that eight fire appliances were deployed to combat the blaze.

Faye Broadway, a resident living nearby, described the distressing scenes to BBC News NI, stating that some neighbours had fled their homes in nightwear. She witnessed two elderly women "in tears" desperately searching for missing pets amid the chaos.

Ms Broadway's partner, David Cadden, recounted the terrifying moment they spotted thick black smoke billowing over their house, followed by flames rising above tree level. "We decided to just take a walk up to make sure that there was no-one in danger, because it looked quite serious," he explained.

Mr Cadden described harrowing scenes of residents evacuating: "I walked up to the back of their houses and the fire was literally a stone's throw away, with ash falling down and embers hitting the roof. They were all running out of the house in their pyjamas, with dogs in their hands, and running across the street."

Firefighters were forced to move crowds back for safety as ash and embers fell on spectators. Some crews were deployed from as far away as Belfast on what proved to be an exceptionally busy night for the service.

Earlier on Friday, firefighters revealed they had responded to 221 gorse fires over the previous five days, with 92% started deliberately. Officials warned that recent dry, sunny weather had "provided a tinderbox landscape" conducive to such fires.

# Cuba Announces Ambitious Shark Conservation Plan

Cuba has unveiled a comprehensive shark conservation strategy developed in partnership with a United States environmental organization, marking a significant step in marine protection efforts.

The plan will require fishermen to systematically record and limit their shark catches while establishing new protected fishing zones. This initiative is particularly crucial given that approximately 20% of the world's 500 shark species inhabit Cuban waters.

Shark populations globally have experienced dramatic declines due to overfishing, the lucrative shark fin trade, and unintentional bycatch. Cuba has previously prohibited the practice of harvesting sharks solely for their fins.

The conservation plan emerged after two years of collaboration with the Environmental Defense Fund (EDF). Daniel Whittle, EDF's Cuba programme director, highlighted that Cuban waters support shark populations through relatively healthy coral reef systems.

"Cuba is considered the crown jewel of the Caribbean, principally because of its incredible coral reef ecosystems, its mangroves, its seagrasses," Whittle explained.

The EDF emphasizes that shark conservation also offers economic benefits, as ecotourism continues expanding and marine resources become increasingly valuable assets. Cuba is now developing a broader regional shark conservation initiative.

# Fox-Sky Deal Decision Delayed Until After UK General Election

The deadline for a decision on 21st Century Fox's proposed takeover of Sky has been extended until after the UK general election, Culture Secretary Karen Bradley announced.

The decision, originally scheduled for 16 May, has been postponed until 20 June to avoid the deal becoming entangled in election politics. Ms Bradley said the extension followed discussions with all parties involved, including Ofcom, the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA), and the Cabinet Office Propriety and Ethics team.

Regulators are currently examining the £11.7bn deal on grounds of media plurality and broadcasting standards. Fox has offered to pay £10.75 per share for the 61% of Sky it doesn't already own, valuing the entire company at £18.5bn.

The proposed acquisition has raised concerns due to media mogul Rupert Murdoch's extensive UK media holdings. Both Sky and Fox are controlled by Murdoch, who also owns The Times and The Sun newspapers. His sons Lachlan and James serve as joint chairmen and chief executive respectively of Fox.

Part of Ofcom's investigation includes assessing whether Sky's potential new owners meet the "fit and proper" standard required of broadcast licence holders.

European competition authorities have already approved the deal, but UK regulators continue their scrutiny of its implications for media concentration.

# Harry Potter Fans Face Four-Hour Online Queue as New Cursed Child Tickets Sell Out

Theatre fans spent hours online on Thursday attempting to secure some of the 250,000 new tickets released at 11:00 BST for Harry Potter and the Cursed Child, only to see them quickly appear on resale websites at inflated prices.

"Failed to get #CursedChild tickets after queuing for four hours," wrote one frustrated Twitter user. "Now loads on sale for hundreds of pounds on StubHub."

Tickets are currently being offered on the secondary marketplace for up to £1,000, despite official vendors Nimax and ATG selling admission to the two-part stage production for significantly less—between £15 and £70 per part.

A spokesperson for the show confirmed that whilst the newly-released tickets had sold out, returned and other late release tickets would become available daily. Additionally, an online lottery held every Friday releases 40 tickets for each performance the following week.

The production has warned customers purchasing from resale websites that they risk being refused admission. "Tickets purchased through either of our official ticketing platforms must not be sold or advertised for sale on the internet, in newspapers or elsewhere. Any ticket advertised for sale in this way will be automatically void," the spokesperson said.

StubHub defended its marketplace, stating that sales are "driven by supply and demand" and that sellers "set the price for what they think the market will bear."

Harry Potter and the Cursed Child became one of the UK's hottest tickets well before opening at London's Palace Theatre in June. Thursday's ticket release followed the publication of Jack Thorne's script, approved by Potter author JK Rowling, which became the fastest-selling book in the UK this decade.

Follow us on Twitter @BBCNewsEnts, on Instagram, or email entertainment.news@bbc.co.uk.

# Space Station Gets Window Clean 250 Miles Up

Two Russian cosmonauts ventured outside the International Space Station on Wednesday to tackle an unusual cleaning job - washing a dirty porthole window whilst floating 250 miles above Earth.

The window had become grimy over the years from exhaust fumes produced by visiting spacecraft docking at the station.

During their six-hour spacewalk, the cosmonauts also installed new equipment and performed routine maintenance work on the exterior of the orbiting laboratory.

This marked the fourth spacewalk at the ISS this year. For station commander Gennady Padalka, it was his tenth career spacewalk, adding to his record as the person who has spent more cumulative time in space than anyone else in history.

# Taliban Attackers Killed After 26-Hour Siege at Kandahar Air Base

**KANDAHAR, Afghanistan** - Afghan security forces killed the final Taliban attacker late Wednesday, ending a devastating 26-hour siege at Kandahar Air Base that left 38 civilians and two police officers dead, the defense ministry announced.

The prolonged assault on one of Afghanistan's largest military installations highlighted significant security vulnerabilities as the last gunman held out alone for several hours before being neutralized. The attack also wounded at least 37 people, including 17 military personnel and four police officers, according to ministry statements.

The Taliban assault began Tuesday when insurgents, described by the militant group as "martyrdom seekers," breached the compound's perimeter. The attackers wore military uniforms and carried light and heavy weapons, according to Tolo News TV. After penetrating the first gate, they occupied an old school building where they exchanged heavy fire with Afghan forces.

During the siege, witnesses reported that militants seized families as hostages, using them as human shields during the firefight. The airport compound houses both Afghan military and civilian sections, as well as a NATO base.

US Army Col. Michael Lawhorn confirmed that the attackers "never physically entered the airfield" and reported no coalition casualties.

The brazen attack, which the Taliban characterized as "thunderous attacks on foreign and hireling personnel," coincided with a regional peace conference in Islamabad where Afghan President Ashraf Ghani appealed to Pakistan for assistance in brokering peace negotiations with the Taliban.

Security analysts described the incident as a major intelligence failure, noting that attackers successfully smuggled weapons into an area supposedly secured by Afghan National Security Forces. The assault follows the Taliban's brief seizure of Kunduz in September, demonstrating the group's continued capability to conduct sophisticated operations.

# London Bombing Victim Led Quiet Life Dedicated to Family

Izabela Brandt, a 38-year-old Polish cleaner, was among the victims of the 7 July 2005 London bombings, killed in the Russell Square blast that claimed 26 lives, including the suicide bomber.

On that fateful morning, Ms Brandt left her Wood Green home at 8:00 AM and boarded a Piccadilly Line train bound for her cleaning job in Gunnersbury. When she failed to arrive at work, her brother Pawel Iskrzynski launched an urgent search, spending days traversing London whilst clutching his sister's photograph.

Police eventually confirmed her death through DNA samples, delivering the devastating news to the family.

Mr Iskrzynski described his sister as an intensely private individual who eschewed smoking and alcohol, maintaining only two close friendships. "She would normally return home from her job and stay indoors and did not pursue leisure activities," he told police in a statement read at the inquest.

Ms Brandt's life had been marked by entrepreneurship and sacrifice. After leaving school in 1981, she established her own restaurant business in Poland. She married Arek Brandt shortly thereafter, and the couple had two children: Hubert and Natalie.

When the restaurant closed in 2002, Ms Brandt made the difficult decision to move to London, leaving her husband to care for their children. The couple separated a year before her death.

In London, she shared accommodation with her brother and worked various jobs, including bar work, before settling into cleaning. She sent most of her wages to Poland to fund her children's education.

Tragically, her daughter Natalie had arrived in the UK on 7 July specifically to visit her mother. Hubert was residing in Sweden at the time of the tragedy.

# Samaritans Sees Record Contact Numbers After Free Helpline Launch

The Samaritans charity has reported a significant surge in people seeking support, handling more than 5.7 million cases throughout 2016.

The organisation attributed the increase of nearly 300,000 contacts compared to the previous year largely to the introduction of a free confidential helpline in autumn 2015. Previously, callers faced a charge of two pence per minute.

The figures, released to mark the beginning of Volunteers' Week, showed total contacts reached 5,703,830 in 2016, up from 5,404,331 in 2015. These contacts included helpline calls, emails, text messages and face-to-face support sessions.

Ruth Sutherland, Samaritans chief executive, emphasized that suicide is both complex and an inequality issue, with factors such as deprivation increasing risk. "Even two pence a minute was enough to deter some callers, which is why we were determined to make all calls to Samaritans free," she said.

Ms Sutherland praised the volunteers for making a difference by supporting growing numbers of people in crisis, but stressed the organisation is "just one part of the equation."

She added that suicide is preventable rather than inevitable, calling on everyone from politicians and health workers to employers and media to play their part.

Volunteers' Week, organised by the National Council for Voluntary Organisations, runs from 1-7 June.

# York's Rougier Street Becomes One-Way for All Vehicles

A major traffic change has been implemented on York's Rougier Street, with all vehicles now required to travel in a westerly direction.

Previously, cars and lorries were restricted to one-way traffic, but buses and taxis used a separate two-way section. The change now means all traffic will travel in a westerly direction.

Safety barriers were introduced earlier this year after a second person was killed crossing the road in two years. Sgt Louise Lucas died after being hit by a bus in March, while Daniel Foss, 37, died in 2013.

The changes were brought in after a review of the system and the withdrawal of the city's Ftr Metro bendy bus - which the layout was designed for.

David Hopkins, cabinet member for environment and transportation, said: "The change to a one-way route for buses and cars will hopefully mean the route is safer for pedestrians."

# Gareth Bale injury: Real Madrid boss Zinedine Zidane uncertain over return date

Real Madrid manager Zinedine Zidane has expressed uncertainty over Gareth Bale's return from injury ahead of the Champions League final.

The Wales international forward, 27, has not played since tearing a calf muscle against Barcelona on 23 April. La Liga title favourites Real face Juventus in the 3 June European final.

"We have to take it day by day but for now he's not with us and I don't know when he will be, but I hope it's soon," said Real boss Zinedine Zidane.

Real have three La Liga games remaining this season, starting with Sunday's home match with Sevilla (19:00 BST). They are second to Barcelona - who visit Las Palmas at the same time - on the head-to-head rule, but have a game in hand.

# African Nations Cup Qualifiers: Djibouti and Madagascar Claim First-Leg Victories

Djibouti celebrated a historic breakthrough in African Nations Cup qualifying, securing a commanding 2-0 home victory over South Sudan in their preliminary round first-leg encounter. The win marks a significant milestone for the East African nation as they seek a place in the main qualifying phase.

Goals from Hamza Abdi Idelh and Med Salam ended Djibouti's prolonged goal drought and put them in pole position to advance to Group C, where they would face formidable opposition in Burundi, Gabon, and Mali in the race to Cameroon 2019.

The victory proved an encouraging debut for Mauritanian coach Moussa Ghassoum, who was overseeing his first match in charge of the Djiboutian national team. Meanwhile, South Sudan's troubling away form continued, extending their winless record on the road with their fifteenth goal conceded in qualifiers while managing just one score.

In Wednesday's other fixture, Madagascar edged Sao Tome e Principe 1-0, courtesy of an own goal from Jordao Diogo. The result marked a winning start for new French manager Nicolas Dupuis, who faced fellow debutant coach Gustavo Clemente on the opposing bench.

Despite missing several key injured players, Madagascar fielded a competitive squad, flying Europe-based players directly to Sao Tome to minimize costs while supplementing them with domestic talent. The winners will advance to Group A alongside Equatorial Guinea, Senegal, and Sudan.

The third preliminary tie featured an Indian Ocean derby, with Comoros defeating Mauritius 2-0 in Moroni on Friday. The result gives Comoros a substantial advantage ahead of Tuesday's return leg at Stade Anjalay in Pamplemousse on April 28.

All three winning teams now hold commanding positions heading into their respective second legs.

# Two Men Seriously Injured in Separate Attacks in Renfrewshire

Two men have been seriously assaulted in separate incidents in Renfrewshire over the weekend.

A 45-year-old man was attacked outside the Anchor Bar in Paisley at approximately 21:30 on Saturday. He was taken to the Royal Alexandra Hospital where his condition was described as stable.

In an unrelated incident, a 30-year-old man sustained facial injuries and head lacerations following an assault on Graham Street in Johnstone at 00:40 on Sunday. He was also transported to the Royal Alexandra Hospital for treatment.

Police Scotland confirmed the two incidents are not connected and have appealed for witnesses to come forward.

# Hatton Garden Raider Used Fake Freedom Pass to Travel to Heist

Brian Reader, the 76-year-old ringleader who admitted involvement in the notorious Hatton Garden heist, used a fraudulent Freedom Pass to travel to central London on the night of the audacious burglary, a court has heard.

The elderly criminal used the counterfeit senior travel card to board the 96 bus from near his Dartford home before alighting at Waterloo East station at approximately 6:30 pm on April 2, prosecutors told Woolwich Crown Court.

The raid, which took place over the Easter weekend, saw thieves make off with valuables worth up to £14 million from safety deposit boxes in London's diamond district.

Detective Constable Matthew Hollands revealed that the Freedom Pass was discovered in Reader's wallet following his arrest. However, the card was not registered in Reader's name but rather in the name of "Mr T McCarthy" and did not bear Reader's photograph.

The court previously heard that Reader withdrew from what has been described as England's "largest burglary" when the gang encountered difficulties accessing the vault on their first attempt.

New evidence presented by Detective Constable Jamie Day, the first Flying Squad officer at the scene, suggested that the still-unidentified red-haired burglar known only as "Basil" appeared to have accessed the building using a key.

CCTV footage, captured by the building's only functioning security camera, showed a white van driven by defendant John Collins arriving at approximately 8:30 pm. Two men wearing high-visibility vests were seen exiting the vehicle. Subsequent footage showed "Basil" granting access to the building via an internal fire escape, followed by other men carrying tools, wheelie bins, and equipment.

In a dramatic courtroom demonstration, jurors were shown a full-size polystyrene replica of the 25cm by 45cm hole drilled through the vault wall. Prosecutor Philip Evans cautioned: "I must point out it says it's for visual purposes only, do not attempt to climb inside."

Three defendants deny conspiracy to commit burglary, whilst a fourth denies conspiracy to conceal or transfer criminal property. Reader and three co-conspirators have already pleaded guilty and await sentencing.

The trial continues.

# Thailand Offers Naval Base for Stranded Migrants as Trafficking Camps Discovered

Thailand has announced it will establish a "floating naval base" to assist thousands of migrants stranded at sea, though authorities insist only those requiring serious medical treatment will be brought ashore. The move comes as the region grapples with a humanitarian crisis involving migrants from Bangladesh and Myanmar, many of whom have been victims of human trafficking.

The Thai Prime Minister, Prayuth Chan-ocha, revealed this week that the naval operation would involve seven ships, two surveillance aircraft, and two helicopters patrolling the Andaman Sea. However, the BBC's Jonathan Head in Bangkok suggests the initiative appears designed to keep migrant boats at a distance rather than demonstrate a genuine commitment to helping those in distress.

"If anyone is injured or sick, they can be treated at hospitals in Thailand but will face illegal entry charges - it is up to them to decide," the Prime Minister stated, emphasizing that migrants brought ashore would still be considered illegal arrivals.

The announcement follows the discovery of horrific trafficking camps in the Malaysian jungle near the Thai border. Malaysian police teams began investigating a series of camps on Tuesday, finding evidence that migrants had been held in makeshift prisons constructed from wood and barbed wire.

Malaysian national police chief Khalid Abu Bakar described the scene as shocking, noting clear signs of torture at the facilities. "We were shocked by the cruelty," he told reporters, though he declined to provide specific details about the abuses uncovered.

Authorities believe the camps were used by human trafficking gangs to hold migrants for ransom before only recently being abandoned. The discovery mirrors similar findings in Thailand at the beginning of May, when graves were uncovered on the Thai side of the border.

Those earlier discoveries prompted Thailand to intensify its crackdown on trafficking routes used to transport Bangladeshi migrants and Rohingya Muslims from Myanmar through Thai territory toward Malaysia. This crackdown had the unintended consequence of forcing traffickers to send migrants by sea instead, leaving thousands stranded in boats that no country initially wanted to accept.

The UN's refugee agency estimates that approximately 3,000 people have now reached land, but another 2,600 may still be adrift at sea.

In Myanmar, authorities have charged 20 people with human trafficking-related offences. The suspects were arrested from a vessel carrying 200 migrants from Bangladesh that was rescued last week.

Under international pressure, Malaysia and Indonesia agreed last week to stop rejecting migrant boats and provide temporary shelter. Thailand has also agreed to stop towing boats away from its territory and has permitted US Navy aircraft searching for migrants to operate from Thai military bases - but only under Thai military command, after initially refusing an American request last week.

Thailand is scheduled to host a regional meeting on Friday to address the ongoing crisis and coordinate a regional response to the humanitarian emergency.

# Deadly Bomb Attack Strikes Pakistani Refugee Camp

**JALOZAI, Pakistan** - A devastating bomb attack has killed numerous people at a refugee camp in Pakistan, with reports indicating victims were queuing for food rations when the explosion occurred.

The blast struck the Jalozai camp, which provides shelter for people fleeing violence in Pakistan's tribal districts along the Afghan border - an area known as a sanctuary for Taliban and al-Qaeda-affiliated militants. While the camp serves a humanitarian purpose, police officials say it has also been exploited as a hiding place by some militant groups.

The explosion, for which no organization has yet claimed responsibility, left a crater at the scene. Police official Fuad Khan reported that the bomb detonated in a car parked near the administration office, where refugees were both collecting rations and registering as new arrivals.

"I saw about 20 casualties around me as the smoke and dust cleared," Khan told AFP news agency. Live television footage captured ambulances rushing victims to nearby hospitals, while authorities worked through wreckage of mangled vehicles to gather evidence.

Such attacks on refugee camps in Pakistan are exceptionally rare. However, the BBC's M Ilyas Khan notes that security forces last week detained individuals connected to the militant group Lashkar-e-Islam. Police suspect Thursday's bombing may have been retaliation for those arrests.

The attack comes at a sensitive time for Pakistan, which on Wednesday announced national elections scheduled for May 11. This will mark the country's first democratic transition from one elected civilian government to another.

Security concerns are overshadowing election preparations, though the outgoing government's reforms now permit political parties to campaign in tribal areas for the first time - part of efforts to combat militancy in these volatile regions.

# Cardiff Blues Confident of Luring Leigh Halfpenny Back to Wales

Cardiff Blues are positioning themselves as the ideal destination for Wales full-back Leigh Halfpenny, with head coach Danny Wilson emphasizing that player welfare and international performance would take precedence over financial considerations.

The 26-year-old star is out of contract with French Top 14 side Toulon at the end of the current season and faces a crucial decision about his future. While the Blues acknowledge they cannot match the lucrative wages offered by wealthy European clubs, Wilson believes they can provide something potentially more valuable: optimal player management to keep Halfpenny in "peak" condition for international duty.

"The best interests of the player internationally would be at the front of our minds," Wilson stated, highlighting a key differentiator in their recruitment pitch.

Halfpenny, who represented the Blues 87 times between 2008 and 2014 before his move to France, would likely be offered a national dual contract (NDC) should he opt to return to Wales. Under this arrangement, the Welsh Rugby Union would fund 60% of his salary, with the region covering the remaining 40%. In exchange, the player's workload would be carefully managed to prioritize his availability and fitness for Wales.

Wilson believes this structured approach to player management represents a significant selling point, particularly given Halfpenny's injury history. The full-back missed the recent Rugby World Cup due to fitness concerns, making the prospect of careful load management increasingly attractive.

"The design of the central contract is to get our best players playing and staying in Wales, and therefore the management of those players has to be a huge selling point," Wilson explained. "Between us and the strong relationship with the Welsh Rugby Union, the player gets the management he wants to peak and perform for Wales."

However, the Blues face stiff competition for Halfpenny's signature. The Scarlets have publicly expressed interest in the British and Irish Lion, while Premiership side Wasps have been strongly linked with a move. Both the Scarlets and Wasps are likely to compete in next season's Champions Cup, whereas the Blues are set for the second-tier Challenge Cup.

Despite these challenges, the Blues hold a significant advantage. Under the binding agreement between the WRU and Welsh regions, Cardiff Blues have first refusal on Halfpenny as the region that originally developed him.

"If Leigh does make a decision he wants to come back to Wales, I'd like to think Cardiff Blues would be high on his list of considerations," said Wilson. "A calibre of player like Leigh Halfpenny will have many options, whether that's regions, clubs over the bridge, clubs in France."

Wilson confirmed the club is in negotiations with several players as they build their squad for next season.

# Bank of England Economist Admits Forecasting Failures in Rare Candid Confession

In an unusually frank admission, Andrew Haldane, the Bank of England's chief economist, has acknowledged that criticisms of economic forecasting failures are justified. Speaking about predictions that missed the mark both before the 2008 financial crisis and regarding Brexit's immediate aftermath, Mr Haldane conceded the critiques were "a fair cop", adding that the economics profession now faces a crisis of confidence.

Mr Haldane drew a striking comparison between economists' failure to anticipate the devastating impact of Lehman Brothers' 2008 collapse and Michael Fish's infamous 1987 weather forecast, when the BBC meteorologist dismissed warnings of a hurricane hours before severe storms battered south-east England. He dubbed it the profession's "Michael Fish moment".

While his comments addressed economists broadly rather than specifically the Bank of England, Mr Haldane maintained support for the Bank's November forecast predicting a "material" slowdown and significant inflation rise in 2017-2018. The Bank correctly anticipated sterling's post-Brexit devaluation, but significantly underestimated consumer confidence resilience.

The admission highlights ongoing challenges in economic modelling, particularly when accounting for unexpected "shock" events. Models underestimated the financial crisis's severity whilst overestimating Brexit's short-term impact, failing to anticipate dynamic policy responses like the Bank's interest rate cuts to historic lows.

Mr Haldane suggested economists should emulate meteorologists, who now employ vastly more data to understand weather patterns. However, he acknowledged a fundamental difference: meteorology is pure science, whilst economics ultimately studies human behaviour—attempting to predict what millions or billions of individuals might do under specific circumstances.

This distinction makes economic forecasting inherently imprecise and challenging. As consumers, businesses, and policymakers respond unpredictably to changing conditions, even sophisticated models struggle to capture the complexity of human decision-making across entire economies.

The rare public acknowledgement of professional limitations represents an important moment of transparency from one of Britain's most influential economic voices.

# Three More Arrested Over Leeds Halloween Bike Chaos

Three more people have been arrested in connection with a Halloween motorcycle ride-out that brought chaos to Leeds city centre, police have confirmed.

About 50 bikers caused mayhem on 31 October when they brought a major route into Leeds to a standstill and rode dangerously through the city centre. Two men, aged 27, and one man, aged 23, have been arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to cause public nuisance. Nine men and a woman who were previously arrested remain on police bail.

Meanwhile, Leeds City Council has been granted a five-year extension to its county court injunction banning similar events.

The injunction allowed officers to stop ride-outs planned to take place before Christmas and on New Year's Eve, police said.

Labour councillor Debra Coupar, executive member for communities at Leeds City Council, said the injunction allowed the authority to "take action against people behaving irresponsibly", but would "not affect people who ride in groups in a law-abiding and sensible fashion".

The order bans more than one motor vehicle meeting in a public place in the Leeds district to drive anti-socially. It also forbids people from promoting or organising any such meet-ups.

In October, witnesses posted videos online showing bikers in convoy, with some pulling wheelies and others riding on the pavement. The scene was described as "utter chaos" by one passer-by and compared with the Mel Gibson film Mad Max.

# Ulster Farmers Split on Brexit as Union Warns of Uncertainty

The Ulster Farmer's Union has revealed deep divisions within farming families over the EU referendum, with its president Ian Marshall telling MPs that there are "husbands and wives who are completely opposed on this".

Speaking to a parliamentary inquiry examining referendum issues, Mr Marshall described the debate as "head versus heart" for many farmers, who are weighing the need for European market access against concerns about loss of identity.

Despite these divisions, the union maintains that in the "absence of a compelling case" for leaving, continued EU membership remains the better option for Northern Ireland's agricultural sector.

Mr Marshall, alongside chief executive Wesley Aston, emphasized that farming currently fails to deliver profits, with the industry heavily dependent on subsidies for survival. They stressed that Northern Ireland's 30,000 farmers require "information, guarantees and assurances to come to an informed decision".

The officials revealed significant financial figures, stating that farmers received £266 million in direct subsidy support in 2013/14, with an additional £83 million supporting the wider rural economy.

During questioning, DUP MP Ian Paisley highlighted ongoing frustrations with the Common Agricultural Policy's complexity, claiming farmers had complained about it throughout his 18 years as an elected representative. He insisted the UK government would continue financial support post-Brexit.

However, Mr Aston outlined that any new UK arrangement would require continued subsidies and reduced red tape. The union officials expressed doubts about whether Westminster would match EU subsidy levels.

Mr Marshall warned that without guarantees, they would have "huge concerns" about any potential new UK scheme, highlighting the uncertainty facing the farming community ahead of the referendum.

# Police Hunt for Missing Prisoner Simon Brown

Police Scotland has launched an urgent search for Simon Brown, a 45-year-old prisoner who failed to return to HMP Castle Huntly near Dundee yesterday evening.

Brown was reported missing at 17:00 after not returning to the open prison. He is described as 5ft 11in tall, bald, of slight build with brown eyes, and walks with a distinctive stoop and limp.

He was last spotted in Dundee's King Street area wearing a black jacket, black trousers and a white T-shirt. Brown was carrying a black and grey holdall featuring a white Puma emblem.

Police Scotland has warned the public not to approach Brown and urged anyone with information to contact them immediately.

# Somalia and North Korea Top Corruption Index as African Powerhouses Show No Progress

Transparency International (TI) has released its annual corruption index, placing Somalia at the top of the list of the world's most corrupt countries, sharing the dubious distinction with North Korea.

The global watchdog expressed concern that it has seen no improvement in African powerhouses Nigeria and South Africa, despite their economic significance on the continent.

The annual index evaluates factors including the prevalence of bribery and the perception that government officials escape punishment for corruption. According to TI, the countries perceived to be most corrupt typically share common characteristics: ongoing conflict, weak institutions such as police and courts, and a lack of independent media.

Somalia has struggled without an effective central government since long-serving ruler Siad Barre was overthrown in 1991. North Korea, one of the world's most secretive societies, shared the spot of most corrupt nation with Somalia.

In contrast, the "cleanest" countries—Denmark, Finland, and Sweden—demonstrate transparency in public spending and maintain judicial systems that don't differentiate between rich and poor, the report states.

Despite the grim overall picture, TI identified pockets of hope. Ghana was highlighted positively, where activists "worked hard to drive out the corrupt," despite being recently rocked by an undercover film showing judges allegedly taking bribes. Senegal emerged as one of the biggest improvers this year, following the government's introduction of a series of anti-corruption laws.

The index underscores the continuing global challenge of corruption, particularly affecting nations already struggling with instability and weak governance structures.

# Long-Lost Spider Species Rediscovered After Century of Absence

A rare spider species believed extinct in Britain has been spotted for the first time in over a century at a Dorset nature reserve.

Hypsosinga heri was on the verge of being removed from the official list of British species when RSPB volunteers made the remarkable discovery at Radipole Lake Nature Reserve in Weymouth. Two female spiders were found among flowers during a routine butterfly survey.

The species had not been seen since sightings at Wicken Fen near Ely, Cambridgeshire, in 1898 and 1912. The volunteers photographed "a very small, brightly-coloured spider on flowers," which was later verified by the British Arachnological Society.

Since the initial discovery several months ago, additional females have been observed at the nearby Lodmoor reserve. However, RSPB volunteer Allan Neilson noted a puzzling absence: "Which begs the question, where are the males?"

The rediscovery offers hope for the species' survival in Britain.

**Scarlets prop Rob Evans facing December return from wrist surgery**

Wales and Scarlets prop Rob Evans will not return to action until December as he continues his recovery from wrist surgery, the region has confirmed.

The 24-year-old has not played since Wales' summer tour to New Zealand in June and has missed the entire season so far.

"We're not expecting to see Rob back until December," a Scarlets spokesperson said.

Evans has been competing with Cardiff Blues' Gethin Jenkins for Wales' starting loosehead position since the 2015 World Cup.

Scarlets head coach Wayne Pivac previously indicated Evans might return near the autumn internationals in August.

# Irish Language Campaign Exceeds Targets as 13,000 Sign Up

A campaign to promote Irish language fluency has vastly exceeded its original goals, organisers announced on Saturday as they marked the initiative's fourth anniversary.

The Líofa campaign, which translates as "fluent" in Irish, was launched by Minister of Culture, Arts and Leisure, Carál Ní Chuilín, in September 2011. Its initial target was to get 1,000 people to sign up and commit to learning and speaking Irish by 2015.

On Saturday, Ms Ní Chuilín revealed that more than 13,000 people have now registered for Líofa, exceeding the original target thirteenfold. The campaign organisers have set an ambitious new goal to enrol 20,000 people on Irish language courses by 2020.

"Irish is a language for everyone and when I launched Líofa in 2011 I never imagined that I would have to revise the target so many times," Ms Ní Chuilín said in a statement. "People from all walks of life have availed of the opportunity to sign up to learn the language."

To celebrate the anniversary, the minister announced that a series of free intensive Irish language courses will be held at various venues across Northern Ireland on Saturday. "The courses are free and are accessible to all and every support will be given to participants both on this course and beyond as they endeavour to improve on their language skills," she added.

The announcement comes despite research showing significant disparities in Irish fluency across the island. Last month, a report by the Republic of Ireland's Economic and Social Research Institute found that 11% of respondents in the Republic could conduct most conversations in Irish, compared to just 2% in Northern Ireland.

# Two Men Arrested Over Fatal Shooting of Eddie Hutch in Dublin

Irish police have arrested two men in connection with the fatal shooting of Eddie Hutch Senior in Dublin last month.

Mr Hutch Snr, 59, was killed at his flat in Poplar Row, North Strand, in the north inner city on 8 February. Police believe it may have been in reprisal for a fatal shooting at a boxing match weigh-in days earlier.

RTÉ reports that the men can be detained for up to seven days.

They were arrested in the Dublin area and are being held at Mountjoy Garda Station and Bridewell Garda Station.

# Paralympic Champion David Smith Faces Fourth Surgery on Spinal Tumour

Paralympic gold medallist David Smith is preparing for his fourth operation on a life-threatening spinal tumour, scheduled for 1 March, as he continues his courageous battle with the condition that has forced him to put his sporting ambitions on hold.

The 37-year-old from Aviemore, who won rowing gold at the London 2012 Paralympics, had been training to represent Great Britain in Para-cycling at the Rio Games. However, the aggressive growth of the tumour has made further surgery unavoidable.

Smith revealed that the tumour causes him constant pain but has also given him an unexpected purpose - inspiring others facing severe illnesses. "It is a love-hate relationship," he told BBC Radio Scotland's The Stephen Jardine Programme. "In a lot of ways it's changed who I am as a person."

The athlete described receiving an emotional email from a family whose son has cystic fibrosis, saying: "Please never give up because our family is holding it together on your strength." Such messages have helped Smith maintain perspective on his situation. "I can't be angry at my situation if my efforts give hope to others," he said.

Despite his health challenges, Smith attempted to delay surgery last September in hopes of competing in Rio. However, earlier this month he acknowledged the tumour had grown dangerously large - threatening to crush his spinal cord and potentially stop his breathing. A cycling accident that caused the tumour to bleed added further urgency to the need for surgery.

Smith credits sport with providing the mental and physical strength to cope with his condition. Remarkably, just seven months after his last surgery in June last year, he cycled up France's Mont Ventoux three times in one day.

The determined athlete has already mapped out a timeline for his return to cycling following the operation.

# Six More Come Forward Following Footballer's Abuse Revelations

Mr Woodward, who played for Bury and Sheffield United, was abused by convicted paedophile Barry Bennell whilst at Crewe Alexandra between the ages of 11 and 15. Bennell, a former football coach, was jailed for nine years in 1998 after admitting sexual offences against six boys.

Cheshire Police confirmed they are contacting the six individuals who have come forward, though it remains unclear whether they are potential victims or witnesses. The force stated no one else is currently under investigation.

Since going public, he said he has been "speechless" at the overwhelming support from fans and former players, and has encouraged other victims to come forward.

# Top Gear Nominated for National Television Award Despite Clarkson Controversy

The BBC's Top Gear has secured a nomination at the National Television Awards despite the controversial departure of its former host Jeremy Clarkson earlier this year.

# Donaldson Strike Keeps Birmingham's Play-off Hopes Alive

Clayton Donaldson's clinical finish earned Birmingham City a crucial 1-0 victory over struggling Bolton Wanderers, keeping their Championship play-off ambitions firmly on track.

The striker tucked away a low cross from Diego Fabbrini at the near post to claim his seventh goal of the season, securing three precious points that lift Blues to within three points of the coveted play-off positions. The victory ended a concerning run that had seen Birmingham fail to win in their previous three outings.

For Bolton, the struggles continue both on and off the pitch. Despite avoiding a winding-up order on Monday after agreeing to a £7.5m takeover, the Trotters remain rooted in second-from-bottom position, their survival hopes looking increasingly bleak.

Former Bolton striker Dean Holdsworth, who heads the consortium set to take control at the Macron Stadium, was once again present in the stands to witness another disappointing performance from his future charges. The home side's attacking impotence was compounded by the absence of top scorer Gary Madine, who was controversially left out by manager Neil Lennon for disciplinary reasons.

Birmingham hardly dominated proceedings but made their moment of quality count when Donaldson expertly flicked home Fabbrini's delivery. The former Watford midfielder, making his first start for Blues, provided the creative spark that had been missing from an otherwise tepid encounter.

The visitors nearly doubled their advantage late on when substitute David Cotterill was thwarted by Bolton goalkeeper Paul Rachubka, who was making his first league start for the club.

Bolton boss Neil Lennon was frank about his side's limitations: "What we need to do is get the embargo lifted and get some players in to bolster the squad. It's wafer thin at the moment. We do need a bit of strength in depth, it's something we've lacked for a while."

Regarding the Madine situation, Lennon remained tight-lipped about specifics but firm in his stance: "You have to set certain standards as a manager. There are some things which you can't tolerate and you have to put a marker down. It's up to Gary, the ball is in his court."

Birmingham manager Gary Rowett was satisfied with the result, acknowledging: "You always felt this was a really pivotal game. We're not a free-scoring team, we didn't use the ball well enough but the one bit of quality in the game we ended up scoring from. We're still very much in the mix, something that, after 32 games, everyone at the club would have been really pleased with."

# Welsh School Celebrates 70 Years Since Historic Opening

Ysgol Gymraeg Dewi Sant, a Welsh-medium school in Llanelli, has celebrated its 70th anniversary with special commemorations at the site where it all began.

Looking ahead, Ms Davies confirmed discussions with Carmarthenshire council regarding a new school building.

# Geraint Thomas Claims Thrilling Stage Two Victory at Tirreno-Adriatico

Britain's Geraint Thomas secured a dramatic solo victory on stage two of the Tirreno-Adriatico cycling race, attacking in the closing kilometres to claim his first win of the season.

The Team Sky rider made his decisive move with approximately 5km remaining of the 228km stage, holding off a charging peloton to cross the line nine seconds clear in Pomarance, Italy. Dutch rider Tom Dumoulin finished second, with Slovakia's Peter Sagan taking third place.

# Two Teenage Boys Arrested in Australia on Terror-Related Charges

The teenagers were apprehended by a counter-terrorism team in a laneway behind a Muslim prayer hall. According to authorities, they were carrying two bayonet-style knives purchased on the day of their arrest, along with handwritten notes pledging allegiance to IS.

The pair did not appear in Parramatta Children's Court and did not apply for bail, which was formally refused. The arrests were part of an ongoing counter-terrorism operation.

Australian Federal Police Deputy Commissioner Mike Phelan emphasized public safety concerns, stating: "Anybody who says they've got the silver bullet to youth radicalisation, please tell me all about it."

The incident follows the arrest of a 22-year-old man charged with committing a terrorist act last month in southwest Sydney. Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull warned in September that the threat of terror attacks in Australia was "real" following IS calls to target prominent Australian locations.

# Medieval Seawall Breach Leaves Gower Coastal Path Cut Off for Three Years

A picturesque section of the Wales Coastal Path near Llanmadoc in north Gower remains impassable three years after winter storms breached a centuries-old seawall, flooding the area and cutting off a beloved local walking route.

The 2014 storms damaged the medieval seawall at Cwm Ivy, allowing seawater to inundate what was previously grassland rich with flowers and wildlife. Natural Resources Wales (NRW) has since ruled that restoring the original coastal path is not feasible, despite mounting pressure from local residents and walking groups.

Local resident Randolph Jenkins, whose family has lived in the area since 1923, expressed frustration at the loss. "Three years ago this marshland was grassland, full of flowers and wildlife. The wall has been here for centuries," he said. "There are so many people who support re-connecting the path - from local walking and rambling groups to the local assembly member."

Following the breach, NRW created a diversion through nearby Cwm Ivy woods to maintain the Wales Coastal Path's continuity. However, locals argue this has spoiled a popular circular walk and diminished the area's appeal.

The impact extends beyond recreation. Café owner Sian Griffiths reported decreased footfall for her business, noting: "There was a lot of places you could go for a walk. That has all gone now."

NRW has proposed alternatives to Swansea council, which owns the path, including constructing a new route away from the marshland or building a wooden or rope bridge. Hywel Manley of NRW confirmed: "The council is responsible for the public footpath, and we have suggested alternatives."

Swansea council stated it is working with multiple organizations to resolve the ongoing issue.

# Vintage Uniforms Mark Belfast Somme Parade

Bands led a procession of men and women, many dressed in vintage military uniforms and carrying replica weapons, through Belfast to commemorate the Battle of the Somme. The parade was organised by the 36th Ulster Division Memorial Association, with a wreath-laying ceremony held at Belfast City Hall.

# Smart Motorway Plan Could Cost Up to £70m for Belfast Routes

A proposal to convert hard shoulders into traffic lanes on Belfast's main motorways could cost between £60m and £70m, according to consultants' estimates.

Transport NI commissioned experts to examine solutions for "recurrent traffic congestion at peak times" on the region's busiest roads. The resulting report recommends transforming sections of the M1 and M2 into "smart motorways", similar to schemes already operating in England.

The plans would see the hard shoulder converted into permanent traffic lanes on the M1 between Stockman's Lane and Blaris, and on the M2 between York Street and Greencastle, in both directions.

# Scottish Labour Must Elect Leader "For Long Haul" After Election Devastation, Says Lamont

Former Scottish Labour leader Johann Lamont has said the party must appoint a leader for the long term if it is to recover from its catastrophic general election defeat in Scotland.

In her first broadcast interview since resigning, Ms Lamont said the scale of the party's election defeat was worse than anyone "possibly imagined". The party must now elect a leader "for the long haul" to recover, she said.

Ms Lamont also praised the SNP and its leader Nicola Sturgeon for running a campaign that "got everything right".

The SNP won 56 out of 59 seats in Scotland in last month's general election. Labour was left with just one MP in Scotland, after losing 40 seats, including those of Scottish Labour leader Jim Murphy, and shadow foreign secretary Douglas Alexander.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Johann Lamont, who led Scottish Labour from 2011 to 2014, said: "Even those of us who were preparing for the worst possible defeat couldn't possibly have imagined what happened.

"We couldn't have predicted it, but we need to analyse it if we're going to survive.

"The instinct of the Labour Party is if there's a problem, change the leader, then sit back, fold your arms and wait to be disappointed because they're sure it's not going to deliver.

"We can't do that this time. We need to elect a leader not on a short term contract, but a long term appointment for the long haul. There is no quick fix to this, there are not any ploys, not any gimmicks, that will get us through the next period."

She said it "defies logic" that Labour MPs of the "highest calibre" lost their seats, but said the SNP "took all before them".

"That therefore means people were putting faith not just in individual candidates, but putting faith in a message that was coming to them from the SNP."

She said the SNP had provided "a lesson in how to run a campaign", and leader Nicola Sturgeon had been "completely in control".

"It seems to me they got everything right, and Nicola Sturgeon has become a politician over many years. She was the most experienced person on the podium during the leaders' debate, and that shone out."

Ms Lamont added that she felt some comments about the new SNP MPs had been "disrespectful".

"Some of the commentary around some of them choosing to take their oath in Gaelic I found personally offensive as a Gael," she said.

"They are a mixed bunch like any bunch of people, but the fact of the matter is they are significantly representing Scotland's interests."

Ms Lamont, who is MSP for Glasgow Pollok, resigned as Scottish Labour leader last October accusing Westminster colleagues of treating Scotland like a "branch office".

"The recovery [of Labour] in Scotland which matters to the whole of the United Kingdom must be shaped in Scotland itself," she said.

Scottish Labour leader Jim Murphy has announced he will tender his resignation later this month having tabled a plan to reform the party. Deputy leader Kezia Dugdale has confirmed she will stand for the leadership.

# New Law Bans Wheel Clamping on Private Land in England and Wales

A new law coming into effect makes it a criminal offence to clamp or tow away vehicles parked on private land in England and Wales, in a move designed to protect motorists from rogue operators.

The Protection of Freedoms Act introduces the ban, which could save drivers an estimated £55 million annually in clamping charges. However, the legislation does not extend to Northern Ireland, while Scotland has already prohibited the practice since 1992.

Under the new regulations, private landowners retain some powers through strengthened ticketing provisions. Unpaid parking charges can now be claimed from the registered keeper of the vehicle, not just the driver who parked it. This change addresses a previous loophole that made it difficult for landowners to pursue payment.

The government has also established an independent appeals service, funded by the British Parking Association (BPA), allowing motorists to challenge parking charges issued on private land by companies enrolled in the BPA's approved operator scheme.

Lord Taylor of Holbeach, the Home Office minister responsible for the clamping law changes, welcomed the reforms: "This common-sense ban will give motorists the protection they deserve against rogue wheel-clamping and towing companies. It will save motorists £55m each year in clamping charges and finally penalise the real criminals - the corrupt firms themselves."

Local Transport Minister Norman Baker added: "These new parking arrangements deliver a fairer legal framework for motorists and landowners, while getting rid of the indiscriminate clamping and towing by private companies for good."

Despite the reforms, both the AA and BPA have expressed reservations, arguing the measures don't provide adequate protection against unscrupulous parking operators. A BPA spokesperson highlighted concerns about little-known by-laws that grant certain landowners, including some railway stations, airports, and port authorities, exemptions allowing them to manage parking on their own terms.

BPA chief executive Patrick Troy acknowledged the significance of the changes whilst noting their limitations: "The Protection of Freedoms Act ushers in perhaps the most significant shake-up of the private parking industry ever seen in this country. However, the regulations do not yet go far enough. An independent appeals service which is not binding on all operators is likely to be a recipe for confusion among motorists."

The AA has also raised concerns that rogue operators may now shift to issuing bogus parking tickets on private land, potentially creating new problems for drivers despite the clamping ban.

# Chile's Lower House Approves Limited Abortion Rights Bill

Chile's Chamber of Deputies has approved a bill that would allow abortion under three specific circumstances, marking a significant shift in the country's restrictive reproductive laws.

The draft, which was submitted by Michelle Bachelet's government, needs Senate approval to become law. Despite being predominantly Catholic, Chile allowed abortion until 1989. But the practice was banned by General Augusto Pinochet in one of the last acts of his military government.

"Incredible, the motion is passed," said the leader of the Chamber of Deputies, Marco Antonio Nunez. Opinion polls say most Chileans approve the change.

The proposal was approved by 66 to 44 votes. The government, which tabled the bill 14 months ago, managed to get the support of some members of the conservative Christian Democrats.

"This is an historic day. We see the political will to let women make their own decisions," said lawmaker Karol Cariola of the Communist Party, which is part of Ms Bachelet's governing coalition.

However, opposition remains strong. "This is a setback for protection of the unborn," said Claudia Nogueira of conservative Independent Democratic Union party.

Chile is one of seven Latin American countries where there is still a total ban on abortion. The others are El Salvador, the Dominican Republic, Haiti, Honduras, Nicaragua and Surinam.

Only Cuba, Guyana, Puerto Rico and Uruguay allow abortions in cases other than rape, incest or threats to a woman's health. In Mexico, only Mexico City has legalised abortion, during the first 12 weeks.

Authorities are treating the manhunt as a high priority given the serious nature of the allegations and public safety concerns in the Kawasaki area.

# Search Planned for Missing Suffolk Woman Sylvia Stuart

A search is set to be organized for a missing Suffolk woman whose husband was found dead near their home earlier this month.

A group is due to set off from The Bell in Wortwell later. Suffolk Police are aware of the search taking place.

Wortwell is near Harleston in Norfolk and about five miles from Weybread. It is an area of fields, hamlets and the River Waveney, which forms the county border.

On Friday, police searched fields near the couple's home in Mill Lane.

Police believe Mr Qazimaj boarded a ferry from Dover to Calais on 4 June, the day after Mr Stuart was found dead. His car was found on a terraced street within sight of the ferry terminal. Any connection he may have to the Stuarts is not known.

The couple's son-in-law Steve Paxman, 61 and from Leicester, was arrested on 5 June in connection with Mr Stuart's death, and released on police bail until 3 August.

# End of an Era: Last VCR Manufacturer Ceases Production After 33 Years

Funai Electric, the last remaining manufacturer of VHS-playing VCRs, is ending production after 33 years, marking the final chapter for a once-revolutionary technology.

The Japanese company, which has been producing VCRs most recently in China for Sanyo, sold just 750,000 units last year—a dramatic decline from its peak of 15 million units annually. The decision comes as sourcing necessary parts has become increasingly difficult.

VCRs were introduced in the 1970s and revolutionized home entertainment, but were eventually superseded by DVD technology. The writing was on the wall years ago: UK retailer Dixons phased out VCR sales 12 years ago due to DVD popularity, and Sony discontinued Betamax video cassettes last year.

Unlike vinyl records, which have experienced a remarkable renaissance among audiophiles and collectors, experts don't anticipate similar nostalgia for VHS formats.

"I don't see VCR becoming like vinyl," said Tania Loeffler, an analyst at IHS Technology. "The quality on VHS is not something I think anyone would want to go back to."

However, Loeffler acknowledged that niche markets, particularly those focused on archival purposes, will likely mourn the loss of VCR availability for accessing historical VHS content.

The end of VCR production closes a significant chapter in consumer electronics history.

# Cyclist Wins Damages After Pothole Crash Left Him With Severe Head Injury

Alan Curtis, 57, from Bushey in Hertfordshire, suffered a "severe head injury" in the crash on The Drive, Rickmansworth, in 2009. He sued Hertfordshire County Council for failing to fix the pothole, which he said was a "real source of danger".

# Thailand-Australia World Cup Qualifier: Fans Told to Wear Mourning Colors

Football associations in Thailand and Australia have instructed fans to wear black, grey, or white clothing for an upcoming World Cup qualifier match, in respect of Thailand's period of national mourning.

The match, scheduled for November 15, comes as Thailand observes a year-long mourning period following the death of King Bhumibol Adulyadej last week. The 88-year-old monarch reigned for 70 years and was regarded by many Thais as semi-divine, making him the world's longest-reigning monarch.

# Mountain Weather Service Warns of Closure Risk Over Funding Dispute

The Mountain Weather Information Service (MWIS) has warned it could be forced to close if it loses crucial support from sportscotland, potentially putting the safety of climbers and walkers at risk.

The non-profit forecasting service said it would stop producing forecasts at the end of this year if funding is not continued. However, sportscotland has dismissed the safety warning as "disappointing and misleading."

The Scottish government sporting body said it remains committed to providing reliable, authoritative mountain weather forecasts and confirmed investment in MWIS would continue until the end of 2023.

Sportscotland said it has been involved in collaborative discussions for over a year with the Met Office and MWIS about building a "resilient and development-focused mountain weather forecast provision for Scotland."

In a statement, sportscotland said: "Our priority is to ensure there is a sustainable mountain forecast for Scotland through the provision of reliable, authoritative forecasts, which are relevant to outdoor activities and enable forecast users to make informed judgements about their chosen activities. Geoff Monk, Galloway-based lead forecaster at MWIS, expressed concern about the situation: "The funding withdrawal by sportscotland, following their previous decision to collaborate with MWIS, was a real shock and jeopardises the safety of those who use the mountains every day."

He added: "All we want is for MWIS to continue to provide a consistent, quality service so that mountain users can enjoy the mountains safely, fully aware of what the weather will throw at them."

# Dortmund Cruise Past Lotte to Set Up Bayern Semi-Final
