# Nigerian Court Sentences Nine to Death for Blasphemy in Kano

KANO, Nigeria - A Sharia court in northern Nigeria has sentenced nine Muslims to death by hanging after they pleaded guilty to blasphemy charges, according to the head of Kano's religious police.

Aminu Ibrahim Daurawa told the BBC that the trial was conducted swiftly and in secret following violent protests that resulted in part of the courthouse being burned down last month. It remains unclear whether the convicted individuals plan to appeal the sentence.

The alleged blasphemy occurred during a religious gathering held in honor of Sheikh Ibrahim Niasse, the Senegalese founder of the Tijaniya sect, which commands a substantial following throughout West Africa. The nine defendants - eight men and one woman - were accused of stating that "Niasse was bigger than Prophet Muhammad," comments that sparked immediate unrest in the predominantly Muslim city.

The controversial remarks triggered violent reactions, with an angry mob burning the venue to the ground. The nine individuals were subsequently arrested to prevent further violence.

"There has been consensus among Muslim scholars that insulting the prophet carries a death sentence," Mr. Daurawa explained to BBC Hausa service. "We quickly put them on trial to avoid bloodshed because people were very angry and trying to take law into their hands."

When news of the verdict emerged, celebrations reportedly broke out in some areas of Kano, according to BBC Kano reporter Yusuf Yakasai.

The Tijaniya sect, founded in Algeria in 1784, is the largest Sufi order in Islam, with followers spanning north and west Africa, South Africa, Indonesia, and beyond. Sheikh Ibrahim Niasse is credited with reviving the sect in the 20th century, and his shrine attracts pilgrims from across the continent. The convicted individuals belonged to the Haqiqa (Realist) faction of the movement.

In Kano and several other northern Nigerian states, Islamic Sharia courts operate alongside secular judicial systems, a development that followed the country's return to civilian rule in 1999.

This case marks the first time a death sentence has been handed down for blasphemy in northern Nigeria. While death sentences have been issued for other offenses such as adultery under Sharia law, none have been carried out to date.

# Mindfulness Therapy as Effective as Anti-Depressants for Depression Relapse Prevention

Mindfulness-based cognitive therapy could offer a viable alternative to long-term anti-depressant medication for people at risk of depression relapse, according to a major new study.

Scientists tested the therapy against anti-depressant pills for people at risk of relapse and found it worked just as well. The therapy trains people to focus their minds and understand that negative thoughts may come and go. In England and Wales doctors are already encouraged to offer it.

Patients who have had recurrent clinical depression are often prescribed long-term anti-depressant drugs to help prevent further episodes. And experts stress that drug therapy is still essential for many.

In this study, UK scientists enrolled 212 people who were at risk of further depression on a course of mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (MBCT) while carefully reducing their medication. Patients took part in group sessions where they learned guided meditation and mindfulness skills.

The therapy aimed to help people focus on the present, recognise any early warning signs of depression and respond to them in ways that did not trigger further reoccurrences.

Researchers compared these results to 212 people who continued to take a full course of medication over two years. By the end of the study, a similar proportion of people had relapsed in both groups. And many in the MBCT group had been tapered off their medication.

Scientists say these findings suggest MBCT could provide a much-needed alternative for people who cannot or do not wish to take long-term drugs. In their report, they conclude it "may be a new choice for millions of people with recurrent depression on repeat prescriptions."

Nigel Reed, who took part in the study, added: "Mindfulness gives me a set of skills which I use to keep well in the long term. Rather than relying on the continuing use of anti-depressants, mindfulness puts me in charge, allowing me to take control of my own future, to spot when I am at risk and to make the changes I need to stay well."

Providing an independent comment on the study, Dr Gwen Adshead, of the Royal College of Psychiatrists, said: "These findings are important from the point of view of people living with depression who are trying to engage in their own recovery. And it provides evidence that MBCT is an intervention that primary care physicians should take seriously as an option."

But he cautioned the research does not suggest MBCT is useful for all types of depression; nor that it should replace anti-depressant treatment for people with severe disorders who have needed hospital treatment or are suicidal.

And experts caution patients should only reduce their anti-depressant medication under medical supervision.

Prof Eduard Vieta, Professor of Psychiatry at the University of Barcelona, Spain, said there needed to be more studies to establish how effective MBCT might be.

Researchers say their next step is to tease out what the active ingredient in mindfulness therapy might be, and to check it compares favourably to other group-based approaches.

# Tracey Ullman Returns to BBC One with Mixed Reviews for New Sketch Show

Tracey Ullman has made her long-awaited return to British television with her new sketch show on BBC One, receiving a range of responses from critics who praised her versatility while questioning whether the format felt fresh enough for 2016.

The show, which aired on Monday evening, featured the 56-year-old comedian's impressions of Dame Judi Dench as a kleptomaniac and German Chancellor Angela Merkel reimagined as a "sex bomb". Among the original characters were Karen, a drugs mule readjusting to contemporary society after spending 28 years in a Thai prison, and Sally Preston, a topless feminist Member of Parliament.

The Times reviewer Alex Hardy was largely positive, declaring the sketch show delivered "mostly hits". She wrote: "Someone confiscate her passport. It's as if a prodigal daughter - last seen mucking about with French, Saunders and pop producers in the mid-1980s - has returned to the UK from 30 gap years in America and wrapped herself instantly round British hearts and funnybones."

Veronica Lee of The Arts Desk highlighted Ullman's ability to maintain her perspective on British culture despite her decades in America. "Last night's opener didn't just have some of her pitch-perfect impressions, but also her keen-eyed observations of British life today. Clearly her long sojourn in the States hasn't blurred her view, nor made it more rosy about dear old Blighty."

Lee particularly praised Ullman's portrayal of the shoplifting Dame Judi Dench and Dame Maggie Smith recording an audition tape for Star Wars as standout moments.

The Independent's Sally Newall said Ullman was "on fine fighting form", noting that "the duds were few and far between". She expressed excitement about upcoming sketches targeting the royal family, mentioning photographs of Ullman dressed as Camilla Parker Bowles and Carole Middleton.

However, not all reviews were glowing. The Telegraph's Michael Hogan described the show as "hit and miss", comparing it to a cross between Victoria Wood and Little Britain. While he found the darker, more surreal material successful, he felt the gentler sketches fell flat. Nevertheless, he concluded: "She might be 56 and rich enough to never need work again, but Ullman's lost none of her youthful bite. Welcome home."

The Guardian's Sam Wollaston was less convinced, calling the show "unashamedly same-old" and criticising it as "not brave or funny enough, like a step backwards from Little Britain, 10 years after Little Britain."

Comedy website Chortle's Steve Bennett questioned whether the show justified its existence beyond Ullman's star power, suggesting it didn't feel like a classic.

Ullman last appeared on BBC television in the early 1980s with A Kick up the Eighties and Three of a Kind, before relocating to America where she created The Tracey Ullman Show for Fox, winning multiple Emmy and Golden Globe awards. That programme notably gave birth to The Simpsons, which began as short animated segments.

# Price Comparison Websites Win Consumer Trust Despite Flaws, Regulator Finds

Price comparison websites have earned high levels of trust and satisfaction from British consumers, despite some significant shortcomings in how they operate, according to new research by the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA).

The regulator launched a comprehensive study of digital comparison tools (DCTs) last September to examine how these increasingly popular services could be improved for consumers. The interim findings, released today, suggest that no full-scale market investigation is currently needed.

"Overall DCT users think these tools work well, making it easier to make informed choices and save money," the CMA said in its update. "Although DCTs are still a relatively new way of purchasing, the survey indicates that consumers are generally confident in the way they use them, and many use more than one site."

The study, which will deliver its final report at the end of September this year, aims to better understand how people use price comparison websites, apps and switching services across multiple sectors of the economy. Beyond energy, the research encompasses insurance, banking, phone and broadband services, and airline flights.

A central component of the research has been a survey of 4,000 consumers, complemented by a mystery shopping project and a comprehensive review of the comparison websites themselves. The findings reveal widespread adoption, with 85% of internet users having used a DCT at some point, and most reporting they use multiple sites to shop around.

However, the research uncovered some concerning gaps in consumer understanding. Only 11% of respondents believed they had been shown all possible deals available in the market. This suggests many comparison sites fail to make clear they might not cover the entire market—a significant flaw in transparency.

Despite this apparent limitation, customer satisfaction remains remarkably high, with 90% of users saying they were happy with the DCTs they had used. Many reported making better purchasing decisions as a result of using these services.

The CMA has identified several potential problems with the price comparison industry that may lead to recommendations for improvement later this year, though specific details were not disclosed in the interim update.

The regulator believes these digital tools could offer even greater benefits to consumers than they currently do, suggesting room for significant improvement in how they operate.

The launch of the CMA's study last year was met with some surprise from consumer groups and small energy suppliers. Critics pointed out that just months earlier, in June 2016, a full-scale CMA inquiry into the UK's energy market had controversially decided that price comparison websites should no longer be required to show deals on which they did not earn a commission—a decision some viewed as "turning the clock back" on consumer protection.

# University of Bristol Scientists Launch Big Tick Project to Combat Rising Lyme Disease Cases

Scientists at the University of Bristol have launched an ambitious campaign to better understand infection levels in ticks and how diseases can be transmitted to humans through their pets.

The Big Tick Project is specifically targeting dog owners to raise awareness about the dangers of tick-borne diseases, particularly Lyme disease. When infected ticks bite dogs, they can subsequently spread the bacterial infection to their human owners.

Public Health England estimates there are approximately 3,000 new cases of Lyme disease in England and Wales annually, though some Lyme disease charities suggest the actual figure could be as high as 15,000 cases per year.

While Lyme disease can often be managed effectively with early detection, it can cause chronic pain and severe fatigue if left untreated, making prevention and awareness crucial.

Project leader Professor Richard Wall explained that tick numbers and related ailments have increased significantly over the past decade. "Data from all types of practices ranging from urban to rural locations will help advance the understanding of the level of diseases and pathogens ticks carry in the UK," he said.

According to Professor Wall, tick distribution has expanded by 17% nationally over the last ten years, with tick numbers increasing in 73% of surveyed locations, highlighting the growing urgency of this public health concern.

# China's Trade Data Shows Continued Weakness in Global Demand

China's export performance showed marginal improvement in July, though the figures remained disappointing and point to continued weakness in global economic activity.

Exports fell by 4.4% compared to a year earlier, which was a slight improvement over June's 4.8% drop but still worse than analysts had been expecting. Imports were also weaker than estimated, down by 12.5%. As China is a crucial driver of the worldwide economy, the data is seen as a snapshot of the global outlook.

The country's exports have fallen for 12 out of the past 13 months. Global uncertainty ranging from low commodity prices to the EU debt crisis and the UK leaving the bloc continues to mute economic activity around the world.

The figures do "not bode well for the state of global demand, given that Chinese exports benefited from a weaker currency," Louis Kuijs of Oxford Economics wrote in a note. "Looking forward, we expect the trade data to remain lacklustre in the coming months, given our outlook of subdued momentum in global trade and China's domestic demand."

In US dollar denominated terms, exports fell to $184.7bn (£141bn) while imports dropped to $132.4bn. This leaves the country with a trade surplus of $52.31bn for the month of July.

The sluggish domestic demand indicates that Beijing's efforts to boost consumption to spur growth have yet to take effect. The fresh data, though, comes on the heels of better-than-expected economic growth in the second quarter. Gross domestic product expanded by 6.7% in the three months to June compared to a year earlier.

# Former Army Serviceman's Job Reinstated After Citizenship Application Refused

A former soldier who lost his job after being refused UK citizenship has been allowed to return to work while his case is reviewed by the Home Office.

Sam Cataki, 36, from Neyland, Pembrokeshire, was dismissed from his position at Milford Haven Port Authority on Wednesday following the rejection of his visa application. The Fijian national, who served in the British Army for 12 years, has now had his job reinstated following public outcry and political intervention.

A petition supporting Mr Cataki has gathered nearly 30,000 signatures, highlighting widespread community backing for the father of two young children, aged one and five.

Stephen Crabb, MP for Preseli Pembrokeshire, said he had received assurances from the UK government that Mr Cataki's application was being handled "with urgency." The MP has been assisting Mr Cataki since 2014 and recently raised his case with Immigration Minister Brandon Lewis.

Mr Cataki, who left the Army in 2013, believes his citizenship application was rejected due to three penalty points on his driving licence. He had been working at Milford Haven for two years before his dismissal.

Despite his job being reinstated, Mr Cataki remains anxious about the final decision. "I am really hopeful now the job has been re-instated, but the thing is we still do not know if they are going to reject it," he said.

The situation has also put his wife Seini's visa status at risk. The couple has spent nearly £6,000 on visa applications for both of them.

"If it wasn't for the media attention and the help of Stephen Crabb I would have just lost my job, that would be it," Mr Cataki added.

Mr Crabb welcomed the development, saying: "This is positive news for Sam, his family and the people of Neyland who have shown strong support for Sam. Hopefully the whole matter will be resolved very shortly."

# Barclays to Pay $13.75m Over Unsuitable Fund Switching Practices

The US Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (Finra) has ordered Barclays Capital to pay more than $10 million in compensation to affected customers, along with a $3.75 million fine, following revelations of inadequate supervision of mutual fund switching practices.

The settlement, which includes a censure but no admission of wrongdoing by Barclays, addresses failings that occurred between January 2010 and June 2015. During this period, the bank failed to properly supervise procedures that resulted in numerous customers swapping one mutual fund for another.

According to Finra, more than 6,100 fund switches took place over the five-year period, with customers losing a total of $8.63 million. In many cases, the benefits of switching funds were undermined by transaction costs, and most customers were not adequately warned about these expenses before proceeding.

The regulator found particularly troubling practices between March and August 2014, when Barclays processed 1,723 fund transactions—39% of those reviewed—that were inconsistent with customers' stated investment objectives, risk tolerance, or existing investment portfolios.

This fine arrives two months after Barclays appointed James "Jes" Staley, a former JP Morgan senior executive, as chief executive. Mr. Staley has indicated a renewed focus on investment banking while simultaneously cutting costs and divesting non-core assets.

The penalty adds to Barclays' recent regulatory troubles. In November, the bank was fined £72 million in the UK for failing to conduct proper due diligence on wealthy clients. The Financial Conduct Authority found that Barclays had arranged £1.88 billion worth of deals for high-net-worth clients in 2011 and 2012 without conducting appropriate checks on those who should have been considered politically high-risk individuals.

# Alliance Party Leader Praises Colleagues at Belfast Conference

Alliance Party leader David Ford addressed his party's annual conference in Belfast on Saturday, using the occasion to pay tribute to departing colleagues and outline his political future following his decision not to seek reappointment as justice minister.

Mr Ford, who has held the justice portfolio since policing and justice powers were devolved to Stormont in 2010, confirmed he will step down from the ministerial role after May's Assembly elections, though he intends to seek re-election as an MLA.

During his speech, the Alliance leader offered warm praise for his deputy, Naomi Long, describing her tenure as the party's "lone voice in the House of Commons." Despite losing her Westminster seat for East Belfast, Mr Ford emphasized that Ms Long had made a significant impact and expressed hope she would join him at Stormont.

"After the flag protests, the insults, the threats, the violence, Naomi added 4,000 votes to what we were told was the high water mark of 2010," Mr Ford said. He attributed her defeat to what he characterized as "a cynical five-party pact" that barely secured 50% of votes in the traditionally unionist constituency.

Mr Ford also recognized the contributions of Judith Cochrane, Anna Lo, and Kieran McCarthy, all of whom will not contest the May elections.

Turning to broader political issues, the Alliance leader challenged other Stormont parties to accelerate efforts toward building a united community, criticizing what he termed their "delay, fudge and waffle." He distributed his criticism evenly, labeling Sinn Féin "economic illiterates" whilst accusing the DUP of subterfuge regarding abortion policy.

Mr Ford concluded by positioning Alliance as "the only party working for everyone," committed to transforming society and building a united community across Northern Ireland's traditional divides.

# Indian Teen Dies After Onlookers Film Instead of Help at Accident Scene

A 17-year-old boy has died in India after bystanders recorded him on their mobile phones rather than providing assistance following a road accident, local media reported.

Anwar Ali was fatally injured when his bicycle collided with a bus in Karnataka state's Koppal district. According to reports, people gathered around the scene to take pictures and videos of the bleeding teenager but failed to offer any help.

The teen was eventually taken to hospital approximately half an hour after the collision. However, he succumbed to his injuries, having bled to death. Medical professionals stated that Ali could have survived if he had received prompt medical attention.

The tragic incident has reignited debate about the widespread reluctance among Indians to assist road accident victims. India recorded 146,133 road deaths in 2015, making it one of the world's deadliest countries for traffic accidents.

Safety campaigner Piyush Tewari explained that the problem stems from systemic issues rather than lack of compassion. "The foremost reason is intimidation by police," he told the BBC. "Oftentimes if you assist someone the police will assume you're helping that person out of guilt."

Other deterrents include fears of being falsely implicated in the accident, becoming entangled in prolonged legal proceedings as a witness, or being pressured to pay hospital fees.

While India's Supreme Court ruled last year that "good Samaritans" would be protected from harassment, and Karnataka has passed similar legislation, correspondents note that many citizens remain unaware of these protections and distrust police compliance.

The case highlights ongoing challenges in encouraging public assistance at accident scenes across India.

Italy's Six Nations campaign has been dealt another blow with the news that centre Michele Campagnaro will miss Saturday's match against Wales in Cardiff through injury.

The Exeter Chiefs player has been a consistent presence for the Azzurri this tournament, starting all of Italy's 2016 Six Nations matches and previously scoring two tries when the team visited Cardiff in 2014.

Zebre centre Giulio Bisegni, 23, who has earned just two caps, has been called up as his replacement. The 23-year-old will be hoping to make an impression in what is a challenging situation for the Italian side.

Italy's injury crisis deepened after their defeat to Ireland, with fly-half Edoardo Padovani, prop Lorenzo Cittadini and lock George Biagi all ruled out. This forces coach Jacques Brunel to make at least four changes to his lineup.

There is some positive news with Racing92 prop Martin Castrogiovanni, 34, returning from suspension, while Perpignan fly-half Tommy Allen and uncapped duo Jacopo Sarto and Tommaso Castello join the 28-man squad.

# G7 Summit: Merkel Pushes Climate Action and Security Talks

**KRUEN, Germany** - German Chancellor Angela Merkel is pressing fellow G7 leaders to commit to ambitious climate goals during the two-day summit at the luxurious Schloss Elmau hotel in the Bavarian Alps.

The German leader is seeking agreement from the group's members - the United States, United Kingdom, Japan, France, Canada and Italy - to limit global temperature increases to within 2 degrees Celsius of pre-industrial levels. Additionally, Merkel is urging G7 nations to contribute to a fund designed to help poor countries most severely impacted by climate change.

The climate and energy discussions dominated Monday's first working session, as Merkel attempts to build momentum ahead of the crucial United Nations climate summit scheduled for Paris this December.

Beyond environmental concerns, the summit has also addressed international security threats. Leaders were joined by Iraqi Prime Minister Haider al-Abadi, Nigerian President Muhammadu Buhari, and Tunisian President Beji Caid Essebsi for discussions on combating radical extremism from groups including Islamic State and Boko Haram.

British Prime Minister David Cameron announced Sunday that the UK would deploy an additional 125 military trainers to Iraq, calling IS "the biggest threat" facing G7 leaders. The militant group continues to occupy significant territories across Iraq and Syria despite ongoing US-led airstrikes.

Meanwhile, Nigeria faces its own battle against Boko Haram, which has conducted attacks since 2009 in its campaign to establish an Islamic state in the region.

The picturesque alpine setting provides a dramatic backdrop for discussions on these pressing global challenges, as world leaders work to forge consensus on both environmental sustainability and international security.

# Hope Powell Joins FA as Coach Educator for Men's Professional Game

Hope Powell, England's most decorated women's football figure, has taken on a groundbreaking role as coach educator within the men's professional game.

The 49-year-old, who became the first woman to achieve the Uefa Pro Licence in 2003, brings extensive experience having scored 35 goals in 65 England caps and managed the women's national team from 1998 to 2013, including leading Great Britain at the 2012 Olympics.

"I am keen to help develop the next generation of coaches in this country," Powell said. "It's a great opportunity to work within the men's professional game."

She hopes to inspire future female coaches entering the field.

# Lost Exmoor Writer's Manuscript Discovered After 45 Years

The Exmoor Society has unveiled its newly organized archive after uncovering remarkable historical treasures during a two-year relocation project.

The society's collection of books, maps, letters and photographs was previously stored in two disorganized and inaccessible old storerooms. However, during the move to new premises in Dulverton from the Parish Rooms, staff made an extraordinary discovery: a lost manuscript by renowned Exmoor writer Hope Bourne, missing for 45 years.

Archivist Dr Helen Blackman revealed additional finds, including several slide collections documenting six decades of landscape changes across the moor and material related to Exmoor's establishment as a national park.

"All of this helps us gain a more complete picture of Exmoor's landscape, people and heritage," Dr Blackman said.

The archive, now based on Dulverton High Street, will be officially opened by Graeme Bonham-Carter. His father, Victor Bonham-Carter, served as society president for over 30 years and authored numerous books about Exmoor. Victor was also a distant relative of British actress Helena Bonham-Carter.

# England Beat Ireland 2-1 to Reach EuroHockey Semi-Finals

England staged a dramatic second-half comeback to defeat Ireland 2-1 in a crucial EuroHockey Championships pool match in Amsterdam, securing their place in the semi-finals.

Ireland, needing only a draw to progress, took an early lead through Matthew Nelson, who deflected in a penalty corner in the 13th minute. The 10th-ranked side appeared set to cause an upset against their higher-ranked opponents.

However, England turned the match around after the break. David Goodfield equalized just one minute into the third quarter, firing home from close range past Irish goalkeeper David Harte.

The decisive moment came when Ireland's Shane O'Donoghue received a 10-minute sin bin for an elbow. England capitalized on their numerical advantage as centre-forward Sam Ward tapped in from close range to complete the comeback.

The victory sees England finish as runners-up in Pool B behind Germany, who defeated Poland 7-3. England will now face hosts Netherlands in Friday's semi-final, while Germany meet Belgium.

This result reverses the outcome of the teams' last EuroHockey meeting in London two years ago, when Ireland won 4-2 in the bronze medal play-off.

England's women's team also advanced to the semi-finals, where they face the Netherlands on Thursday at 19:00 BST after finishing top of their pool.

# Celebrated Zimbabwean Writer Chenjerai Hove Dies in Exile

Renowned Zimbabwean author and poet Chenjerai Hove has died while living in exile, according to his wife Tekla Hove. The exact cause of death remains unclear, though he had been suffering from liver problems and had fallen ill three weeks prior to his passing.

Mr Hove, widely regarded as one of the leading figures in post-colonial African literature, died with his wife and sister by his side - marking the first time they had been together since 2001, when he left Zimbabwe.

The celebrated writer went into self-imposed exile in 2001 after facing harassment from authorities due to his outspoken criticism of President Robert Mugabe's government. Despite his deteriorating health in recent weeks, friend and colleague Helge Lunde, executive director of the International Cities of Refuge Network, said Mr Hove remained "bright and clear until the end."

Mr Lunde described the late writer as "a great writer, novelist, poet and playwright," but emphasized that "first and foremost he was a freedom fighter, fighting for human rights in his country."

Mr Hove's literary achievements were exceptional, with his work drawing deeply from Shona oral traditions. His novel "Bones" is particularly celebrated for its powerful allegories and imagery rooted in his native language and culture. He demonstrated remarkable command of both English and Shona throughout his career.

Among his four novels was "Masimba Avanhu" (Is This the People's Power?), which examined the situation of women in Zimbabwe. This work, combined with his political criticism, brought him to the attention of authorities, according to the International Writers Project at Brown University.

Throughout his exile, Mr Hove continued writing, producing numerous poems that frequently explored themes of separation. He also contributed plays and proverbs to the BBC and remained committed to his role as a social commentator.

Speaking to BBC's Focus on Africa radio programme last year, Mr Hove articulated his sense of duty: "As a citizen, as an African, as a Zimbabwean.... to look at our lives and at whether our leaders are enhancing our dignity or taking it away."

His literary excellence was recognized through numerous prestigious awards, including the Zimbabwe Writing Award in 1987, the Noma Award for Publishing in Africa in 1989, and a German-Afrika Award for freedom of expression in 2001.

After Zimbabwe's independence in 1980, Mr Hove emerged as one of the country's most important literary voices, mentoring new talent alongside other celebrated writers such as Charles Mungoshi and Dambudzo Marechera.

The family is currently hoping to fly Mr Hove's body back to Zimbabwe for burial, though funeral arrangements have not yet been finalized. His death in exile raises poignant questions about Zimbabwe's treatment of its greatest artistic talents.

Jamaica international Garath McCleary has signed a new contract with Reading until the summer of 2019.

The 29-year-old winger's previous deal was due to expire at the end of the season.

McCleary joined the Royals from Nottingham Forest on a free transfer in May 2012 and has made over 200 appearances for the club.

"I'm very happy Garath has signed a new deal," Reading manager Jaap Stam said. "He's been a very important player for us this season."

McCleary has scored eight goals in 23 Championship appearances this campaign.

# Protesters Call for Closure of Aberthaw Power Station

Environmental campaigners have staged a protest at Aberthaw Power Station in the Vale of Glamorgan, demanding its closure and the creation of more renewable energy jobs in the area.

The demonstration comes after the European Court of Justice ruled in September that the coal-fired station had been emitting illegal levels of air pollution, highlighting growing concerns about its environmental impact.

In response to the court's findings, plant operators RWE announced they would invest £5 million in new technology designed to "significantly lower" emissions of toxic nitrogen oxides from the facility. A company spokesman also confirmed the station would reduce its generation levels this year to ensure continued operation within its Environmental Permit whilst remaining competitive.

However, environmental activists dismissed these measures as insufficient. Alyson Austin from the United Valleys Action Group criticized the investment, saying: "This is a sticking plaster for a severed arm, it's just not good enough."

Ms Austin argued that the station's closure was inevitable and called for proactive planning: "We need to put something positive in place of Aberthaw. Renewable energy could provide thousands of jobs." She urged that workers at the station should be "re-skilled" now to facilitate the transition to cleaner energy.

The protest brought together multiple environmental organizations, including Reclaim the Power, Bristol Rising Tide, and the Coal Action Network.

RWE defended the station's continued operation, emphasizing its importance for energy security. A spokesman stated that the combination of reduced operating hours and lower emissions would allow Aberthaw to "provide security of electricity supply for Wales and beyond into the 2020s."

The company highlighted that UK generation margins had reached record lows multiple times during the winter, prompting warnings from National Grid. They described Aberthaw as "an important bridge to the UK's vision of a renewable future" and crucial for balancing renewable technologies.

The spokesman acknowledged the situation was "regrettably a challenging time" for the more than 200 employees as staff structures undergo updates.

# Man Jailed for Brutal Rape and Sexual Assault in Guildford

A man has been sentenced to 18 years for a horrific attack on an 18-year-old woman in Guildford, Surrey.

Avan Mogridge, 32, of Church Street, Stamford, Lincolnshire, was convicted at Guildford Crown Court of dragging his victim into a wooded area off Parkway on the morning of October 22, 2016. He was found guilty of two counts of rape, two counts of sexual assault, and one count of making a threat to kill. He will remain on the sex offenders register for life.

The young woman was on her way to work when she was attacked at approximately 06:15 GMT. Mogridge pulled her into woodland adjacent to the pavement, where he held her down, threatened her life, and subjected her to a prolonged sexual assault lasting around an hour.

The attack was interrupted when two members of the public discovered the assault in progress. They immediately intervened and contacted police, leading to Mogridge's arrest at the scene.

In a victim impact statement read to the court, the survivor described the devastating effect the attack had on her life: "I used to be a bubbly and confident girl and enthusiastic about life and living it. I had dreams for my future. I am now traumatised, scared, drained and frightened. One day in October, because of one person, my life turned upside down and my dreams disappeared."

Detective Constable Tim Faltermeyer of Surrey Police praised the victim's courage throughout the judicial process and expressed gratitude to the couple who intervened. "This was a horrifying and traumatising hour-long attack on an innocent young woman," he said, adding that the case demonstrates how seriously Surrey Police treats sexual assault reports.

Mogridge will serve 14 years in custody followed by four years on licence.

# Stalker Michael Lane Jailed for Murder of Shana Grice After Police Failures

A man who murdered his ex-girlfriend after police fined her for wasting their time when she reported his stalking has been jailed for life.

Shana Grice, 19, was found with her throat cut in the smoke-filled bedroom of her Brighton flat in August 2016. Michael Lane, 27, had placed a tracker device on her car during a campaign of harassment, his trial heard.

Sentencing Lane, Mr Justice Green said he would serve a minimum of 25 years. The judge also criticised police over their contact with Miss Grice.

Lewes Crown Court was told Miss Grice had contacted police several times about Lane's unwanted attention. The jury heard that after making one complaint to Sussex Police about Lane, Miss Grice was issued with a fixed penalty notice for wasting police time because she did not disclose she had been in a relationship with him.

Mr Justice Green, criticising Sussex Police, said: "You jumped to conclusions. In other words, she was treated as the wrongdoer and having committed a criminal offence, and Michael Lane was treated as the victim.

"There was seemingly no appreciation on the part of those investigating that a young woman in a sexual relationship with a man could at one and the same time be vulnerable and at risk of serious harm," he said. "The police jumped to conclusions and Shana was stereotyped."

He said that after penalising Miss Grice for time-wasting, police then treated all further complaints by her with "scepticism". The judge said another consequence was that Lane felt police would not act if he continued his "obsessive stalking".

Miss Grice's mother, Sharon Grice, said Lane had been harassing, stalking and pressuring her daughter for more than a year.

In a statement following Lane's sentencing, she and Miss Grice's father Richard Green said their daughter would have still been alive if Sussex Police had acted on her complaints.

They said: "Shana had complained to the Sussex Police about his stalking her over five times but this was treated as being of low risk and she was given a fine for wasting police time."

They described Lane as a "dangerous and obsessive man" who had shown "arrogance and cowardice" by pleading not guilty and blaming others for his actions.

"He compounded this by relying on the wholly inadequate police assessment of risk to Shana to suggest he was no danger to her.

"We firmly believe Shana would be alive today if Sussex Police had acted to protect Shana on the many occasions she complained about Lane, rather than issue her with a fine for wasting police time."

The Independent Police Complaints Commission (IPCC) has begun an investigation.

# Syrian Jets Strike Kurdish Positions in Hassakeh City, Sparking Tensions

Syrian government warplanes have conducted air strikes against Kurdish security forces in the northeastern city of Hassakeh, marking a rare escalation between two parties that have largely avoided direct confrontation throughout Syria's five-year conflict.

The UK-based Syrian Observatory for Human Rights reported that Kurdish security forces had been targeted in the strikes. The Syrian military has not commented on the incident, but sources said the Kurds had seized government buildings in Hassakeh and the nearby city of Qamishli. Both sides were later reported to have agreed to a ceasefire, though tensions remain high.

However, the Kurdish Democratic Union Party's Popular Protection Units (YPG) militia said it would "not be silent" over what it called an act of flagrant aggression, warning that "every hand spattered with the blood of our people will be held to account."

Kurds made up between 7% and 10% of Syria's population of 24.5 million before the uprising against President Bashar al-Assad began five years ago. Although they were denied basic rights and suffered decades of political suppression by the Arab-led state, most Kurds avoided taking sides when protests swept the country in 2011.

When government forces withdrew from Kurdish areas to concentrate on fighting rebels elsewhere in mid-2012, Kurdish militias swiftly took control, led by the YPG. The Kurds later established autonomous administrations but allowed the government to retain footholds in Hassakeh and Qamishli.

Both sides have largely avoided clashes over the past four years, with the government focusing on fighting rebel groups and the Kurds battling so-called Islamic State. However, tensions have increased recently following the Kurds' unilateral declaration in March of a new federal region—a move rejected by both the government and opposition forces.

The latest clashes reportedly erupted in Hassakeh on Tuesday and spread to several locations around the city by Wednesday. A YPG spokesman said the air strikes hit Kurdish districts and positions of the Asayish, Kurdish security personnel. "There are martyrs and wounded," Redur Xelil told Reuters.

The YPG has emerged as a major fighting force in northern Syria over the past two years, becoming a key ally of the US-led coalition against Islamic State, complicating the delicate balance of power in the region.

# Rail Electrification Costs Could Double Due to Network Rail Failures, MPs Warn

Network Rail's severe planning and budgetary failures have caused significant delays to the Great Western Main Line electrification project and could see costs double, according to a damning report by the Public Accounts Committee (PAC).

The estimated cost of the ambitious electrification scheme increased dramatically between 2014 and 2015, rising from £1.6bn to £2.8bn - and that figure does not even include the planned extension to Swansea. Network Rail has acknowledged the problems and said changes have now been implemented to control costs.

The line from London to Oxford and Bristol Parkway was originally scheduled to be electrified in 2016, with the extension to Cardiff due in 2017 and Swansea in 2018. However, the project has faced repeated setbacks.

In June, UK Ministers "paused" the Midland Main Line and TransPennine route electrification schemes due to spiralling costs, though they maintained that the Great Western Main Line scheme remained "a top priority". Despite this assurance, the Public Accounts Committee heard in October that there was now no firm completion date and costs could reach £2.8bn.

The PAC report criticised the Office of Rail and Road (ORR), the industry regulator which calculated the original £1.6bn estimate, saying it had not been robust enough in scrutinising Network Rail's plans or ensuring the organisation addressed known risks.

The MPs warned that the delays will put public money at risk, as the Department for Transport will have to pay up to £400,000 per day to rent new trains that cannot be used until the line is electrified.

Committee chair Meg Hillier delivered a stinging verdict: "Network Rail has lost its grip on managing large infrastructure projects. The result is a twofold blow to taxpayers: delays in the delivery of promised improvements and a vastly bigger bill for delivering them."

Plaid Cymru MP Jonathan Edwards expressed "real concern that spiralling costs for compensation to the train operator will compromise when the scheme will be finished". He called for an end to the "profit-for-dividend model, which sees the shareholders of a private company benefiting from the inevitable disruption to a public infrastructure scheme".

An ORR spokesman acknowledged that escalating costs and delays were "unacceptable" and agreed a review of its role was "appropriate" following changes to Network Rail's ownership and finances. "We need to learn the lessons," he said.

Network Rail admitted the industry had been "overly ambitious" about what could be achieved with available funding. A spokesman said: "Our understanding of how best to plan and deliver major new electrification schemes was not good enough."

The organisation has now made "significant changes" to how it plans and delivers investment programmes, ensuring schemes progress only once reliable cost estimates can be established. Network Rail noted that electrifying the Great Western Main Line was "extremely complex" on an operational railway, with efforts to minimise disruption to line-side neighbours increasing costs.

The midfielder will miss Oxford's crucial fixtures before returning for their final push.

# KKK Group to Hold Rally at Historic Gettysburg Battlefield

A white supremacist organization will hold a controversial event on October 5 at the historic Gettysburg battlefield in Pennsylvania, where one of the Civil War's bloodiest battles took place in July 1863.

Park officials announced they are legally required to permit the gathering under US freedom of speech protections, despite the site's profound historical significance. The Battle of Gettysburg resulted in as many as 50,000 soldiers being killed or wounded during three days of fierce fighting.

The battlefield holds particular importance in American history as the location where President Abraham Lincoln delivered the Gettysburg Address in November 1863. During the cemetery dedication ceremony, Lincoln delivered what would become one of the most famous speeches in American history, envisioning "a new birth of freedom" emerging from the conflict between northern free states and southern slave-holding states.

The Ku Klux Klan, formed after the Civil War, has a notorious history of violence and is recognizable by its white-hooded ceremonial attire. Richard Preston, leader of the Confederate White Knights of the Ku Klux Klan, described his organization to local media as "white separatist," stating their goals include removing President Barack Obama from office and implementing stricter immigration policies.

"This is about America for Americans," Preston said. "The only thing we want is our country back."

The group previously conducted a membership rally at Maryland's Antietam battlefield earlier this month, another Civil War site known for being the war's deadliest single-day battle.

In an official statement, the National Park Service explained their obligation: "As custodians of land owned by the American people, the National Park Service has a responsibility to make that land available for exercising [free speech] rights."

Park officials confirmed they would work to protect park resources and ensure other visitors are not negatively impacted by the event.

# Welsh GPs Await Government Decision on Recruitment Incentives

General practitioners and health planners across Wales are anxiously awaiting the Welsh government's response to their appeals for support in addressing recruitment challenges in struggling areas.

However, senior medical figures have expressed reservations about the effectiveness of financial incentives as a solution. Professor John Bligh, head of Cardiff University's school of medicine, warned that such incentives have produced "variable results" in practice.

The recruitment crisis has become increasingly acute, with Hywel Dda University Health Board recently taking direct control of two GP practices after they failed to find replacements for retiring doctors. Catherine Davies, the health board's executive director for primary care, emphasised that career development opportunities were more important than financial inducements.

"It's about offering career development. We want to attract the brightest, the best, the most driven," Ms Davies said. "While it is a helpful tool to have, it's by no means the golden bullet answer."

Professor Bligh echoed these sentiments, stating: "I would much rather doctors chose to work in an area because that's where they wanted to work, as opposed to having a debt reduction scheme or some similar process."

The statistics paint a concerning picture. Whilst GP numbers in Wales have increased by 10% over the past decade to 2,006, the ageing population and mounting workload pressures are taking their toll. Dr Paul Myers, representing the Royal College of General Practitioners in Wales, noted that many experienced GPs "can't wait to finish."

The British Medical Association estimates Wales requires at least 200 trainee GPs annually to maintain adequate staffing levels. Yet the current quota of 136 training positions frequently goes unfilled.

Dr Ruth Hussey, chief medical officer for Wales, acknowledged recruitment difficulties in certain areas. A comprehensive primary care workforce plan, addressing sustainability challenges and potential solutions, will be published later this month.

The issue will be examined further on Eye on Wales, BBC Radio Wales, Sunday 5 July at 12:30 BST.

# Cyclist Forced Off M5 Motorway Given Conditional Discharge

A cyclist who rode on the M5 motorway has been given a conditional discharge after appearing at Exeter Magistrates' Court.

Balin Hobbs, 52, was cycling on the hard shoulder of the M5 when police intercepted him and forced him from the road into a service station near Cullompton, Devon. He pleaded guilty to riding a pedal cycle on a motorway and resisting arrest.

The court imposed a 12-month conditional discharge and ordered Hobbs to pay a £20 victim surcharge.

## Three-Day Journey From London

In a remarkable demonstration of his commitment, Hobbs cycled to Devon from London to attend the court hearing because it was against his spiritual beliefs to be driven in petrol or diesel vehicles. The journey took him three days, and he slept on the courtroom steps the night before his appearance.

The incident occurred on the afternoon of April 29 when Hobbs was heading towards Bristol on his bicycle. Police caught up with him on the M5, but he overtook the police car before officers forced him from the road two miles later at Junction 28, where he entered a service station.

The court heard that Hobbs wrestled with officers during his arrest as he was placed into a police van. "You are putting me in shackles for no reason," he protested.

## Defendant Represents Himself

Hobbs, whose address was given as Hennock, Devon, but who is currently living in London, represented himself in court. He admitted being on the motorway, stating: "I was definitely on the M5 on my bike." However, he claimed police had "intimidated, harassed and harangued" him, explaining: "I did not intend to cycle on the M5 but I had to try and find my way to Bristol and then London."

Hobbs, who had no previous convictions, mounted his bike following the hearing to begin his journey back to London.

# Nepal Bomb Blast Kills Two Near Government Offices

At least two people were killed and six others injured in a bomb explosion outside the Nepal Oil Corporation offices, officials confirmed on Wednesday.

The blast occurred at 1:25pm local time (0740 GMT) in an area near government buildings and the district court. Nepal police spokesman Binod Singh told Agence France Presse that authorities have cordoned off the site and deployed a special investigative team to gather evidence.

# German Man Arrested After Fatal Knife Attack at Bavarian Train Station

A knife attack at a train station in Bavaria has left one person dead and several others injured, including one victim in a life-threatening condition, German authorities confirmed Tuesday.

The incident occurred shortly before 05:00 local time (03:00 GMT) on Tuesday morning at Grafing station, located approximately 40 kilometers east of Munich. A 27-year-old German man attacked four people before being overpowered and arrested by police.

The suspect, identified as a German national apparently from the Hessen area of central Germany, attacked one victim on a train and others at various locations around the station, including outside the building. Footage from the scene showed bloody footprints on both a train and the station platform.

Bavarian Interior Minister Joachim Herrmann described the incident as a "terrible attack" and stated there were no indications the man was from a migrant background. He added, "So far there are no findings that are relevant for state security," though police initially said a political motive had not been ruled out.

Grafing's mayor, Angelika Obermayr, expressed shock at the violence. "The idea that people get on an S-Bahn train on a beautiful morning or do their paper round and then become victims of a maniac is terrible," she said.

# UK Government Announces Alan Turing Institute for Big Data Research

The British government has unveiled plans to establish the Alan Turing Institute, a major research facility dedicated to advancing big data analytics and algorithm research. The institute, named after the legendary World War Two code-breaker, will receive £42 million in government funding over five years.

Chancellor George Osborne announced the initiative during his Budget speech in the House of Commons, emphasizing Britain's ambition to become a global leader in data science. "I am determined that our country is going to out-compete, out-smart and out-do the rest of the world," he declared.

The institute will focus on developing new methods for collecting, organizing, and analyzing large datasets—capabilities that have become increasingly crucial in the modern economy. According to the government, big data applications can help businesses improve manufacturing processes, refine marketing strategies, and deliver more efficient services to customers.

Universities and other interested organizations will be invited to submit bids for the funding to establish and operate the facility. The competitive process aims to ensure the institute benefits from the strongest possible academic and research partnerships.

The timing of the announcement is particularly poignant, coming just months after Alan Turing received a posthumous royal pardon in December 2013. Turing, who lived in Osborne's constituency, made groundbreaking contributions to the Allied victory in World War Two through his work at Bletchley Park, where he helped crack the German Enigma code.

Tragically, Turing's life was cut short following his 1952 conviction for "gross indecency" after having a relationship with a 19-year-old man. He was chemically castrated as punishment and stripped of his security clearance, ending his vital code-breaking work. The conviction reflected the discriminatory laws of the era that criminalized homosexuality.

In his Budget speech, Chancellor Osborne paid tribute to Turing's legacy: "Alan Turing did more than almost any other single person to win the war, and was persecuted for his sexuality by the country he helped save. I am delighted that he has finally received a posthumous royal pardon."

While welcoming the initiative, the think tank Policy Exchange suggested that government itself should make greater use of big data technologies in public services.

# Northern Ireland's Changing Landscape: How Peace Transformed the Physical Scars of the Troubles

BBC News NI examines the dramatic physical transformations across Northern Ireland's landscape that mirror the region's journey from conflict to peace, through photographs of key landmarks from the Troubles era.

During the height of the Troubles, the simple act of shopping in Belfast city centre required passing through military-style security checkpoints. Royal Avenue, one of Belfast's premier shopping streets, was accessible only through security gates where police routinely searched bags for explosives. Today, those imposing barriers have been completely removed, allowing shoppers to move freely through the bustling commercial district.

The rural landscape of County Armagh once bristled with sangars – fortified observation posts that formed a crucial part of the British Army's defensive strategy. These structures were designed to control both the landscape and movement of people across Northern Ireland. One such installation, known as Watchtower Golf Five Zero or Borucki Sangar in Crossmaglen, was named after Private James R Borucki of 3 Para, who was killed by a remote-controlled bomb concealed in a bicycle.

The security infrastructure began to disappear rapidly following the IRA's decommissioning of weapons in 2005. Within weeks, demolition work commenced on watchtowers and military bases throughout the region. By August 2007, the British army's emergency operation in Northern Ireland officially ended, marking a significant milestone in the peace process.

Perhaps no structure symbolizes the Troubles more powerfully than the Maze prison. Constructed on a former airfield in the early 1970s, this sprawling complex housed paramilitary prisoners from both sides of the conflict. Demolition began in 2006, and nearly all the notorious H-blocks have since been razed. While controversial proposals to convert the site into a peace centre remain shelved, the location now serves as home to the Ulster Aviation Society and hosts the Balmoral Show, a cornerstone event in Northern Ireland's agricultural calendar.

In Derry's Bogside area, the iconic slogan "You are now entering Free Derry," painted on a gable wall in 1969, remains standing – though it's now the sole remnant of an entire row of terraced houses. The so-called normalisation process has seen numerous Army barracks and police stations demolished, including the prominent Andersonstown facility in west Belfast, which was torn down in 2005.

The border between Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland once meant lengthy queues and rigorous identity checks at what was termed the "hard border." Those delays are now largely a memory.

Street art has also evolved with the times. While hundreds of murals painted by Republicans and Loyalists during the Troubles still exist, new artwork celebrating contemporary life has emerged. One notable transformation saw a UFF mural replaced with a colourful patchwork quilt featuring words about women and their roles in families and communities.

The most visible remaining legacy of division are the "peace walls" – permanent barriers erected in the 1970s to separate Catholic and Protestant neighbourhoods in Belfast. The Crumlin Road wall became the first to be removed, and Northern Ireland's power-sharing government has committed to dismantling all peace walls by 2023, representing perhaps the final physical chapter in the region's journey toward reconciliation.

# Two Sam Mitchells: The Strangers Who Became Internet Famous

What started as a curious Facebook friend request has blossomed into one of 2017's most heartwarming internet stories, capturing global attention and proving that sometimes the best connections happen by pure chance.

It all began when Sam Mitchell, a 19-year-old plasterer from Tasmania, Australia, decided to reach out to a complete stranger on social media. The reason? They shared not just a first name, but a full name, including middle names.

"You may be wondering why I have sent you a friend request. I had to because we share the same name. Middle name as well. Good day sir," the Australian Sam wrote to his British namesake.

The 22-year-old London backpacker responded quickly with surprising news: "Yeah, and what is stranger is that I've just moved from the UK to Australia."

What happened next became the stuff of internet legend. Four hours after that initial exchange, Australian Sam and his friends, fueled by enthusiasm and beer, pooled their money together to purchase a plane ticket for British Sam to fly from Victoria to Tasmania for New Year's Eve, departing the very next morning.

"The idea of flying him down got tossed about," Australian Sam told the BBC. "The more beers we had, the better the idea became."

After collecting their new friend from Launceston Airport, the group organized the "Sam Mitchell Olympics," featuring competitions including a sack race using laundry buckets, taste-testing challenges, and beer pong. The festivities culminated at a bar where the two Sams rang in 2017 with a kiss at midnight.

"It was strictly platonic, but it was very nice for me knowing that he had chosen to kiss me at midnight, instead of his girlfriend who he has been with for four years," British Sam joked.

The story quickly went viral, with media outlets and websites around the world celebrating the unlikely friendship. Pedestrian called it "The games. The drinks. The mateship. The pash," while Mashable described it as an "extremely cute bromance." Techly declared it "a story for the digital age."

British Sam reflected on the phenomenon: "It seems to be a story that everyone is really enjoying amongst all the bad news over the past year."

Before parting ways, the friends made a promise to stay connected. They've even discussed organizing an international "Sam Mitchell Olympics" by next New Year's Eve, bringing together Sam Mitchells from around the world.

"We'll definitely have a drink and a few laughs at some point," British Sam said.

Police are investigating the movements of Anis Amri, the Berlin attack suspect, after discovering an unused Dutch SIM card in his backpack, according to French and Italian media reports.

The fact that Amri was able to travel across Europe despite being subject to a European arrest warrant has raised significant security concerns. Investigators are also working to determine whether the 24-year-old had accomplices.

# Cancer Patient's Dance Video Goes Viral, Inspiring Millions

A heartwarming video of a cancer patient dancing during chemotherapy has captured the hearts of more than two million viewers on Facebook and Instagram within just two days of being posted.

Praying for you. Thank you for inspiring others. Sharing with my Facebook friend that has breast cancer. She needs this."

# Northern Ireland Records One of Lowest Road Death Tolls in 80 Years

Northern Ireland has recorded one of its lowest road death tolls in eight decades, according to PSNI Superintendent David Moore, though officials stress that any loss of life on the roads remains unacceptable.

Speaking about the 2013 figures, Superintendent Moore emphasized that while the numbers represent significant progress, "one death is one too many." The statistics show 58 people lost their lives on Northern Ireland's roads during the year.

Environment Minister Mark H Durkan highlighted the critical importance of further reducing road deaths and serious injuries. "It only takes one bad choice to ruin a life. We all share the road, so we all share the responsibility to prevent these collisions," he said.

Minister Durkan announced the government's ambitious new target of zero road deaths, urging all road users to "commit to sharing the road to zero." This aligns with the Road to Zero safety campaign, launched in April 2013, which focuses on portraying the human impact of road deaths by highlighting the devastating effect on bereaved families.

Subject to executive approval, a Road Traffic Amendment Bill is planned for introduction in 2014. The legislation would introduce tougher measures against drink-driving and address the disproportionately high number of young people killed on the roads.

The 2013 statistics reveal that 24 victims were drivers, 12 were passengers, 10 were motorcyclists, seven were pedestrians, and three were cyclists. Tragically, two children died on Northern Ireland's roads last year, down from five in 2012.

Superintendent Moore delivered a straightforward message about road safety: "If everyone slowed down, did not drive after drinking or taking drugs, wore a seatbelt and drove with greater care and attention, then more people would live. It really is that simple."

Since records began in 1931, 14,626 people have died on Northern Ireland's roads, with 75,070 suffering serious injuries since 1971. Road deaths peaked in 1972 with 372 fatalities, while 2012 saw the lowest number on record.

# British Gymnasts Shine at European Championships with Multiple Medal Haul

British gymnasts delivered a stellar performance at the European Championships in Romania, with Ellie Downie and Courtney Tulloch leading a remarkable medal rush for the team.

# Mental Health Trust Deaths Rise Sparks Investigation Concerns

Norfolk & Suffolk Foundation Trust (NSFT) has been criticised for not doing enough to understand why patient deaths have risen dramatically, following an independent investigation.

The trust recorded 157 deaths in 2015-16, a significant increase from 88 deaths in 2012-13. The figures also showed 105 deaths in 2013-14.

Verita, commissioned by NSFT to investigate the rise, found that whilst the trust's investigation process meets national requirements, there is insufficient analysis to establish the underlying causes of these deaths.

The investigation revealed several areas requiring improvement. Internal reports into each death lacked consistency, support for bereaved families needed enhancement, and there was inadequate evidence that the trust's board had discussed each unexpected death thoroughly.

However, the report cautioned that data collection was not standardised across the UK, meaning "limited means for making meaningful comparisons" about death rates between different trusts.

Michael Scott, NSFT chief executive, emphasised patient safety as paramount, stating: "One avoidable death is one too many - that is why we commissioned this investigation." He confirmed that recommendations were "already, or will be, acted upon."

A separate report by NHS England's Nursing and Quality Directorate offered some reassurance, concluding that since April 2015, NSFT had reported deaths appropriately under the NHS Serious Incident framework and "investigated in a timely and appropriate manner."

The trust was originally commissioned the investigation after statistics showed it had a higher number of deaths than other mental health trusts in the UK. NSFT was placed in special measures by the Care Quality Commission in February 2015.

# Teenager Stabbed to Death in Hoxton Estate Attack

# Second Walker Dies on Ben Nevis Route in Same Week

The Lochaber team has recently reported dealing with an "exceptional amount" of call-outs in recent months, highlighting the increased pressure on mountain rescue services.

# Football clubs pay tribute to Daniel Wilkinson

Football clubs across Yorkshire and beyond are preparing to honour Daniel Wilkinson, the former Hull City youth player who tragically died following a medical emergency during a match.

The Evo-Stik Northern Premier League has requested all fixtures this week include a minute's silence in Wilkinson's memory.

Following his time at Hull, Wilkinson's career included stints at North Ferriby United, Scarborough Athletic, Harrogate Town, Goole Town, and Rushall Olympic before joining Shaw Lane this summer.

England striker Harry Kane has withdrawn from the squad for Tuesday's friendly against Spain at Wembley to continue his recovery from an ankle injury with Tottenham.

The 23-year-old has played just 73 minutes for Spurs since damaging his ankle against Sunderland on 18 September. He was an unused substitute for England's World Cup qualifying win over Scotland on Friday.

"The sessions we're going to do aren't what Harry needs at this time," said interim England boss Gareth Southgate. "It was never really my intention to start him in a game and I think it's important that he gets a different training programme to what we're going to follow over the next couple of days."

England have not called up a replacement for Kane, leaving Daniel Sturridge, Jamie Vardy, Marcus Rashford, Wayne Rooney and Theo Walcott as striker options.

Spain's visit to Wembley is the fourth and final fixture Southgate was given responsibility for, but with England still top of their 2018 World Cup qualifying group, he is heavy favourite to get the job on a full-time basis.

Kane, who scored his third league goal of the season on his return from injury in the north London derby against Arsenal, will be available for Spurs' fixture against West Ham on Saturday.

# Jersey Could Print More Banknotes to Boost Government Returns

The States of Jersey is considering increasing its banknote issuance limit from £100m to allow greater investment opportunities and boost government returns.

Russell Crowe, head of the States' treasury and investment management unit, explained that Jersey currently sells locally issued banknotes to high street banks in exchange for UK pounds. The proposed increase would enable the government to invest more sterling, significantly improving returns "from almost nothing".

Draft legislation is scheduled for presentation to the States in January, though Mr Crowe indicated this could be brought forward if Christmas shopping season demand increases substantially. Currency circulation is expected to rise from £83m to approximately £98m during the festive period.

Robert Kirkby from the Jersey Chamber of Commerce expressed surprise at continued cash usage in today's digital age. He noted it would be "interesting to see the impact" of younger "digital natives" on consumer spending habits in the coming year, suggesting traditional cash usage may decline as technology-savvy generations mature.

# Girl, 6, Bitten by Police Dog During Chase in Manchester

A six-year-old girl suffered multiple bite wounds after being attacked by a police dog during a pursuit in Newton Heath, Manchester, on Tuesday evening.

Phoebe Malone was playing outside with friends when she was bitten by the dog as officers chased a suspect who had fled from a stolen vehicle that crashed into a wall on Blackstone Walk.

Her mother, Sarah Malone, described the traumatic incident that occurred at approximately 19:55 BST. "My son saw what happened from the window and shouted: 'Mum, Phoebe's been bitten by a police dog,'" she said.

Mrs Malone rushed outside to find her daughter surrounded by police officers. "She was just sat on the chair and there was loads of police around her and she was just shaking," she recalled. "They asked me if I could get her in the house because she's cold, we need to get her warm."

The youngster sustained ten wounds, with two described as very deep. "They said if it was two inches more, it could have gone for her arteries, so it was serious," Mrs Malone explained. Phoebe was taken to hospital and kept overnight for observation.

Mrs Malone expressed her shock at the incident, saying: "I just can't believe it's happened to a little girl, let alone my daughter." She criticised the police decision to release the dog in an area where children were playing and called for a review of dog handler training procedures.

Greater Manchester Police confirmed the incident occurred during pursuit of a driver who abandoned a stolen Fiat Punto following the crash. A spokesman said: "A police dog was deployed to pursue the offender and during the chase a six-year-old girl was unfortunately bitten."

While police described the injuries as "not believed to be serious," the incident has been automatically referred to the force's Professional Standards Branch for investigation. GMP has launched an internal review into the circumstances surrounding the attack.

# Ronnie O'Sullivan Critical of Form Despite Recent Success

Five-time world champion Ronnie O'Sullivan has downplayed his recent tournament victories, claiming he has been "overachieving" despite winning his sixth Masters in January and his fourth Welsh Open title in February.

The snooker star made the surprising admission following his 4-3 defeat to world number 31 Michael Holt at Venue Cymru on Tuesday in the opening round of the World Grand Prix.

"I know I won the Welsh Open and the Masters but, the Masters, I only won it because everyone played pretty abysmal against me," O'Sullivan told BBC Radio Wales. "Winning two tournaments was a bit too much return for how I've been playing."

The 42-year-old was gracious in defeat, praising his opponent's performance. "Well done to Michael. He played a good match and deserved his win. He played better on the day," O'Sullivan said.

However, he remained critical of his own form, stating: "I wasn't really on form. I was pleased with how I stuck in there and tried to turn it around but my game just wasn't strong enough."

O'Sullivan suggested he has been "papering over the cracks" and acknowledged significant work is needed before the World Championship in Sheffield. "For me to do well at Sheffield, I'm going to need to find some consistency. I need to do some work between now and when Sheffield starts."

Holt, who produced breaks of 119 and 88 to secure victory, was delighted with his performance. "It's great to beat him. He's the best player," Holt said. "It's up there with one of my best wins."

Holt will face either Liang Wenbo or Graeme Dott in Thursday's second round.

# Boy, 12, Dies from Asthma After Hospital Discharge Failures

A 12-year-old boy died from an asthma attack just five days after being discharged from a London hospital where doctors failed to recognise the severity of his chronic condition, an inquest has concluded.

Michael Uriely was taken to the Royal Free Hospital in London twice within 24 hours in August 2015, but medical staff failed to diagnose his condition as chronic asthma despite clear warning signs. Coroner Dr Shirley Radcliffe stated that had Michael been given a high dose of steroids during his hospital stay, "it's unlikely he would have died."

The tragedy began on 18 August when Michael's parents brought him to hospital following a violent coughing and vomiting episode that left him struggling to breathe. He was released by 8pm that evening, but suffered another severe attack in the early hours and was rushed back to A&E.

Although he was kept overnight during the second admission, doctors failed to connect the two visits or recognise the seriousness of his condition. Two internal investigations also failed to identify his chronic asthma. Michael was discharged the following day and died from an acute asthma attack on 25 August.

Dr Radcliffe told Westminster Coroner's Court that "alarm bells should have begun to ring" when Michael was admitted twice within 24 hours. She said a "totally inadequate" medical history was obtained and staff missed a crucial opportunity to recognise the severity of his condition.

"The history and signs were there to be seen and understood, but sadly it wasn't recognised and he was discharged essentially on the same treatment he had been on," the coroner said.

Following the tragedy, the Royal Free Hospital appointed two specialist respiratory clinicians, opened a dedicated asthma clinic, and introduced a new strategy for treating children with asthma.

Michael's parents, Ayelet and Roy Uriely, described their son as "an extraordinary boy, both in personality and intelligence" who had been diagnosed with asthma at age two and began learning chess aged three. He "doted on his younger twin sisters, who adored him."

The inquest heard that since Michael's death, seven other children in London have died from asthma.

# Olympic Silver Medallist Becky James Retires from Cycling to Pursue Baking Career

**Media playback is not supported on this device**

Welsh cycling star Becky James has announced her retirement from professional cycling at the age of 25, revealing plans to transform her cake-making hobby into a full-time baking business.

The double world champion and Olympic silver medallist made the surprise announcement on Wednesday, 17 August, explaining that the decision crystallized just two weeks earlier. "I thought 'this is what I want to do' and it just clicked," James said. "I came to the decision it was the right thing for me to do and I'm feeling very excited."

James's cycling career reached its pinnacle in 2013 when she won world sprint and keirin titles, followed by silver medals in the same events at the 2016 Rio Olympics. Her Olympic success was particularly remarkable given she had endured a two-year battle with knee injuries and illness, during which she "gave up" her life for a year to concentrate on qualification.

Speaking on BBC Radio Wales' Good Morning Wales programme, the Abergavenny athlete revealed she had spent a year-long break after Rio contemplating her future. "It's been up and down," she explained. "I was on such a high after the Olympics, and then you have a massive dip and it's really hard to get out of that rut."

**Media playback is not supported on this device**

James acknowledged experiencing the "post-Olympic blues" that many elite athletes face after major competitions. "People say you have the post-Olympic blues and I definitely had that, but then I came out of that dip and I was half training and trying to figure out what to do," she said.

The announcement comes less than a month after James indicated she was looking forward to returning to competitive action. However, she insists the timing feels right and she harbours no regrets about her career.

"I kind of gave up my life the year before Rio because I wanted to give it everything," James reflected. "So I gave up my life, I shipped off my dog Lola to George (boyfriend, rugby player George North) and committed everything just to get to Rio."

Looking back on her achievements, James expressed contentment with her legacy. "I'm so happy with everything I've achieved in my career. I didn't feel like I was desperate to carry on to the next Olympics, I'm so chuffed with what I've done."

The decision to retire stemmed from James's realization that her heart was no longer fully committed to cycling. "If it wasn't what I wanted to do I knew in my heart I wouldn't achieve what I'd want to," she explained. "I couldn't do anything half-hearted - if I didn't really want to do it I knew I wouldn't achieve my goals and be the best I could be."
