# Arsenal Chief Gazidis Defends Transfer Strategy Despite Fan Criticism

Arsenal chief executive Ivan Gazidis has defended the club's cautious approach to the transfer market, insisting they cannot compete financially with wealthier rivals.

The club have made one major signing this summer, buying Granit Xhaka from Borussia Monchengladbach for £35m. "We can't afford to outgun competitors that have far more money. We have to be very careful, very selective," Gazidis told the New York Times.

The 51-year-old reiterated his support for manager Arsene Wenger, denying it is based on a "sense of nostalgia". Wenger has overseen 20 consecutive top-four finishes in the Premier League, but the last of his three league titles came in 2004. Some supporters protested at the end of last season, calling for a change in manager.

The Frenchman insisted that the club would "add what we missed" during the transfer window to close the 10-point gap to champions Leicester, but his pursuit of France forward Alexandre Lacazette has been frustrated with Lyon turning down a £29.3m offer.

Arsenal were the only club in Europe's top five leagues not to buy an outfield player in last season's summer transfer window. Goalkeeper Petr Cech, signed for £10m, was the only arrival, despite the club having almost £200m in cash reserves.

But Gazidis - who spoke of "an escalation in our financial firepower" in 2013 - claims that the Premier League's large and relatively evenly-shared television deal means money is less decisive than it was.

"The constraints within the Premier League are less and less about pure finances. More relatively important become things like how well you identify players, how well you develop players, what kind of sports science you have, your analytics, your psychology," he added. "All of these support areas around what we do increasingly become bigger differentiators."

# Brexit Uncertainty Persists Despite Rising Business Optimism

A survey by accountancy firm Deloitte has revealed a notable uptick in business confidence among finance directors, though Brexit concerns continue to dominate corporate thinking.

The fourth-quarter survey of 119 finance directors found that 27% were more optimistic about business prospects, up from just 16% in the third quarter. The improvement has been attributed to better-than-expected GDP growth figures.

However, the research showed that two-thirds of respondents remain anxious about Brexit's potential impact on their operations. Before the referendum, chief financial officers identified Brexit as their most significant business risk. Confidence plummeted to levels not seen since the global financial crisis immediately after the vote, prompting companies to curtail investment and spending.

"Since then the UK has proved more resilient than expected and talk of the UK falling into recession has abated," the Deloitte report noted.

Despite this resilience, most finance bosses anticipate continued economic uncertainty. Nearly half plan to adopt defensive measures, including spending cuts and building cash reserves. Approximately 48% expect slowdowns in hiring and merger and acquisition activity over the coming year.

# Osteopath Struck Off After Illegally Parking in Disabled Space During Court Hearing

An osteopath who brazenly parked in a disabled bay while admitting to blue badge fraud has been struck off the professional register.

Nigel Graham, 56, from Southbourne, was appearing at Southampton magistrates' court in June 2015 to plead guilty to parking offences when BBC cameras captured him committing another violation outside the very same courthouse. His illegally-parked vehicle received a parking ticket, which remained attached to the windscreen as the car was driven away.

Inside the courtroom, Graham admitted to five counts of false representation to avoid parking fines across Southampton, Bournemouth and Christchurch, plus one count of illegally using a disabled person's blue badge. The badge belonged to his deceased mother and had been fraudulently applied for after her death.

The magistrate described his actions as "despicable dishonest offences committed over a long period of time with no regard to bona fide blue badge holders." Graham received a suspended jail sentence and 120 hours of community service.

In May, the General Osteopathic Council ruled that Graham's conduct was fundamentally incompatible with professional practice. The council noted that he "continued to obfuscate" during their hearing and demonstrated "no insight into the seriousness of his criminality."

The "degree and persistence" of his dishonesty led to his removal from the osteopathic register, effectively ending his career in the profession.

# Man Convicted of Murdering Derby Student After "Fit" Comment

A man has been found guilty of murdering a 22-year-old student who was stabbed in the heart following a trivial comment about a woman's appearance in Derby city centre.

Haris Mohammed was convicted at Nottingham Crown Court of killing Tom Webb on 19 January after one of Mr Webb's friends remarked that a young woman was "fit". The jury rejected Mohammed's claims that he acted in self-defence after Mr Webb allegedly swung a bottle at him.

The trial heard that Mr Webb had been with two friends buying food and drink from Tesco in St Peter's Street when one of them made the comment about a passing woman being attractive. One of Mohammed's friends overheard the remark and informed him about it.

Mohammed, who had been in a nearby McDonald's, then decided to pursue Mr Webb's group as part of what prosecutor Michael Auty QC described as "an angry mob".

"Haris Mohammed had no need to become involved at all," Mr Auty told the court. "Neither he nor anyone else was in any danger. And yet he led others off in pursuit of Thomas Webb. He wanted confrontation. He wanted to demonstrate his power."

The prosecutor emphasised that Mr Webb was "entirely innocent" and Mohammed had no reason to attack him. "Haris Mohammed could have walked away at any time. He could have stayed in McDonald's," he said.

Mohammed used a butterfly knife with a blade approximately seven centimetres long to stab Mr Webb. The weapon was later recovered from within a McDonald's cup found in a raised planter where Mohammed had been in the immediate aftermath of the killing.

Outside court, Mr Webb's mother Rachel paid an emotional tribute to her son. "Tom was everything to me," she said. "I have no mother, I have no father, I have no other children, no husband or partner. Tom was my entire family and I'll miss him, but I have his memory."

When asked about Mohammed, she said simply: "I feel for his family."

Detective Chief Inspector Dave Cox, who led the investigation, said: "Not only is a family grieving for the loss of a young man, another family will now be grieving for a teenager who will undoubtedly spend a long time behind bars."

Mohammed will be sentenced on 29 July.

Wycombe Wanderers have completed the signing of former Bristol City defender Liam Fontaine on a permanent deal. The 31-year-old spent a decade at Ashton Gate, amassing 247 league appearances before moving to Aberdeen in 2014. After joining Wycombe last summer, he was loaned to Eastleigh in November.

The League Two club have also secured Huddersfield Town defender Will Boyle, 21, on a free transfer, with the youngster signing an 18-month contract at Adams Park.

# Tourist Convoy Ambushed in Afghanistan, Multiple Westerners Injured

A group of twelve Western tourists travelling through Afghanistan came under attack when their convoy was ambushed by Taliban militants, Afghan officials confirmed to the BBC on Thursday.

The tourists, comprising eight British nationals, three American citizens, and one German, were being escorted by Afghan army personnel en route to Herat city when attackers struck using small arms fire and an improvised explosive device in the Chesht-e-Sharif district.

Jailani Farhad, spokesman for Herat's governor, confirmed the attack details, though it remains unclear exactly who sustained injuries. Several tourists reportedly suffered light wounds and are receiving treatment. The German foreign ministry has stated that its citizen was unharmed in the assault.

A Taliban spokesman claimed responsibility for the ambush, highlighting the persistent dangers on Afghanistan's main roadways where militant attacks and kidnappings by the insurgent group remain frequent.

Afghan interior ministry spokesman Sediq Sediqqi told Tolo news that the group had been travelling from Bamiyan to Herat via Ghor province. The tourists are currently being held at an Italian military hospital in Herat city, with plans for evacuation to Kabul. Security reinforcements have been deployed to the attack site.

Despite the ongoing insurgency and warnings from Western governments against non-essential travel, Afghanistan continues to attract small numbers of adventure tourists annually. Bamiyan province, known for its ancient cultural sites and natural landscapes, remains particularly popular with foreign visitors organized through specialized adventure tourism companies.

# Gilbert Stages Dramatic Comeback to Defeat Carter at UK Championship

World number 21 David Gilbert produced a remarkable recovery to defeat two-time World Championship runner-up Ali Carter 6-5 in a thrilling encounter at the UK Championship.

The Derby player found himself trailing 3-0 in what looked set to be an early exit from the tournament. However, Gilbert turned the match around with an impressive display of scoring, including a half-century and two century breaks, followed by another 50 to establish a 5-3 advantage.

"It was looking like it would be an early bath," admitted the 35-year-old Gilbert. "But I got a bit lucky going in at 3-1 down and then I actually started playing really well. I started off and was useless. Maybe I was too chilled."

The decisive frame proved to be a tense affair, with Carter missing several opportunities early on. Gilbert capitalised on his opponent's errors, clearing to the black in what he described as "probably the best clearance I have ever made."

Gilbert, who has already secured £15,000 for his best UK Championship run, will face either Ding Junhui or Jamie Jones in the last 16.

"I was a bit lucky, but I will take it. It's a big win for me," Gilbert said. "Happy days."

# Millions of Energy Customers Could Save Hundreds by Switching Tariffs

More than 1.7 million Npower customers could save as much as £261 annually simply by switching to a different tariff with the same supplier, according to new figures released by energy regulator Ofgem.

The data reveals the extent to which British households are overpaying for their energy. As many as 6.6 million British Gas customers could save £129 a year by moving to cheaper deals, though British Gas disputes this figure, claiming that recent price changes mean the actual saving is now £43.

The figures also expose a troubling trend: the vast majority of customers with some suppliers remain on expensive standard variable tariffs. SSE has the highest proportion, with 91% of its customers on standard variable tariffs, compared to just 9% at First Utility.

Across the UK as a whole, 66% of households remain on standard tariffs, which are typically more expensive than fixed-rate deals. This has sparked controversy within the industry and drawn criticism from consumer advocates.

However, Npower has challenged the £261 savings claim, arguing that fixed-price deals are usually limited to a certain number of customers. Once the quota is reached, the deal is withdrawn, meaning many customers may not actually be able to access the advertised savings.

The revelations come after business and energy secretary Greg Clark met with energy suppliers last month amid claims that companies were profiteering from customers on standard variable tariffs. While the industry has denied these accusations, three of the biggest suppliers have frozen their tariffs through winter in response to public pressure.

"Millions of people across Britain continue to pay too much for their energy," said Mr Clark. "The measures announced today are a positive step to help more people benefit from increased choice and competition."

Citizens Advice welcomed the comparison table but called for energy companies to do more proactively. "We'd like to see energy companies do more off their own back to help customers who are on a low income, like moving them to a cheaper deal," said Gillian Guy, chief executive of Citizens Advice.

Meanwhile, the Competition and Markets Authority has confirmed plans to assist the 10 million households that have remained on standard tariffs for more than three years. From next year, suppliers must inform Ofgem which customers haven't switched tariffs. With customer consent, they will receive details of better deals to encourage switching.

# FTSE 100 Slips as Rolls-Royce Tumbles on Heavy Losses

London's benchmark FTSE 100 index closed marginally lower on Thursday, dropping 10.36 points, or 0.14%, to finish at 7,286.56.

Travel firm Tui led the gainers, surging 5.27% after reporting narrowed first-quarter losses. The company's performance was driven by robust UK bookings, which jumped 10% in volume compared to the previous year. RBS and Capita also posted solid gains.

However, Rolls-Royce suffered the steepest decline, plummeting 3.99% after announcing a massive pre-tax loss of £4.6bn. The aerospace giant was weighed down by costs from a bribery settlement and currency-related contracts impacted by sterling's depreciation following the Brexit referendum.

In currency markets, the pound weakened 0.49% against the dollar to $1.2464 and fell 0.25% versus the euro to 1.1790 euros.

# Court of Appeal Dismisses Challenge to £85 Car Park Overstay Charge

A motorist who challenged an £85 parking fine for overstaying a two-hour limit has lost his case at the Court of Appeal, in a decision that could have significant implications for private parking enforcement across the UK.

Barry Beavis, 48, from Chelmsford, received the charge letter from car park operator ParkingEye after exceeding the time limit at a facility in Chelmsford in April 2013. He refused to pay, arguing the charge was excessive and unfair.

The case progressed through the courts after Mr Beavis received a court summons and saw the charge increase to £150. Last May, Cambridge County Court ruled the £85 charge was lawful and did not breach the Unfair Terms in Consumer Contracts Regulations.

Mr Beavis subsequently appealed the county court decision, but three Court of Appeal judges unanimously dismissed his challenge. They concluded the amount charged "is not extravagant or unconscionable".

ParkingEye defended the charges as "a commercially-justified deterrent" necessary to discourage motorists from over-staying at the site, which is located close to the railway station and law courts.

Following the judgment, Mr Beavis expressed his frustration, stating: "I am absolutely furious that they have not upheld the law as it stands but have created new law." He is now considering taking his case to the Supreme Court, the highest court in the land.

Prof Stephen Glaister, director of the RAC Foundation, called the outcome "deeply frustrating" for the motorist.

However, the British Parking Association welcomed the court's decision, saying it "provided clarity on the use of contract law for parking on private land". The association stated it would not expect members to increase charges following the judgment, noting that "only a small minority of motorists fall foul of such conditions".

The ruling confirms that current private parking charges are considered lawful and reasonable under existing regulations.

# Fox Hunting Debate Reignites in House of Lords

A heated debate over fox hunting has erupted in the House of Lords, with prominent figures clashing over animal welfare and the future of the controversial ban.

Lord Mancroft, chairman of the Council of Hunting Associations, sparked controversy by claiming that hunting organizations are "the only two organisations clearly which have any interest in the welfare of the animals concerned." He made the remark during a Lords debate on the fox hunting ban, which the government has now shelved for at least two years.

The Hunting Act, introduced by Tony Blair's Labour government in 2004, prohibits the use of dogs to hunt foxes and wild mammals in England and Wales. The law has remained a contentious issue, dividing politicians and the public alike.

Labour's Baroness Jones strongly opposed any attempts to overturn the ban, calling fox hunting "cruel, inhumane and ineffective." She noted that Prime Minister Theresa May's support for hunting during the election campaign had proved "massively unpopular on the doorstep."

Lord Mancroft defended his position by arguing that Baroness Jones showed "absolutely no interest in the welfare of the quarry species who were supposedly the object of this Act." He claimed that populations of both foxes and hares have declined since the hunting ban was implemented.

Before the general election, a leaked email from Lord Mancroft suggested that Mrs. May's poll lead represented "the chance we have been waiting for" to overturn the ban. However, following the Conservatives' loss of their Commons majority, the government confirmed it would not bring forward a vote during this Parliamentary session.

Government spokeswoman Baroness Vere acknowledged the passionate views on both sides. She shared her experience of attending her first hunt earlier this year, expressing amazement at the diversity of participants "from all walks of life."

Labour peer Baroness Mallalieu, president of the Countryside Alliance, criticized current legal fox control methods, including snaring and night shooting. She urged the government to develop "a method which is stable, which is acceptable on both sides of the argument and which puts animal welfare at the forefront."

Baroness Vere responded that no control methods were "without difficulty," adding that the entire framework of wildlife legislation would be reviewed once Britain leaves the EU and regains control of such laws.

# Rangers striker Martyn Waghorn targets Scottish Cup semi-final return

Rangers striker Martyn Waghorn is targeting a return to action in next month's Scottish Cup semi-final against Celtic after making progress in his recovery from a knee injury.

The 26-year-old has been sidelined since mid-February but remains hopeful of featuring in the crucial Old Firm clash at Hampden Park.

"I'll push myself but I have to be cautious too," Waghorn told Rangers' website. "If everything goes well then there is a chance I could be involved against Celtic but that is just if everything goes spot-on."

The former Wigan Athletic forward has been in prolific form this season, netting 28 goals for the Scottish Championship leaders, including four in the cup competition. His last appearance came in the fifth-round replay victory over Kilmarnock, where he scored a penalty before sustaining the injury.

"The last six or so weeks have been tough, playing Dundee in the cup game and then knowing we have Celtic coming up - hopefully I can get fit and in contention for that," he added.

Waghorn emphasized the importance of being fully fit before returning to action. "I have to be 100 per cent ready - I want to push myself but I don't want to push myself too far in case we get further on in the competition or rule myself out of the latter stages of the season.

"I'm a little bit ahead of schedule. It is going well but I don't want to say it is going great until I can go outside because I haven't tested it as much, we'll know more in the next week to 10 days about whether I am ready to come back."

# Lincoln City Edge Closer to National League Title Despite Red Card Drama

Lincoln City moved three points clear at the top of the National League with a hard-fought 1-0 victory over relegation-threatened Chester FC in a dramatic encounter marred by two red cards and touchline confrontations.

Harry Anderson emerged as the unlikely hero, scoring just six minutes after replacing the injured Lee Angol. The substitute pounced on a hard, low cross from the left that broke fortuitously, slotting home from close range to secure three precious points for Danny Cowley's side.

The victory gives Lincoln breathing space over second-placed Tranmere Rovers, who suffered a home defeat to Forest Green, but it came at a cost. The Imps were forced to play the final 15 minutes with ten men after substitute Alan Power was shown a straight red card for a late challenge on Chester captain Luke George, remarkably just three minutes after entering the fray.

The drama intensified during seven minutes of added time when Chester's Kane Richards received his marching orders for a late tackle on Bradley Wood. The incident sparked an angry confrontation between both benches, highlighting the tension of a match with huge implications at both ends of the table.

Chester, desperately needing points to secure their National League status, proved stubborn opponents and could count themselves unfortunate not to take something from the match. Before Anderson's decisive strike, the visitors created several promising opportunities. Wade Joyce and James Alabi both unleashed powerful drives that sailed narrowly over the crossbar, while Richards found himself clean through on goal only to be thwarted by a superb recovery tackle from Sean Raggett.

Lincoln's attacking threat in the first half came primarily through Nathan Arnold and Elliott Whitehouse, though both fired over from promising positions. Paul Farman was relatively untroubled until the break, but the second half proved far more challenging for the Lincoln goalkeeper.

After the interval, Chester pressed hard for an equalizer. Alabi's low left-footed effort was cleared off the line, and the visitors felt aggrieved when appeals for a penalty were waved away after Richards went down under Alex Woodyard's challenge. Farman produced the save of the match to deny Elliott Durrell's spectacular long-range drive, clawing the ball away brilliantly.

The match saw numerous bookings, with Luke Waterfall, Alex Woodyard, and Paul Farman cautioned for Lincoln, while Ryan Lloyd, Elliott Durrell, and Lucas Dawson went into the referee's notebook for Chester.

Despite the challenging circumstances, Lincoln's resilience ensures they maintain pole position in the race for automatic promotion with the finish line now firmly in sight.

# HMRC Seeks NHS Records Access to Identify Scottish Taxpayers

HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) is seeking access to NHS records as it struggles to identify taxpayers eligible for Scotland's new income tax regime, prompting Labour to demand both governments take control of the situation.

The tax collection agency has admitted that preparations for implementing the Scottish Rate of Income Tax (SRIT) have "proved more complex than was initially anticipated," leading to an increased risk rating for the project. However, HMRC maintains the initiative remains "on track for successful delivery."

From April 2016, the Scottish Parliament will gain the power to set income tax rates for the first time in its history. The new system will only apply to those who spend most of the tax year resident in Scotland, requiring HMRC to accurately identify Scottish taxpayers from among the wider UK population.

In a letter to the Commons public accounts committee dated 16 January, HMRC's tax assurance commissioner Edward Troup acknowledged the challenges facing the project. The agency has raised concerns that some individuals may attempt to dodge tax by falsifying their main residence when rates differ between Scotland and the rest of the UK.

To combat this potential abuse and improve accuracy, HMRC wants to cross-reference its data with NHS records. The Scottish government is currently consulting on whether to grant this access, with the consultation period running until 25 February. No decision has yet been taken on the matter.

Shadow Scottish Secretary Margaret Curran criticised both governments' handling of the situation, stating: "This letter confirms what Scottish Labour has been saying all along - that HMRC and the Scottish government are struggling to identify all Scottish taxpayers. Both our governments need to get a serious grip of this."

The Scottish government has distanced itself from responsibility, stating that administering the tax is a matter for the UK government and HMRC.

Despite the challenges, there has been some positive news regarding costs. HMRC has revised downwards its estimated expenditure for setting up the new tax from £40-45 million to £35-40 million.

As an alternative data source, HMRC has also suggested using the electoral register to identify Scottish residents. The agency noted that voter registration is particularly high following last year's independence referendum. However, this proposal may prove controversial, as the Scottish government previously strongly objected when local authorities suggested using electoral data to pursue poll tax arrears.

Mr Troup emphasised the agency's thorough approach, stating: "We need to be sure that we have thoroughly explored all the available options for improving the accuracy of information we hold."

A Scottish government spokesman confirmed: "A consultation is ongoing as to whether HMRC should be allowed administrative data to assist their identification of where people should pay tax."

# Trouble at Prison Near Doncaster Quelled Overnight

A disturbance involving a "small number" of inmates on one wing at a Category C prison near Doncaster has been brought under control overnight, the Prison Service confirmed.

One prisoner sustained injuries during the incident but did not require hospital treatment. No staff members were harmed.

The facility, which houses approximately 1,000 inmates, was found to have "high" levels of violence during HM Inspectorate of Prisons' latest inspection in February.

Notable inmates reportedly include former England footballer Adam Johnson, who is serving a six-year sentence for grooming and engaging in sexual activity with a 15-year-old girl.

# Hanson Academy Sends Hundreds of Students Home Over Uniform Policy

Hanson Academy has sent home more than 240 pupils over three days as head teacher Elizabeth Churton's strict uniform policy crackdown continues.

The Bradford school turned away 152 students on Tuesday, followed by 63 on Wednesday and 33 on Thursday during the ongoing enforcement campaign. The controversial policy has sparked a divided response from parents on the school's Facebook page.

Students are being sent home for various uniform infractions, including wearing hoop earrings, having two or more earrings per ear, or sporting patterned trousers. The rules also prohibit unnatural hair colours and ban students from wearing jumpers, jackets or coats indoors. Strict regulations also apply to footwear.

Single parent Diane Hickey said her 13-year-old daughter was sent home twice – on both Tuesday and Wednesday – for wearing black pumps, shoes the girl has worn to school for the past two years.

"I'm not buying her a new pair of shoes. I'm a single parent. I can't afford a new pair of shoes," Miss Hickey said. "I don't think it's fair she's been sent home twice. She's embarrassed we can't afford new footwear."

Miss Hickey added: "I think it's ridiculous. I am keeping her home today because what's the point in making her walk to school if she's going to be sent home?"

In a statement, Mrs Churton defended the policy, explaining that students with uniform issues that could be resolved were sent home to rectify them, with parents contacted.

"As forewarned, some students were sent home for this reason," she said. "They were sent home to change and the majority rectified this immediately and returned to school ready to learn."

The principal emphasized that rules are an important part of preparing students for "adult life."

# Harper Lee Secures Future of To Kill a Mockingbird Play in Monroeville

The beloved stage adaptation of To Kill a Mockingbird will continue to be performed in its spiritual home of Monroeville, Alabama, after author Harper Lee intervened to save the production.

The announcement comes after Dramatic Publishing, the licensing firm that previously controlled the performance rights, chose not to extend its agreement for the production. Lee responded by establishing the Mockingbird Company, which will take over producing the play starting in 2016, with proceeds benefiting local communities.

Dramatic Publishing expressed its support on Facebook, stating it was "thrilled" with the arrangement. "We are also happy to announce that the play will be performed by Mockingbird Players, who have acted this American classic so well for so long," the company wrote. "We believe that this is the best way (from the stage) to celebrate Ms Lee's masterpiece throughout the greater Monroeville area."

The decision has been warmly welcomed by the community. A Facebook campaign called Save Monroeville's To Kill a Mockingbird play had been actively lobbying for the production's continuation. Supporter Johnny Johnson commented: "Thank you Miss Harper Lee, you have made Monroe County proud," while Meagan McDonald added: "Thank you for working towards an agreement!! What a blessing for Monroeville!!"

The Monroe County Heritage Museum has staged the show for years, though its relationship with Lee has been complicated. In 2013, the 88-year-old author sued the museum over unauthorised merchandise sales, following the museum's opposition to her federal trademark application. That dispute has since been resolved.

Current performances are completely sold out through next month, driven partly by anticipation surrounding Lee's upcoming second novel, Go Set a Watchman. The book, written in the 1950s but shelved on editorial advice, will be published on 14 July, marking Lee's first release since the 1960s.

To Kill a Mockingbird, published in July 1960, has sold over 40 million copies worldwide, won the Pulitzer Prize, and inspired an Oscar-winning film starring Gregory Peck. The novel's exploration of race, class, and innocence continues to resonate with audiences globally.

# Ofcom Investigates Britain's Got Talent Over Dog-Swap Controversy

Broadcasting regulator Ofcom has launched an investigation into ITV's Britain's Got Talent after receiving 1,150 complaints about the show's finale.

The controversy centres on dog trainer Jules O'Dwyer, who used a second dog called Chase to perform a tightrope walk because her Border Collie, Matisse, was afraid of heights. The switch was not made clear to viewers during the broadcast.

ITV boss Peter Fincham subsequently admitted the programme should have been transparent about using a different dog.

"We've opened an investigation to determine whether viewers of ITV's Britain's Got Talent final, who may have paid money to vote, were misled about the competition," an Ofcom spokesman confirmed.

O'Dwyer and Matisse narrowly won the final, watched by 13 million people, securing a £250,000 prize and a Royal Variety Performance spot.

# ICC Chairman Shashank Manohar Resigns After Less Than a Year

Shashank Manohar has resigned as chairman of the International Cricket Council (ICC) after less than a year in the role.

The 59-year-old was elected as the body's first independent chairman on a two-year term in May last year. Manohar, a two-time president of the Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI), said the decision was because of personal reasons.

"I hope the ICC achieves greater heights in future," the Indian added.

The ICC confirmed it had received Manohar's resignation on Wednesday, adding that it would "assess the situation" before making any further announcements.

Manohar had previously sought to reduce the power of England, Australia and India - the so-called Big Three - on the ICC's decision-making executive committee.

Speaking in February 2016, he stated: "No member of the ICC is bigger than the other."

A final decision on a new governance structure was due to be taken at a meeting in April.

# Rare European Wolf Cubs Filmed Playing at Highland Wildlife Park

Adorable European Wolf cubs, born just four weeks ago, have been captured on camera playing at the Highland Wildlife Park in a heartwarming display that has delighted staff and conservationists alike.

The arrival of the cubs came as an unexpected surprise to zookeepers, as their parents successfully bred only two months after arriving at the facility. Staff had anticipated the pair would not breed until next year at the earliest, as part of the carefully managed European breeding programme.

The mother, Aurora, was born at the Highland Wildlife Park in 2013, while the male, Loki, was born in 2012 in the Netherlands. Despite being first-time parents, the pair have adapted remarkably well to their new roles.

Keeper Kellie Ross, who cares for the wolves, described the magical moment she witnessed the cubs playing. "We have set up cameras with motion sensors and I was down changing the memory card," she explained. "I was lucky enough to be there at the same time the cubs were out playing."

Ross expressed feeling privileged that the parents trusted staff enough to allow the siblings to remain outside the den while she was nearby. "It is lovely to see them playing like normal puppies. It really is something special," she said.

Bradley Yule, the zoo's network manager, emphasized the significance of the birth. "This is an important event in the role of our zoo and these pups will enhance the population," he stated. "They will also serve as ambassadors to help reduce the pressure on wild environments where these wolves come from."

The cubs, which have yet to be named, represent hope for the conservation of European Wolves. Loki has been observed feeding and sharing food with Aurora, who continues to carefully rear her young in their den.

# Carlisle United Sign Former Chelsea Youth Player Isaiah Wright

Carlisle United have completed the signing of 20-year-old defender Isaiah Wright on a short-term contract, following his departure from Chelsea after a decade with the Premier League club.

Wright, who joined Chelsea's academy at the age of 10, signed his first professional deal with the Blues in 2013. However, persistent injuries significantly impeded his progression into the first team, with the full-back's appearances limited to youth team, reserve, and under-21 fixtures.

"It's very exciting for me, it's been a long journey since I left Chelsea," Wright told BBC Radio Cumbria. "I'm excited and in love with the fans and the club already."

The Waltham Forest-born player has been on trial at Brunton Park for some time and is joined by Alexander McQueen, who has also returned to the club on a short-term deal.

Reflecting on leaving Chelsea, Wright admitted: "It was quite upsetting because it was a big part of my life for so long. That said, I was also ready to take the next step and start pushing for first-team football because that's my end goal."

# Parents Reunited with Daughter After False Abuse Allegations Seek to Move On

Craig Stillwell and Carla Andrews are determined to rebuild their lives after a harrowing ordeal that saw their daughter Effie removed from their care for nearly eight months over false allegations of child abuse.

The Aylesbury couple, both 23, were accused of causing grievous bodily harm to their infant daughter after she collapsed last August at five months old. Mr Stillwell was arrested at Stoke Mandeville Hospital, and Effie was immediately placed into foster care while Buckinghamshire County Council pursued a case in family court to secure permanent local authority care.

For months, the devastated parents were limited to seeing their daughter just three times weekly for 90-minute supervised visits at a contact centre. However, the council's case collapsed when medical experts discovered Effie suffered from Ehlers-Danlos syndrome type IV, a rare genetic condition that causes易 bruising and can mimic signs of physical abuse.

Despite being cleared and having Effie returned to their care, the couple say they have not received an apology from the council. They report that social workers have visited their home twice since their daughter's return, causing ongoing distress.

"I want to move on with Effie without having any more interference," said Miss Andrews. "I want to shut the door and tell them to leave us alone to get on with our lives because we have proved our innocence."

Mr Stillwell echoed his partner's frustration, expressing their desire to simply resume normal family life.

Buckinghamshire County Council declined to comment on the specific case but stated that social care decisions "draw evidence from multiple sources" and follow proper assessment procedures.

The family now hopes to put this traumatic chapter behind them and focus on Effie's ongoing medical needs.

# Police Investigate "Body in Boot" Report That Turned Out to Be Dog Duvet

A Norfolk man received an unexpected visit from police after a concerned member of the public mistook a duvet in his car boot for a wrapped body.

Chris Richmond, 30, was going about his daily business at a petrol station in Fakenham, Norfolk, when another customer spotted what they believed to be suspicious circumstances. The distressed witness contacted police, reporting they had seen what appeared to be a body wrapped in a duvet in the boot of Mr Richmond's Land Rover Freelander.

Officers attended Mr Richmond's home near Wells-next-the-Sea to investigate the report. Upon inspection, they quickly discovered the "body" was actually bedding for his pet dogs that he keeps in the vehicle.

Mr Richmond, who had been filling cans for his strimmer and refuelling his car at the station, said his boot had been open throughout his visit. He recalled that another vehicle had pulled in behind him during the incident.

"The police officer did say himself it was a bit of an odd call," Mr Richmond told the Eastern Daily Press. "I'm not criticising them for doing their job. If I was daft enough to go out with a dead body in my car in the middle of the day, they could have got a good lead."

While initially annoyed by the questioning, Mr Richmond has since come to appreciate the humorous side of the misunderstanding.

Norfolk Police confirmed they received the call at 13:55 BST regarding suspicious circumstances. After visiting the registered owner's address and examining the dog bed in the boot, officers determined no further action was necessary.

The incident serves as a reminder of the importance of public vigilance, even when suspicions prove unfounded.

# Florida Woman Uses Scent Preservation Kit to Help Find Missing Relative

A Florida woman's forward-thinking preparation paid off when she used a two-and-a-half-year-old scent sample to help locate a missing family member, according to the Citrus County Sheriff's Office.

The anonymous woman had stored the scent using a specialist preservation kit back in January 2015. These kits can preserve a person's unique scent for up to seven years, making them valuable tools in missing person investigations.

Scent preservation works by rubbing a pad on a person's underarm and sealing it in a sterile jar. Police dogs can then smell the sample before beginning their search. Manufacturers claim these kits are more effective than using clothing because they contain pure scent, uncontaminated by environmental odors or smells from other people.

Dogs possess a far superior sense of smell compared to humans, and trained police dogs can detect drugs, locate people, and even find corpses. Various police forces worldwide, including those in China and Germany, maintain databases of scent samples from suspects and crime scenes.

However, the technique has critics. A 2006 study in New South Wales, Australia, found that only 25 percent of people identified by sniffer dogs actually carried drugs when searched.

Despite these concerns, the Florida case ended successfully. The missing person was located, and the helpful police dog celebrated with a well-deserved ice cream, the Sheriff's Office announced on Facebook.

# Man in Critical Condition After Dumfries Assault

Police are investigating a serious assault in Dumfries after a man sustained critical head injuries early Saturday morning.

Officers were called to Queensberry Street at approximately 01:15 on Saturday. The victim was initially taken to Dumfries and Galloway Royal Infirmary before being transferred to the Western General Infirmary in Edinburgh, where he remains in critical condition with a head injury.

Detective Chief Inspector Colin Burnie said: "Our investigation is ongoing to establish the circumstances surrounding this incident and officers are currently carrying out door-to-door inquiries and studying CCTV footage to gather more information on this incident and whoever is responsible."

# Crusaders Cruise Into Irish Cup Semi-Final with Comfortable Victory Over Carrick

Crusaders booked their place in the Irish Cup semi-final with a dominant 3-0 victory over Carrick Rangers, with Paul Heatley starring in a man-of-the-match performance at Seaview.

The Crues will face Glenavon in the last four at Windsor Park on 2 April, setting up what promises to be an intriguing encounter.

Heatley opened the scoring in spectacular fashion, finding the net with a looping header over debutant goalkeeper Ryan Morrell in the 16th minute after the ball was deflected into his path from Jordan Forsythe's left-foot cross. He then turned provider on 33 minutes, delivering a low cross from the right which Colin O'Carroll tapped home from six yards out for the second.

Heatley completed his impressive display eight minutes after the break with a cool right-foot finish that slid past Morrell and went in off the post to make it 3-0.

Carrick's afternoon went from bad to worse as they had Aaron Smyth and Brian McCaul dismissed. Smyth received a straight red card for fouling Heatley, denying him a clear goalscoring opportunity to complete his hat-trick. Midfielder McCaul was shown a second yellow card to compound a disappointing day for the struggling Premiership side.

Crusaders manager Stephen Baxter was respectful of their semi-final opponents: "The last time we met Glenavon in a semi-final, we lost, so we will hope to reverse that this time around. They are a fabulous team who defend well and have goal threats all over the park. It will be a great occasion for everyone, played on a beautiful surface."

# Brexit: Northern Ireland businesses face "enormous paperwork" if UK leaves customs union

A leading European law expert has warned that Northern Ireland businesses could face "an enormous amount of paperwork" depending on the UK's decision on customs union membership after Brexit.

Professor Michael Dougan made the remarks as the UK prepares to decide whether to remain in the EU customs union following its departure from the European Union. Staying in the union would prevent the UK from negotiating independent trade agreements, but leaving would subject goods moving between the UK and EU to customs procedures and likely tariffs.

The decision carries particular significance for Northern Ireland, as departure from the customs union would transform the Irish border into a customs frontier, potentially creating substantial challenges for cross-border trade.

## Customs enforcement inevitable

Speaking to the Northern Ireland Affairs Committee, Professor Dougan, an expert at the University of Liverpool, stated that some form of customs enforcement would be unavoidable. Beyond tariffs, he emphasized that customs borders involve "regulatory enforcement" covering product standards and other requirements.

"There does have to be a frontier, it does have to involve checks and does have to involve pre and post border formalities," he told the committee.

Dr Stephanie Reynolds, also from the University of Liverpool, explained that EU customs controls rely on an "electronic risk management system" identifying "high risk" cargo before border arrival. Modern customs operations have increasingly moved toward paperless systems, with most declarations filed electronically.

She noted that Authorised Economic Operator status provides expedited access to simplified procedures and allows some shipments to be 'fast-tracked.' Most cargo inspections now use "non-intrusive methods" such as x-rays.

## Nordic model examined

The experts cited the Norway-Sweden border as an example of a "well-managed, fully co-operative" frontier, despite Sweden's customs union membership and Norway's non-membership.

BBC Northern Ireland has visited the main Nordic crossing to assess traffic and business impacts and explore potential lessons for Northern Ireland. Reports on the subject are being broadcast across all BBC platforms, including The View on BBC One Northern Ireland at 22:45 GMT Thursday.

# Scottish Film-maker Champions Wild Swimming in Cold Highland Waters

A passionate film-maker and photographer is inspiring others to embrace wild swimming in Scotland's icy waters through his captivating documentaries and social media presence.

Calum Maclean, based in Inverness, has built a following by documenting his adventures swimming in rivers, lochs and seas across Scotland. His work, shared online and through BBC The Social, showcases the raw beauty and exhilaration of cold-water swimming in some of the country's most spectacular locations.

His dedication to exploring new swimming spots is now the focus of a television series on BBC Alba, the Gaelic language channel. "Into the Water" (Dhan Uisge) features Mr Maclean at stunning locations throughout the Highlands, islands and Argyll, including the dramatic waters of Loch Maree in Torridon, the remote beaches of Sanna in Ardnamurchan, and a challenging swim between Seil and the island of Luing.

Safety remains paramount for the experienced swimmer. Before attempting difficult sea swims, he carefully researches tides and currents, and consults with local boatmen about water conditions. "I never jump straight into cold water - so always acclimatise for a minute first," he explains. "It's the first 90 seconds that take your body to get used to it, to help avoid cold water shock."

His pre-swim routine involves thorough assessment: checking water depth and temperature, identifying underwater hazards like rocks or branches, planning exit points, and evaluating currents or rip tides. Though he sometimes swims alone, he stresses his experience and knowing personal limits, always exiting before feeling dangerously cold.

Despite the challenges, Mr Maclean emphasises that Scotland offers many locations suitable for novice wild swimmers. He attributes wild swimming's growing popularity to its addictive nature: "You go once and then you've just got to go again."

The activity has experienced a significant boom, with groups forming on social media worldwide to share information about natural swimming pools and organise group swims. Mr Maclean believes this surge reflects people's desire for connection with nature and the unique thrill that wild swimming provides.

# Brazilian Man Dies After Cow Falls Through Roof Onto His Bed

A Brazilian man has died after being crushed by a cow that fell through his roof while he was sleeping.

The one-tonne cow was grazing on a hill behind the small house, in the town of Caratinga, when it stepped onto the asbestos roof, which collapsed under its weight. Joao Maria de Souza, 45, was lying in bed when the animal fell on him.

He was taken to hospital and died the day after, reportedly of internal bleeding. Mr Souza was conscious and appeared to be in a good condition, but he had to wait too long to be seen by a doctor, relatives said.

Local media says this is the third such incident in the region in the past three years. There were no casualties in the two previous incidents.

In the first occasion, there was no one inside the house when the cow fell through the roof. In the second incident, a baby and a small child were sleeping next to the spot where the animal fell, in what was described at time as a miraculous escape.

Caratinga is in a hilly area of Minas Gerais, a Brazilian state traditionally known as a cattle raising and dairy producing region.

# Uganda Election: Museveni Leads with 61% as Observers Criticize Poll Conditions

Uganda's long-time President Yoweri Museveni appears headed for victory in the country's presidential election, with more than 80% of ballots counted showing him securing 61% of the vote. His main challenger, Kizza Besigye, trails with 34% and is currently under house arrest. Full results are expected within hours.

The election has drawn sharp criticism from European Union observers, who highlighted significant concerns about the electoral process. EU Chief Observer Eduard Kukan acknowledged that "voters actively participated in the campaign events and expressed a remarkable determination while waiting for the long hours on the election day to cast their ballots."

However, he noted that "the National Resistance Movement's domination of the political landscape distorted the fairness of the campaign," pointing to an "intimidating atmosphere" created by the governing party.

The voting process has been marred by sporadic violence, opposition allegations of electoral fraud, and government-imposed blocks on social media sites and messaging apps. Mr. Besigye was arrested on Friday on suspicion of planning to publish his own results, which would violate electoral laws. Kampala police chief Andrew Felix Kaweesi stated authorities would detain him until official results are announced.

This marks the fourth electoral contest between the former allies, who once fought together as guerrilla fighters, with Mr. Besigye serving as Mr. Museveni's personal doctor.

President Museveni, who seized power in 1986, is credited with restoring stability to Uganda but faces growing criticism for increasingly authoritarian tendencies. Former Prime Minister Amama Mbabazi is in distant third place and is also reportedly under house arrest.

**Music Festival Celebrates Milestone 10th Anniversary in Wester Ross**

A popular music festival in Wester Ross marked its 10th anniversary over the weekend with sold-out performances on Friday and Saturday. Approximately 2,500 revellers attended each day to enjoy headline acts including Utah Saints, Twin Atlantic, Shed Seven, and The Undertones, alongside Alabama 3, Public Service Broadcasting, and Hunter and the Bear.

In a testament to the event's popularity, this year's festival sold out before any performers were even announced, highlighting its strong reputation among music fans in the Scottish Highlands community.

# Trump and Clinton Debate: Rivals Find One Nice Thing to Say

In an unusually tense television debate on 10 October 2016, US presidential rivals Donald Trump and Hillary Clinton broke protocol by refusing to shake hands at the start.

The frosty encounter saw heated arguments over multiple issues, notably Mr Trump's controversial remarks about women.

Despite the hostile atmosphere throughout, both candidates managed to find something positive about their opponent when prompted. Mrs Clinton praised Mr Trump's children, whilst he acknowledged her determination and refusal to quit.

The debate highlighted the deeply strained relationship between the two presidential hopefuls.

# South Korean Ferry Captain Lee Joon-seok Sentenced to Life in Prison for Sewol Disaster

GWANGJU, South Korea — A South Korean appeals court on Tuesday sentenced the captain of the sunken ferry Sewol to life in prison, overturning his previous 36-year jail term and significantly increasing his punishment for one of the country's worst maritime disasters.

Lee Joon-seok, now nearly 70 years old, was at the helm when the ferry capsized and sank in April 2014, killing more than 300 people, most of them high school students on a field trip. While he had been found guilty of gross negligence in November and sentenced to 36 years in prison, the appeals court determined his actions warranted the harshest possible punishment short of execution.

The judge at the Gwangju High Court delivered a scathing verdict, comparing Lee's decision to abandon the sinking vessel to a doctor deserting sick and dying patients in a hospital. The captain's actions, the judge said, left passengers trapped on his ship "in a state of fatal and indescribable suffering."

Prosecutors had argued for the death penalty, telling the court that Lee deserved the ultimate punishment for abandoning his passengers. They emphasized that his actions led to the deaths of 250 high school students and "inflicted an incurable injury on their parents," according to Yonhap news agency.

Despite the life sentence, families of the victims protested outside the court, demanding even harsher punishment. "He should have received death penalty. Imprisonment for life? They want to give life sentence to a person so that he can peacefully die when he is old?" asked Jeon Myung-sun, whose son Jeon Chan-ho died in the disaster, according to the Associated Press.

Lee had been captured on video and in photographs leaving the ship while passengers remained trapped inside the sinking vessel. While he apologized for abandoning passengers, he argued that he never intended to sacrifice their lives and claimed he was "confused" during the incident.

The appeals court also handed down revised sentences to 14 other crew members, ranging from 18 months to 12 years in prison. These sentences were actually lighter than their previous jail terms of five to 30 years. Judge Jeon Il-ho explained that the new sentences took into account that the crew members were following orders from the captain.

"We drew a distinction between the captain Lee Joon-seok who has a grave responsibility and crew members who took orders from the captain," Reuters quoted the judge as saying. "And we considered health conditions of the crew members and actions they took in the rescue operation as well as how they boarded the ferry Sewol."

The Sewol disaster, which occurred on April 16, 2014, triggered widespread mourning across South Korea and became one of the worst maritime disasters in the country's modern history. Investigations revealed the tragedy was caused by a combination of factors including illegal redesigns of the vessel, overloading of cargo, the inexperience of the crew member steering the ship, and lax government safety regulations.

President Park Geun-hye has vowed to implement reforms and agreed to demands from grieving relatives to salvage the ferry. Nine bodies remain missing from the disaster.

The tragedy continues to resonate in South Korean society. Over the weekend, thousands of protesters peacefully demonstrated in Seoul against the government's handling of the disaster, following clashes with riot police at another protest that left dozens injured.

# Labour Leadership Race Intensifies as Corbyn Leads Polls Amid Party Tensions

The Labour Party leadership contest has erupted into open warfare, with left-wing candidate Jeremy Corbyn calling for politics to be conducted in a "comradely and friendly" manner amid escalating attacks from party grandees and rival candidates.

The controversy intensified after former Cabinet minister Alan Milburn joined Tony Blair in warning against a Corbyn victory, declaring that Labour would have a "death wish" if it shifted leftward. Fellow leadership candidate Liz Kendall went further, describing a potential Corbyn win as a "disaster" for the party.

The stark warnings came after a YouGov poll for The Times placed Mr Corbyn significantly ahead in the leadership race, with 43% of first preference votes, compared to Andy Burnham on 26%, Yvette Cooper on 20%, and Ms Kendall trailing in fourth place with just 11%.

The prospect of a Corbyn victory has sent shockwaves through the party establishment. Labour donor John Mills told The Guardian that Mr Corbyn's election could trigger an "SDP-style split" – referencing the 1981 breakaway that formed the Social Democratic Party – and predicted that wealthy donors would withdraw their financial support.

Mr Mills, who has donated to Ms Kendall's campaign, suggested that "some of the major donors" would be "less likely to give" if Mr Corbyn won, raising questions about the party's financial viability under his leadership.

Responding to the barrage of criticism, Mr Corbyn struck a conciliatory tone, telling the BBC: "I think politics should be conducted on a comradely and friendly basis, and if people disagree with each other then say what they disagree on, and let's keep these silly remarks to themselves."

Ms Kendall firmly rejected suggestions that she should withdraw from the race to consolidate opposition to Mr Corbyn. "I'll be fighting for what I believe in until the very end," she declared, arguing that "turning back to the politics of the 1980s and losing elections does nothing to help the people" Labour wants to support.

The controversy follows comments from former Prime Minister Tony Blair, who warned that Labour would not win from a "traditional leftist platform" and suggested that those with Mr Corbyn's politics should "get a transplant." One of Mr Blair's former advisers even described MPs who nominated Mr Corbyn to ensure a broad debate, but don't support him, as "morons."

However, not all Labour figures agree with the attacks on Mr Corbyn. Former deputy prime minister Lord Prescott criticized Mr Blair for "abusing" Corbyn supporters and urged the party to "calm down."

Mr Milburn emphasized that Labour could only win the next election by occupying the centre ground, warning that any leftward lurch would be fatal for the party's electoral prospects.

Despite leading in the YouGov poll among party members, a subsequent Ipsos Mori survey of the general public showed Mr Burnham ahead, with 27% saying he would make a good prime minister, compared to 22% for Ms Cooper, 17% for Mr Corbyn, and 16% for Ms Kendall.

As the leadership contest continues, the deep divisions within Labour over its future direction show no signs of healing, with establishment figures increasingly alarmed at Mr Corbyn's unexpected surge in popularity among party members.

# Vettel Set to Test Modified 'Halo Two' Safety Device at Austrian Grand Prix

Sebastian Vettel is expected to trial the latest version of Formula One's controversial cockpit protection system during Friday's opening practice session, as the sport continues its push to enhance driver safety.

The four-time world champion will complete at least one lap with the 'Halo Two' device fitted to his car, giving engineers and officials their first on-track look at the modified design. The system, intended to shield drivers from impacts with large airborne debris, represents an evolution of the original halo concept tested in March.

While the visual changes may be subtle, significant modifications have been made to both materials and dimensions. Most notably, the new iteration uses titanium rather than steel construction, offering improved strength-to-weight ratios. However, the FIA has indicated this may not represent the final material specification when the device becomes mandatory in 2017.

Beyond performance testing, the governing body's medical team will assess how the halo affects driver extraction procedures in emergency situations—a crucial consideration for race safety protocols.

The FIA has informed teams that cockpit protection will form part of next year's sweeping regulation changes, designed to make cars faster and more visually striking. However, officials continue refining the final design to optimize the balance between safety benefits, driver visibility, and cockpit access.

The halo's development comes after Red Bull's alternative 'aeroscreen' concept failed mandatory impact tests, which simulate a wheel striking the device at 250km/h. Though the FIA hoped to continue aeroscreen development for potential 2018 introduction, Red Bull has suspended work to focus resources on their 2017 challenger.

# New Welsh Plant Species Named After Sir David Attenborough

A newly discovered plant species found in the Brecon Beacons has been named in honour of Sir David Attenborough.

The Attenborough Hawkweed belongs to the daisy family and is believed to have evolved in the Welsh mountains since the last ice age. These plants are close relatives of dandelions, sharing similar-looking flowers.

Sir David expressed his delight at the tribute, saying he was "thrilled" by the honour. "Bestowing a name on a new species is surely one of the greatest of biological compliments and I am truly grateful," he said.

Dr Tim Rich, the plant taxonomist who made the discovery and named the species, described finding it as "a really exciting moment and something that you dream of as a naturalist."

He explained his choice: "I decided to name this special little plant found in the mountains of the Brecon Beacons after David Attenborough as he inspired me to study ecology when I was 17."

# Indian Court Orders Fresh Investigation Into Mohammad Akhlaq Lynching Case

A court in northern India has ordered a fresh investigation into the 2015 killing of Mohammad Akhlaq, who was beaten to death by a mob over allegations of storing beef in his home.

Mohammad Akhlaq was beaten to death by a group of men in Dadri in the northern Indian state of Uttar Pradesh. Eighteen people are on trial for his murder. The slaughter of cows, considered sacred by Hindus, is banned in many Indian states.

The court in Gautam Buddh Nagar, near the Indian capital, Delhi, gave the order after hearing a petition filed by one of Mr Akhlaq's neighbours.

Mohammad Danish, Mr Akhlaq's son, said he "hoped a fresh investigation will bring out the truth". "I am hoping for a fair probe. The real facts will be revealed then," he told the CNN-IBN news channel.

A lab test cited widely in the aftermath of the killing in September had said that the meat allegedly found in his refrigerator was mutton and not beef. However, a new lab report, revealed in June by the lawyers of 18 people on trial for his murder, said that the meat in question was, in fact, beef.

Later, it was also revealed that the meat was never in his house, but found inside a bin near his home.

Although police have said that the type of meat is irrelevant to the murder case, the defence team has been using the new test results to demand the release of the 18 suspects on the grounds that they were "provoked" into attacking Mr Akhlaq.

Uttar Pradesh is one of the 10 Indian states where the slaughter of cow, calf, bull and bullock is completely banned. However, the slaughter of buffaloes and the sale and consumption of its meat is permitted.

# Russia Names 68 Athletes for Rio Olympics Despite Doping Ban

Russia has named 68 track and field athletes it hopes will compete at the Rio Olympics, despite the country's athletics federation remaining suspended over doping allegations.

Athletics' governing body first imposed the ban in November following allegations of widespread state-sponsored doping in the country. The Russian Olympic Committee (ROC) and its athletes last week appealed against the decision to the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas). A final decision is due by 21 July.

The International Association of Athletics Federations (IAAF) has said a handful of Russian athletes could compete in Rio as "neutral athletes". To do so, they must meet a number of criteria, including being repeatedly tested outside their homeland.

Russian doping whistleblower Yuliya Stepanova has been cleared to run and was described as a "symbol" for clean competitors.

The All-Russian Athletics Federation (Araf) on Tuesday published a list of the 68 athletes it said had met its criteria for taking part in the Olympics, which start on 5 August. Two-time Olympic pole vault champion Yelena Isinbayeva and London 2012 high jump gold medallist Ivan Ukhov are included.

Araf said each of its athletes has "sent an individual request to the Olympic Games" to be checked by the IAAF, as "Araf is not now a member". It said it had also appealed about the "overall legality of adding extra criteria for the participation of sportsmen competing at the Olympics".

The International Olympic Committee's deadline to achieve qualifying criteria for the Games is 11 July, though the ROC says that would be extended should Cas rule in favour of its athletes.

After approximately 30 years, the zoo ended its agreement to provide apes for advertising, though chimpanzees from abroad continued appearing in tea adverts until 2003.

Choppers' journey began in Liberia, where she was rescued from poachers as a baby by a British couple in 1973. They brought her to Twycross for care, but her life in television had lasting damaging effects on her natural behaviour.

Only in her later years did Choppers begin to exhibit typical chimpanzee behaviour. Following the death of her companion Louis—who played Mr Shifter in the PG Tips adverts—in July 2013, keepers introduced Choppers to the zoo's larger chimpanzee group.

# Girl's Hair Trapped in Lanzarote Hotel Pool Filter for Two Minutes

A young girl from Leeds fell unconscious after her hair became trapped in a swimming pool filter at a holiday resort in Lanzarote, leaving her underwater for more than two minutes.

Darcey Morgan was pulled to safety by fellow holidaymakers at the H10 Rubicon Palace in Playa Blanca during a family holiday in April. Her mother, Alex Morgan, described the incident as "terrifying" and said her daughter turned blue before losing consciousness.

The 32-year-old mother was staying at the resort with her husband Gareth, 35, and their three children when the accident occurred. Darcey received CPR by the poolside before being rushed to hospital in Arrecife, where she was kept overnight for observation.

"It took over two minutes to get her hair free, by which time she was unconscious. She was blue," Mrs Morgan said. "There are no words for what I was feeling. It's every parent's worst nightmare."

Darcey lost four clumps of hair in the incident but has since made a full recovery.

Mrs Morgan said she reported the incident to hotel management but claimed they "did nothing" in response. "The swimming pool was not closed, the waterfall and the filter remained on," she said.

Following the accident, Mrs Morgan said other guests came forward to report they had previously raised concerns about the filter with staff. She claimed one boy had his swimming trunks sucked into the device just two days before Darcey's ordeal.

However, First Choice said it had received no other reports regarding the filter and confirmed the device had been switched off immediately after being informed of the incident.

# KPMG Under Investigation Over Rolls-Royce Bribery Scandal

The Financial Reporting Council has launched an investigation into KPMG's auditing of Rolls-Royce, raising fundamental questions about the effectiveness of corporate financial oversight following one of Britain's most significant corruption scandals.

Earlier this year, Rolls-Royce paid £671 million in fines, including £498 million to the Serious Fraud Office, and issued an apology after being found guilty of paying millions in bribes to middlemen over decades to secure lucrative orders. The engineering giant's long-standing auditor, KPMG, had been examining the company's accounts for 26 years, yet apparently failed to detect the widespread illegal activity.

KPMG has stated it is cooperating with the investigation and remains "confident in the quality" of its work. However, critics are asking how a detailed professional audit could miss such systematic and recurring corruption. The case has reignited debate about the fundamental purpose and effectiveness of corporate auditing.

The Rolls-Royce scandal, along with previous high-profile failures at Enron, WorldCom, Tesco, and during the financial crisis, highlights structural problems at the heart of auditing and financial oversight.

The first issue is that auditors are neither police nor regulators. They cannot simply seize whatever documents they wish. Instead, they largely must work with information the company chooses to provide. This makes it relatively easy for a determined company to mislead its auditors—a defence frequently offered by audit firms when questioned about failures.

The second problem concerns the commercial relationship between auditors and their clients. Auditors are contractors paid by the very companies they examine. The "Big Four" accounting firms—PwC, KPMG, EY, and Deloitte—audit over 90% of major company accounts. They compete for this lucrative business, creating inherent incentives to maintain favour with those who employ and pay them.

KPMG audited Rolls-Royce for 26 years, earning tens of millions of pounds and inevitably developing close relationships. Similarly, PwC audited Tesco for 32 years before agreeing not to seek reappointment following that company's accounting scandal. Such long associations hardly provide ideal conditions for maintaining tough, arms-length scrutiny.

While outright corruption remains rare, unconscious bias favouring a client paying substantial fees over decades is difficult to avoid.

Recent regulatory changes require large public companies in the FTSE 350 to tender their auditing contracts every ten years, though they need only change auditors every twenty years. Critics argue this still allows excessive coziness to develop.

Auditors do face penalties occasionally. The record fine in the United States is $8 million, whilst in the UK it stands at £3 million. These sums are minuscule compared to fines levied on misbehaving companies and relative to the enormous size of major accounting firms.

The fundamental problem remains: major accountancy firms have historically enjoyed substantial rewards whilst facing relatively little risk, raising questions about whether current structures can deliver the independent oversight investors and the public require.

# Prison Drug Problem 'Threatens to Overwhelm' HMP Ranby

A damning report has revealed that the widespread availability of so-called "legal highs" at a Nottinghamshire prison is threatening to overwhelm its healthcare services.

The HM Inspectorate of Prisons found that New Psychoactive Substances (NPS) pose a significant challenge at HMP Ranby, which houses approximately 1,000 male inmates. These substances are chemically designed to mimic already-banned drugs.

Deputy Chief Inspector Martin Lomas said the jail faces the urgent task of "destabilising the supply of NPS which threatens to overwhelm it."

The report also raised serious concerns about six suicides occurring within just 17 months at the facility.

"NPS remains a real concern in prisons," Spurr stated, adding that a new testing regime would be implemented across the country from April. He emphasised that authorities would work closely with police to disrupt supply chains and take "robust action" against those supplying or using NPS in prisons.

Despite these challenges, inspectors noted some positive developments, including fewer prisoners reporting feelings of being unsafe or victimised, though these figures remained significantly higher than comparable prisons.
