# Malaysia PM Calls Myanmar Violence Against Rohingya Muslims "Genocide"

Malaysian Prime Minister Najib Razak has described the treatment of Rohingya Muslims in Myanmar as "genocide", urging the international community to take action against what he called systematic persecution.

Mr Razak made the comments in an opening statement to members of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) gathering in Kuala Lumpur. The OIC is made up of 57 countries with large or majority-Muslim populations. It is holding the emergency session to discuss what it says is a humanitarian crisis faced by the Myanmar minority.

Approximately 65,000 Rohingyas have fled Myanmar's Rakhine state since Burmese soldiers began intensive counter-terrorism operations there in October.

Describing the situation as "a cause of great and immediate concern", Mr Najib said: "Far too many people have lost their lives in Myanmar. Many have suffered appalling deaths, and those that have lived through the atrocities have witnessed or endured unspeakable cruelty. That in itself is a reason why we cannot keep silent."

The situation also threatens to create "a new home for terrorist groups", he said, as "militant elements could infiltrate and possibly radicalise this oppressed community".

## What is the OIC?

Formerly known as the Organisation of the Islamic Conference, the 57-member organisation is largely made up of majority-Muslim countries. It was established in 1969 in the wake of an arson attack by an Australian Christian on the al-Aqsa mosque in Jerusalem.

Its aims include the promotion of co-operation among member states, safeguarding Islamic holy places and working towards eradicating racial discrimination and colonialism. But despite its size, numerous committees and stated scope, it has limited resources at its own disposal.

## What is happening in Rakhine state?

After lethal attacks in October on security forces in Maungdaw district in Myanmar (also called Burma), the authorities launched a counter-insurgency operation that critics claim has involved widespread killings, rape and the destruction of Rohingya villages.

The government of Myanmar has denied the accusations and has suggested Rohingya burned their own homes down to attract international attention. It has also prevented NGOs and international media, including the BBC, from entering the region to investigate the claims.

In his speech, Mr Najib called on the Burmese government to allow humanitarian aid in.

The country's leader Aung San Suu Kyi has previously asked for "space" from the international community to deal with the issue. After a trip to Rakhine state, former UN Secretary General Kofi Annan also said he would not describe the violence against the Rohingya as "genocide".

But John McKissick, a senior official in the UN's refugee agency, told the BBC in November that Myanmar is seeking the ethnic cleansing of the Muslim minority from its territory.

## Who are the Rohingya?

The estimated one million Muslim Rohingya are seen by many in mainly Buddhist Myanmar as illegal migrants from Bangladesh. They are denied citizenship by the government despite many having lived there for generations.

Communal violence in Rakhine state in 2012 left scores dead and displaced more than 100,000 people. They face widespread discrimination and mistreatment.

# El Salvador Gang Truce Leads to Sharp Drop in Murders

El Salvador has witnessed a dramatic decline in violent crime following a historic truce between the country's most feared street gangs, according to police figures released this week.

Authorities reported that killings have fallen nearly 24% overall this year, with May murders plummeting by more than 50% compared to the same period last year. Justice and Public Security Minister David Munguia Payes credited the gang ceasefire, stating it "has had an important effect on the drop in violence."

The unprecedented peace deal between Mara Salvatrucha (MS-13) and Barrio 18, two gangs notorious for ruthless violence, was brokered by the Catholic Church. The agreement came after gang leaders were transferred from maximum security facilities to prisons with more relaxed conditions.

President Mauricio Funes emphasized that his government did not directly negotiate with the gangs but merely facilitated the accord.

On 19 June, imprisoned gang members held ceremonies marking the first 100 days of the truce. Gang leaders signaled willingness to make the pact permanent. "We want a definitive ceasefire," gang leader Oscar Armando Reyes told the Associated Press, though he stressed the government must provide concrete job proposals.

El Salvador's gangs originated from immigrant street gangs in the United States and have evolved into powerful trans-national criminal organizations with thousands of members.

The successful truce has captured attention in neighboring Honduras and Guatemala, countries also plagued by high murder rates and gang violence.

# Norway Accuses Fitness Tracker Companies of Breaking Data Privacy Laws

Norway's Consumer Council (NCC) has filed a formal complaint against four major fitness tracker manufacturers, accusing them of violating local data protection laws.

The consumer watchdog said Fitbit, Jawbone, Garmin and Mio had all failed to comply with Norwegian regulations governing how companies handle consumer information. According to the NCC, the firms collected excessive amounts of personal data without adequately informing users about who could access it or how long it would be retained.

The complaint has now been submitted to Norway's data protection authority for investigation.

Finn Myrstad, director of digital services at the NCC, criticized the companies for operating under "asymmetrical and obscure terms" that forced users to surrender personal information in exchange for using the fitness tracking devices.

"We fear that this information can be exploited for direct marketing and price-discrimination purposes, and that basic privacy principles are being neglected," Mr Myrstad said in a statement.

The allegations emerged from a detailed research project conducted by the council examining the terms and conditions employed by the four wristband manufacturers. The investigation found that users had minimal access to information about what data was collected, who viewed it, and how it was utilized.

"It is important that we don't give up basic rights in order to use the products and services of the future," Mr Myrstad emphasized.

In response to the complaint, Jawbone issued a statement saying it was reviewing the NCC report. The company insisted it only shares user data with explicit permission, such as when integrating with third-party applications.

A Jawbone spokesman described the company as a "custodian" of user data, noting that users can download their information and request deletion at any time.

The BBC has contacted all four companies for comment.

# Portsmouth's Spinnaker Tower to be Painted Blue and Gold After Red Design Backlash

Portsmouth City Council has revised its controversial plans to rebrand the iconic Spinnaker Tower following a public outcry that saw more than 10,000 residents sign a petition against the original colour scheme.

The landmark tower will now be painted blue and gold instead of red and white, after the council's initial design sparked fury among local residents who objected to the use of Southampton Football Club's colours on one of Portsmouth's most recognisable structures.

The rebranding is part of a £3.5 million sponsorship deal with airline Emirates, announced earlier this month. The tower will be renamed the Emirates Spinnaker Tower, with the new livery set to be in place in time for the America's Cup World Series sailing event in July.

More than 100 litres of red paint that had already been purchased for the original scheme will now be donated to charities and community organisations across Hampshire, the council confirmed.

## A City Divided

The revised blue and gold design reflects Portsmouth's traditional colours, matching those of the city and its football team. Blue has long been associated with Portsmouth, making the new scheme more palatable to local residents.

Donna Jones, leader of Portsmouth City Council, defended the decision and the subsequent U-turn. "We have listened to the public and created a new blue, gold and white design that is in keeping with suggestions from residents," she said. "This gives us a unique opportunity to promote Portsmouth around the world."

Ms Jones emphasised that the financial terms of the Emirates deal remained unchanged despite the design revision. She stressed the importance of the funding for the cash-strapped council: "We wouldn't have to do any of this if we weren't so desperately short of money. We have a primary school places crisis at the moment - this money is going towards building new classrooms."

## Opposition Criticism

However, the Liberal Democrat opposition has criticised the council's handling of the entire affair. Councillor Ben Dowling said the saga had made Portsmouth the "laughing stock of the country."

"It's good that the new design isn't red but we still have some fairly serious questions about the process that has taken place," Mr Dowling said. "Most Portsmouth people are asking 'why didn't we just get asked in the first place?' - someone surely would have pointed out that red wasn't the best idea."

## Moving Forward

Sir Tim Clark, President of Emirates, acknowledged the public feedback: "We listened to the feedback and worked with the council to adapt the designs in order to create something that Portsmouth residents will be proud of."

An application for advertising consent has been posted on Portsmouth City Council's website, though it currently faces 13 objections. Several objectors have complained about the lack of detailed visual representations accompanying the application, making it difficult to assess the full impact of the proposed changes.

The branding will remain in place for five years, until June 2022, if approved at a planning committee meeting scheduled for 7 July. The 560-foot tower, which opened in 2005, is owned by the council but operated by a private company.

# Te'o Commits to Worcester Warriors Despite Injury-Hit Season

Ben Te'o has pledged his commitment to Worcester Warriors for next season, dismissing speculation about his future despite an injury-disrupted campaign at Sixways.

The New Zealand-born rugby league convert, 30, has played infrequently this season after joining from Irish side Leinster in the summer of 2016. He has suffered two separate concussion injuries, added to his England calls.

# Former GP Andrew Johnson receives additional jail time for historical sex abuse

# Viral Appeal Leads to Overwhelming Support for Down's Syndrome Football Team

A Londonderry-based football team for young people with Down's syndrome has been inundated with offers of support after a social media plea went viral, featuring Republic of Ireland winger James McClean.

The Oxford Bulls, established with help from the Foyle Down's Syndrome Trust, were struggling to find opponents when manager Kevin Morrison made an appeal on social media. McClean responded by getting in touch and visiting the team, with a video of his visit spreading rapidly across social platforms.

"The response had been so good the team could play every week for two years," said a delighted Mr Morrison. "Our first competitive match will now take place in Sion Mills on 24 April."

The impact on the young players has been profound. Seamus Breslin, parent of one player, said his son "finishes school on a Friday and then plans his whole weekend around football. He absolutely loves it."

John Morris, another parent, described how his son had become a local celebrity since McClean's visit, with people taking pictures of him in shops. "With James McClean coming down, they've become famous," he said. "The exposure has been unbelievable. Manchester City, Liverpool FC and UEFA have even been in contact."

One mother praised the club for giving her 10-year-old son confidence and helping him make friends. "They've been treated like heroes and we couldn't believe the story was even in French Canadian papers," she said.

The Foyle Down's Syndrome Trust provides various activities for young people and adults with the condition.

# Asda Reports Sales Decline Despite Market Share Gains

Asda, the UK supermarket chain owned by US retail giant Wal-Mart, has reported a 1.6% decline in like-for-like sales during the third quarter, marking a reversal from the 0.6% growth recorded in the previous quarter.

Despite the drop in sales at stores open for more than a year compared with the previous three months, chief executive Andy Clarke expressed satisfaction with the company's performance, noting that Asda continues to gain market share in challenging conditions.

"A year ago we took clear action to address the changes in our market and implement a five year strategy to redefine value retailing. That is a long term strategy that won't be delivered overnight," Mr Clarke said.

He emphasised that whilst the company's focus on value for money and online shopping expansion was proving successful, market conditions remained extremely difficult. "The last quarter has seen a shockwave go through our industry and others are starting to respond to the challenges they face. I expect that we will see another tough quarter and I'm under no illusions that the battle continues to rage."

Asda, which competes with Sainsbury's for the position of Britain's second-largest supermarket behind market leader Tesco, took aim at competitors' promotional tactics during a press briefing. Chief merchandising officer Barry Williams criticised rival supermarkets' heavy use of vouchers, describing several Morrisons promotions as akin to "quantitative easing" and "desperate measures."

"You can win a quarter with a voucher.... We're not immune from the turbulence, but we judge our performance over a much longer period of three to five years," Mr Williams said, adding he had never seen as many money-off vouchers in his 25-year career.

The comments came shortly after Sainsbury's announced £150m in price cuts as part of its new customer strategy. Mr Clarke dismissed this as "a drop in the ocean," claiming Asda's price advantage over Sainsbury's already exceeds double digits.

He also asserted that Asda's Everyday Low Prices strategy is narrowing the gap with discount retailers, stating: "We are pulling away from the other three. There are very clear winners and losers in our market."

# Aldershot Town Cruise to Emphatic 6-0 Victory Over Guiseley

Aldershot Town recorded their biggest league victory since December 2013 with a commanding 6-0 demolition of Guiseley at the EBB Stadium on Saturday.

The Shots dominated proceedings from the opening whistle and came agonisingly close to breaking the deadlock in the 14th minute when Bobby-Joe Taylor headed home from a James Rowe cross, only for the effort to be ruled out for offside.

However, the home side's persistence paid off just six minutes later when Matt McClure curled a beautiful effort into the far post to give Aldershot a deserved lead. The striker's shot clipped the inside of the upright before nestling into the net, sending the home supporters into raptures.

Guiseley briefly threatened when they had a goal disallowed, but any hopes of a comeback were swiftly extinguished as Aldershot turned on the style. Callum Reynolds doubled the advantage before Jim Kellerman added a third to put the contest beyond doubt.

The hosts weren't finished there, though, as Shamir Fenelon grabbed a fourth goal before the interval to cap off a remarkable first-half performance that left the visitors shellshocked.

The second period continued in similar fashion, with James Rowe adding his name to the scoresheet with a thunderous 20-yard drive into the bottom corner. McClure then completed the rout with his second goal of the afternoon, rounding off the comprehensive 6-0 victory.

The match saw several bookings, with Guiseley's John Rooney and Robert Atkinson shown yellow cards in the first half, whilst Connor Brown and Aldershot's Will De Havilland joined them in the referee's notebook after the break.

Both managers made changes throughout the contest, with Guiseley introducing Callum McFadzean, Reece Thompson, and Kayode Odejayi in search of a consolation, whilst Aldershot brought on Scott Rendell, Jake Gallagher, and Nick Arnold.

The emphatic victory will provide a significant boost to Aldershot's confidence as they continue their league campaign.

# Thai Activist Charged with Lese-Majeste for Sharing BBC Profile of New King

Thai activist Jatupat Boonpattararaksa has been detained and charged with insulting the monarchy after sharing a BBC Thai profile of the new king on Facebook, marking the first lese-majeste charge since King Maha Vajiralongkorn's ascension to the throne.

The 64-year-old monarch officially became king on Thursday, nearly two months after his father's death. Mr Jatupat, known for his involvement in anti-government protests, was arrested in Chaiyaphum province in north-eastern Thailand, with charges filed in Khon Kaen city.

Under Thailand's strict royal defamation law, the activist faces up to 15 years in prison if convicted. Human rights organizations have criticized the military-backed government for allegedly weaponizing lese-majeste legislation to suppress political opposition.

King Vajiralongkorn succeeded his father, the widely revered King Bhumibol Adulyadej, who died on October 13 at age 88 after reigning for seven decades. The case highlights ongoing tensions surrounding free speech and royal criticism in Thailand's current political climate.

# Judge Criticises Fertility Clinic Over Legal Parent Forms Error

A fertility clinic has been sharply criticised by a High Court judge after paperwork errors left a woman fighting in court to be recognised as the legal parent of her own children.

The case involved a same-sex couple who underwent fertility treatment at IVF Hammersmith Limited. One of the women gave birth to twins after the treatment. But her partner, who was the biological mother, had to go to court to be declared a legal parent - because the wrong forms were filled in at the clinic.

The case is among 15 similar ones brought to the High Court.

The president of the Family Division, Sir James Munby, said the clinic's lawyers had been "grossly insensitive" in their handling of the case.

He granted the woman - identified only as X - a declaration that she was a legal parent of the twins in February.

Giving his reasons for Wednesday's judgement, he said the women had been left "shocked and angry" when the clinic's error came to light.

Sir James said the women had paid more than £15,000 for their treatment with IVF Hammersmith Limited.

He described how the clinic's solicitors sent a "crass and insensitive" letter to the women, offering them £1,000 in compensation.

Sir James said in his ruling: "The offer of money, whatever the amount, was merely adding insult to injury.

"If an offer of financial compensation was appropriate at all, the idea that £1,000 began to approach a realistic figure was so wide of the mark as to be not merely insulting but almost offensively so.

"If ever there was a situation calling for empathy, understanding, humanity, compassion and, dare one say it, common decency, never mind sincere and unqualified apology, it is surely this."

The clinic's director had expressed regret in a witness statement and said there were now procedures to try and avoid any repeat of the situation.

Sir James described this as a "mealy-mouthed observation".

This case is among eight, involving a number of clinics, which have been resolved at the High Court, after the UK's fertility regulator identified the form-filling errors.

A further seven cases are still awaiting a final court hearing. It is thought as many as 85 couples could be affected in total.

A spokeswoman for IVF Hammersmith said: "We understand the stress the process and hearing has caused and we are sorry for this.

"We would like to reiterate that we have learned from this case.

"To safeguard all other patients receiving donor sperm, since 2013 we have introduced witnessing to the process, run dedicated staff training and operated continuous audits."

# Apple iPhone 7: Petition Launched to Keep Headphone Socket

**A petition calling on Apple to retain the standard headphone socket on its forthcoming iPhone 7 has attracted more than 200,000 signatures.**

Online reports suggest Apple plans to omit the 3.5mm socket to make the iPhone 7 thinner and more waterproof, with more room for the battery. The Fast Company reported it would rely on the Lightning cable port, currently used for charging, for sound output. Others suggest Apple will ship the iPhone 7 with wireless headphones.

The Sum of Us, a website "fighting for people over profits", which organised the petition, said: "Not only will this force iPhone users to dole out additional cash to replace their hi-fi headphones, it will singlehandedly create mountains of electronic waste that likely won't get recycled."

Tech website The Verge said: "Removing [the] headphone [socket] from phones is something that no-one is asking for and has serious drawbacks including poor compatibility and accessibility, [and] DRM [digital rights management] audio [ie with built-in copyright enforcement]."

## Public Reaction Mixed

Many complained on Twitter that removing the socket would render expensive headphones useless. Some complained having to use the Lightning port would mean "no music while charging". One tweeted: "I am OK with Apple removing the headphone [socket] as long as they bundle Lightning EarBuds with the iPhone 7."

Others said that they would not be upgrading.

But not everyone is convinced that losing the jack is a bad idea. John Gruber, who writes the technology blog Daring Fireball and is regarded as an authority on all things Apple, makes the point that losing the jack would make more room for a larger battery.

"Removing the analogue headphone jack is inevitable. This is what makes Apple different. They will initiate a painful transition for a long-term gain," he writes. "In five years we'll look at analogue headphone jacks the way we look at all the other legacy ports we've abandoned."

## Apple's Audio Strategy

Apple introduced support for headphones over its Lightning cable in 2014. In the same year, it paid $3bn (£2bn) for the acquisition of headphone maker Beats.

And the Mac Rumours website suggests Apple could be preparing bespoke headphones for the phone. It noted that a trademark application had been filed for the term "AirPods" in October last year. And while Apple was not directly linked to these applications, the site said, "the pattern of filings is consistent with Apple's usual strategy".

If the rumours prove true, it will not be the first time Apple has abandoned what it sees as outdated technology. In 1998 it released the iMac G3 without a floppy disk, leaving many questioning the wisdom of the move. But, just more than a decade later, Sony - a pioneer of the floppy disk - announced it was killing off the storage device.

# Hamilton Critical of Own Form Despite Victory at UK Championship

Nottingham-born snooker player Anthony Hamilton delivered a scathing assessment of his own performance despite advancing to the last 64 of the UK Championship with a hard-fought 6-5 victory over Craig Steadman.

The 43-year-old, who once reached number 10 in the world rankings, showed little optimism about his chances ahead of his Saturday evening clash with former world champion Graeme Dott.

"It was rubbish - seriously. I can't play any worse," Hamilton told BBC Sport after his opening-round success. "It was a good attitude but rubbish snooker. I am rubbish now a lot of the time."

Hamilton, who turned professional in 1991, enjoyed a distinguished career that included five years in the world's top 16. He reached two ranking event finals and competed in four World Championship quarter-finals, with his last appearance in the last eight coming in 2007.

However, recent years have been challenging for the veteran player. Plagued by a persistent neck injury, Hamilton had slipped to number 50 in the world rankings by the time the York tournament began.

Despite praising the quality of the tables at the venue, Hamilton lamented his declining form. "The tables are gorgeous," he said. "A few years ago I would have been making 80 every poke, now I am making eight every poke. I am getting old basically. It's no fun but it's better than working."

Interestingly, Hamilton suggested that facing a top-class opponent like Dott might actually work in his favour. "I will probably play better against a top player," he explained. "They go for their shots, force the issue and if they miss they are in position so the chances come easier. You get fewer chances but the chances are better. I might be able to glean some old school form."

He added: "Graeme might be a bit too clever for me now I am old and rubbish. But if I play well then I have a chance, it's simple."

Hamilton's match against Steadman was complicated by an unusual incident before play began. The Muswell Hill resident was docked a frame for being late after waiting in the wrong location.

"I came out of the dressing room and saw some players standing around waiting and just joined them," Hamilton explained. "My lot were over the other side, but obviously I didn't know that. I was only there a couple of minutes. By the time I got there I was late so I got docked a frame."

Despite accepting responsibility, Hamilton suggested there had been insufficient information about the dual assembly points. However, he recovered from the setback, noting: "I got over it straight away and that was the only time I played well."

# Government Suffers Defeat on Constituency Boundary Review

The coalition government has suffered a significant defeat in the House of Lords over plans to redraw parliamentary constituency boundaries, with Liberal Democrat ministers breaking ranks to vote against their Conservative partners for the first time.

The House of Lords approved a cross-party amendment to delay the review of parliamentary constituencies until 2018, effectively pushing the changes beyond the next general election. The amendment passed with a substantial majority of 69 votes, marking a dramatic rupture in the coalition partnership.

Prime Minister David Cameron now faces a critical decision on whether to attempt to overturn the Lords vote when the legislation returns to the House of Commons. However, with Deputy Prime Minister Nick Clegg having instructed Liberal Democrat MPs to oppose the boundary changes, the prospects for a Conservative victory appear slim.

At the heart of the dispute is the Conservative plan to reduce the number of MPs from 650 to 600, including a reduction from 40 to 30 seats in Wales, where constituencies typically have smaller electorates. Political analysts have suggested the review could deliver approximately 20 additional seats to the Conservatives, potentially proving crucial to their chances of winning the next general election.

Conservative MP Glyn Davies, who observed the Lords debate, acknowledged the vote would "really put cat among pigeons." He questioned on Twitter whether the government would attempt to reverse the amendment, noting that the 69-vote majority would embolden opposition in the Commons.

Speculation has emerged that David Cameron might seek support from smaller Westminster parties. However, the Scottish National Party quickly dismissed such prospects, stating: "There have been no discussions and no deal will be done on the boundary review." The SNP also criticised what they described as "fall-out and petty score-settling between the Tories and Lib Dems," suggesting the entire process may have been "a waste of time and waste of money."

Plaid Cymru, whose three MPs form a joint parliamentary party with the SNP's six representatives, appeared equally reluctant to negotiate unless the UK government offers substantial devolution of powers from Westminster to Cardiff Bay. Even with such concessions, the parliamentary arithmetic appears unfavourable for the Conservatives.

The political uncertainty has prompted the Conservative Party to select candidates for 2015 based on existing constituency boundaries rather than the proposed new ones.

Downing Street confirmed the government would attempt to overturn the Lords vote in the Commons. A spokesman said: "The PM remains of the view that we should have fewer MPs to cut the cost of politics, and more equal size constituencies so that people's votes have more equal weight."

However, Nick Clegg's comments suggest the prime minister faces an uphill battle. The Deputy Prime Minister told the BBC: "We are leaving the boundary changes on the statute book but we are saying that we should miss a beat and do it in the next parliament not this one."

# Bosworth Sets British Record Despite Stomach Issues in Olympic Race Walk

British race walker Tom Bosworth finished sixth in the Olympic 20km race walk despite battling illness, but celebrated breaking the national record by a significant margin.

China's Wang Zhen claimed gold in a time of one hour, 19 minutes and 14 seconds, improving on his bronze medal from London 2012. His compatriot Cai Zelin took silver, also bettering his fourth-place finish from four years ago. Australia's Dane Bird-Smith rounded out the podium with bronze.

Bosworth had positioned himself among the race leaders during the opening hour before Wang and Cai pulled away in the final stages. Despite the challenging circumstances, the British athlete remained philosophical about his performance.

"I can't be disappointed with sixth place at the Olympics but I could have done better as I had a dodgy stomach last night and that affected me a little bit," said Bosworth.

He added: "To break the British Record by such a margin and at the Olympics is a dream come true. It was just an amazing experience. I'm so happy I cannot put it into words."

The performance marks a career highlight for Bosworth despite the physical difficulties he faced during the competition.

# Studio in Talks to Adapt Brexit Campaign Book for Television

An unnamed Hollywood studio is reportedly in negotiations to adapt "The Bad Boys of Brexit" into a television series, with Benedict Cumberbatch rumored to play Nigel Farage, the former UKIP leader and prominent Brexit campaigner.

The potential six-part adaptation is based on former UKIP donor Arron Banks's book, which chronicles the chaotic journey of Mr Farage's Brexit campaign. According to the Sunday Times, talks between the studio and Mr Banks are scheduled to take place next month in Los Angeles.

Mr Farage, speaking to BBC News, confirmed he was not directly involved in the project but joked about the casting speculation: "I have to play myself, obviously." However, he suggested the adaptation's appeal extends beyond Brexit itself, noting that interest has been generated because the story is "linked directly to Mr Trump's presidency itself."

The connection to American politics appears to be a key selling point. Mr Farage appeared alongside then-candidate Donald Trump on the campaign trail last year, with Trump expressing hopes of replicating Brexit's upset of the political establishment. Since then, Mr Farage has become a frequent visitor to the United States, working as a Fox News contributor and maintaining close ties with the Trump administration. He was notably the first British politician to meet Trump after his inauguration and has dined with the president at his Washington DC hotel.

"As an idea it [Brexit] has taken America by storm," Mr Farage told BBC News, adding that he is often "accosted in the street" by Americans wanting to discuss the topic.

Publisher Biteback describes the book as a tale that lurches "from comedy to crisis (often several times a day)" during the EU referendum campaign. Biteback boss Iain Dale told the Daily Mail there is a "real appetite for this kind of thing" in America, citing the success of political dramas like House of Cards.

The script has reportedly been written from the perspective of Gerry Gunster, an American pollster who advised Mr Banks's Leave.EU campaign. Andy Wigmore, a close associate of Mr Banks, revealed they were approached about the adaptation just before Christmas while visiting Trump in New York, initially thinking it was a "joke" before realizing it was "very serious."

Mr Farage has ruled out a fourth bid for UKIP leadership.

# MPs Reject Calls to Postpone EU Referendum Date

The House of Commons has decisively rejected a motion to delay the EU referendum, despite a cross-party appeal from representatives of devolved administrations who warned the June date would interfere with regional elections.

The motion was defeated by 286 votes to 70 on Tuesday, following an impassioned debate in which MPs from Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales expressed concerns about the timing of the referendum.

The DUP's deputy leader, Nigel Dodds, led the calls for postponement, urging the government to respect the wishes of the devolved administrations. "It needs to be treated with the respect it deserves," he told the Commons. "We hear a lot about the respect agenda and about taking on board the views of the administrations in the devolved countries of the UK and this now needs to be put into practice."

The first ministers of Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales have all written jointly to Prime Minister David Cameron expressing opposition to a late June referendum date. Nicola Sturgeon, Carwyn Jones and Arlene Foster warned that holding the vote so soon after devolved elections would "confuse" the process and make it difficult for them to campaign effectively.

However, Mr Cameron has maintained his position that voters will be capable of distinguishing between the different polls.

During the debate, Mr Dodds emphasised that the European debate should "not impinge on other elections due to take place this year, including to the Scottish Parliament as well as the Welsh and Northern Ireland Assemblies."

Independent MP Lady Sylvia Hermon, despite supporting the UK's continued EU membership, backed the call for delay. She urged the prime minister to confirm he would visit Northern Ireland to campaign, but only after the Assembly elections.

The UUP's Danny Kinahan used a Doctor Who analogy to illustrate his concerns about the uncertainty surrounding the referendum. "It's like we're trying to make a decision and all those that want to leave are charging into the Tardis," he said, adding that he wanted "the electorate to know what they are voting for."

The SDLP's Margaret Ritchie argued that a period of purdah from March to June would be undemocratic, as "it prevents ministers, it prevents MPs and it prevents members of devolved administrations from properly representing their constituents."

Despite these concerns, the government has pressed ahead with its proposed referendum date.

# Syrian Surgeon Struggles with Language Test to Resume Medical Career in UK

A Syrian surgeon who fled his homeland and was granted asylum in the UK is unable to practice medicine because he cannot pass the required English language test, despite Wales facing a significant shortage of doctors.

Hussam arrived in the UK in 2014 using a fake passport, escaping a country torn apart by civil war. While he has been granted asylum and safety, his professional life remains in limbo. Before he can register with the General Medical Council (GMC) and apply for positions as a surgeon, he must achieve an 80% mark on a specialized English language examination.

Despite taking the test five times, Hussam has been unable to reach the required threshold. His brother Shadi, also a qualified doctor from Syria, faces the same predicament, having failed the test on five occasions as well. The brothers have now opened a currency exchange shop on City Road to support themselves financially.

"I didn't come here because I wanted a better life. I was forced to come here to find a life," Hussam explained. "I used to be a surgeon and suddenly my life has been changed.... I was forced to leave."

Shadi argues that the language requirements are unreasonably demanding: "To reach this level we need to have a very high level of English language. Even the native speakers can't reach this level."

The situation is particularly frustrating given that the British Medical Association has reported Wales is short of 400 doctors, highlighting the cruel irony of qualified medical professionals being unable to fill desperately needed positions.

Hussam's decision to flee Syria came after several of his colleagues disappeared following arrests by government forces. He believes they were taken to Saydnaya prison, a facility that Amnesty International has accused of executing up to 50 people daily without proper trials. "It's a nightmare. I don't know yet if they are alive or not," he said, adding that he feared it was only a matter of time before authorities came for him.

Upon arriving in Cardiff, Hussam learned English through the refugee charity Oasis and subsequently worked for the organization, helping other refugees navigate housing and asylum claims. However, two-and-a-half years later, his dream of returning to medicine remains unfulfilled.

"Before I came here I thought it would be a few months and I would get the language and be able to communicate with people and be at a hospital. But after two-and-a-half years I'm still dreaming about it," he said.

The longing for his former profession is so strong that Hussam regularly visits the University Hospital of Wales in Cardiff, standing outside the accident and emergency department. "I come here quite often, I miss being a doctor," he admitted.

Despite the setbacks and occasional doubts about whether leaving Syria was the right decision, Hussam maintains hope: "One day you will see me here wearing the uniform and you can say, 'hello Dr Hussam'."

Hussam's story is featured in the BBC Wales documentary "Strangers in a strange land."

# Doctors Urged to Monitor Colleagues Over Antibiotic Prescriptions in Fight Against Drug Resistance

Doctors should monitor each other's prescribing habits and resist pressure from demanding patients as part of urgent new measures to tackle the growing crisis of antimicrobial resistance, according to draft guidelines from the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE).

The proposals come after years of failed policies to reduce antibiotic use, with prescription rates rising by 6% between 2010 and 2013. Alarmingly, experts estimate that half of all antibiotic prescriptions during this period were "inappropriate," despite repeated warnings about the catastrophic threat posed by drug-resistant infections.

Prof Mike Baker, director of the centre for clinical practice at NICE, acknowledged the severity of the situation. "Antibiotic use has gone up and up and up each year despite a number of initiatives to damp down on their use," he said. "We have to turn this tanker around."

The guidelines, which establish best practice for the NHS, introduce several controversial recommendations, including the concept of peer pressure among medical professionals. "Health professionals should question the practices of colleagues when they are not in line with local and national guidelines," Prof Baker told the BBC News website. "I think peer pressure has to be a part of any strategy to reduce antimicrobial use."

The draft rules also address the difficult issue of patient expectations, urging doctors to become more comfortable refusing requests for antibiotics. "Patient pressure is a real problem and it puts GPs under pressure, and they can be afraid of not prescribing antibiotics even when they know it's wrong," Prof Baker explained.

Under the proposed guidelines, doctors would spend more time explaining to patients why antibiotics are unsuitable for many conditions. The recommendations also encourage wider use of "watchful waiting" strategies, where antibiotics are only prescribed if a patient's condition fails to improve naturally.

However, Prof Baker stressed that the approach required careful judgment. "These ideas were not a 'blunt instrument' and doctors needed to 'walk a tightrope,'" he warned, noting that withholding antibiotics inappropriately could lead to serious complications such as sepsis in some cases.

The stakes could not be higher. Without effective antibiotics, routine surgeries, chemotherapy treatments, and organ transplants become impossibly dangerous. The rise of resistant bacteria threatens to strip doctors of one of their most powerful weapons against infection, potentially returning medicine to a pre-antibiotic era.

England's chief medical officer, Prof Dame Sally Davies, welcomed the initiative. "Preserving the effectiveness of the antibiotics we have is absolutely crucial and everybody, including patients, has a role to play," she said, encouraging prescribers to participate in the consultation process.

Dr Maureen Baker, chairwoman of the Royal College of GPs, supported the team approach outlined in the guidelines. "Antibiotics have served us well in treating infections for over 60 years, but as a society we have become too dependent on them and they are now seen as a 'catch-all' for every illness and infection," she said.

The Royal College emphasized that GPs, practice teams, and pharmacists must work together to discuss alternatives with patients seeking antibiotics for minor illnesses, most of which resolve naturally over time. The consultation on these draft guidelines represents a crucial step in addressing one of the most serious threats to modern healthcare.
